## Abstract

We reconstruct the ordinary Riemann Hypothesis argument rooted at riemannHypothesis : RiemannHypothesis := rhOfAll in the supplied Lean project. The underlying mathematical argument is credited to Levent Alpöge and Claude; this manuscript is a human-readable reconstruction prepared by Jeremy Rodgers for referee checking. We preserve the source’s hypotheses, conventions, and quantified estimates, reconstruct all forty-five handoff gap groups and all fourteen original frontier branches across Sections 2–17, match every established literature input by precise statement and source, and assemble the full argument from the terminal row and local-parameter witnesses to ordinary RH in Proposition 17.4 and Theorem 17.5 (including the uniform Breuil–Kisin Mittag–Leffler containment in Proposition 7.102, the ramification-based prime-cyclic base-change induction in Proposition 7.114, the global face-cutting strictness of the integral Siegel fan in Lemma 10.65, and the explicit accounting for Mathlib’s total-function value at s = 1 in ZF). Standard published theorems cited along the way are explicitly identified. A transitive UTF-8 textual source scan of the local modules imported by Main.lean (175,187 modules) reports zero missing local modules and zero textual axiom, sorry, or admit declarations; that textual scan is distinct from a Lean 4 kernel check, as no local Lean 4 elaboration or kernel typechecking of the pinned environment has been run here. Review passes applied to this manuscript were targeted audits of specific steps and interfaces rather than a complete line-by-line independent verification of all pages.

## 1 Scope, source and standard of proof

The target is the ordinary Riemann Hypothesis for the meromorphic continuation of ∑_{n≥1}n^{−s}. The source actually proves a stronger half-plane assertion for all Dirichlet characters and then specializes it to the character modulo one. We follow that argument; we do not assume that it is enough merely to state its stronger intermediate assertions.

The underlying mathematical argument is credited to Levent Alpöge and Claude, as requested and as described by the supplied project’s provenance. This manuscript is a human-readable reconstruction of that supplied argument prepared by Jeremy Rodgers; it introduces no original extensions. Its source authority is the archive rh-main.zip, SHA-256

02a2877f92f3a6579181209838e7e8de08ba472e87cf8404f56a0e4f42ed8f19.

Project source paths below are relative to lean/src. Established Mathlib statements are read at the exact revision 0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474, pinned by the project. This fixes, in particular, the conventions for the values assigned at poles, primitive characters, local reciprocity and complex powers.

A citation in this manuscript has two jobs: to state the mathematical result being used, and to identify a source precise enough to check that result. At an application we check the hypotheses, normalization and quantifiers. A project declaration bearing a literature-related name is not, by itself, a literature citation. All forty-five handoff gap groups and all fourteen original frontier branches are reconstructed across Sections 2–17, and their exact wiring into the terminal argument is assembled in Section 17 (Proposition 17.4 and Theorem 17.5), with all fourteen original frontier branches accounted for in Section 18. Standard published theorems enter only at their explicitly checked statements.

The earlier expansion is preserved in RH_Exposition and the checkpoint recorded in data/scope-and-freeze.json. The large supporting expansions are used to recover actual arguments, not as a substitute for an argument in the present paper. Routine foundations of algebra, topology and analysis may be cited at referee level. We no longer attempt to print every generated Lean declaration or every implementation detail of those foundations.

The original fourteen frontier branches are retained in the compact input map. They are an initial check-list, not a proof that all essential mathematical inputs have been found. Coverage is decided by tracing the actual terminal argument and checking each mathematical contract. A transitive UTF-8 textual source scan of the local modules imported by Main.lean (175,187 local modules) records zero missing local modules and zero textual axiom, sorry, or admit declarations. That source scan is strictly weaker than a Lean 4 kernel check: no local Lean 4 elaboration or kernel typechecking of the full pinned environment has been obtained here, and a successful typesetting build does not supply formal verification. Likewise, the post-assembly checks applied to this manuscript were targeted audits of specific proofs and interfaces rather than a complete line-by-line independent referee verification of every page.

## 2 The precise target and the endpoint reduction

## Conventions and established analytic inputs

<!-- Source PDF page 6 -->

2.1 Conventions and established analytic inputs

We write ζ for the continued Riemann zeta function and L(s, χ) for the continued Dirichlet L-function of a character χ modulo a positive integer N. For positive real x we use x^{s}= exp(s log x) with the real logarithm. The Lean functions are total functions: a value is assigned even at a pole. All substantive applications below either avoid the pole or explicitly retain the source’s convention at it.

The exact target definition in Mathlib/NumberTheory/LSeries/RiemannZeta.lean:185--186 is the following proposition:

$$
\forall s\in\mathbb C,\qquad \zeta(s)=0,\quad \neg\exists n\in\mathbb N\;s=-2(n+1),\quad s\ne 1\quad \Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{Re}s=\frac12.
$$

The quantified n starts at zero, so the excluded values are exactly −2, −4, −6, . . .. No restriction to the critical strip has been silently inserted.

We use the following established analytic results in their precise forms. Each is a theorem in the pinned source; the source paths and names identify the exact version being cited.

(i) ζ(0) = −1/2: riemannZeta_zero, Mathlib/NumberTheory/LSeries/RiemannZeta.lean:151--152.

(ii) If w ̸= −n for every n ∈ℕ and w ̸= 1, then

$$
\zeta(1-w)=2(2\pi)^{-w}\Gamma(w)\cos(\pi w/2)\zeta(w).
$$

This is riemannZeta_one_sub in the same file, lines178–180. The displayed identity, rather than the informal comment preceding it in that file, fixes the normalization.

(iii) Γ(w) ̸= 0 for Re w > 0: Complex.Gamma_ne_zero_of_re_pos, Mathlib/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/

Gamma/Beta.lean:454--457.

(iv) For z ∈ℂ,

$$
\cos z=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists k\in\mathbb{Z}\ z=(2k+1)\pi/2.
$$

This is Complex.cos_eq_zero_iff, Mathlib/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/Trigonometric/Complex.lean:33--42.

(v) For the character modulo one,

$$
L(s,1_1)=\zeta(s)\qquad (s\in\mathbb{C}).
$$

This equality of the total functions is DirichletCharacter.LFunction_modOne_eq, Mathlib/NumberTheory/LSeries/DirichletContinuation.lean:67--69.

For the elementary nonvanishing of (2π)^{−w} we need only 2π > 0 and the exponential formula above: an exponential is nonzero. This checks the same nonzero-base condition used by Complex.cpow_ne_zero_iff in the source.

## The functional-equation argument

<!-- Source PDF page 7 -->

2.2 The functional-equation argument

Proposition 2.1. Suppose

$$
\forall w\in\mathbb{C},\qquad\operatorname{Re}w>\frac12,\quad w\ne1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\zeta(w)\ne0.
$$

Then the Riemann Hypothesis in (1) holds.

Source: Formalism/GammaFactorNonvanishing/RhOfRight.lean:5--62; Formalism.VW.rh_of_right.

Proof. Let s satisfy the three hypotheses on the left of (1). If Re s > 1/2, (5) contradicts ζ(s) = 0. If Re s = 1/2, the conclusion already holds. It remains to exclude Re s < 1/2.

First s ̸= 0, since otherwise ζ(s) = −1/2 by (i). Set w = 1 −s. Then Re w = 1 − Re s > 1/2 and w ̸= 1. For every n ∈ ℕ, the real part of −n is nonpositive, whereas Re w > 0; hence w ̸= −n. These verify every hypothesis of (ii), so (2) applies. Its left side is zero.

The factors 2 and (2π)^{−w} are nonzero. The factor Γ(w) is nonzero by (iii), since Re w > 0. The factor ζ(w) is nonzero by (5), since Re w > 1/2 and w ̸= 1. To handle the remaining factor, suppose cos(πw/2) = 0. By (iv), πw/2 = (2k+1)π/2 for an integer k. Cancelling the nonzero real number π gives w = 2k + 1, and therefore s = −2k. If k < 0, then k ≤−1 and Re s = −2k ≥2, contrary to Re s < 1/2. If k = 0, then s = 0, already excluded. If k > 0, set n = k −1 ∈ℕ; then s = −2(n + 1), contrary to the nontrivial-zero hypothesis. Thus the cosine factor is also nonzero. The right side of (2) is consequently a product of nonzero complex numbers, contradicting its zero left side. This excludes the remaining case.

Definition 2.2. Write EC for the statement

$$
\forall N\ge1\;\forall\chi\bmod N\;\forall s\in\mathbb C,\qquad \operatorname{Re}s>\frac12,\quad (\chi\ne 1_N\text{ or }s\ne1)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad L(s,\chi)\ne0.
$$

This is exactly UpperTheory.EveryCharacter in Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/CharacterBoxes/EveryCharacter.lean:13--14. The typeclass condition NeZero N means N ̸= 0; for N ∈ℕ it is exactly the stated

```text
N ≥1.
```

Proposition 2.3. The statement EC implies ordinary RH.

Source: Formalism/GammaFactorNonvanishing/CritLine.lean:29--32; Formalism.VW.rh_of_every.

Proof. For Re s > 1/2 and s ̸= 1, specialize (6) to N = 1 and χ = 1_{1}. The disjunction in that statement holds through s ̸= 1. Equation (4) therefore gives ζ(s) ̸= 0. Proposition 2.1 applies.

2.4 The reduction from primitive characters

A primitive-character object ψ consists of a positive modulus d, a primitive Dirichlet character χ_{ψ} modulo d, and the indicated primitivity certificate. Write ZF for

$$
\forall\psi\;\forall s\in\mathbb C,\qquad \operatorname{Re}s>\frac12\quad\Longrightarrow\quad L(s,\chi_\psi)\ne0.
$$

This is the source’s Formalism.HC.ZeroFreeAll: Formalism/SharpRestriction/RamificationFrobenius/TotientGaloisClasses/ExplicitFormulaErrorOfHostConditions.lean:11--18. For the primitive trivial character modulo one, L(s, 1_{1}) = ζ(s) by (4), so the universal quantifier in (7) also includes the total function’s assigned value at s = 1. We account for that point explicitly, matching the case split in Formalism/SharpRestriction/RamificationFrobenius/TotientGaloisClasses/Landau.lean:508--516: for s ̸= 1, the analytic nonvanishing of the regularized function ζ_{1}(s) = (s −1)ζ(s) (riemannZetaOne_eq_mul_of_ne_one) yields ζ(s) ̸= 0, whereas at s = 1 the assigned value of Mathlib’s total function ζ(1) is nonzero by the pinned Mathlib theorem riemannZeta_ne_zero_of_one_le_re. By contrast, both EC (6) and ordinary RH (1) explicitly exclude s = 1 for the trivial character, so the total function’s convention at the pole s = 1 plays no role in ordinary RH itself.

Proposition 2.4. The assertion ZF implies EC.

Source: Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/CharacterBoxes/Imprimitive.lean:5--35; UpperTheory.Top.imprimitive.

Proof. Fix N ≥ 1, a character χ modulo N, and s with σ = Re s > 1/2 and (χ ̸= 1_{N} or s ̸= 1). Let d = cond(χ) and let χ^{′} be its primitive character. The conductor facts in Mathlib/NumberTheory/DirichletCharacter/Basic.lean give d ̸= 0, d | N, primitivity of χ^{′}, and changeLevel_{d|N}(χ^{′}) = χ (conductor_ne_zero, conductor_dvd_level, primitiveCharacter_isPrimitive, and changeLevel_primitiveCharacter, the last at310–312). Thus ψ = (d, χ^{′}) is one of the objects quantified in (7), and L(s, χ^{′}) ̸= 0.

We also have χ^{′} ̸= 1_{d} or s ̸= 1. If s ̸= 1 this is immediate. Otherwise the original disjunction gives χ ̸= 1_{N}; if χ^{′}= 1_{d}, changing level would give χ = 1_{N}, a contradiction. Here change of level preserves the trivial character, the theorem changeLevel_one in the same pinned file.

We may therefore apply the exact continuation identity DirichletCharacter.LFunction_changeLevel, Mathlib/NumberTheory/LSeries/DirichletContinuation.lean:150--154:

$$
L(s,\chi)=L(s,\chi')\prod_{p\mid N}(1-\chi'(p)p^{-s}).
$$

The product ranges over distinct prime divisors of N; primes dividing d cause no problem since χ^{′}(p) = 0. All the identity’s hypotheses have been checked: both moduli are nonzero, d | N, and the preceding disjunction holds for χ^{′}.

For every prime in this product, p > 1 and |χ^{′}(p)| ≤1. The latter is the exact character bound DirichletCharacter.norm_le_one, Mathlib/NumberTheory/DirichletCharacter/Bounds.lean:33--37. Our complex-power convention gives |p^{−s}| = p^{−σ}< 1. Hence |χ^{′}(p)p^{−s}| ≤p^{−σ}< 1, so 1 −χ^{′}(p)p^{−s}̸= 0. The finite product in (8) is nonzero, as is its first factor. This proves (6) with its full modulus and character quantifiers.

## The analytic window principle

<!-- Source PDF page 8 -->

## 3 The analytic window principle

The analytic argument needs an upper bound on arbitrarily distant power-length windows, rather than an estimate at every sufficiently large point. We first prove this implication for finite positive combinations of

<!-- Source PDF page 9 -->

Dirichlet characters. We then specify the uniform estimate and host existence statement required to produce those windows.

Throughout this section, L(s, χ) denotes the meromorphic continuation of ∑_{n≥1}χ(n)n^{−s}. Characters are extended by zero off the units. The character of conductor 1 gives ζ(s). In the analytic arguments below, the simple pole of ζ(s) at s = 1 is always excluded from the zero sets Z_{F} (just as s = 1 is excluded for the trivial character in EC and ordinary RH). When interfacing with the stronger total-function statement ZF (7) of Section 2, nonvanishing of Mathlib’s total function ζ at s = 1 is supplied separately by riemannZeta_ne_zero_of_one_le_re, following the exact case split at s = 1 versus s ̸= 1 in Formalism/SharpRestriction/RamificationFrobenius/TotientGaloisClasses/Landau.lean:508--516. For a positive real number y, complex powers mean y^{s}= exp(s log y), using the real logarithm.

We use the classical facts that a nonprincipal Dirichlet L-function is entire, is nonzero at 1, and has its Euler product in ℜs > 1, and that ζ(s) = (s −1)^{−1}+ γ + O(s −1) near 1. The precise reference state-ments checked for these facts are DLMF §25.15(i), equations (25.15.1)–(25.15.2), (25.15.9), and (25.2.4)– (25.2.5).^{1}

3.4 Levels and the order of the uniform choices

```text

=⇒∀χ ∈K ∀s, ℜs > θ =⇒ L(s, χ) ̸= 0.
```

This is the analytic principle needed by the subsequent construction. The special values of the weights have played no role in its proof; their positivity is what makes (11) nonzero.

Proposition 3.4 (Uniform small-scale reduction). Fix a level ℒ and λ > 1. Suppose there are fixed real numbers e_{D}, e_{L} and ϵ_{1} > 0 with the following property. For every 0 < ϵ < ϵ_{1} there is a set W_{ϵ} ⊆ ℝ containing windows [Y, Y^{λ}] arbitrarily far to the right, and a threshold x_{ϵ}, such that

```text
G_{ℒ}(x) ≤x^{1/2+(eD+eL+7)ϵ} (x ∈W_{ϵ}, x ≥x_{ϵ}).
```

Then every character in K has no zero in ℜs > 1/2.

Proof. Given s with ℜs > 1/2, put

m = min(ℜs −1/2, 1/2) > 0, θ = 1/2 + m/2.

Then 0 < θ < 1 and θ < ℜs. Choose 0 < ϵ < ϵ_{1} so that (e_{D} + e_{L} + 7)ϵ ≤m/2; for example any positive ϵ no greater than min(ϵ_{1}/2, m/(2(|e_{D} + e_{L} + 7| + 1))) works. For x ≥ max(x_{ϵ}, 1) in W_{ϵ}, monotonicity of x^{t} in t gives G_{ℒ}(x) ≤x^{θ}. Discarding a bounded initial part of W_{ϵ} preserves its arbitrarily distant windows: when requesting a window initially, require its left endpoint to exceed that bound. Apply (17) to exclude a zero at s.

<!-- Source PDF page 15 -->

The placement of the quantifiers in this proposition is essential. The exponents e_{D}, e_{L} are chosen before ϵ, while the family, the admissible set, and its threshold may depend on ϵ. At a fixed ϵ, the constants controlling its family must work at every sufficiently large admissible x, and not be chosen again after x is specified. No uniformity over all primitive characters is asserted: the level, its conductor data, and all fixed constants may depend on the primitive character under consideration.

For completeness, every primitive character ψ belongs to a level of the kind used here. Take the finite cyclic subgroup generated by ψ in the character group of its conductor, replace each member by its inducing primitive character, take no exceptional character, and put o equal to the size of that cyclic group. The trivial member induces the conductor 1 character. Taking the inducing primitive character commutes with inversion: the conductor of an inverse equals the original conductor, because induction commutes with inversion in both directions, and injectivity of induction identifies the two primitive characters. Thus the resulting finite set is conjugation-stable. The primitive character inducing ψ is ψ itself, so it is indeed contained in this cyclic level. Consequently proving the small-scale hypothesis for these cyclic levels suffices for the primitive-character conclusion used in the reduction 2.4.

3.9 Reading the host characters and the level weights

The following description states exactly the host information used by the analytic argument. Let r : (ℤ/Nℤ)^{×} ↠Γ be surjective. For ψ ∈Γ̂, let χ_{ψ} be the character modulo N whose value at a unit is ψ(r(u)), and let p_{ψ} be its inducing primitive character. Different ψ’s give different p_{ψ}’s: equality of their primitive characters gives equality after induction to N, then equality on the image of r, which is all of Γ. In particular p_{ψ} = 1 if and only if ψ = 1.

For a prime p, write N = p^{k}N_{p}^{′} with p ∤N_{p}^{′}. Take the local units U_{p} to be the kernel of reduction of (ℤ/Nℤ)^{×} to (ℤ/N_{p}^{′}ℤ)^{×}. The Chinese remainder theorem gives a unit fr_{p} that is 1 modulo p^{k} and p modulo N_{p}^{′}. Define I_{p}= r(U_{p}) and F_{p}= r(fr_{p}). Then

```text
b_{ψ}(m) = p_{ψ}(m) (m ≥1). (30)
```

To prove this it suffices to consider m = p^{j}. The character ψ is trivial on I_{p} exactly when χ_{ψ} factors through N_{p}^{′}, or equivalently when p does not divide its conductor. This last conductor criterion follows directly from the Chinese remainder decomposition of the unit group into its prime-power factors: for each factor choose the least exponent through which its character factors. Their product is the conductor, and a divisor of N is an inducing modulus exactly when each of its exponents is at least the corresponding least exponent. If the restriction is trivial, the inertia average equals ψ(F_{p})^{j}= p_{ψ}(p)^{j}, by the defining congruence of fr_{p} modulo the conductor. If the restriction is nontrivial, translation by an inertia element on which it is nontrivial makes the average zero, and p_{ψ}(p) = 0 because p divides its conductor. This proves (30).

For ψ ̸= 1, choose ℓ(ψ) = L^{′}(1, p_{ψ})/L(1, p_{ψ}). The value ℓ(1) can be set to zero: it is not used in the definition of G_{D}(1; y) = G(y), and no principal logarithmic derivative at the pole is needed. Equation (30) then gives G_{D}(ψ; y) = 𝒢_{pψ}(y) for every ψ.

The required inertia pattern follows from the usual concrete host conditions as well. Namely let N = Qqd, where q, d are distinct odd primes, d ≡7 (mod 8), 4 | Q, and gcd(Q, qd) = 1. Suppose

## What a tied family must supply

<!-- Source PDF page 27 -->

3.10 What a tied family must supply

At a fixed ϵ > 0, a family has an admissible set W, an index set I_{x} at each x, and for each index a host, its finite group H_{x,i}, and a distinguished node set T_{x,i}. The node labels are injective maps from these groups into a common set of integer labels. The family specifies a common node-label set 𝒯 (x), with

𝒯 (x) = {val(t) : t ∈T_{x,i}}.

A tie at x chooses an index i_{0}, writes H = H_{x,i0}, and supplies the entire quantitative package of Proposi-tion 3.12. Its translation set is the whole group H, with translation map the identity. At each u ∈H its finite nonempty word set and slope data may come from a separately chosen family index pt(u). The tie identifies all group, size, weight, inertia and Frobenius coordinates used in the quantitative package with those of these family members. The identifications include x_{datum} = x, ϵ_{datum} = ϵ, the bounds e_{Div} ≤ e_{D}, e_{Loss} ≤ e_{L}, datum c_{HH} ≤c_{HH}, and the fixed constants K, e_{K}. All the scalar, thin and cost hypotheses displayed above are required at every u ∈H. For the nodes it requires

t ∈T ⇐⇒ val(t) ∈𝒯 (x).

For the second set it requires T_{2} = {ja_{0} : j ∈D_{2}} for some finite set of integer digits D_{2}, where A_{0} = ⟨a_{0}⟩. These conditions are the mathematical content of the tie that is used here; the geometric construction of such ties is a separate existence assertion.

Proposition 3.13 (Transfer from a tie). The tie at x gives the quantitative package at the distinguished host i_{0}, with its actual node set T_{x,i0}, required in Proposition 3.12.

Proof. First T = T_{x,i0}. Indeed t ∈ T means that val(t) is the label of a member t^{′} ∈ T_{x,i0}. Injectivity gives t = t^{′}. Conversely any such member has its label in 𝒯 (x). Next the identity translation map has image all of H, so its image contains A_{0}. Every element of T_{2} is an integer multiple of a_{0}, hence lies in A_{0}. All slope-data hypotheses, identities of the arithmetic count and main term, node-size estimates, bounds for B_{0}, N_{c}, and comparisons of constants are already among the tie conditions. Their assertions for every u ∈H imply their assertions for u ∈A_{0}. The compatible logarithmic derivative is unchanged because the identified reciprocity homomorphism is the same homomorphism used to define I_{p}, F_{p}. This verifies every required component.

Suppose there is one constant C_{E} and a threshold such that its hosts at every index satisfy (31) and (32), together with the other explicit-formula conditions, for all sufficiently large x. Suppose fixed K, c_{HH}, e_{K}, chosen before x, give ties at every sufficiently large x ∈W. Then for every sufficiently large x ∈W,

```text
_{Gℒ(x) ≤x}1/2+(e_{D}+e_{L}+7)ϵ_{.}
```

Proof. Choose the uniform threshold from Proposition 3.12, and enlarge it to the explicit-formula and tie thresholds. At an admissible x beyond it, choose the tie’s distinguished index i_{0}. Proposition 3.13 gives the quantitative package there; the explicit-formula bounds hold at that same index because their hypothesis holds at every index. The uniform level estimate therefore applies.

Together with Proposition 3.4, this shows exactly what is required from the family construction: for each cyclic level, fixed e_{D}, e_{L} and ϵ_{1} > 0, then for every 0 < ϵ < ϵ_{1} a family with arbitrarily distant power windows and the two eventual properties in Corollary 3.14. In particular, the arithmetic estimate at

Definition 8.1 alone does not supply the ties or the explicit-formula host bounds.

3.15 The character boxes and the thin estimate on a host

Fix a host field as in Lemma 3.20, with modulus Q_{S}, distinct primes q, d, and finite abelian frame A. Write Q_{odd} for the odd part of Q_{S}. A character of the host means the primitive Dirichlet character attached to a character of its Galois group. Its conductor divides Q_{S}qd: the latter character is obtained from the unit group modulo Q_{S}qd, and passing to its primitive character divides this modulus.

Lemma 3.33 (Real-character decomposition and host boxes). Suppose M > 0, Q_{odd} | M, every prime dividing Q_{S} divides 2M, and PairGood(M, ϵ, Y, X, q, d) holds. For each real primitive host character χ whose conductor f_{χ} is divisible by q or d, put j = 1 if d | f_{χ}, and j = 0 otherwise. Then

```text
f_{χ} ≤8Q_{odd}(e^{Y ϵ/5}e^{jY ϵ/5(log Y )2}, )
L(s, χ) ̸= 0 ℜs > 399/400, |ℑs| ≤8Me^{Y ϵ/5}e^{jY ϵ/5(log Y )2} .
```

In particular every such real L-function has no real zero greater than 399/400. The six quadratic boxes and the three QDq(X, ϵ, 4) bounds used in HostGood follow from the same pair.

Proof. A real Dirichlet character takes the values 1, −1 on units. At an odd prime p, the subgroup 1+pZ/p^{v}Z has odd order, so maps trivially to {1, −1}; its local conductor exponent is at most one. At 2, a quadratic character factors through modulus 8. Indeed the units modulo 2^{v}, for v ≥ 3, are generated by −1, 5; the elements congruent to 1 mod 8 are exactly the even powers of 5, so every quadratic character kills them. The cyclic description follows from v_{2}(5^{2r}−1) = r+2, proved by the factorization 5^{2r+1}−1 = (5^{2r}−1)(5^{2r}+1). The conductors at levels below 8 satisfy the same bound.

By the Chinese remainder theorem, the local factor at either q or d is consequently trivial or the unique quadratic character at that prime. The remaining local factors give a real primitive character ρ of conductor dividing 8Q_{odd}. Thus there are i, j ∈{0, 1} with

```text
f_{χ} = f_{ρ}q^{i}d^{j}, χ(a) = ρ(a)(a/q)^{i}(a/d)^{j}. (63)
```

The equality includes nonunits: a positive local exponent gives zero on a nonunit at that prime. Each nontriv-ial quadratic factor at a new prime is primitive, and a product of primitive characters of coprime conductors

<!-- Source PDF page 50 -->

is primitive. To see the latter assertion, if the product factored through a proper divisor, fixing all but one CRT coordinate to 1 would force that local primitive factor to factor through a proper divisor as well. This also proves the exact conductor equality. In particular j is exactly the indicator of d | f_{χ}; and i, j cannot both be zero under the hypothesis of the lemma.

Every integer coprime to 2Mqd is coprime to f_{χ}, since every prime factor of Q_{S} divides 2M. Therefore (63) is an inducing relation in precisely the sense used in the definition of PairGood. Also f_{ρ} | 8M. Its real-character clause gives the stated zero box. The pair’s upper bounds

```text
q ≤e^{Y ϵ/5}, d ≤e^{Y ϵ/5(log Y )2}
```

and f_{ρ} ≤8Q_{odd} give the conductor bound. At a real argument the height condition is automatic. This proves the first two assertions.

For completeness, the six small boxes use ρ = 1 or the primitive quadratic character χ_{8}(a) = (2/a), and (i, j) = (1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1). On odd a, quadratic reciprocity gives

(−q/a) = (a/q), (−d/a) = (a/d) (q, d ≡3 mod 4).

The conductor of χ_{8} is exactly 8: if it factored through a proper divisor, it would factor through 4, whereas 5 ≡ 1 mod 4 and χ_{8}(5) = −1. The corresponding conductors therefore have the same product form as above, and primitive uniqueness identifies any proposed inducing character with this product. The three bounds at X instead use ρ = 1 and these same nonzero (i, j). The pair gives ‖𝒢_{χ}(X)‖≤ X^{1/2+ϵ/2} and |L^{′}(1, χ)/L(1, χ)| ≤4 log X. Since X ≥Y > 1, the first bound is at most X^{1/2+ϵ}, exactly the required QDq bound. These are the arguments of CharacterBoxes/RealSplit.lean:43--160, RealBox.lean:13--112 and PairRows.lean:9--215,264--320.

Lemma 4.4 (Counting the distinct kernels). If G is a finite abelian group and T is a finite set of subgroups with cyclic quotients, then ∑

```text
φ([G : H]) ≤|G|.
H∈T
```

Proof. For a cyclic quotient G/H of order m, its faithful complex characters are specified by the primitive mth roots assigned to a generator. There are φ(m) of them. Composing with the quotient map gives distinct characters of G whose kernel is exactly H. Characters obtained from different H have different kernels, so the resulting sets are disjoint. They lie in the character group of G. To count that group, write G as a product of finite cyclic groups: a character is specified independently by a root of unity of the appropriate order on each cyclic generator. Their number is the product of the cyclic orders, namely |G|. Counting the disjoint subsets proves the inequality.

Lemma 4.7 (Coefficient independence of the normalized lengths). Suppose two finite coefficient rings 𝒪, 𝒪^{′} and their characters have the same values in ℚ_{ℓ}. The corresponding strict cohomology kernels have finite length simultaneously, and their normalized lengths are equal.

Proof. First suppose 𝒪 ⊆𝒪^{′}. The second ring is finite and torsion free over the first, and hence finite free, because the first is a discrete valuation ring. Its positive rank makes the extension faithfully flat. Write d for the relative ramification index. Tensoring the coefficient exact sequence with 𝒪^{′} identifies

```text

```

𝒪^{′}⊗_{𝒪} Frac(𝒪)/𝒪 ≃ Frac(𝒪^{′})/𝒪^{′}.

This is compatible with the Galois action: both characters have the same values under the inclusion, and so do their inverse and cyclotomic twists.

Choose a finite free basis of 𝒪^{′} over 𝒪. Continuous cochains with the extended discrete coefficients are then finite direct sums of the original cochains. This identification commutes with the coboundary operators and all local restriction maps. The same finite direct sum commutes with the product of the local terms. Flatness preserves kernels and images, so it identifies the strict cohomology kernel M^{′} over 𝒪^{′} with 𝒪^{′}⊗_{𝒪}M. The strict local conditions are therefore preserved, rather than replaced by unrestricted cohomology.

If M has a composition series, each simple factor is the residue field 𝒪/ϖ. Its tensor extension is 𝒪^{′}/ϖ𝒪^{′}, of length d over 𝒪^{′}, since ϖ is a unit times the dth power of a uniformizer of 𝒪^{′}. Exactness along the series gives

length_{𝒪}′ M^{′}= d length_{𝒪} M.

Finiteness is also reflected. Tensoring any strictly increasing finite chain of submodules with a faithfully flat module keeps its successive quotients nonzero. Thus arbitrarily long strict chains in M give such chains in M^{′}. A module of finite length cannot have them. This proves the equivalence of finite length, including the case in which the allowed extended length is infinite.

The same uniformizer computation applied to ℓ gives E_{𝒪}′ = dE_{𝒪}. Dividing the two length identities proves equality of normalized lengths when they are finite. If they are infinite they are infinite on both sides; the source’s separate conversion to a real value agrees as well because it uses the same convention on both infinite lengths.

Extend the two characters to it; they agree because their values in the ambient field agree. Apply the inclusion case to each and combine the two equalities.

4.3 The precise Kato input

For this subsection, H_{f}^{1}(L, V ) has its ordinary Bloch–Kato meaning: a continuous cohomology class is unramified at finite places away from ℓ and becomes a coboundary after tensoring with B_{cris} at places above ℓ. For a stable lattice T ⊂V , the discrete Selmer group uses, locally, the image of these finite rational classes in H^{1}(L_{v}, V /T). These are exactly the conventions in Kato’s §14.1.

<!-- Source PDF page 69 -->

Background fact 4.10 (Noncentral critical Selmer finiteness). Let f be a normalized newform of weight k ≥2, and let V_{f} be its two-dimensional cohomological ℓ-adic representation over a finite coefficient field. For a finite abelian extension L/ℚ, 1 ≤ r ≤ k −1 and 2r ̸= k, every stable lattice in V_{f}(r) has finite discrete Bloch–Kato Selmer group over L.

This is Kato [44, Theorem 14.2(1), pp. 235–236]. It imposes no good-ordinary hypothesis; that hypoth-esis belongs to the different Iwasawa statement, Theorem 17.4. The representation here is Kato’s cohomo-logical V_{f}, of Hodge–Tate weights 0, 1 −k, and the twist is the cyclotomic twist.

Lemma 4.11 (From finite discrete Selmer to rational vanishing). If the discrete Bloch–Kato Selmer group of a stable lattice T ⊂V over a number field L is finite, then H_{f}^{1}(L, V ) = 0.

Proof. Choose a finite set of places S containing the coefficient prime and all ramification of V . The finite local conditions place the rational Selmer group in H^{1}(G_{L,S}, V ). The coefficient exact sequence 0 →T → V →V /T →0 sends it into the discrete Selmer group: each local finite rational class maps to its allowed local image by definition. The source is a vector space over the coefficient field and in particular is a divisible abelian group. Its image in a finite group is divisible and must be zero. Exactness therefore places every rational Selmer class in the image of H^{1}(G_{L,S}, T).

This image is a bounded lattice in H^{1}(G_{L,S}, V ). One can check boundedness directly from the usual finite coefficient construction: H^{1}(G_{L,S}, T) is the inverse limit of the finite groups H^{1}(G_{L,S}, T/ℓ^{n}T), and its image is a finitely generated integral module in the finite-dimensional rational cohomology. Finiteness of the finite groups follows from the finiteness of extensions of bounded degree unramified outside S; the passage to rational cohomology is localization of this integral module. If a nonzero vector x and all ℓ^{−n}x belonged to this lattice, a coordinate functional nonzero on x would give integral coordinates of valuations tending to minus infinity, a contradiction. Since the Selmer group is a vector space contained in that lattice, it is zero.

Proposition 4.12 (The odd-weight twist and finite characters). Let e ≥1, let f have weight 2e + 1, and let φ be a finite-order Galois character factoring through a finite abelian extension of ℚ. Then

Apply Fact 4.10 with k = 2e + 1, r = e and then Lemma 4.11. This gives H_{f}^{1}(L, V_{f}(e)) = 0.

The restriction of a finite local class is finite: an unramified cocycle remains unramified after restricting inertia, and a B coboundary remains a coboundary after restricting the local Galois group. Thus restriction

## The local subquotients in definite base change

<!-- Source PDF page 82 -->

4.6 The local subquotients in definite base change

The base-change input in the publication package concerns the definite unitary group over a CM field E, with E/E^{+} unramified at every finite place. For an automorphic irreducible representation π of rank n ≥1, its preliminary output is a finite isobaric list: positive ranks n_{i} summing to n, discrete automorphic GL_{ni}(𝔸_{E}) representations V_{i}, their local irreducible smooth factors σ_{i,w}, and their infinitesimal characters m_{i,τ}. Each V_{i} has the prescribed normalized conjugate-self-dual cuspidal ascent. Put

```text
I_{w} = σ_{1,w} × · · · × σ_{c,w},
```

where the product is normalized parabolic induction in GL_{n}(E_{w}). The preliminary statement also supplies an irreducible subquotient P_{w} of I_{w} at every finite place. Its additional assertions are the following: P_{w} is spherical when π is unramified at w; at an inert unramified place its Satake parameter is the specified base-change parameter of π; at a split place it is a local factor of π along the split identification; and ∑_{i}m_{i,τ} is the infinitesimal character prescribed by the weight of π. The inert assertion quantifies over every compatible completion involution, uniformizer and residue cardinality. These conventions are retained in the statement rather than replaced by a statement about almost every place.

Background fact 4.21 (Unitary local products). For a nonarchimedean local field of characteristic zero, normalized parabolic induction of a finite list of irreducible unitarizable representations of general linear groups is irreducible and unitarizable.

This exact assertion follows from Tadić’s classification: Theorem D(ii) writes each factor as a product of the specified unitary building blocks, and Theorem D(i) makes the concatenated product irreducible and unitary [6, pp. 338–339, Theorem D]. The nonarchimedean and characteristic-zero hypotheses hold here because E_{w} is a finite extension of a p-adic field. The factors are unitarizable because they are local factors of the discrete automorphic representations V_{i}, realized in the unitary discrete spectrum. Thus this is the full unitary-product assertion required by the bridge, without a genericity or a temperedness assumption.

Proposition 4.22 (Removing the auxiliary local subquotients). The preliminary isobaric base-change state-ment just specified implies the source’s DefiniteN: the same conclusions hold for I_{w} itself, in place of P_{w}, at every place.

Proof. Keep the ranks, discrete representations, local factors and infinitesimal characters supplied by the preliminary statement. For a fixed w, Fact 4.21 makes I_{w} irreducible. By the definition of subquotient there is an invariant subspace S ⊆ I_{w} and a surjective intertwiner S → P_{w}. The target is nonzero, so S ̸= 0. Irreducibility gives S = I_{w}. The kernel of the intertwiner is an invariant subspace of I_{w}; it cannot be all of I_{w}, since the map is surjective onto a nonzero space. It is therefore zero. The intertwiner is an isomorphism.

An isomorphism of representations carries fixed vectors to fixed vectors. It also commutes with every finite Hecke operator, because it commutes with the action of every group element and hence with the in-tegrals, or finite double-coset sums, defining those operators. Consequently it preserves sphericality and all the Satake eigenvalue identities. Composing or inverting this isomorphism in the local-factor intertwiner preserves the split local-factor assertion as well. Transfer the three local assertions from P_{w} to I_{w} in this way. The construction applies independently at every w and does not change any quantifier on the inert-place data.

The actual supplier of the preliminary statement in the source is a trace-formula and finite-spectral con-struction, proved in full in Subsections 4.7 and 4.8 below. The following small but essential selection step explains why a finite candidate family fixed before T varies suffices.

Lemma 4.23 (A finite candidate list works at every inert place). Fix π and a set S of at most one specified split place. Suppose there is a finite list of spectral candidates D_{1}, . . . , D_{k} such that each has the required infinitesimal characters, matches π at all but finitely many split places, and matches at every place of S. Suppose moreover that for each finite set T of places, one of these same candidates has the required inert Satake identities at every unramified nonsplit place of T. Then one candidate has the required identities at every unramified nonsplit place.

Proof. If none did, choose for each j an unramified nonsplit place w_{j} where D_{j} fails. The set T = {w_{1}, . . . , w_{k}} is finite. The hypothesis gives an index j whose candidate works throughout T, in particular at its own w_{j}, a contradiction. This also rules out the empty candidate list: apply the finite-set hypothesis to T = ∅ to obtain an index. The chosen candidate retains its infinitesimal and split-place assertions since those hold for every member of the list.

The quantifier order in this lemma is substantive. Its finite list is fixed before T varies; merely construct-ing a new list for each T would not prove its conclusion. The next three subsections discharge both directions of the definite base-change boundary in full. Subsection 4.7 constructs the complete reduction baseChangeN_of from the three-clause finite spectral candidate contract CandFin to BaseChangeIsobaricN, including the uniform finite-family quantifier inversion from RunT to RunFin, commutative C*-algebra peak-element extrac-tion from asymptotic trace bounds, singleton split-place rigidity and swap, cuspidal conjugate-self-duality, local split/unramified/ramified subquotient realization, and the unconditional wiring to DefiniteN and BcSpeh. Subsection 4.8 proves the finite spectral candidate contract candFin : CandFin, completing UpperTheory.BaseChangeIdentities.baseChangeN. Subsection 4.9 then proves the reverse weak base-change descent descWeakAll and descWeak via unitarity, regular-factor normalization, split-place Jacquet–Shalika rigidity, and global twisted-vs-unitary trace comparison.

Proposition 4.24 (Local split, unramified inert, and ramified subquotients). Let D ∈ Pre(E, n) and let w be a finite place of E.

1. Split places. Suppose w is split in E/F and P is a smooth irreducible representation of GL_{n}(E_{w}) that is a subquotient of I_{w}(D) and occurs as a local component of π along p : U_{n,w} → GL_{n}(E_{w}). If π is unramified at w, then P is K_{w}-spherical. Moreover, P satisfies all four clauses of AtPlace at w.

2. Unramified nonsplit places. Suppose there exist factor Satake multisets b_{1}, . . . , b_{c} such that each σ_{i,w} is K_{GL}(w, N_{i})-spherical with Satake parameter b_{i}. Then there exists a smooth irreducible subquotient P of I_{w}(D) that is K_{w}-spherical and has Satake parameter ∑^{c}_{i=1}b_{i}.

3. Ramified nonsplit places. For every finite place w, I_{w}(D) admits a smooth irreducible subquotient P. If π is not unramified at w, then the inert Satake clause of AtPlace holds vacuously for P at w.

Next we establish the global comparison, conjugate-self-duality, local rigidity, and Grothendieck-ring permutation properties for Full candidates. Crucially, because a Full candidate already controls both cofinitely many split places and all unramified nonsplit places, comparing two Full candidates yields cofinite global Satake agreement directly on E, without any Galois-representation or Chebotarev step.

Proposition 4.25 (Global Satake agreement, conjugate-self-duality, and local rigidity). For every CM field E/F satisfying Unr, n ≥1, and π satisfying IsAutRepU:

1. Almost-everywhere unramifiedness and Satake agreement (FullSat). The representation π is unram-ified at cofinitely many finite places of E. For any D, D^{′} ∈ Pre(E, n) satisfying Full(π, D) and Full(π, D^{′}), there exists a cofinite set of finite places w of E at which D and D^{′} share a common Satake multiset: ∃B, D.Sat(w, B) ∧D^{′}.Sat(w, B).

2. Conjugate-duality of Satake parameters (FullTheta). Every D ∈ Pre(E, n) satisfying Full(π, D) is θ-stable: at cofinitely many finite places w of E, there exists B with D.Sat(w, B) and D.Sat(u, B^{−1}) for every conjugate place u of w (meaning u ∩𝒪_{F} = w ∩𝒪_{F} and either u ̸= w or w is nonsplit).

3. String classification, cuspidal conjugate-self-duality, and local rigidity (Strings, CuspCsd, LocRigid). Every D ∈ Pre(E, n) satisfying Full(π, D) is regular algebraic (D.Reg), every discrete factor V_{i} of D satisfies CsdAsc, and for any two D, D^{′} satisfying Full(π, D) and Full(π, D^{′}), there exists a bijection e : Fin(D.c) ≃ Fin(D^{′}.c) such that D.σ_{i,w}^{∼}= D^{′}.σ_{e(i),w} at every finite place w of E.

4. Permutation invariance of subquotients and Satake multisets (PermSub, PermSat). If D, D^{′}∈ Pre(E, n) and e : Fin(D.c) ≃ Fin(D^{′}.c) satisfy D.σ_{i,w}^{∼}= D^{′}.σ_{e(i),w} at a finite place w, then I_{w}(D) and I_{w}(D^{′}) have the exact same smooth irreducible subquotients and the exact same Satake multisets at w.

Proof. (1) Pick a nonzero vector φ ∈ π; its stabilizer in the finite adelic unitary group U_{n}(𝔸_{E,f}) is open. If for each w we pick y_{w} ∈ U_{n,w} with c_{w}(y_{w}) ∈ K_{w} failing to fix φ when such an element exists (and y_{w} = 1 otherwise), then y_{w} → 1 in U_{n}(𝔸_{E,f}) along the cofinite filter of places w, because at each fixed place u only the at most two primes above u ∩𝒪_{F} have nontrivial u-component. Hence y_{w} eventually lies in the stabilizer of φ, proving π is unramified at cofinitely many places (eventually_isUnramU). For any D ∈ Pre(E, n), each discrete factor V_{i} is spherical at cofinitely many places; taking a nonzero K_{w}-fixed vector in I_{w}(D) and applying exists_sat_multiProd shows that at cofinitely many places w, D has a factor Satake tuple S_{i} and every nonzero K_{w}-fixed vector in I_{w}(D) is a Satake eigenvector for ∑_{i}S_{i} (eventually_sat). If D, D^{′} satisfy Base(π, D) and Base(π, D^{′}), then at cofinitely many split places w, π is unramified and both D, D^{′} satisfy SplitAt(π, w) via subquotients P, P^{′} of I_{w}(D), I_{w}(D^{′}). By Proposition 4.24(1), P and P^{′} are K_{w}-spherical; lifting K_{w}-fixed vectors across the subquotient surjections via compactness of K_{w} transfers the Satake parameters ∑_{i}S_{i} and ∑_{j}S_{j}^{′} to P and P^{ ′} (hasSatGL_of_isSubquotient). Since P and P^{′} are both local components of π at the split place ∑ w, they have the same Satake parameter (hasSatGL_of_isCompAlong_split), forcing ∑_{i}S_{i} =_{j}S_{j}^{′} (splitSatPre). Combining the split and nonsplit cases gives FullSat (rFullSat).

Theorem 4.26 (From RunFin to BaseChangeIsobaricN via singleton split-place swap). The finite-selection hypothesis RunFin implies BaseChangeIsobaricN. In particular, the same placewise assembly reduces BaseChangeIsobaricN to the abstract triplet (RunSplit, RunInert, Rigid) in BaseChangeIsobaricNOf.lean.

Proof. Fix (E, n, π) with Unr(E), n ≥1, and IsAutRepU(π). Apply Lemma 4.23 (full_of) with S = ∅ to obtain D ∈ Pre(E, n) satisfying Full(π, D). By Proposition 4.25(3), every discrete factor V_{i} of D satisfies CsdAsc. We construct a smooth irreducible representation P_{w} satisfying AtPlace for D at every finite place w of E by three mutually exclusive cases:

• w is split. Apply Lemma 4.23 again with the singleton set S = {w} to obtain D_{w} ∈ Pre(E, n) satisfying Full(π, D_{w}) and D_{w}.SplitAt(π, w). Let P_{w} be a smooth irreducible subquotient of I_{w}(D_{w}) that occurs as a local component of π at w. By Proposition 4.25(3,4) (LocRigid and PermSub), D and D_{w} agree up to permutation of local factors at w, so P_{w} is also a subquotient of I_{w}(D). Proposition 4.24(1) then shows P_{w} satisfies AtPlace for D at w.

• w is nonsplit and π is unramified at w. Since Full(π, D) holds, InertAt(π, D, w) supplies factor Satake multisets b_{i} for D.σ_{i,w} whose sum B equals bcParam(n, α) for every compatible (s, ϖ, q, α). Propo-sition 4.24(2) produces a K_{w}-spherical irreducible subquotient P_{w} of I_{w}(D) with Satake parameter B; since w is nonsplit, the split clause is vacuous, so P_{w} satisfies AtPlace at w.

• w is nonsplit and π is ramified at w. Proposition 4.24(3) supplies a smooth irreducible subquotient P_{w} of I_{w}(D) for which the unramified, inert, and split clauses are all vacuous, giving AtPlace at w.

Choosing P_{w} at each w gives all ten fields of IsBaseChangeN, proving fieldN_of and fieldN_of_run. The parallel abstract reduction core_of/baseChangeIsobaricN_of replaces full_of + LocRigid + PermSub by the axiomatized (RunSplit, RunInert, Rigid) interface and executes the identical three-case placewise assembly.

Theorem 4.29 (Reduction from CandFin to BaseChangeIsobaricN). The three-clause finite spectral candidate contract CandFin implies BaseChangeIsobaricN.

Proof. We verify the three inputs FrameEx, FrameBound, and FrameRead to bci_of, and then compose the proved pipeline of Propositions 4.28 and 4.27 with Theorem 4.26.

Step 1: Unitary-side trace identity (uSide). For any (E, n, λ) with Unr(E) and n ≥1, any section S, and any finite-adelic level K^{′}, the space of definite unitary automorphic forms of weight λ and level K^{′} decomposes as a finite direct sum ⊕_{i∈ι}(π_{i} ∩V_{fix}(K^{′})) of finite-dimensional spaces (unitaryAutForms_weight_level_finite_sum_fixed_vectors), with each π_{i} admitting unique admissible local components σ_{i,w} (exists_unique_admissible_localComponent_definiteUnitary) and every irreducible automorphic π_{0} of weight λ and level K^{′} matching some π_{i} at every w ∈S. For every separable test family f, trace additivity over the direct sum equates ∑_{i∈ι} Tr(hop(f)|_{πi∩Vfix(K}′_{)}) to the global Hecke trace, which equals dim(W_{λ}) times the rational geometric side (heckeTrace_weightForms_eq_dim_mul_rationalClasses). Factoring orbital integrals across w ∈ S (twistedOrbitalIntegral_product_eq_finprod), stabilizing the rational geometric side (geomURat_eq_geomU), expressing each spectral summand as dim(W_{λ})∏_{w∈S} twTr(σ_{i,w}, f_{w}) (trace_hecke_levelVectors_eq_dim_mul_local_traces), and cancelling the nonzero factor dim(W_{λ}) yields uSide : USide.

Step 2: Run frames from CandFin (frameEx_of_fin). Fix an initial frame F_{0} : Frame0(h_{R}, π, S) (con-structed unconditionally in frameEx0) and a finite set T of places. Enlarge the unramified nonsplit subset of T to a nonempty finite set T^{′} ⊆ Sec \ (S_{0} ∪ Bad) of unramified nonsplit places equipped with local Hermitian splitting matrices b_{w} (exTbOf). Invoke Step 1 (uSide) to obtain the finite unitary family fam of weight F_{0}.λ containing an index i_{0} whose local components match π on Sec. By candIndep, the candidate predicate F_{0}.Cand(F_{0}.loc(T^{′}, c, e, b)) is independent of (c, e, b); applying CandFin at (c, e) = (0, 0) supplies the finite eigenvalue sets Z_{i,w} of (C1), the finite split-place covers {D_{w,j}} of (C2), and the uniform Iwahori dimension bound m_{0} of (C3).

• At each w ∈T^{′}, π_{w} is unramified with unitary Satake parameter α_{w}^{′} (frameInert_all), yielding via coneEigOf a monotone Satake tuple ξ for bcParam(n, α_{w}^{′} ) and a nonzero Iwahori-fixed eigenvector y on which every cone-supported Hecke function g_{cw} acts by polynomial evaluation at ξ. Because each Z_{i,w} is finite, polynomial interpolation on the strictly ordered cone coneGL(n, 2) (locC) produces finitely supported c_{w} such that g_{cw}(y) = y, while nonvanishing of the endoscopic Jacquet evaluation at any (ξ_{a}, ξ_{b}) ∈Z_{i,w} forces both ξ_{a}, ξ_{b} monotone and the µ-twisted multiset sum µ^{n}_{w}^{−ai}ξ_{a} + µ^{a}_{w}^{i}ξ_{b}= bcParam(n, α) (using muVal and satCompAt).

• At each w ∈S_{0}, since {D_{w,j}} is finite and each I_{w}(D_{w,j})^{Kw′} is finite-dimensional, locE constructs a K_{w}^{′} -bi-invariant Hecke function e_{w} fixing a nonzero K_{w}^{′} -vector of fam.σ_{i0,w} while annihilating all K_{w}^{′} -fixed vectors of every irreducible subquotient τ ̸∼= P_{w} (where P_{w} is the local component of π at w) occurring in any D_{w,j}, hence in any candidate D. Set m_{S}(w) := 1 + max_{j} dim_{ℂ} I_{w}(D_{w,j})^{Kw′}.

Define the damping exponent m := m_{0} + sup_{w∈S0} m_{S}(w) + 1 ≥ 1. From uMod_of (using spherical_one_of_local_algebra, spectral_trace_of_model_algebra, and unitary_model_holds) we obtain the finite-dimensional unitary block module R carrying the operator R.u = g_{U}(m) and the commuting diagonal Hecke algebra; by eig_B (using gcHecke and powEig), R contains a nonzero eigenvector v in block i_{0} with R.u(v) = v. This constructs a RunFrame(F_{0}, T) and proves FrameEx.

Step 3: Trace-formula word identity and norm bound (frameBound). Given a run frame F : RunFrame(F_{0}, T) with structure proof h : F.Struct (frameOk), consider the induced generator data G = F.toGenIn(h_{D}, h) (GenIn). Any element a of the star-algebra generated by G.gen expands as a finite linear combination ∑_{j∈J}c_{j}w_{j} of words in the generators and their adjoints (adjWords). By the local word-matching identities LocWord and LocMatch, the trace-formula word identity wordId (WordIdAt) equates each power trace Tr((R.u)^{k}w_{fin}) on the unitary module to a finite sum ∑_{s} cc_{s} · sc_{s} · ellSum2(· · · ) of endoscopic elliptic orbital sums across the blocks s ∈F_{0}.C.ι. Applying the block growth estimate in∑ BlkGrowth to each block s bounds the s-th summand by C_{s}(1 + k)^{Ns}‖‖(β_{s}^{m}_{j}c_{j}w_{j,s})^{k}‖‖, which yields GBound (gBound_words, hW_frame, frameBound_of).

Step 4: Gelfand character reading (frameRead). Let (s, χ) be a block and contractive star-character satisfying the hypotheses of GRead for G = F.toGenIn(h_{D}, h), with χ(B_{s}) ̸= 0. First, for any generator a with eigenvalue c on v, if c ̸= 0 then χ evaluates to c directly, while if c = 0 then adding the unit-eigenvalue generator a_{0} (for which a_{0}v = v) gives (a+a_{0})v = v ̸= 0, whence χ(a)+1 = χ(a+a_{0}) = 1 and χ(a) = 0 (chi_pin, gRead_of, chiTr). Next, ReadLimit (proved from eFinal_holds in readLimit_of_efinal) extracts a nonzero eigen-limit (s_{1}, s_{2}, F_{lim}, χ_{a}, χ_{b}) in block s with F_{lim} lying in the paired automorphic space of the trees s_{1}, s_{2} and carrying the uniform level and K_{∞}-types of F_{0}. Evaluating archimedean derivative test functions against χ pins (χ_{a}, χ_{b}) to the target archimedean parameters (F_{0}.A_{s}) (ident_of), and preOfTree_holds + joinEx_holds assemble a candidate tuple (P_{a}, P_{b}, D) satisfying F_{0}.Cand(F.d) with the required weights and cofinitely many split matches (q_of, blockCand_of). Because χ(B_{s}) ̸= 0, the m-th iterate of the separating convolution operator convF(β_{L}) does not vanish on F_{lim} (powNeOf_holds). We extract the three remaining clauses of TOut:

• Split matching on S (candS_of): At any split w ∈S ⊆S_{0}, restricting the nonvanishing m-th iterate to place w produces a nonzero m-th iterate of the split matrix operator of e_{w} on K_{w}^{′} -fixed vectors. Since e_{w} kills every K_{w}^{′} -fixed vector of every irreducible subquotient τ ̸∼= P_{w} and m > m_{S}(w) > dim_{ℂ} I_{w}(D)^{Kw′}, any nilpotent filtration on non-P_{w} subquotients would vanish at power m; thus P_{w} must occur as a subquotient of I_{w}(D) (readS).

• Inert Satake matching on T (inert_d): At any unramified nonsplit w ∈ T ⊆ T^{′}, restricting the nonvanishing m-th iterate to place w yields a nonvanishing m-th iterate of the diagonal cone operator q_{T} on the Iwahori-fixed space of pairAt(P_{a}, P_{b}, w), whose dimension is ≤ m_{0} < m. Hence some Iwahori-Jacquet eigenpair (ξ_{a}, ξ_{b}) ∈Z_{s,w} has nonzero cone evaluation (readT); by Step 2 (F.choiceT), ξ_{a}, ξ_{b} are monotone and their µ-twisted sum equals bcParam(n, α), giving InertAt(π, D, w) via expRead and joinSat_holds.

Together with the K_{∞}-type hypothesis W_join of F_{0}, this establishes TOut(π, S, T, F_{0}.K, F_{0}.W, D) (candTOut_of, frameRead_of), proving FrameRead.

Step 5: Final chain. By genEx_of, Steps 2–4 together with frameEx0 and frameOk yield GenEx. Lemma 4.31 (Openness of the slot-projected adelic levels). For every a ≤ n and d = F_{0}.loc(T^{′}, c, e, b), the subgroups lev_{1}(Sec, d, a) ≤ GL_{a}(𝔸_{E,f}) and lev_{2}(Sec, d, a) ≤ GL_{n−a}(𝔸_{E,f}) are open. In particular, LevOpen holds.

Because Sec is a conjugation section and θ_{F}^{2} = id, every finite place u of E either lies in Sec or is conjugate to a unique split place v ∈ Sec (while nonsplit places satisfy ̄v = v). It follows that g ∈ K_{f}(E, m) = ∏_{u}K_{GL}(u, m) if and only if cpn_{m}(s)(g) ∈K_{GL}(s.pl, m) for all s ∈ Slot(Sec), and correspondingly x ∈K_{f}(E, a) × K_{f}(E, n −a) if and only if cp_{H}(s)(x) ∈K_{2}(a, n −a, s.pl) for every slot s, where cp_{H}(s) = cpn_{a}(s) × cpn_{n−a}(s).

P, P^{′}∈ Pre E n satisfy Strict, then prodAt(P, w) ≃ prodAt(P^{′}, w) as GL_{n}(E_{w})-representations for every finite place w.

Proof. For (1), define the base gapped tuple

g_{0}(m)(i) = 2(m −i) (i ∈ Fin m). (89)

Consecutive coordinates of g_{0}(m) decrease by 2, so g_{0}(m) is gapped (gap0), and for every i ∈ Fin m the single-coordinate bump g_{0}(m) + 1_{i} still decreases by at least 1 at every step, so it remains gapped (gap1) while satisfying pw(ξ, g_{0}(m) + 1_{i}) = pw(ξ, g_{0}(m)) ξ_{i} (pw_shift). Suppose (ξ_{a}, ξ_{b}) and (ξ_{a}^{′}, ξ_{b}^{′}) give the same ev_{2} on all gapped pairs. Evaluating at (g_{0}(a), g_{0}(b)) and cancelling the nonzero factors dl_{w}(g_{0}(a)) dl_{w}(g_{0}(b)) yields M = pw(ξ_{a}, g_{0}(a)) pw(ξ_{b}, g_{0}(b)) = pw(ξ_{a}^{′}, g_{0}(a)) pw(ξ_{b}^{′}, g_{0}(b)) ̸= 0. Evalu-ating at (g_{0}(a) + 1_{i}, g_{0}(b)) and cancelling the nonzero modulus factors and M gives ξ_{a}(i) = ξ_{a}^{′}(i) for every i; evaluating at (g_{0}(a), g_{0}(b) + 1_{j}) similarly gives ξ_{b}(j) = ξ_{b}^{′}(j) for every j.

For (2), each coset-sum operator hkG for dc2 acts as a linear endomorphism T_{x,y} on ρ (hk_lin: either finitely supported on cosets, giving a finite linear combination of group operators, or zero by the definition of finsum). By induction on finite sets (li_eig), nonzero simultaneous eigenvectors of a family of linear endomorphisms with pairwise distinct eigenvalue characters are linearly independent. By (1), distinct (ξ_{a}, ξ_{b}) yield distinct eigenvalue characters, so choosing one nonzero eigenvector in ρ^{I2(a,b,w)} per (ξ_{a}, ξ_{b}) produces a linearly independent family inside a finite-dimensional space; hence the set of occurring (ξ_{a}, ξ_{b}) is finite (fin_eig).

For (3), fix a representative pair (P_{A}(j_{a}), P_{B}(j_{b})). By Proposition 4.34(3), both τ_{1} = prodAt(P_{A}(j_{a}), w) and τ_{2} = prodAt(P_{B}(j_{b}), w) are admissible, so τ_{1}^{I(a,w)} and τ_{2}^{I(b,w)} are finite-dimensional. Whenever (P_{a}, P_{b}) is strictly equivalent to (P_{A}(j_{a}), P_{B}(j_{b})), Proposition 4.34(1) yields equivalences on both factors, hence an equivalence pairAt(P_{a}, P_{b}, w) ≃ τ_{1} ⊠τ_{2} (extTensorEquiv), which preserves the I_{2}-fixed dimension by Proposition 4.34(2) and carries JEig eigenvectors into Z_{ja,jb} because intertwining bijections commute with coset-sum Hecke operators (∪ Ev.hk_map, Ev.jeigR_equiv, CF.eig_one). Taking Z =_{ja,jb}Z_{ja,jb} and m = max_{ja,jb}m_{ja,jb} over the finite index set Fin k_{A} × Fin k_{B} proves (3).

4.9 Weak base-change descent and split-place rigidity

Subsections 4.7 and 4.8 (together with Proposition 4.22 and Lemma 4.23) handle base change from a definite unitary group to GL_{n}(𝔸_{E}). In the reverse direction, both the patching package feeding the threshold counts in Section 4 and the full descent DescOffT used in Proposition 7.110(b) require weak base-change descent from a regular algebraic conjugate-self-dual cuspidal representation π of GL_{n}(𝔸_{E}) to the definite unitary group U(n) over E^{+}. In this subsection we reconstruct the complete proof of has_of_split, descWeakAll, and descWeak. Every step below is proved unconditionally in the supplied Lean source with zero axioms and zero sorries across all 36,328 modules in its transitive dependency cone; we note explicitly where a lower Lean module discharges a classical automorphic or trace-formula interface (Jacquet–Shalika bounds and Rankin–Selberg poles, cuspidal finiteness and multiplicity one, the definite unitary trace formula, endoscopic stabilization, the unit fundamental lemma, and twisted trace-formula asymptotics).

Throughout this subsection, let E be a CM field with maximal totally real subfield E^{+} such that E/E^{+} is unramified at every finite place (GlobalTheory.BCT.Unr E), and write Pl(E) for the set of finite places of E, c(w) (cPl w) for the complex-conjugate place of w ∈ Pl(E), and q_{w} = N(w) > 1 for the residue cardinality of w. For a finite multiset B in ℂ^{×}, set inv(B) = {α^{−1} : α ∈ B}. An isobaric datum D ∈ CD(E, n) consists of a length c ≥0, positive ranks N_{1}, . . . , N_{c} ≥1 with ∑^{c}_{i=1}N_{i} = n, and cuspidal isomorphism classes P_{i} ∈ CG(E, N_{i}). We write D.Sat(w, B) if there exist Satake multisets b_{i} for P_{i} at w with ∑_{i}b_{i} = B, D.Has(π) if (N_{i}, P_{i}) = (n, [π]) for some i, and D.Reg if for every complex embedding τ : E ↪→ ℂ the summed infinitesimal character ∑_{i} infChar_{τ}(P_{i}) equals infOfWeight(λ_{τ}) for some dominant weight λ_{τ} ∈ DomWeight(n) (so every entry has the form k + (n −1)/2 with k ∈ℤ).

Proposition 4.38 (Unitarity and θ-stability of conjugate-self-dual cuspidal representations). Let E be a CM field, let n ≥1, and let π be a cuspidal automorphic representation of GL_{n}(𝔸_{E}) satisfying DualIsConj (a nondegenerate invariant bilinear pairing between π and its complex-conjugate twist under conjOp). Then π is conjugate self-dual (IsCsd), normalized on the real split center (IsNormalised), unitary (IsUnitary), and θ-stable as an automorphic subspace (ThetaFix).

Proof. We first produce a nondegenerate invariant bilinear pairing between π and its inverse-transpose twist (Paired for invTOp), using the Jacquet–Shalika strong multiplicity one theorem (jacquetShalikaRigidity, proved unconditionally in the source from Rankin–Selberg poles rsPole and the local bound jacquetShalikaBound). Write π = π_{0} ⊗χ where π_{0} is normalized on the real split center (cuspidal_eq_twist_normalised). Let dualSubC(π_{0}) denote the space of functions obtained from π_{0} by applying the conjugate-linear inverse-transpose map D. Because π_{0} is normalized and cuspidal, its space embeds into L^{2}(GL_{n}(E)\GL_{n}(𝔸_{E})^{1}) via an injective equivariant map u (memL2_normalised_cusp_form, using cuspFormsBoundedGL), and at cofinitely many finite places w the Satake multiset of dualSubC(π_{0}) coincides with that of π_{0} (hasSat_dual). By jacquetShalikaRigidity.strong_multiplicity_one, there is a (𝔤, K_{∞}) × GL_{n}(𝔸^{∞}_{E})-equivariant isomor-phism T : dualSubC(π_{0})−→^{∼} π_{0} (dualSubC_iso). The composite J = T ∘D : π_{0} →π_{0} is a conjugate-linear

bijection intertwining invTOp with the action on π_{0}. Therefore

```text
B_{0}(φ, ψ) = ⟨u(Jψ), u(φ)⟩_{L}2
```

is a nondegenerate ℂ-bilinear pairing witnessing Paired for π_{0} and invTOp: invariance under finite adelic and maximal compact elements follows from right-invariance of Haar measure, while Lie-algebra skew-symmetry holds by inner_lie_skew' (paired_of_dualSubC_iso). We now combine B_{1} (for invTOp) with the given pairing B_{2} (for conjOp). By admissibility and finite-ness of cuspidal forms (formsFiniteGL, exists_idempotent_finiteRank_adjoint_cuspidal), there exists a nonzero finite-rank idempotent P ∈ End_{ℂ}(π) admitting formal adjoints P_{1}, P_{2} with respect to B_{1}, B_{2}. Choose v ∈ π with Pv ̸= 0 and a linear functional g ∈ π^{∗} with g(Pv) ̸= 0. Then f = g ∘P satis-fies f ∘P = f, so nondegeneracy on the finite-dimensional image of P supplies vectors ψ_{1}, ψ_{2} ∈π with B_{1}(φ, ψ_{1}) = f(φ) = B_{2}(φ, ψ_{2}) for all φ ∈ π, and ψ_{1} ̸= 0 since f(v) ̸= 0. Both invTOp and conjOp are involutive (invTOp_involutive, conjOp_involutive). By irreducibility of π and the common represented functional, there is a ℂ-linear isomorphism S : π−→^{∼} π intertwining invTOp with conjOp, which gives π.IsCsd (isCsd_of_paired).

Let ω be the central character of π (exists_hasCentral). Conjugate self-duality implies that the archimedean derivative dχ_{ω} satisfies dχ_{ω}(t) = −dχ_{ω}(t) for every real scalar t ∈ ℝ (CsdUnitary.dchi_theta), so dχ_{ω}(t) = 0 and hence ω(exp(t)) = 1. Thus π is trivial on the real split center, i.e. IsNormalised (isNormalised_of_isCsd). The same triviality shows that the 1-dimensional representation 1 ⊗ ω is normalized, hence unitary, so ω is a unitary Hecke character and π is unitary (isUnitary_of_isNormalised), proving unitOf. Finally, pulling back π along the global involution θ yields a cuspidal subspace isomorphic to π by IsCsd, which coincides with π itself by cuspidal multiplicity one (cuspMultOneGL), yielding thetaFixOf.

Lemma 4.39 (Infinitesimal-character normalization of regular isobaric factors). Let E be a CM field, n ≥ 1, π a cuspidal representation of GL_{n}(𝔸_{E}) satisfying DualIsConj, and D ∈ CD(E, n) a regular isobaric datum (D.Reg) such that for cofinitely many split places w ∈ Pl(E) there exists a multiset B with D.Sat(w, B) and [π].HasSat(w, B). Then for every index i of D, the factor D.P(i) admits a representative ρ_{i} ∈ CuspSub(E, D.N(i)) that is normalized (IsNormalised) and unitary (IsUnitary).

w non-split w^{−1} w∈Pl(E) w diverges (not_summable_all); thus the complement {w : IsSplitAt w} cannot be finite. Intersecting with the cofinite matching hypothesis gives a split place w and Satake multisets b_{j} for D.P(j) such that B =∑_{j}b_{j} is the Satake multiset of π at w.

Fix an index i, put a = D.N(i) ≥ 1, and pick a representative ρ of D.P(i). Choose s ∈ ℂ so that ρ_{0} = ρ⊗| det |^{s} is normalized on the real split center (exists_twist_isNormalised), and put z = −s, so that D.P(i) = [ρ_{0}] ⊗| det |^{z}. We show z = 0 (twist_zero). Twisting by | det |^{z} translates every infinitesimal character multiset by +z (absInf): infChar_{τ}(D.P(i)) = infChar_{τ}(ρ_{0}) + z.

Proposition 4.40 (Split-place Jacquet–Shalika rigidity). Let E be a CM field with E/E^{+} unramified at all finite places, let n ≥1, and let π ∈ CG(E, n) be unitary. Let J be a finite index set, and for each j ∈J let a_{j} ≥1 and P_{j} ∈ CG(E, a_{j}) be unitary. Suppose that for cofinitely many split places w ∈ Pl(E) there exist Satake multisets b_{j} for P_{j} at w such that ∑_{j∈J}b_{j} is the Satake multiset of π at w. Then there exists j ∈J with (a_{j}, P_{j}) = (n, π).

Set χ = µ^{2}. Then χ is unitary, unramified at cofinitely many places with |χ_{w}(ϖ_{w})| = 1, and satisfies χ_{w}(ϖ_{w}) = (−1)^{2} = 1 at every non-split place w. Moreover, for every i ∈ℕ, π ⊗χ^{i} is unitary, and at any infinite place v of E the

Proof. For (i), shrink K to an integral level subgroup K^{′} (levShrink) and induct strongly on N (readJ_all, cuspReadI_of). The case N = 0 is trivial with D = CD.nil. For N ≥1, every automorphic form φ_{k} is either cuspidal or has a nonzero constant term along some standard maximal parabolic of block sizes (r, s) with r + s = N and r, s ≥1; by pigeonhole on this finite partition (readJ_or), we treat the two cases separately:

• Cuspidal case (cuspCaseJ): each φ_{k} lies in a cuspidal representation π_{k} = π_{0,k} ⊗| det |^{zk} with π∑_{0,k} normalized (cuspMem, normTw). Summing the infinitesimal characters yields z_{k} → z_{0} := (_{τ}m_{0}(τ).sum)/(N[E : ℚ]). Hence the π_{0,k} eventually have uniformly bounded infinitesimal characters, level K^{′}, and K_{∞}-type W, so they range over a finite set (cuspFin). Extracting a constant subsequence π_{0,σ(k)} = π_{0} gives D = [π_{0}] ⊗| det |^{z0} with D.Inf(m_{0}), ¬D.Has(π) for π ∈ X (by normUniq and the exclusion hypothesis on φ_{k}), and Satake eigenvalue convergence (satComb, absInf, mtoLaws).

• Non-cuspidal constant-term case (ctCaseJ): taking the constant term along (r, s) produces eigenforms (φ_{1,k}, φ_{2,k}) on GL_{r} and GL_{s} whose shifted infinitesimal characters sum to m_{k} with shifts −s/2 and +r/2 (stepT). Because m_{0} has only finitely many multiset partitions (splitLim), passing to a subse-quence converges to a pair (p_{1}, p_{2}) of target infinitesimal characters. Applying the strong induction hypothesis to r < N and s < N yields finite families (D_{1,j1}) and (D_{2,j2}), whose twisted concate-nations (D_{1,j1} ⊗| det |^{−s/2}) ⊞(D_{2,j2} ⊗| det |^{r/2}) (cdAddG) have ranks ≤ max(r, s) < N (hence automatically avoid X), sum to m_{0}, and satisfy Satake convergence (satComb).

Theorem 4.42 (Global twisted-vs-unitary trace comparison dichotomy). Let E be a CM field with E/E^{+} unramified at all finite places, let n ≥1, and let π be a regular algebraic cuspidal representation of GL_{n}(𝔸_{E}) satisfying DualIsConj that admits a Satake multiset at every non-split finite place w. Then at least one of the following holds (RunTh):

(a) There exists an automorphic representation σ of the definite unitary group U(n)(𝔸_{E}+) (IsAutRepU) that is unramified at every non-split finite place w (IsUnramU) and satisfies that for cofinitely many split places w there exist an irreducible smooth representation τ of GL_{n}(E_{w}) and a Satake multiset B with τ occurring as a local component of σ at w, HasSatGL(w, τ, B), and [π].HasSat(w, B).

<!-- Source PDF page 110 -->

(b) There exists a regular isobaric datum D ∈ CD(E, n) with ¬D.Has(π) that has an inert-self-dual Satake multiset (inv(B) = B) at cofinitely many non-split places and matches the Satake multiset of π at cofinitely many split places.

Proof. Choose a unitary Hecke character µ for E/E^{+} with odd archimedean exponents e(v) (muEx) and let λ = l_{1} be the dominant weight attached to π by Proposition 4.41(iii). Pick a section S ⊂ Pl(E) and a finite set Z ⊂S of split places containing all places where π or µ ramifies (using the hypothesis that π is spherical at every non-split place, while µ is unramified at every non-split place) together with a good split place w_{1} ∈Z (rChoice). At every w ∈Z, choose a local component τ_{w} of π and a compactly supported smooth function f_{w} on GL_{n}(E_{w}) with trc(τ_{w}, f_{w}) ̸= 0 (levelFn), and at w_{1} choose f_{w1} supported on matrices with separable characteristic polynomial (regFn); then every twisted constant term ct_{0}(µ, a, b, f) satisfies RegAt2 at w_{1} (regCt). Write B(w) for the Satake multiset of π off Z.

Unitary trace formula (uSide, rUEval). Theorem 4.43 (Split-matching rigidity and weak base-change descent). Let E be a CM field with E/E^{+} unramified at all finite places, let n ≥1, and let π be a cuspidal automorphic representation of GL_{n}(𝔸_{E}) satisfying DualIsConj.

(i) (has_of_split) If D ∈ CD(E, n) is regular (D.Reg) and matches the Satake multiset of π at cofinitely many split places, then D.Has(π).

(ii) (descWeakAll) If π is regular algebraic and admits a Satake multiset at every non-split finite place,

then there exists an automorphic representation σ of the definite unitary group U(n)(𝔸_{E}+) that is unramified at every non-split finite place and matches the Satake multiset of π at cofinitely many split places.

(iii) (descWeak) In particular, UpperTheory.V.Z.Desc.DescWeak holds: for every prime p, every finite set S

of places of E^{+} containing all places above p such that every place of E over S is split, every rank 2 ≤ n ≤ 4, and every regular algebraic cuspidal representation π of GL_{n}(𝔸_{E}) satisfying DualIsConj that admits a Satake multiset at every place of E not lying over S, there exists a definite unitary automorphic representation σ as in (ii).

Proof. For (i), Proposition 4.38 (unitOf) shows that [π] is unitary, and Lemma 4.39 (partNorm absInf) shows that every factor D.P(i) of D is unitary. Applying Proposition 4.40 (splitRigid) to [π] and the finite family (D.N(i), D.P(i))_{i∈Fin(D.c)} yields an index i with (D.N(i), D.P(i)) = (n, [π]), which is precisely D.Has(π).

For (ii), apply Theorem 4.42 (runTh). If the second alternative held, it would supply a regular isobaric datum D ∈ CD(E, n) with ¬D.Has(π) matching π at cofinitely many split places, contradicting (i). Hence the first alternative holds, proving descWeakAll.

For (iii), since 2 ≤n implies 1 ≤n, and every non-split place w ∈ Pl(E) cannot lie over S (as every place over S is split by hypothesis), the off-S Satake hypothesis supplies a Satake multiset for π at every non-split place. Applying (ii) therefore yields UpperTheory.V.Z.Desc.DescWeak.

4.10 The F8 patching package and literature-level realization

This subsection reconstructs the complete fifteen-field record UpperTheory.V.Af.HypothesesH' constructed by published_hypotheses_from_patching_alt together with the fifty-six-field record LiteratureRankNHypothesis that feeds it from our already-closed upstream suppliers: the unconditional CM Galois correspondence Row0b recT (Theorem 7.116 in Subsection 7.15), definite-to-isobaric base change baseChangeN (Subsections 4.7 and 4.8, Theorem 4.36), and weak base-change descent descWeak (Theorem 4.43 in Subsection 4.9). We treat no record assignment as a proof: every field of LiteratureRankNHypothesis is accounted for explicitly (separating project-specific suppliers, derived Lean reductions, and established classical literature statements), and every component of HypothesesH' is proved in detail. Downstream consumption of the resulting HypothesesH' object by ends0_alt, sp4In0_alt, linkedUnlE_holds_alt, and katoTwoW_of_printsH is handled in Subsection 4.11, while the KatoTwoW/Bcr l model identification is handled in Subsection 4.4.

(i) Local GL_{n} and finite-group package (loc : LitLocAlt, 18 fields): Bernstein–Zelevinsky finiteness (bz), Bernstein–Tadić irreducibility of unitary products (bern, Background fact 4.21), geometric lemma (geo), Zelevinsky polynomial-ring structure (zel), irreducibility of totally disjoint products (disj), Moy–Prasad Jacquet isomorphism (mp), tempered products of square-integrables (temp), essentially

Proposition 4.48 (Quadratic and cyclic base change, imaginary-quadratic GL_{2} descent, and definite quater-nion algebras). The base-change, descent, and quaternion fields bc, cyc, cyc2, and quat of HypothesesH' hold unconditionally:

degree Galois extension M/K of totally complex number fields and every n ≥1, base-change lifting (modulo norm-character self-twists), Galois-invariant descent for regular infinitesimal characters, and fibre uniqueness modulo norm characters hold (Z.Bc.CycC).

(iii) Imaginary-quadratic GL_{2} descent (cyc2:= Or.inl RankTwoDescent.descS): for every imaginary

Theorem 4.55 (Rank-four symplectic image density and promodularity). For every h_{H} : HypothesesH', the theorem sp4In0_alt applied to h_{H} establishes SymplecticFourImageDense: for every large host (h, t), every odd prime ℓ, every coefficient ring c, every 0 < e < t, every ψ ∈X_{h}(ℓ, e), and every good symplectic datum D of Case II or Case III (OfCase), one has D.Fin0, D.NoEnd, and an isomorphism ι : ℚ_{ℓ}≃ℂ such that every irreducible characteristic-zero symplectic deformation on D is regular algebraic automorphic over ℚ (AllIrr for IsAut4Alt).

Proof. Write h_{N} = h_{H}.litN and h_{A} = h_{H}.toClassicalTheorems. The proof constructs five inputs from h_{H} and feeds them to Cu.sp4In_alt = main4_alt:

(1) Unramified cohomology and Hida inputs (adjoint_lift_of_prints): builds U : UnramifiedInputs combining U.coh : CohomologyHyp (from locPrints_of_litN and h_{N}.coh), h_{H}, Core.modU_of_printsH, levEx, lamEx, and b0Ex applied to phiAll of cohP_alt.

(2) Ferrero–Washington ℓ-rank bound (FW.ferreroWashington): proved unconditionally in Lean (uniform bound on |Cl(𝒪_{K}′)/ℓCl(𝒪_{K}′)| along cyclotomic ℤ_{ℓ}-towers of abelian number fields), yielding via x2 a uniform dimension constant C on tame towers so that a deep layer satisfies 30(C + 1)^{2}≤T.d.

(3) Case-II initial seed (seedIIs_alt): combines h_{H}, hilbert_eisenstein_weight_one_holds, Lit.oneUse, and automorphic induction indAutLP_of_printsH_upQuad_upSol_indCs (from quadratic base change h_{H}.bc and cyclic base change h_{H}.cyc) through propMHolZ_alt, mixSeed_of_alt, mixOfP, and seedII_of_p_alt, establishing SeedIIAlt.

(4) Case-III tensor-induced initial seed (fourth_initial_of_prints_h): given a Case-III tower T_{0} with quadratic subfield K^{′} such that g_{0} /∈ G_{K}′, tauEx' constructs an algebraic character κ of K^{′}, and rhoExP (driven by propEGP_of_printsH) constructs an odd-weight modular representation ρ of G_{ℚ} of weight k ≥18m + 3 together with an auxiliary prime w and character θ killing roots of unity (hence unramified away from w and trivial on deep towers by theta_unramified_of_kills_roots_of_unity). Then rank_four_automorphy_of_tensor_of_base_change_of_induction base-changes ρ to P_{0} on K^{′} (h_{H}.bc), chooses j ∈{1, . . . , 9} (Cu2.goodJ) separating the four archimedean weights of P_{0} ⊗Y and its complex conjugate, ascends over M = K^{′}⊔L for every abelian CM field L ⊇⊇K^{′} (h_{H}.cyc and awChain_of_printsH), verifies SplitBad via polOf4_alt and sphOfUnrW_alt (using polarization sign adjustment exists_polarized), and applies quadratic automorphic induction indAutCs_of_alt from M to L (Cu2.tenInd) to prove that tenB(ρ_{1}, τ)|_{GL} is regular algebraic cuspidal with full witness AllW. Packing the symplectic pairing, continuity, residue congruence, and initiality (tower_is_initial_of_ok) yields SeedIVAlt.

(5) Potential modularity ideals on deep fit towers (pmEx_of_printsH): given any fit deep tower T, exists_two_links_same_kappa_not_dvd_of_fit_deep produces two rank-four unitary Hida links K, K^{′} with distinct auxiliary places (v0_ne) and maps φ : B.B → X.B, φ^{′} : B^{′}.B → X.B from universal ordinary determinant rings carrying modular ideals J_{0}, J_{0}^{′} (from U.modU). Set J = J_{0} · φ + J_{0}^{′}· φ^{′} on X.B (promodular_existence_of_local_zero). Then:

• a power of 𝔪_{X.B} lies in the ideal generated by J and the weight parameters (exists_pow_maximalIdeal_le_of_modular_phi);

• regularity of the modular deformation quotient holds at modular points (modular_deformation_quotient_regular_at_point_alt);

• at every seed point y of X.A, local_zero_of_modular_p verifies X.LocZero J y by shifting the weights to even gaps, deducing automorphy via ptAutR'_alt and point_representation_weights, transporting ideals via hida_modular_ideal_map, and invoking eigenbasis_rank_four with adjoint_lifting_of_cohomology (from Th.core_alt_bis);

• characteristic-zero purity follows from pmPur_w_alt (using h_{J}.end1), and rank-four automorphy over ℚ follows by gluing pmAutO_alt across the two coprime auxiliary places via glueN and descending via pmDown_alt.

This supplies PMExAlt.

We now assemble ProModAlt for every ambient field 𝔞 and residual star representation (r, u) on D:

• In Case II (Ctx2), proMod_of_pmEx_of_ctx2_of_kPair_of_star selects a tame tower T_{0} (exists_tame_tower_ok_two), uses deep_tower_residue_chain_exists (fed by seedIIs_alt) to pass to a tower T_{1} carrying a residual chain from the lattice model P^{′} to the Case-II seed Q, chooses a deep layer T with 30(C + 1)^{2} ≤ T.d via (2), and applies last_step: X.LocZero at the seed Q supplies SomeIn at the residual endpoint, and allIn_of_chain with residual_charpoly_rank_four propagates membership in J back along the chain to P^{′}, proving ProModAlt.

• In Case III (Ctx3), promodularity_case_three_of_chain_reduction uses existsTensorSeedTower_holds to select T_{0}. Over a finite base change T_{1} killing the Gysin locus W_{2} (diesEx), chainIV_alt builds a four-step residual chain u →q_{3} →q_{4} →q_{2} →Q mod 𝔪 of Good4 points alternating between lineP and lineM moves (gysinPs, gysinAl) connecting u to the Case-III seed Q from (4). Finally, modularity_rank_four_of_promodularity_case_three converts ProModAlt into three conse-quences: nonexistence of characteristic-p star points (contradiction_star_promodular, giving Con), characteristic-zero purity (pureW_of_proModular_of_isZero, giving PurityAtPoints), and characteristic-zero automorphy (aut_n_alt, giving AutmAlt). Applying fin0_no_end_all_irr_of_good_con_purity_aut yields D.Fin0 ∧D.NoEnd ∧∃ι, D.AllIrr(IsAut4Alt ι), proving SymplecticFourImageDense.
