Proposition 4.56 (Shared-package sphericalization and wiring into Kato vanishing). Let h_{H} : HypothesesH'. Combining h_{H} with the unconditional quadratic base-change theorem UpperTheory.ConvolutionTheory.R2.quadBC2 and the internal Bcr l Bloch–Kato evaluation twoS (vanishOrdL_of_zetaUr, reconstructed in Sub-section 4.4 and Proposition 4.12) yields katoTwoW_of_printsH on h_{H}, establishing KatoTwoW.

Proof. Put P = h_{H}.toClassicalTheorems and h_{R} = rowOf' P.litN.aut.gal. We construct the four spheri-calization layers that feed twoS from h_{H}:

(1) Split-at-ℓ quadratic base change and polarization (base_change_split_of_printed_quad_bc): given an odd prime ℓ and an irreducible continuous V : G_{ℚ} → GL_{2}(ℚ_{ℓ}) with finite-order determinant at-tached to a regular algebraic cuspidal representation π of GL_{2}(𝔸_{ℚ}), choose an imaginary quadratic field K/ℚ in which ℓ splits together with an element s /∈ G_{K} lying in the kernel of V (Cq.exQuad). Then V |_{GK} remains irreducible (range_of_sign, isIrr_comp), ruling out self-twist of π by the quadratic character of K (noTwist_of_prints), so quadBC2 lifts π to a regular algebraic cuspidal representation Q of GL_{2}(𝔸_{K}) with V |_{GK} attached to Q. Using the symplectic self-duality V^{∨} ≃ V ⊗(det V )^{−1} (dualTw_det) and an algebraic Hecke character χ^{′} on K of fixed archimedean sign (heckeChar_sign_fixed) matching (det V )χ_{ℓ}, Satake comparison at cofinitely many places polarizes Q (polar_of_lift, via Jacquet–Shalika and Gelfand–Kazhdan). At a split place w | ℓ of K, the com-pletion isomorphism K_{w} ≃ℚ_{ℓ} equates Satake multisets of π_{ℓ} and Q_{w} (sat_iff).

(2) Local sphericality and Frobenius-Satake matching above ℓ (local_k_of_printed_rec_compat_sph_frob and locQ_of_alt): for a polarized regular algebraic cuspidal representation Q on GL_{2}(𝔸_{K}) whose attached r has a D_{A}-flag above w | ℓ with inertia characters χ^{e}_{ℓ}, χ^{−}_{ℓ}^{e} (e ≥ 1), the exponent difference m_{i} −m_{j} ∈{0, ±2e} is never 1, so κ_{i} ̸= κ_{j}χ_{ℓ} on I_{A} (cycIne). Local-global compati-bility (compatTOf on (h_{R}, plainRec), recTExists, winPt) then forces the Weil–Deligne representation of r|_{GKw} to have level 1 (weil_deligne_above_of_printed_results), so the local component has a GL_{2}(𝒪_{Kw})-fixed vector (recSph_alt), admits a Satake multiset B, and matches the Frobenius value of κ_{0} to a Satake parameter b ∈B (weilDeligne_frobenius_eigenvalue_of_full_flag, recFrob_alt).

<!-- Source PDF page 134 -->

Combining (1) and (2) inside locQ yields LocQ over ℚ, and frobRoot_alt converts this for any newform g of level prime to ℓ into a root α = ℓ^{e}b of the Hecke polynomial at ℓ (FrobRoot).

(3) Twist-stable sphericality from the automorphic witness (sphOfWit and twWit_alt): given an admitted representation W carrying the automorphic witness WitAQ and any finite-order character φ killing µ_{M}, alg_cyclotomic_of_printed_results and aIsoTwOf_alt transport the witness to W ⊗φ (twWit_alt), and sphOfWit applies LocQ to conclude SphAt for (ι, e, W).

(4) Unramified level and exclusion of χ_{ℓ} as a flag character (srcS_alt and sources_of_spherical): given an admitted W with D_{ℓ}-flag characters κ_{0}, κ_{1} satisfying κ_{0}|_{Iℓ} = χ^{e}_{ℓ}χ, κ_{1}|_{Iℓ} = χ_{ℓ}^{−e}χ(det W), and det W|_{Iℓ}= 1, Kronecker–Weber (kwAbs) on ker(det W) provides N ≥1 so that φ := (det W)^{−1}χ^{−1} kills µ_{Nℓ}. Then W ⊗φ has inertia flag characters (χ^{e}_{ℓ}, χ_{ℓ}^{−e}) and admits an attached weight-(2e + 1) newform g (twNew_alt). By SphAt, the cuspidal representation attached to g has a Satake multiset at ℓ, so h_{H}.ssR forces ℓ ∤ M(g) (not_dvd_level_of_satake_hecke_poly_cofinite). Applying frobRoot_alt at a Frobenius σ gives a Hecke root α = ι(u)^{±1} where u = (κ_{0}φ)(σ)χ_{ℓ}(σ)^{−e} has ℓ-adic norm 1; by odd-weight purity (newform_unit_root_not_root_of_unity_odd_weight), α is not a root of unity. If κ_{0}|_{Dℓ} = χ_{ℓ}, then comparing infinite-order χ_{ℓ}|_{Iℓ} with finite-order χ forces e = 1, whence u = φ(σ) would be a root of unity, contradiction; if κ_{1}|_{Dℓ} = χ_{ℓ}, inertia forces χ^{e}_{ℓ}^{+1}|_{Iℓ} = χ|_{Iℓ}, again contradicting infinite order. Thus SrcS holds.

Finally, for any Used datum (W, θ) with newform f of weight 2e + 1 and witness WitAQ, applying twoS to P.litN.coh and srcS_alt evaluates vanishOrdL_of_zetaUr on both W ⊗1 and W ⊗θ (since θ = det W on the admissible pair and sphAt_tw preserves SphAt under finite-order twists), yielding both Bloch–Kato Selmer vanishings required by KatoTwoW.

4.12 Construction of the uniform rank-three congruence integer

Writing (c) = 𝔪_{𝒪}^{k} over the DVR 𝒪, we have len_{𝒪}(Hom_{𝒪}(k_{𝒪}, 𝒪/(c))) ≤ 1, and induction along a composition series of Q_{j} (length_hom_le) gives len_{𝒪}(Hom_{𝒪}(Q_{j}, 𝒪/(c))) ≤ len_{𝒪}(Q_{j}) = cotLen(x, 𝒜, j, F) < ∞. Since k_{𝒪} is finite, a finite-length 𝒪-module N has cardinality |k_{𝒪}|^{len𝒪(N)}; injectivity of ψ gives |M| ≤| Hom_{𝒪}(Q_{j}, 𝒪/(c))| and hence len_{𝒪}(M) ≤ cotLen(x, 𝒜, j, F) (len_le_of_inj).

## What the sixty-field package asserts

<!-- Source PDF page 170 -->

4.15 What the sixty-field package asserts

The structure UnitaryGroupThirdPlaceHypotheses has exactly sixty fields, at lines 23–82 of BernsteinUnitaryProductIrreducible.lean. The record published_results_eigen assigns all sixty, in the same order, at lines 667–726 of EveryCharacterOfLiteratureOfVWin.lean. The field statements are mathematical inputs, not conse-quences of having written that record. Four of its entries can already be resolved directly from the proofs above and in the local chapter.

Both greenCuspidal and greenRegularCharacters are provided by the verified Green parametrization and Proposition 4.1. The former is precisely its polynomial-label statement, including the degree and all

<!-- Source PDF page 171 -->

choices of roots; the latter is the regular-character statement preceding that proposition. The field depthZeroSupport' is exactly Lemma 5.11: a depth-zero irreducible subquotient of a parabolic induction forces depth-zero vectors in each cuspidal inducing factor. Its source quantifies over every nonarchimedean local field, as does that proof.

The fourth entry has a different meaning. The type of the field named siegelEisensteinSimplePole is the abbreviation UnusedSlot72, whose definition is True. Its supplier is the proof trivial. The unique proof of this proposition fills the field without asserting a pole, a residue or even an Eisenstein series. No analytic conclusion can be extracted from this entry alone.

The fields galoisRepOfPolarizedCuspidal and localGlobalAboveL retain the full CuspUAlt and CarUAlt statements, including their normalization and their quantification over arbitrary compatible period mod-els. Their conversion from the geometric Galois theorem is the shared obligation in Section 7. Likewise the integral crystalline fields require the simultaneous model comparison of Input 6.78; naming a standard crystalline-lattice theorem does not construct those model isomorphisms.

The separate first-input record, ThetaLocalInputs, has fifty-three fields and fifty-three matching assign-ments. Twenty of its mathematical types are also fields of the sixty-field record; their combined list has ninety-three distinct top-level types. In particular the first-input record still includes the convergent Rallis inner-product assertion, the two real/metaplectic and local Howe comparison assertions, the specified Kudla splitting, and the global theta invariance assertion. They are not supplied merely by the finite-field Green result.

There are also three nested packages. The nonendoscopic package has local representation, global automorphic–Galois, cohomology, joining and Hecke functional-equation components. The geometric com-patibility package has twelve components: Weil representation, discrete-series existence and classification, analyticity, trace-class, smooth factorization and Flath factorization, Siegel–Weil, doubling and unramified doubling, partial Hecke continuation and the height-counting assertion. The local link package has seven: the specified B comparison, global reciprocity, Bloch–Kato, local Tate duality, local Euler characteristic,

cris local finiteness and the integral prismatic comparison. A proof of the sixty-field conjunction must account for these components as well; they are not replaced by the field names. Every project-specific component above is now discharged across this manuscript – galoisRepOfPolarizedCuspidal and localGlobalAboveL by The-orem 7.116, baseChangeDefiniteUnitary by Proposition 4.30 and Theorem 4.36, nLink and the crystalline comparisons by Subsections 6.6 and 6.7, AbelianDeRham by Proposition 10.32 and Subsections 10.8–10.9, the theta-integral and local-matching assertions by Subsections 4.21–4.22, and the full literature-level record reconciliation by Subsection 4.10 – and all sixty and fifty-three fields enter the final assembly in Section 17 (Proposition 17.4 and Theorem 17.5).

Lemma 4.81 (The norm-one density used by the determinant). Let E/F be a CM quadratic extension, assume E/ℚ is Galois, and let T be a finite set of finite places of F. Write U_{1}(𝔸_{F} ) = {z ∈𝔸^{×}_{E}: zz̄ = 1}. A closed subgroup of this group that contains U_{1}(F) and all the local U_{1}(F_{v}) at the fully split places outside T is the whole group.

Proof. First record an idele version. Let M ⊂𝔸^{×}_{E} be a closed subgroup containing E^{×}, one fixed positive infinite idele e with |e|_{𝔸E} > 1, and the entire local E_{w}^{×} outside a finite exceptional set whenever Nw is prime. The quotient 𝔸^{×}_{E}/M is a compact abelian group. To see compactness, the norm-one idele-class group is compact, and division by a power of e puts the modulus of any idele into [1, |e|]. Compactness of the norm-one class group is the usual ideal-class and unit-lattice argument: use finitely many ideal-class representatives for finite valuations, a compact product of finite local units, and a bounded fundamental parallelepiped for the logarithms of the global units at infinity. The remaining archimedean angular factors are compact. Adjoining the bounded modulus interval consequently gives a compact set surjecting onto the displayed quotient.

If that quotient had a nonidentity point, separation of points by continuous characters of a compact abelian group would give a nontrivial unitary idele-class character trivial on M. Lemma 4.80 rules this out. Thus M is the whole idele group.

Now let N be the closed subgroup in the statement. Use adelic Hilbert90 to form the continuous surjec-tion

```text
q : 𝔸^{×}_{E}−→U_{1}(𝔸_{F} ), q(y) = y/̄y.
```

For clarity, local Hilbert90 gives a preimage at each place. At almost every inert place the quadratic extension is unramified; subtracting its valuation by a base-field uniformizer makes that preimage a unit. At a split place a norm-one pair (a, a^{−1}) has preimage (a, 1). The chosen preimages therefore form an idele, which proves adelic surjectivity. The subgroup M = q^{−1}(N) is closed and contains E^{×}, since q(k) = k/k^{̄} ∈U_{1}(F). It contains a positive infinite idele e fixed by conjugation, because q(e) = 1.

Exclude the primes over T and the finitely many primes ramified in E/ℚ. If Nw = p is prime outside this set, its inertia degree and ramification index over p are both one. Galoisness makes all such indices equal. The identity efg = [E : ℚ] then shows that p splits completely in E. In particular the place v under w is fully split and outside T. For a local idele y supported at w, q(y) is supported at v and has norm one, so it belongs to N. Thus M contains all the degree-one local groups required by the idele version. That version gives M = 𝔸^{×}_{E}, and surjectivity of q gives N = U_{1}(𝔸_{F} ).

Lemma 4.83 (Enlargement and linearity of polynomial matching). If a pair matches over S and S ⊂ T, with the ramification set contained in S, it matches over T. The set of polynomial matching pairs, allowing such a finite set, is a complex vector subspace of the product of the two function spaces.

Proof. For v /∈S the images of the two vacua coincide; call that vector z_{v} ∈Π_{v}. The multilinear map

```text
⊗Π_{v} −→⊗Π_{v}, ⊗u_{v} −−→ ⊗u_{v})⊗(( ⊗ z_{v}))
v∈S v∈T v∈S v∈S v∈T\S
```

is well defined by the universal property of the finite tensor product, with factors placed in their indexed positions. Tensoring it with the identity on Π_{∞} carries the equality over S to the equality over T. The unchanged local functions outside S are exactly these vacua, so this is the desired enlarged matching equality.

The pair (0, 0) is represented by empty sums. For two matching pairs choose the common set T_{1}∪T_{2} and enlarge both equalities by the first argument. Multiply the archimedean factors in the first pair by any c ∈ℂ and concatenate its finite sums with those of the second pair. Linearity of p_{∞} and of the tensor product turns their images into c times the first tensor sum plus the second. The same operation on both sides preserves the equality, proving closure under (x, y) →→cx + y and hence the vector-subspace assertion.

Lemma 4.84 (The good-place action on matching pairs). Fix a split finite place v and a splitting embedding E → F_{v}. Assume the local quotient maps are onto and the two local Weil actions respect their common quotient: equal quotient images have equal quotient images after the simultaneous right action of any h ∈ U(W)(F_{v}). Assume also that the global action supported at v acts on a pure adelic function by its local action at v and leaves all other factors unchanged. Then the simultaneous action of h preserves polynomial matching.

Choose a linear section s : Π_{v} →𝒮_{v} of p_{v}, and set A = p_{v}Os. Compatibility applied to sy and any x^{′} ∈𝒮_{v}^{′} with p^{′}_{v}x^{′} = y gives Ay = p^{′}_{v}O^{′}x^{′}. Conversely, for any x ∈𝒮_{v} choose x^{′} with p^{′}_{v}x^{′} = p_{v}x. Compatibility and the preceding equality give p_{v}Ox = p^{′}_{v}O^{′}x^{′} = A(p_{v}x). Lemma 4.85 (The two factorizations used by the theta argument). Let A, B, H be complex vector spaces, let P ⊂ A × B be a vector subspace, and let B_{0} ⊂ B be a vector subspace. Suppose I : A → H and I^{′}: B →H are linear and

For any s, t ∈ℂ there are linear maps C : A →H and C^{′}: B →H such that

```text

C^{′}(b) = C(a) ((a, b) ∈P).
```

<!-- Source PDF page 179 -->

Proof. On P_{0} = P ∩(A×B_{0}) define k(a, b) = sI(a)+tI^{′}(b). It is linear. If the first coordinate vanishes, the second vanishing hypothesis gives k(0, b) = 0. Consequently k descends to the image of the first-coordinate projection: if two elements have the same first coordinate, their difference is (0, b −b^{′}) ∈P_{0} and has zero k-value. Choose a vector-space complement of that image in A, and extend this descended linear map by zero on the complement. The resulting C satisfies the first displayed equality.

Now consider (a, b) →→C(a) on all of P. If b = 0, then (a, 0) ∈P_{0} because 0 ∈B_{0}, and the equality just proved gives C(a) = sI(a) + tI^{′}(0) = 0, using the first vanishing hypothesis. It therefore descends through the second-coordinate projection of P. Extend the descended map by zero on a complement of that projection’s image in B; call the extension C^{′}. By its construction C^{′}(b) = C(a) for every pair in P.

Lemma 4.88 (Finite orbits from countable algebraic dimension). Let G be a locally compact Hausdorff group, let U be a complex vector space of countable algebraic dimension with an action ρ, and suppose there is an injective linear map j : U →C(G, ℂ) satisfying j(ρ(g)x)(h) = j(x)(hg). For every x ∈U and every compact C ⊂G, the span of {ρ(g)x : g ∈C} is finite dimensional.

Proof. Choose a finite or countable basis of U. The spans U_{S} of its finite subsets form a countable covering of U. Viewed in the Hausdorff product space ℂ^{G}, each j(U_{S}) is closed: a finite-dimensional subspace of a Hausdorff topological vector space is closed. The orbit map g →→j(ρ(g)x) is continuous in that product topology, since each coordinate is j(x)(hg). The closed sets E_{S} = {g : ρ(g)x ∈U_{S}} cover G. The Baire theorem for locally compact Hausdorff spaces gives a nonempty open set N ⊂ E_{S} for one finite S; fix

```text
g_{0} ∈N.
```

For each k ∈C, the open set kg_{0}^{−1}N contains k, and its orbit of x lies in ρ(kg_{0}^{−1})U_{S}. A finite number of these sets cover C. The corresponding finite sum of translates of U_{S} is finite dimensional and contains the entire orbit over C.

Proposition 4.89 (The invariant-form line used by the theta proof). Let G, U, j, ρ be as in Lemma 4.88. Suppose U is a nonzero irreducible G-module, G has a compact open subgroup K, and there is a compact Ω⊂G such that, for every g ∈G, some g^{′} ∈Ω satisfies j(x)(g) = j(x)(g^{′}) for every x ∈U. Let c be a positive-definite invariant Hermitian form on U, linear in the first argument, and let b be any invariant sesquilinear form, also linear in its first argument. Then b = λc for some λ ∈ℂ. No boundedness hypothesis on b is required.

These finitely many linear functionals, together with their K translates, detect vectors: if ℓ_{i}(ρ(k)x) = 0 for every i, k, then j(x) vanishes on Ω by the displayed equivariance, hence on all of G by the covering property, and injectivity of j gives x = 0.

Fix 0 ̸= f ∈ U and put V = span ρ(K)f. It is finite dimensional by the preceding lemma. Let ℋ = Hom_{K}(V, U). The map ⊕

```text
ℋ −→ V^{∗}, L −−→(ℓ_{i} ∘L)_{i}
i
```

is injective. If its value is zero, then, for v ∈ V , ℓ_{i}(ρ(k)Lv) = ℓ_{i}(Lρ(k)v) = 0 for every i, k; detection gives Lv = 0. Thus ℋ is finite dimensional. The sum Z =∑_{L∈ℋ}L(V ) is consequently finite dimensional, is K-stable and contains V , since the inclusion of V is one of the maps L. Its orthogonal complement Z^{⊥} is also K-stable, by invariance of c.

We claim b(Z, Z^{⊥}) = 0. Fix y ∈Z^{⊥} and let Y = span ρ(K)y ⊂Z^{⊥}; this space is finite dimensional. Finite-dimensional Riesz representation gives a linear map T_{Y} : U →Y characterized by

```text
c(T_{Y} x, w) = b(x, w) (w ∈Y ).
```

Invariance of the two forms and nondegeneracy of c|_{Y} make T_{Y} equivariant for K: test T_{Y} ρ(k)x and ρ(k)T_{Y} x against every w ∈Y , and replace w by ρ(k^{−1})w. For every L ∈ℋ, the composite T_{Y} L : V →U is therefore another member of ℋ. Its image lies in Z by definition and in Y ⊂Z^{⊥} by construction. Hence it is zero. Thus b(Lv, y) = c(T_{Y} Lv, y) = 0; taking their span proves the claim.

Apply finite-dimensional Riesz representation again, now to Z, to obtain T_{Z} : U →Z with c(T_{Z}x, w) = b(x, w) for w ∈Z. The endomorphism T_{Z}|_{Z} has an eigenvector 0 ̸= x ∈Z, since Z is a nonzero finite-dimensional complex space. Write its eigenvalue as λ. On Z we have b(x, w) = c(λx, w) = λc(x, w). On Z^{⊥} both sides vanish by the claim. Decompose an arbitrary w ∈ U into its projection onto the finite-dimensional Z and its orthogonal remainder to obtain the same equality for every w.

Finally N = {x : b(x, w) = λc(x, w) for every w} is a G-stable vector subspace. For stability, write any w as ρ(g)ρ(g^{−1})w and apply invariance of both forms. It contains the nonzero eigenvector just con-structed. Irreducibility gives N = U, which is exactly b = λc.

Lemma 4.90 (Countable polynomial Schwartz rank). For the source’s compatible Hermitian/skew-Hermitian Cartan and Darboux models, the polynomial Fock space and the polynomial adelic Schwartz space have countable algebraic dimension over ℂ.

Proof. Write X for the finite-dimensional real archimedean configuration space and β for the real bilinear pairing in the standard additive character. The differentiated Heisenberg operator in the Darboux coordinates is

```text
D(a, b)f(y) = ∂_{a}f(y) −2πiβ(y, b)f(y).
```

For each choice ϵ of signs at the finitely many infinite places, the Cartan operators induce a real complex structure J_{ϵ} on X ⊕X. Its vertical-to-horizontal block is invertible. In fact at each infinite place the com-patible Cartan symplectic pairing ω(v, J_{ϵ}v) is definite, with a possible overall sign ϵ_{w}. If v = (0, b) and J_{ϵ}v were also vertical, the pairing would vanish because the vertical subspace is Lagrangian. Definiteness forces b = 0 there. This proves injectivity place by place and hence on their product; equality of the finite dimensions gives surjectivity. This is why the source uses the compatible Cartan structure, rather than an arbitrary complex structure on the Darboux space.

Let G_{ϵ} be the simultaneous annihilator space defined by D(J_{ϵ}p)f = iD(p)f for every p ∈ X ⊕X. Evaluation at zero is injective on it. Indeed suppose f(0) = 0, fix x ∈X, and choose b such that J_{ϵ}(0, b) = (x, b^{′}) using the invertible block. The annihilator equation at y = tx gives

```text
_{dt}^{d}f(tx) = t c_{x}f(tx), c_{x} = 2πi(β(x, b^{′}) −iβ(x, b)).
```

Consequently the derivative of f(tx) exp(−t^{2}c_{x}/2) is zero. This function equals its value at zero, namely zero. The exponential never vanishes, so f(x) = 0. As x was arbitrary, f = 0. Thus dim G_{ϵ} ≤1.

There are finitely many sign choices. Choose a real basis p_{1}, . . . , p_{m} of X ⊕X and generators for the sum of these finite-dimensional G_{ϵ}. The complex span of all vectors

```text
D(p_{i1}) · · · D(p_{ik})f_{ϵ} (k ≥0)
```

is countably generated, contains all these annihilator spaces, and is stable under every D(p_{i}). Real linearity in p makes it stable under every Heisenberg differential operator. The polynomial space is the smallest subspace with precisely these containment and stability properties, so it is a subspace of this countably generated space and has countable dimension.

The finite adelic configuration space has a countable compact-open basis. One obtains it by prescribing congruence neighborhoods at finitely many places and the integral lattice elsewhere; the places, congruence depths and residue classes involved are all countable. Every locally constant compactly supported function is a finite linear combination of compact-open characteristic functions from the finite set algebra generated by this basis. To verify this, cover its compact support by finitely many basic sets on which it is constant and refine into their finitely many disjoint Boolean pieces. This set algebra is countable. Thus the finite adelic Schwartz–Bruhat space also has countable dimension. The map sending an archimedean function and a finite adelic function to their product is bilinear. Its image contains all the pure adelic generators used to define polynomial Schwartz data. The tensor product of two countably generated spaces is countably generated, proving the second assertion.

Corollary 4.91 (The kernel and irreducible quotient in the line argument). In the definite setting, suppose the matching space P_{0} is stable under the full right action and let

N_{0} = {(Φ, Φ^{′}) ∈P_{0} : (Φ, 0) is polynomial matching}.

Proposition 4.86 holds.

Its smaller member is still in the full-rank-cone subspace, so the second zero-pair assertion gives B_{y} = 0. Thus both maps, and every K_{s,t}, vanish on N_{0}.

The kernel of B is invariant, contains N_{0} and is proper because B is nonzero. The stated irreducibility property gives ker B = N_{0}. Hence U = P_{0}/ ker B is an irreducible module and B embeds it in continuous functions on the right automorphic quotient. It has countable algebraic dimension by Lemma 4.90, since P_{0} is a subspace of the product of the two polynomial data spaces. The function embedding is equivariant for right translation. A compact representative set for the right automorphic quotient gives the covering property in Proposition 4.89. A compact open subgroup of the full right adelic group is obtained by taking its compact archimedean group and any compact open subgroup of its finite adelic group.

The form c(x, y) = ⟨B_{x}, B_{y}⟩_{W} is positive definite: zero norm makes the continuous function B_{x} zero everywhere, and then x = 0 in U. Each b(x, y) = ⟨K_{s,t}(x), K_{s}′_{,t}′(y)⟩_{W} descends to U by the kernel equality. Haar right invariance makes b, c invariant. Their products are integrable because the functions are continuous on a compact quotient. All hypotheses of Proposition 4.89 now hold, giving exactly the required scalar identity for all matching pairs.

Lemma 4.92 (Finite function tensors have no extra relations)∏. For finitely many sets X_{i} and vector subspaces V_{i} ⊂ℂ^{Xi}, the product-function map ⊗_{i}V_{i} →ℂ^{iXi} is injective. Consequently any chosen linear maps V⊗_{i} → Q_{i} carry two finite pure-tensor presentations of the same product function to the same element of

```text
_{i}Q_{i}.
```

Proof. A proposed relation uses only finite-dimensional subspaces W_{i} ⊂ V_{i}. Evaluations at points of X_{i} span W_{i}^{∗}: otherwise their common annihilator in W_{i} would contain a nonzero function vanishing at every point, a contradiction. Choose bases of the W_{i} and express each coordinate functional as a finite linear combination of evaluations. If the product function is zero, applying these finite evaluation combinations separately in each variable makes every tensor-coordinate coefficient zero. The tensor is therefore zero. This proves injectivity on every finite relation, hence on the full algebraic tensor product. Applying the tensor product of the chosen maps proves the consequence.

For adelic pure functions one first fixes all coordinates outside the finite tensor set. The vacua are nonzero, and are standard integral characteristic functions at almost every place. Choose a nonzero value of each exceptional vacuum and an integral point at every other place. These choices form a finite adele, and their product is nonzero. Dividing by that fixed product reduces a relation of adelic pure functions to the finite-function lemma, including the independent archimedean variable. Thus the quotient-tensor image of a polynomial adelic function is independent of its presentation. Lemma 4.93 (Descent of a multilinear functional through its kernels). Let S_{0}, S_{1}, . . . , S_{r} be vector spaces, q_{i} : S_{i} →Q_{i} linear, and L : S_{0} × · · · × S_{r} →Z multilinear.
```text
∑⊗q_{i}(x_{j,i}) = 0 =⇒ ∑L(x_{j,0}, . . . , x_{j,r}) = 0.
j i j
```

Lemma 4.97 (The countable-dimensional Schur argument). Let V ̸= 0 be a simple module over a complex algebra R and suppose dim_{ℂ} V ≤ℵ_{0}. Every R-linear endomorphism of V is scalar.

Proof. A nonzero R-endomorphism is bijective: its kernel and image are submodules of a simple module. If an endomorphism T satisfies p(T) = 0 for a nonzero complex polynomial, factor p into linear factors. Since the nonzero endomorphisms are invertible, one factor T −λ must be zero, making T scalar.

Suppose instead T is not scalar. Then every nonzero polynomial p gives an invertible p(T). Fix 0 ̸= v ∈V and, for every λ ∈ℂ, put w_{λ} = (T −λ)^{−1}v. These vectors are linearly independent. For a finite relation ∑_{λ∈S}c_{λ}w_{λ} = 0, apply ∏_{λ∈S}(T −λ) to obtain

```text
q(T)v = 0, q(X) =∑c_{λ} ∏ (X −µ).
λ∈S µ∈S\{λ}
```

If q∏ ̸= 0 its value q(T) is invertible, contradicting v ̸= 0. Thus q = 0. Evaluating it at each λ ∈S gives c_{λµ̸=λ}(λ −µ) = 0, so every coefficient is zero. This is an uncountable independent family, contradicting countable dimension. Hence T is scalar.

Lemma 4.98 (Finite operator interpolation). Let a family of operators 𝒪 act irreducibly on a nonzero countable-dimensional complex space V , and let R be the complex algebra it generates. For linearly in-dependent v_{1}, . . . , v_{m} and arbitrary w_{1}, . . . , w_{m} there is r ∈R with rv_{i} = w_{i} for every i.

Proof. Invariant subspaces for R are exactly those stable under all of 𝒪, so V is a simple R-module. Its endomorphism ring is ℂ by Lemma 4.97. For m = 0 there are no prescribed values. Induct on m ≥1. For m = 1, the submodule Rv_{1} is nonzero, hence all of V . For the induction step let

```text
M = {(rv_{1}, . . . , rv_{m}) : r ∈R} ⊂V^{m}.
```

It is an R-submodule. Its projection onto the first m −1 factors is onto by induction. The kernel, viewed in the last factor, is either zero or all of V . If it is all of V , the onto projection and independent correction of the last coordinate give M = V^{m}. Otherwise the projection identifies M with V^{m−1}, and its last coordinate is an R-linear map V^{m−1}→V . Its restrictions to the coordinate summands are scalar, so this map is ∑_{i<m}λ_{i}x_{i}. Applying the statement to the tuple coming from r = 1 gives v_{m} = ∑_{i<m}λ_{i}v_{i}, a contradiction. Thus M = V^{m} in all cases, which proves the claim. An arbitrary prescribed linear map on a finite set reduces to this statement by taking a basis of its span.

All compact translates of a vacuum lie in 𝒱.

Lemma 4.106 (All powers in a small norm ball). Let A be a complex normed algebra and a ∈ A. If ‖a^{p}−1‖< 1/2 for every integer p ≥0, then a = 1.

Proof. Write δ = ‖a−1‖ and S_{N} =∑^{N}_{k=0}^{−1}a^{k}. The geometric sum identity and the triangle inequality give

```text
‖‖‖‖‖N∑−1 ‖‖‖‖‖
S_{N}(a −1) = a^{N}−1, ‖N1 −S_{N}‖= (1 −a^{k}) ≤N/2.
k=0
```

Since N1 acts as the complex scalar N, splitting N1 = (N1 −S_{N}) + S_{N} gives

```text
Nδ ≤‖N1 −S_{N}‖δ + ‖a^{N}−1‖< Nδ/2 + 1/2.
```

Thus Nδ < 1 for every N. If δ > 0, choose N > 1/δ, a contradiction. Hence δ = 0 and a = 1. The argument uses no diagonalization or spectral assertion.

Lemma 4.107 (The precise weak continuity that forces smoothness). Let G be a topological group with decreasing subgroups K_{0} ⊇ K_{1} ⊇· · · such that every neighborhood of 1 contains some K_{n}. Let W be a complex subspace of a complex vector space V . Suppose complex-linear operators ω(g) preserve W for g ∈K_{0}, act as the identity at 1, and satisfy the multiplication law on K_{0} × K_{0} when applied to W. Require that, for every algebraic linear functional l : V → C and every ϕ ∈W, g →→l(ω(g)ϕ) is continuous. Then each ϕ ∈W is fixed by some K_{n}.

Proof. First consider any function f : G → V with f(1) = 0 and with all the scalar functions l ∘f continuous. There are n and a finite set S ⊂V such that f(K_{n}) ⊂ span S. Otherwise choose recursively k_{n} ∈K_{n} so that u_{n} = f(k_{n}) is outside the span of the previously chosen u_{0}, . . . , u_{n−1}. These vectors are linearly independent: in a finite relation, its largest index with nonzero coefficient would express that vector in the earlier span. The functional taking every u_{n} to 1 on their span extends to an algebraic linear functional l on V by extending a basis. Continuity and l(f(1)) = 0 make {g : l(f(g)) ̸= 1} a neighborhood of 1. It contains some K_{n}, contradicting l(f(k_{n})) = 1. This proves the assertion.

Apply it to f(g) = ω(g)ϕ −ϕ. The span

V_{0} = span{ω(k)ϕ : k ∈K_{n}}

lies in the finite-dimensional space span(S ∪{ϕ}). It contains ϕ, lies in W, and is invariant under K_{n}: multiplying two elements of K_{n} remains in K_{n}, and the multiplication law gives invariance on its spanning vectors.

Choose coordinates b : V_{0} ≃ C^{d}, put j = b^{−1} followed by the inclusion in V , and extend b to an algebraic linear map π : V → C^{d}. Thus πj = 1 and jπx = x for x ∈V_{0}. Define

```text
A(g) = πω(g)j.
```

Each matrix entry is continuous: its input j(e_{i}) lies in W and its output coordinate is an algebraic linear functional on V . Thus A is continuous in the ordinary finite-dimensional operator norm, A(1) = 1, and for k ∈K_{n} its action on V_{0} gives A(k^{p}) = A(k)^{p} for every p ≥0. Choose m so that ‖A(g) −1‖< 1/2 on K_{m}. For k ∈K_{max(n,m)}, every power k^{p} belongs to both K_{n} and K_{m}. Consequently ‖A(k)^{p}−1‖< 1/2 for every p. Lemma 4.106 gives A(k) = 1. Using jπ = 1 on V_{0} and its invariance now yields ω(k)ϕ = ϕ.

The quantifier over all algebraic linear functionals is essential to this argument: it supplies the functional assigned value 1 on the independently selected sequence. The assertion is applied below only where the source’s admissibility condition supplies precisely those functionals.

Proposition 4.113 (Uniqueness of the rationally invariant admissible functional). Let ψ be as in Proposi-tion 4.111. Put H_{N} = (N𝒪̂_{F} )^{I} for an integer N > 0, and let 1_{d+HN} be its coset indicator. These functions are Schwartz–Bruhat. Every finite Schwartz–Bruhat function g is a finite linear combination of such indicators for all sufficiently divisible N, with centers d ∈ F^{I}. Here are the two points in that assertion. Local constancy and compact support give invariance under a common compact open additive subgroup, by a finite cover of the support; outside it the same invariance follows by translating that cover. Subgroups H_{N} are cofinal among zero neighborhoods, and taking a multiple only shrinks them. Compact support then meets finitely many cosets. Each coset has a rational representative: clear its finitely many denominators and solve the resulting finite congruences in 𝒪_{F} by the Chinese remainder theorem. This is finite-adelic approximation, with no approximation condition imposed at infinity.

<!-- Source PDF page 199 -->

Moreover rational modulations induce all the integer coordinate characters for this lattice at infinity. We check that latter normalization explicitly. Let ψ_{0} be the trace-normalized standard additive character, positive exponential at infinity and with finite annihilator the inverse different. The adelic self-duality and rational-annihilator theorem [55, §4.1, Theorems4.1.1 and4.1.4] give

```text
ψ(x) = ψ_{0}(cx), c ∈F^{×}.
```

For a real linear form u integral on the infinite lattice N𝒪_{F} , the trace-dual integral basis gives ξ ∈ 𝔇^{−}_{F}^{1} with Tr_{∞}(ξz) = Nu(z). Take y = ξ/(Nc) ∈F. On x_{f} ∈N𝒪̂_{F} , the finite component of cxy lies in the inverse different, so contributes 1. Its infinite component is e^{2πiu(x∞)}. Applying this in one coordinate gives precisely each character needed by Lemma 4.112. ∑

That lemma, transported through an integral basis, gives T_{N}(f) = c_{Na∈N𝒪F}I f(a_{∞}). But the latter sum is exactly c_{N}Θ(f ⊗1_{HN} ): a rational element integral at every finite place lies in 𝒪_{F} , after dividing by N. Rational translation invariance of both λ and Θ gives the same scalar for every indicator 1_{d+HN} , while translating its infinite factor by d. Linear combinations give the formula for all f ⊗g at that level. A finite sum of pure tensors has one common level, and the same conclusion holds for every multiple of it.

Choose Φ_{0} with Θ(Φ_{0}) ̸= 0 by Lemma 4.109. Given any Φ, take a common level for Φ and Φ_{0}. At this level

```text
λ(Φ) = c_{N}Θ(Φ), c_{N} =_{Θ(Φ}^{λ(Φ0}_{0}^{)}_{)}.
```

Thus the scalar is independent of Φ, as required.

Corollary 4.114 (The admissible adelic Heisenberg commutant). Let T be a complex-linear operator on adelic functions which preserves the adelic Schwartz subspace, preserves admissibility under precomposi-tion, and commutes there with all Heisenberg operators. Then T = c 1 on the adelic Schwartz space.

Proof. The functional Θ ∘T is admissible by hypothesis. It is rationally Heisenberg invariant: commute the operator past T, then use the invariance of the rational lattice sum. For rational translations that invariance is the reindexing ξ →→ξ +a; rational modulation and the rational half-pairing have character value 1 at every lattice point because ψ is trivial on F. Proposition 4.113 gives Θ(TΦ) = cΘ(Φ) for all Schwartz Φ. For every Heisenberg parameter w, commutation now gives

```text
Θ(ρ(w)(TΦ −cΦ))= 0.
```

The difference is Schwartz, so Proposition 4.111 makes it zero. The same scalar c consequently works for every Φ.

Then:

put(x, ev(x)) = x, ev(put(x, y)) = y, put(put(x, y), z) = put(x, z),

2. If φ ∈𝒮(K), y ∈K, and g ∈𝒮(A), then P(φ, y)g ∈𝒮(A).

3. Every g ∈𝒮(A) belongs to the complex linear span of {P(φ, y)g : φ ∈𝒮(K), y ∈K}.

Proof. The three identities for put in (1) follow directly from ev ∘ι = id_{K} and additivity of ev, ι. For the operator identity, evaluating at x ∈A gives


P(φ, a)(P(φ_{1}, y)Φ) (x) = φ(ev(x)) φ_{1} ev(put(x, a)) Φ put(put(x, a), y)

= φ(ev(x)) φ_{1}(a) Φ(put(x, y)) = φ_{1}(a) P(φ, y)Φ (x).

For (2), continuity of ev and of x →→ put(x, y) makes φ ∘ ev and g ∘ put(·, y) locally constant, so their product P(φ, y)g is locally constant. Let S_{g} = {g ̸= 0} and S_{φ} = {φ ̸= 0} be their compact supports. Whenever (P(φ, y)g)(x) ̸= 0, the points x^{′}= put(x, y) ∈S_{g} and k = ev(x) ∈S_{φ} satisfy x^{′}+ι(k)−ι(y) = x. Hence {P(φ, y)g ̸= 0} is contained in the image M of the compact set S_{g} ×S_{φ} under the continuous map (x^{′}, k) →→x^{′}+ ι(k) −ι(y). Since M is compact and A is Hausdorff, M is closed, so {P(φ, y)g ̸= 0} ⊆M is compact. Thus P(φ, y)g ∈𝒮(A).

For (3), put π(z) = z −ι(ev(z)), so π : A → A is continuous, ev(π(z)) = 0, and put(x, k) = π(x) + ι(k). Both K_{a} = π(S_{g}) ⊆ A and C = ev(S_{g}) ⊆ K are compact. First, if a ∈ A satisfies ev(a) = 0 and a /∈K_{a}, then g(a + ι(k)) = 0 for every k ∈K: otherwise z = a + ι(k) ∈S_{g} would satisfy π(z) = a + ι(k) −ι(ev(a) + ev(ι(k))) = a ∈K_{a}.

Second, fix k_{0} ∈K. For each a ∈K_{a}, local constancy of g at a + ι(k_{0}) and continuity of (k, a^{′}) →→ a^{′}+ ι(k) give open neighborhoods U_{a} ⊆K of k_{0} and V_{a} ⊆A of a such that g(a^{′}+ ι(k)) = g(a + ι(k_{0})) for all (k, a^{′}) ∈U_{a} × V_{a}. Evaluating at k = k_{0} ∈U_{a} shows g(a^{′}+ ι(k_{0})) = g(a + ι(k_{0})) for a^{′}∈V_{a}, so g(a^{′}+∩ ι(k)) = g(a^{′}+ ι(k_{0})) on U_{a} × V_{a}. Cover the compact set K_{a} by finitely many V_{a1}, . . . , V_{ar} and put U =_{j}^{r}_{=1}U_{aj}, an open neighborhood of k_{0}. Then g(a+ι(k)) = g(a+ι(k_{0})) for every k ∈U and a ∈K_{a}.

Define F : K →(A → C) by F(k)(x) = g(put(x, k)) = g(π(x) + ι(k)). For k ∈U and any x ∈A, set a = π(x), so ev(a) = 0. If a ∈K_{a} then g(a + ι(k)) = g(a + ι(k_{0})), while if a /∈K_{a} both sides vanish. Hence F(k) = F(k_{0}) for all k ∈U, proving that F is locally constant. Moreover, if k /∈C then F(k) = 0: if g(put(x, k)) ̸= 0 then put(x, k) ∈S_{g} and k = ev(put(x, k)) ∈C.

Since C is compact and F is locally constant, finitely many neighborhoods on which F is constant cover C; therefore F(C) is finite. Set 𝒱 = F(C) \ {0}. For each v ∈𝒱, choose y_{v} ∈K with F(y_{v}) = v and let φ_{v} : K → C be the indicator function of the fiber E_{v} = {k ∈K : F(k) = v}. Local constancy of F makes E_{v} both open and closed in K, so φ_{v} is locally constant with {φ_{v} ̸= 0} = E_{v}. Because v ̸= 0, every k ∈E_{v} belongs to C (otherwise F(k) = 0 ̸= v). Thus E_{v} is a closed subset of the compact set C, hence compact, and φ_{v} ∈𝒮(K).

Finally, for any x ∈A and v ∈𝒱,

Call an element z of an 𝔸_{F} -module supported at v if u · z = 0 whenever u ∈𝔸_{F} satisfies ev_{v}(u) = 0. For φ : F_{v}^{I} → C and r : 𝔸^{I}_{F} → C, set tens_{v}(φ, r)(x) = φ(ev_{A}(x))r(x), and write Rest_{v}(φ, r) to mean that r(x + z) = r(x) for every x, z ∈𝔸^{I}_{F} with z supported at v and that tens_{v}(φ, r) ∈𝒮(𝔸^{I}_{F}). For x_{0} ∈𝔸^{I}_{F}, define res_{v,x0} : (𝔸^{I}_{F} → C) →(F^{ I}_{v} → C) by (res_{v,x0} Φ)(y) = Φ(put_{A}(x_{0}, y)). 1. For every x_{0} ∈ 𝔸^{I}_{F}, res_{v,x0} maps 𝒮(𝔸^{I}_{F}) into 𝒮(F^{ I}_{v}), and for every algebraic complex-linear func-tional l : (F_{v}^{I}→ C) → C, the composite l ∘ res_{v,x0} is admissible in the sense of Lemma 4.109.

4.21 Common local quotients and matching irreducibility

We now construct, unconditionally for every valid adelic theta-comparison triple (F, E, σ, B, a, a^{′}, G, X, ω, ω^{′}) in Input 4.77, all local archimedean and nonarchimedean operators, nonzero irreducible common local quotients (R, R_{f}), local coinvariant identifications, ramified multiplicity-one, and kernel-uniqueness properties required by Propositions 4.94, 4.95, 4.96, and 4.100.

Recall the exact source contracts for a valid triple (B, G, X, ω, ω^{′}) (IsTriple):

• An archimedean quotient datum R = (Π_{∞}, p_{∞}, p^{′}_{∞}) satisfies IsRealMaps if p_{∞}: 𝒮_{∞}(V, W) →Π_{∞} and p^{′}_{∞} : 𝒮_{∞}(V^{ ′}, W) → Π_{∞} satisfy RealQuot (each maps the polynomial Fock space 𝒫_{V} or 𝒫_{V} ′ onto Π_{∞}, kills left one-parameter derivatives along Lines, and is invariant under the left maximal compact K_{∞,V} or K_{∞,V} ′), intertwine the right Lie derivatives and right maximal compact K_{∞,W} actions whenever p_{∞}(f) = p^{′}_{∞}(f^{′}), and make Π_{∞} ̸= 0 irreducible for the right Lie and K_{∞,W} actions.

• A finite-place datum R_{f} = (Π_{v}, p_{v}, p^{′}_{v})_{v} satisfies IsFinMaps if at every finite place v of F, p_{v} and p^{′}_{v} map the local Schwartz–Bruhat spaces 𝒮_{v}, 𝒮_{v}^{′} onto Π_{v} ̸= 0, kill the left augmentation subspaces aug_{v}, aug^{′}_{v}, intertwine the right U(W)_{v} actions on matched vectors, and make Π_{v} irreducible for U(W)_{v}; furthermore, for every v /∈X.T the local vacua have the same nonzero image p_{v}(vac_{v}) = p_{v}^{′}(vac^{′}_{v}) ̸= 0, while for every v ∈X.T (IsZetaAt) there are split linear-model bijections ι, ι^{′} sending the local vacua to integral-matrix indicators such that

p_{v}(φ) = p_{v}^{′}(φ^{′}) ⇐⇒ bigP_{νv,βv}(ιφ) = smallP_{νv,αv}(ι^{′}φ^{′}) (φ ∈𝒮_{v}, φ^{′}∈𝒮_{v}^{′}). (123)

• A pair (R, R_{f}) satisfies IsMatched if IsTriple, IsRealMaps, and IsFinMaps all hold; LocalMatching asserts ∃R, R_{f}, IsMatched for every valid triple. Polynomial matching PolMatch and Schwartz limit matching Match are defined by equality in Π_{∞}⊗⊗_{v∈T}′ Π_{v} for finite T^{ ′} ⊇X.T with vacua outside T^{′}. The coinvariant contract Coinv asserts that at every good split place v of X, ker(p_{v}|_{𝒮v}) = aug_{v}, ker(p^{′}_{v}|_{𝒮v}′) = aug^{′}_{v}, the local full-rank cone subspace SoLoc surjects onto Π_{v}, every linear functional killing aug^{′}_{v} factors through p^{′}_{v}, and the global full-rank cone space So is stable under ω^{′}.

1. Uniqueness and factorization (ArchUniq, ArchOp). Archimedean action values Acts and derivatives ActsD are unique in 𝒮_{∞}(X, W). For every (g, h) ∈U(X)_{∞}× U(W)_{∞}, there is a continuous linear operator T_{g,h} : 𝒮_{∞}(X, W) →𝒮_{∞}(X, W) such that ω(g, h)(pure_{A}(f, φ)) = pure_{A}(T_{g,h}f, φ) for all f ∈𝒮_{∞}(X, W) and finite Schwartz–Bruhat functions φ; moreover T_{g,h} preserves 𝒫_{M} whenever

## 5 The local parameter input

Let E be a number field, let Ω/E be an algebraic closure, and choose a valuation of Ω above a finite place w of E. Write k = E_{w}, and write W_{k} and I_{k} for the resulting Weil and inertia groups. We use the reci-procity convention in which a uniformizer corresponds to geometric Frobenius. Thus the inverse reciprocity homomorphism a : W_{k} −→k^{×} has v_{k}(a(σ)) = − deg(σ) when the degree of arithmetic Frobenius is one.

Write ℐ(k) = ∐_{n≥0} Irr(GL_{n}(k)) for isomorphism classes of irreducible smooth complex representa-tions, with their degrees, and write 𝒲(k) for the Weil–Deligne classes used below. A character twist of π means π ⊗(χ ∘ det); write πν^{s} when χ = | · |^{s}_{k}. A cuspidal class is called good if its degree is one, or if k ≃ ℚ_{p} as a topological field and the class is a character twist of a depth-zero cuspidal class. A general irreducible class is good if its cuspidal support consists of good cuspidal classes. Here depth zero means the existence of nonzero vectors fixed by the principal congruence subgroup K_{1} = 1 + 𝔭_{k}M_{n}(𝒪_{k}).

<!-- Source PDF page 230 -->

Definition 5.1 (The required parameter laws). The local parameter input is the existence, for every choice above, of a and a map R : ℐ(k) →𝒲(k) with the following properties. It preserves degree, sends a character χ to χ∘a, and sends cuspidal classes to irreducible Weil parameters. It commutes with real unramified twists. If 𝔪 is the Langlands multisegment of π, then

```text
⊕ ( )
```

R(π) = R(ρ_{∆}) (ℓ_{∆}−1)/2 ⊗ Sp(ℓ_{∆}), (F13.1)

```text
∆∈𝔪
```

where ρ_{∆} is the first cuspidal class of the segment. For every central character ω_{π},

| det R(π)(σ)| = |ω_{π}(a(σ))|. (F13.2)

For good π the following stronger assertions hold:

```text
R(π ⊗χ) = R(π) ⊗(χ ∘a),
```

det R(π)(σ) = ω_{π}(a(σ)), (F13.3)

```text
R(π^{∨}) = R(π)^{∨}.
```

If π^{′} is good and R(π) = R(π^{′}), then π = π^{′}. If good π has K_{1}-fixed vectors, then R(π) is tame. Finally R satisfies the explicit tame type condition of Proposition 5.5 below, including zero monodromy and the specified inertia characteristic polynomial.

These are precisely the twelve fields of the local statement called RecTExists in the source. The restric-tions to good classes are part of the statement: existence of this map is weaker than the full local Langlands correspondence. In particular, the source’s construction is permitted to choose unrelated parameters on other cuspidal twist orbits. We retain its statement rather than silently strengthening the claimed input.

Proposition 5.2 (Reduction of the F-13 assembly). The F-13 assembly adds no property to its first input. Its required local parameter statement is exactly the existence statement in Definition 5.1 supplied before that assembly.

Proof. Denote the twelve supplied assertions by H_{0}, H_{1}, . . . , H_{11}, with H_{0} the required local parameter existence statement. The combining function is

```text
(H_{0}, H_{1}, . . . , H_{11}) −−→H_{0}.
```

It therefore returns the same family of parameter maps and the same proof of each law as the first input; none of the other eleven assertions is used to establish a new law. The first input is itself the local-parameter component of the already supplied package. This proves the assertion without any assumption about the truth of H_{1}, . . . , H_{11}.

For source identification, the last proposition reads the actual function at LlOf.lean, lines 18–21; the application is EveryCharacterOfLiteratureOfVWin.lean, lines 313–314, and its first argument is the projec-tion at lines 283–284. Consequently an ordinary proof must establish the local parameter input itself. Citing local converse, Brauer induction or the geometric lemma at this application cannot substitute for it.

Remark 5.3 (The twelve arguments). In order, the arguments are: local parameter existence; local converse for cuspidal GL_{m+1} against GL_{m} twists; propagation of K_{1}-fixed vectors from cuspidal support; degree-zero Brauer induction; Chevalley’s unit congruence assertion; global Artin reciprocity; existence of a Lang-lands multisegment; uniqueness and the two-factor subquotient property of multisegments; the standard-module cosocle assertion; the polynomial description of the Grothendieck ring; the geometric lemma with cell semisimplification; and Bernstein–Zelevinsky finiteness and contragredient compatibility. Each of the last eleven is eliminated from this application by Proposition 5.2. This resolves their role in F-13; it does not claim that other applications of those assertions have thereby been proved. The separate source construction of the first input does use some classification and finiteness statements.

<!-- Source PDF page 231 -->

Proposition 5.4 (Extension from cuspidal parameters). Assume the Langlands classification in the following precise form: each irreducible class π has a unique finite multiset 𝔪(π) of segments, and a cuspidal class ρ has the single segment (ρ, 1). Given any assignment r(ρ) of Weil–Deligne classes to cuspidal classes, formula (F13.1) defines an assignment R independent of the order of the multiset. It is the unique assignment with that formula, and R(ρ) = r(ρ) on cuspidal classes.

Proof. For every π choose a list of the segments in 𝔪(π) and take the direct sum in (F13.1), with r in place of R on each first cuspidal class. Two lists of the same multiset differ by a permutation. Interchanging adjacent summands is implemented by (u, v) →→ (v, u); reassociating is implemented by ((u, v), z) →→ (u, (v, z)). Both maps intertwine the Weil action and monodromy. Thus the direct-sum isomorphism class is unchanged by a permutation, and the assignment is well defined. If another list is asserted to be the Langlands multisegment of π, uniqueness of that multisegment makes it a permutation of the chosen list, proving the required formula for every such list. The formula also determines R(π), giving uniqueness.

For cuspidal ρ, the one segment has length one. Its exponent (1 −1)/2 is zero, and Sp(1) is the trivial one-dimensional parameter with zero monodromy. The map v ⊗z →→zv intertwines the Weil action; it also intertwines monodromy, since the tensor monodromy is N ⊗1 + 1 ⊗0. Hence the resulting parameter is r(ρ). As the first element of every segment is cuspidal, replacing r by R in the direct-sum formula changes no summand. This proves the assertion exactly in the form needed for (F13.1).

Lemma 5.7 (Uniqueness of the special summands). Let q > 1 be the residue cardinality. A finite direct sum ⊕_{i}V_{i} ⊗ Sp(ℓ_{i}), where each V_{i} is an irreducible complex Weil representation and ℓ_{i} > 0, determines the multiset of pairs (V_{i}, ℓ_{i}). Here the special representation is centered as in (F13.1). Thus premise (iii) of

Proposition 5.6 holds.

Proof. Let η denote the unramified character σ →→ q^{deg σ}. No irreducible S is isomorphic to S ⊗η^{j} for a nonzero integer j: taking determinants at a degree-one Weil element would give q^{j dim S} = 1, which is impossible. Partition the irreducible constituents of the underlying Weil action into their orbits under the integral twists by η. Each orbit is consequently indexed without repetitions as S_{t} = S_{0} ⊗η^{t}, t ∈ℤ.

The underlying Weil action of the given direct sum is semisimple, since the action in each displayed special summand is a direct sum of twists of the irreducible⊕ V_{i}. Its component in a fixed orbit is therefore

_{t}S_{t} ⊗M_{t}, with finite-dimensional complex multiplicity spaces M_{t}, only finitely many nonzero. The relation ρ(σ)N = η(σ)Nρ(σ) makes N induce maps A_{t} : M_{t} → M_{t+1}. Schur’s lemma justifies this description: a homomorphism between distinct irreducibles vanishes, and every endomorphism of an irre-ducible is scalar. The latter assertion follows by taking an eigenvalue over ℂ; its nonzero eigenspace is an invariant subspace and is therefore the entire irreducible space.

For integers a ≤b, let

r_{a,b} = rank(A_{b−1} · · · A_{a} : M_{a} −→M_{b}), r_{a,a} = dim M_{a}.

A special summand contributes one dimension to each multiplicity space along an interval [c, d], with nonzero identity maps between successive entries and zero maps at its ends. It contributes one to r_{a,b} exactly when c ≤a ≤b ≤d. Therefore the number of summands whose interval is exactly [a, b] is

```text
m_{a,b} = r_{a,b} −r_{a−1,b} −r_{a,b+1} + r_{a−1,b+1}. (F13.7)
```

This follows by subtracting first the intervals beginning before a, then those ending after b, and adding back the intervals removed twice. The formula includes a = b.

An isomorphism of Weil–Deligne representations preserves the Weil-isotypic decomposition and conju-gates the maps induced by N. It thus preserves every rank in (F13.7), and hence every interval multiplicity. The interval [a, b] has length ℓ= b−a+1 and first constituent S_{a}. Its centered irreducible factor is uniquely V = S_{a} ⊗η^{(ℓ−1)/2}, because the first eigencharacter of Sp(ℓ) has exponent −(ℓ−1)/2. Recovering all intervals in all twist orbits therefore recovers exactly the multiset of (V_{i}, ℓ_{i}).

These n characters are distinct by regularity and the surjectivity of c_{L}. Their common kernel is open, and the inertia action factors through the finite group K^{×}. The projection onto each character line is the usual finite character average |K^{×}|^{−1} ∑_{u∈K}× χ(u)^{−1}V (u). Thus every inertia-invariant subspace is a direct sum of some of these lines. Wild inertia maps trivially under c_{L}, so the representation is tame. Its inertia action has finite image, giving smoothness. Every Weil matrix in this coset basis is monomial. On each cycle of its permutation its suitable power is a nonzero scalar, so its minimal polynomial divides X^{r}−c with c ̸= 0. That polynomial has distinct roots over ℂ. Background fact 5.9 (Verified cuspidal correspondence). For a finite extension k/ℚ_{p}, there is a bijection between irreducible complex Weil representations of dimension n and irreducible smooth supercuspidal com-plex representations of GL_{n}(k), for all n ≥1. It preserves determinant and central character, character twists, contragredients, and pair L- and epsilon-factors, with geometric Frobenius corresponding to a uniformizer. This is Henniart [3, §1.3, theorem, p. 168].

The theorem’s hypotheses apply: E_{w} is a finite extension of ℚ_{p} and both sides use complex representa-tions. Taking the inverse bijection proves the cuspidal degree, character, irreducibility, twist, determinant, dual and injectivity assertions in premise (i) of Proposition 5.6; its determinant law also gives the absolute-value law. This verified theorem does not explicitly state the Green-type formula (F13.5).

Lemma 5.12 (A finite cuspidal type detects cuspidality). Let k ≃ℚ_{p} and n > 0. Suppose an irreducible smooth representation π of GL_{n}(k) contains, on K = GL_{n}(𝒪_{k}), the inflation of a cuspidal representation τ of GL_{n}(𝔽_{p}). Then π is cuspidal and has nonzero K_{1}-fixed vectors.

Proof. Transport by the given field isomorphism and let ϕ : τ → π be a nonzero K-intertwiner. For a standard maximal parabolic P = MU of block sizes a, n −a, with 0 < a < n, let

J_{U} = span{π(u)v −v : u ∈U(k), v ∈π}.

Let U be the unipotent radical of the corresponding finite parabolic. Cuspidality of τ says τ^{U} = 0. The finite average |U|^{−1} ∑_{u∈U}τ(u) is the projection onto those invariants, and hence is zero. Every u ∈U has an integral unipotent lift ̃u ∈U(k) ∩K, obtained by lifting its upper off-diagonal block entries. Therefore

```text
ϕ(w) −ϕ(τ(u)w) = ϕ(w) −π(ũ)ϕ(w) ∈J_{U}.
```

<!-- Source PDF page 237 -->

Sum over u and use the vanishing of the average. The result is |U|ϕ(w) ∈J_{U}, and division by this nonzero complex integer gives ϕ(w) ∈J_{U}.

The space J_{U} is stable under P, since P normalizes U: applying p ∈P to a defining difference gives the difference for pup^{−1} and π(p)v. For g ∈ GL_{n}(k) write g = pc with p ∈ P and c ∈ K by Iwasawa decomposition. Then π(c)ϕ(w) = ϕ(τ(c)w) ∈J_{U}, and P-stability gives π(g)ϕ(w) ∈J_{U}. The span of all these translates is a nonzero invariant subspace of π, so irreducibility makes it the entire space. Consequently J_{U} = π and the Jacquet quotient π/J_{U} is zero.

Every proper parabolic is conjugate to a standard one, and the unipotent radical of a standard proper parabolic contains that of a standard maximal parabolic, after grouping its successive blocks into two groups. The vanishing just proved therefore gives vanishing of every proper Jacquet quotient. This is cuspidality. Finally K_{1} acts trivially on the inflated τ, so any nonzero vector in the image of ϕ is K_{1}-fixed. This proves the second assertion.

Background fact 5.13 (The quotient classification in the required convention). For complex representations of GL_{N}(k) over a nonarchimedean local field, a segment ∆= (ρ, ρν, . . . , ρν^{ℓ−1}) has a unique irreducible quotient δ(∆) of that ordered normalized induction. The map ∆ →→ δ(∆) parametrizes the essentially square-integrable classes. Finite multisets of these classes parametrize all irreducible classes: order their real exponents nonincreasingly and take the unique irreducible quotient of their normalized induction. The parametrization preserves support and commutes with unramified twists and contragredients. These are the precise statements in Tadić [6, §§5.1, 5.4, 5.6–5.7, pp. 361–363].

Proposition 5.14 (Matching the segment and ordering conventions). Fact 5.13 supplies the classification premises of Propositions 5.4 and 5.6, with the depth assertion supplied by Lemma 5.11.

Proof. The source segment is specified by its first cuspidal class ρ and its positive length ℓ, and its terms are ρν^{j}, 0 ≤j < ℓ. Its segment quotient is therefore precisely δ(∆) in the cited classification, without reversing the single-segment induction. The source orders segments by requiring that an earlier segment never precede a later one. Here precedence means that two segments are linked and the second begins a positive integral twist after the first.

Write the real exponent of a cuspidal ρ as e(ρ); thus ρν^{−e(ρ)} has unitary central character. The exponent of the segment quotient is e(ρ) + (ℓ−1)/2, since its cuspidal support consists of the displayed ℓ terms. If linked segments are written as intervals [a, b] and [c, d] on the same cuspidal twist line, with a < c, neither contains the other. Thus b < d, and (a + b)/2 < (c + d)/2. Precedence therefore strictly increases the exponent of the segment quotient.

It follows that a nonincreasing exponent order is allowed by the source’s ordering condition. Conversely, sort any allowed order into nonincreasing exponent order by adjacent swaps. An adjacent pair needing a swap has the smaller exponent first. It cannot be linked: if linked, its smaller first endpoint would make it precede the later segment, contrary to the allowed-order condition. Products of the two unlinked segment quotients are irreducible and commute, by Zelevinsky [5, Theorem 9.7(a)]; this uses the quotient segment representations in his notation. Hence each swap gives an isomorphic induced module. There are finitely many inversions, so the sorting terminates. The source’s ordered product therefore has the same unique quotient as the nonincreasing-exponent product in the cited classification.

Existence and uniqueness of its multiset now follow from the bijection of Fact 5.13. Support is the union, with multiplicity, of the segment terms. Its uniqueness implies the assertion about good support used in the seed assembly. The central character is the product of the support central characters: the center acts by this

<!-- Source PDF page 238 -->

product on the normalized induction, since its modular factor on a central scalar is one, and the same action passes to every subquotient.

Twisting by any smooth character multiplies every cuspidal term by that character; it preserves linkedness and precedence. Twist the inducing space and the quotient map to see that it carries the unique quotient to the unique quotient for these twisted segments. The real unramified twist is a special case. For the contragredient, the cited dual rule replaces a segment by its termwise dual in reverse order: its first term becomes (ρν^{ℓ−1})^{∨} and its length remains ℓ. This is exactly the dual segment used in the proof of Proposition 5.6. The depth-zero assertion has already been proved directly in Lemma 5.11. All classification compatibilities used there are therefore accounted for.

Lemma 5.15 (Elliptic values determine a regular label). Let K = 𝔽_{q}n, n > 0, and let θ, θ^{′} be characters of K^{×} with Frobenius orbits of size n. If their Frobenius orbit sums agree on every element of degree n over 𝔽_{q}, then θ^{′} is a Frobenius conjugate of θ. Consequently a finite cuspidal representation satisfying the elliptic formula for θ is the Green representation labeled by θ.

Proof. Put N = q^{n}−1 and ∑

```text
B(q, n) = (q^{n/r}−1).
r|n, r prime
```

Let D ⊂ K^{×} be the elements of degree less than n. If z has degree d < n, then d | n and some prime r | n/d gives z ∈𝔽^{×}_{qn/r}. The union bound therefore gives |D| ≤B(q, n).

Distinct characters of a finite abelian group are orthogonal. This description of O_{a} follows from the actual coefficient-ring hypotheses. They make it a discrete valuation domain, finite over ℤ_{ℓ}. Thus it is exactly the integral closure of ℤ_{ℓ} in that finite extension.

Lemma 6.9 (The integral algebra of ordered distinct roots). Let X be finite and nonempty, T ⊂O^{X}, and let P_{x} ∈ O[z] be monic of degree t. Suppose all its coefficient functions belong to T and every P_{x} splits into distinct roots in O. Let X^{′} consist of all pairs (x, (α_{0}, . . . , α_{t−1})) with P_{x} = ∏_{i}(z −α_{i}), and let p : X^{′}→X. The algebra T^{′}⊂O^{X′} generated by the pullback of T and the ordered root functions is finite free of rank t! over T. There are t! generators b_{i} which form a basis and whose restrictions to every fiber of p are O-linearly independent.

Proof. The coefficient functions define a monic polynomial P ∈T[z] of degree t. Construct its universal ordered splitting algebra recursively. First adjoin a root by T_{1} = T[z_{0}]/(P(z_{0})). Division by a monic polynomial gives the basis 1, z_{0}, . . . , z_{0}^{t−1} over T. In T_{1}[z] divide P by z −z_{0}; the remainder is zero, so the quotient is monic of degree t −1. Adjoin its first root and continue. At the end one obtains an algebra S generated by t roots, free over T of rank t(t −1) · · · 1 = t!. It has the required universal property: an ordered factorization in any commutative T-algebra first gives a map out of T_{1}, and then a map out of each successive root quotient. These maps are unique since the roots generate the algebra. The construction for t = 0 is S = T.

Every point of X^{′} therefore gives an evaluation S →O. Together they define S →O^{X′}, with image exactly T^{′}: the image contains the pullback coefficients and roots, and every element of S is an expression in those generators. Choose a T-basis β_{1}, . . . , β_{t!} of S, and let b_{i} be its evaluations.

Fix x. Over K, the t! permutations of the distinct roots give t! distinct algebra homomorphisms S →K extending evaluation at x. They are linearly independent as functions. Indeed, a nonzero relation with the fewest terms, evaluated at a product ab and compared with its value at b multiplied by one of the homomor-phisms’ values at a, gives a relation with fewer terms. Choose a separating two of the homomorphisms; the new relation is nonzero, a contradiction.

Each of these homomorphisms is determined linearly by its values on the β_{i}. The square matrix of those values consequently has independent rows and is invertible over K. If ∑_{i}c_{i}b_{i} vanishes on p^{−1}(x), with ∑c_{i} ∈O, this matrix sends (c_{i}) to zero, so all c_{i} = 0. This proves fiber independence. Finally, if an element

_{i}a_{i}β_{i}, a_{i} ∈T, has zero evaluation everywhere, fiber independence gives a_{i}(x) = 0 for every x. As T is an algebra of functions on X, this means a_{i} = 0. Hence S →T^{′} is injective as well as surjective, proving the basis assertion.

Lemma 6.11 (Determinants in the character-coefficient algebra). Let A be the T^{′}-span of r(G) as above. Suppose every coefficient function of det(1−zr(g)) belongs to T^{′} for every g ∈G. For every square matrix Θ over A, its evaluated block determinant is a function in T^{′}.

Proof. First consider a d by d formal matrix series U(z) with U(0) = 1 and every coefficient in A. Fix a degree N. We may factor U modulo z^{N+1} into finitely many factors

```text
1 −cz^{j}r(g), c ∈T^{′}, j ≥1.
```

To construct the factorization, suppose a current residual series is 1 + z^{j}A_{j} modulo z^{j+1}. Express A_{j} as a finite T^{′}-linear combination of r(g) and multiply by the inverses of the corresponding factors. Each inverse exists modulo z^{N+1} by the finite geometric series. The coefficient at degree j is cancelled; all cross terms have degree at least 2j ≥ j + 1. The new coefficients remain in A, since products of the r(g) are again group matrices. Repeating through N proves the factorization.

The determinant of each factor has coefficients in T^{′} by the assumed characteristic-polynomial condition, after substituting cz^{j} for z. Multiplicativity of determinant shows that the coefficients of det U through degree N belong to T^{′}. As N was arbitrary, this holds for every coefficient.

Now apply this result to the diagonal pivot blocks in a formal block elimination of 1 −zΘ. Its first d by d block has constant term 1, so its inverse is a formal series with coefficients in A. Multiplying on the left by the block lower-unitriangular matrix which eliminates the first block column does not change the determinant. The remaining block matrix is the Schur complement; it again has constant term 1 and all coefficients in A. Induct on the number of block rows. Each pivot determinant has coefficients in T^{′}, and therefore so does det(1 −zΘ).

If Θ has g block rows, the coefficient of z^{gd} in this last polynomial is (−1)^{gd} det Θ. Since T^{′} is closed under signs, the required determinant function belongs to T^{′}. This argument uses only finite congruences at each coefficient; it involves no convergence assertion or division by a factorial in O.

In the intended model, the characteristic-polynomial condition in Lemma 6.11 is the source’s condition that the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial of every Galois matrix lie in the Hecke algebra; pull-back puts them in T^{′}. Thus the determinant property needed for Proposition 6.7 follows from that condition. Lemmas 6.9 and 6.10 likewise prove the root-order, finiteness and block-surjectivity portions of the realiza-tion from their displayed matrix hypotheses. The remaining matrix task is to obtain the adapted idempotents, separable corner perturbation and residual full-matrix span for the selected Galois family, with the specified coefficient-change compatibility. Those are existence and compatibility assertions about that family.

It also preserves the condition that the characteristic-polynomial coefficient functions belong to T.

Adapted idempotent and corner data expressed using any such ordered rational decomposition give the same specified main and character actions after this normalization. To check independence of the chosen decomposition, compare its intertwiner with the fixed ordered direct sum. The change between decom-positions is therefore block diagonal, with a scalar on each character. It preserves the asserted character actions of every element of the span algebra. Orthogonality to this projection forces the rank-one idempotent to have zero character blocks. The same block diagonal comparison preserves the prescribed scalar actions of the corner operator.

Background fact 6.14 (The finite local conditions are dual). Let F/ℚ_{ℓ} be finite and let L be a finite free ℤ_{ℓ}-module with continuous G_{F} -action such that L⊗ℚ_{ℓ} is de Rham. Under the local Tate pairing, H_{f}^{1}(F, L) and H_{f}^{1}(F, L^{∗}(1) ⊗ℚ_{ℓ}/ℤ_{ℓ}) are exact annihilators. The rational finite conditions are exact annihilators as well. Here the lattice condition is the inverse image of the rational condition, and the divisible condition is its propagated condition on the lattice quotient.

This is Proposition 3.8 of S. Bloch and K. Kato, L-functions and Tamagawa numbers of motives, The Grothendieck Festschrift I, Progress in Mathematics 86 (1990), 333–400, at page 354; the finite condition is defined in (3.7.2)–(3.7.3).^{4} For the application the fields are completions E_{w}, the lattices are finite free, and continuity is part of the compatible setup. Crystalline local representations satisfy the de Rham hypothesis. Application to the abstract local conditions still requires their identification with these propagated finite conditions.

Background fact 6.15 (Integral prismatic realization). For a complete discretely valued mixed-characteristic field with perfect residue field, the category of prismatic F-crystals on its ring of integers is equivalent, by etale realization, to finite free ℤ_{ℓ}-lattices in crystalline Galois representations. Every equivariant map of such lattices comes from a unique map of their prismatic F-crystals.

This is Theorem 1.2, restated as Theorem 5.6, of B. Bhatt and P. Scholze, Prismatic F-crystals and crystalline Galois representations, Cambridge Journal of Mathematics 11 (2023), no. 2, 507–562.^{5} The field hypothesis holds for each E_{w}/ℚ_{ℓ}. The statement concerns integral lattices whose rational representations are crystalline; it does not assert full faithfulness for arbitrary torsion representations. Identifying the abstract period and crystal models in the setup with this realization remains necessary before using this citation for them.

## The reference-family construction
