6.4 Period rationality and the remaining division bounds

The remainder argument uses the same selected realization as the arithmetic comparison. Its rationality statements cannot be obtained by replacing that realization by an unrelated one with the same ranks. We spell out the two linear arguments used to transport its columns.

Lemma 6.86 (Descent through the canonical period section). Let K ↪→ ℂ be a number-field embedding σ, let W be a finite-dimensional K-space, and let j : W →W_{ℂ} be its scalar-extension map. Let V_{0} be a finite-dimensional complex Hermitian space, ι : V_{0} →W_{ℂ} a surjection and U = ker ι. Write sec : W_{ℂ} → U^{⊥}⊂V_{0} for the inverse of ι|_{U}⊥. Suppose e : K^{d}≃W, p : K^{n}→K^{d} is surjective, the vectors a(F) ∈V_{0}, F ∈K^{n}, span V_{0} over ℂ, and

```text
ι(a(F)) = j(e(pF)).
```

If a complex linear period functional L : V_{0} →ℂ and a K-linear functional β : K^{d}→K satisfy

```text
L(a(F)) = σ(β(pF)) (F ∈K^{n}),
```

then

L(sec(j(e(y)))) = σ(β(y)) (y ∈K^{d}).

In particular the transported period pairing takes its values in the specified embedded field σ(K).

Proof. Define a complex linear functional Λ on W_{ℂ} by extending the K-linear functional βe^{−1} in a K-basis of W. Thus Λ(j(e(y))) = σ(β(y)). The two complex linear functionals L and Λι agree on all a(F) by the displayed identities, and hence agree on their complex span V_{0}.

For the concrete section calculation, choose F with pF = y and put a(F) = u + q by orthogonal projection to U ⊕U^{⊥}. Then ι(u) = 0 and ι(q) = j(e(y)), so q = sec(j(e(y))). Evaluating L = Λι at q gives the claimed value. This also shows why it is necessary to identify the kernel and the canonical section: the calculation is unaffected by the component u precisely because the descended functional vanishes on that kernel.

Here is the image computation used to verify the span premise. If p and c are commuting idempotents on a finite-dimensional K-space, the operator induced by c on im p has image im(pc). One inclusion follows from p(cv) = cv for pv = v, and the other from pcw = c(pw). It fixes im(pc) pointwise. Choosing bases for these two images and extending scalars shows that the corresponding complex operator has image the complex span of the rational good-image basis. This proves the image and span assertions for the level and good idempotents in the selected column realization. The other premise in the lemma is the actual period factorization: in the source its scalar factor at the base level is 1, so the period on these generators equals the embedded algebraic column pairing β(pF). Applying the lemma to every row parameter and period functional, and transporting by the selected rational identifications of the row and column spaces, proves rationality of their pairing. This use requires that period factorization for the same chosen realization.

Lemma 6.87 (The full lattice obtained from the selected local lattices). Let K be a number field and W a finite-dimensional K-space. Fix a full O_{K}-lattice L_{0}. At each finite prime v let L_{v} be a full O_{K,v}-lattice in W, with L_{v} = (L_{0})_{v} except at finitely many primes. Then

L = {w ∈W : w ∈L_{v} for every v}

is finite over O_{K} and spans W over K. An invertible K-linear map carries it to a finite full lattice.

<!-- Source PDF page 316 -->

Proof. For each exceptional prime choose a sufficiently large denominator which bounds L_{v} on both sides by scalar multiples of (L_{0})_{v}. Choose one nonzero integer a whose valuations at these finitely many primes exceed all those requirements. At every other prime the same two inclusions hold automatically. Thus

```text
aL_{0} ⊂L ⊂a^{−1}L_{0}.
```

For the upper inclusion, use that an element of K integral at every finite prime belongs to O_{K}, in coordinates of a fractional-ideal decomposition of L_{0}. Equivalently this is the characterization of a fractional ideal by its prime valuations. The module on the right is finite and O_{K} is Noetherian, so its submodule L is finite. The module on the left spans W, since a ̸= 0, giving fullness. The image of a finite generating set generates the transported lattice, and invertibility transports its K-span onto W.

In the column construction each local lattice is the image of the prescribed algebraic lattice under an invertible matrix ι_{v}. Their types equal the base type except on the finite twisting support. The lemma therefore applies to the glued row lattice. The selected linear isomorphism to the remainder space sends that lattice to the source’s remainder lattice, so the latter is finite and spans the entire remainder space. No dimension comparison alone would prove this lattice assertion.

Lemma 6.88 (Transport and absorption of the sharp functional bound). Fix one selected primitive realization. Suppose its remainder lattice is identified isometrically with the abstract remainder lattice, and its positive period weights κ agree under the specified embedding bijection. Write λ_{0} = log |G|. If its passage inequality is

µ_{max}(R) ≤x^{C}b − mean(log κ) + 14λ_{0},

then the same realization satisfies

µ_{max}(R) + mean(log κ) ≤x^{max(C,1)+1}b

provided x ≥ 56, b ≥ 1 and λ_{0} ≤ 4b. These assertions are uniform in all selected indices once their displayed premises hold uniformly.

Proof. The isometry identifies every rational subspace with its image, preserves its integral lattice and metric, and hence preserves its degree and slope. Taking the supremum of the slopes gives the same maximal slope on both sides. The identified weights give equal sums of their logarithms; the embedding bijection gives the same normalizing cardinality, so the means agree too. Transport the passage inequality by these two equalities and add the common mean to obtain

µ_{max}(R) + mean(log κ) ≤x^{C}b + 56b.

Put d = max(C, 1). Since x ≥ 56 > 1, we have x^{C} ≤ x^{d} and x^{d}(x −1) ≥ x(x −1) ≥ 56. Thus x^{C}+ 56 ≤x^{d+1}, and multiplication by b ≥0 proves the assertion.

For a family take the maximum of the finitely many thresholds for the row bounds, primitive realization, dimension-size estimate, passage construction, the original family domain and the number 56. This threshold is chosen for the family before its index is chosen. Every input then refers to the same selected realization at that index; the displayed calculation introduces no further choice of realization.

The final remainder assertion has four components: a frame-number bound, eventual rationality of the period pairing, eventual fullness of the remainder lattice, and eventual nonnegativity of ℒ_{a} = log(a rd(E)). The last follows from a ≥ 1 and rd(E) ≥ 1. The two middle components follow from the preceding descent and lattice lemmas once the selected primitive period factorization and local lattice identifications are supplied. 6.5 Closure under selections and the remaining arithmetic input

Lemma 6.89 (Transport to selected subclasses). Suppose a property P(ℱ) holds for every admissible family. Then it holds for every admissible family taking values in any fixed class 𝒜 of hosts, for each selected subclass of 𝒜, and for each extension for which the underlying family is still admissible. In particular the family bound just proved passes to each selected row in the host construction, with its original family constant.

Proof. For a family taking values in 𝒜, discard the additional membership assertion and apply the universal statement to the underlying admissible family. For a selected subclass or an admissible extension, apply the same operation to its underlying family. The conclusion for an individual selected row is evaluation of this family statement at that row. The resulting estimate retains the constant chosen for that family. No new supremum over families and no new analytic uniformity is introduced.

This is the mathematical content of the source’s passage from the all-family two-prime assertion to the closed assertion and then to its linked version. The local parameter input of Section 5 does not prove a new estimate in this passage: its parameter identifies the selected rows to which the already universal estimate is applied.

The next step in the endpoint is the existence of a full collection of host hypotheses. The two-prime estimate is one input to that step. The construction also requires compatible theta matching, agreement of the theta integrals, a covolume estimate, evaluation and functional grids, and simultaneous realization of all the selected rows. Their constants and selections must be compatible with the same admissible family. Neither Proposition 6.85 nor Lemma 6.89 establishes these realization assertions. In particular, proving a bound for an empty class of compatible setups would not establish their existence.

6.7 Simultaneous arithmetic realization on the selected family

We now complete the arithmetic comparison stream by proving all six clauses of Input 6.78 simultaneously on every compatible setup GlobalTheory.NLink.SetupAlt and deducing the pointwise split-case bound Up-perTheory.N.conclusion_split_alt and the uniform two-prime family bound UpperTheory.N.at23_family_alt. The argument combines four ingredients: (1) construction of the canonical integral block-ring objects (RingDef, RingTop) from primitive matrix data; (2) unramified residue-field enlargement and determinant-comparison descent removing the residue-field cardinality restriction in Proposition 6.7; (3) simultaneous realization of the column lifts, strict Selmer/Sha/class-group identifications, and Tate-dual row quotients on the integrally normalized family; and (4) assembly on the selected family from the already-proved local crystalline lifting, invariant-annihilator, and trivial-block theorems (Proposition 6.62 and Corollaries 6.69 and 6.76) together with the conjugate row–column declarations at ℓ= 2 and split odd primes.

## The geometric trace formula and the Galois row

<!-- Source PDF page 337 -->

## 7 The geometric trace formula and the Galois row

The geometric branch is used to supply Galois representations attached to regular algebraic polarized cuspidal automorphic representations. Its output is stronger than the existence of a representation with the expected unramified Frobenius polynomials: it includes specified local comparisons at the coefficient prime. We state that output first, then explain the geometric trace calculation and the two distinct passages from geometric realizations to one representation. These passages must be distinguished because the first geometric assertion permits different representations at different places.

## The precise output required of the row

<!-- Source PDF page 337 -->

7.1 The precise output required of the row

Let E be a CM number field, E^{+} its maximal totally real subfield, E/E an algebraic closure, ℓ a prime, and ι : ℚ_{ℓ}≃ℂ a field isomorphism. Write G_{E} = Gal(E/E). The source fixes a local Langlands recognition predicate ℛ_{v}. Thus ℛ_{v}(r_{c}) says that a map r_{c} from irreducible representations of GL_{a}(E_{v}) to Weil–Deligne representations has the prescribed normalization. Quantification over r_{c} below is part of the assertion, rather than a choice of a different normalization for each application.

Here is a convenient way to record exactly the weaker local relation used in the final row. For two local Weil–Deligne objects x, y, write x ⪯_{v} y if the following conditions hold:

(i) dim x = dim y.

(ii) If every commutator [s, t] has characteristic polynomial (T −1)^{dim y} on y, and y satisfies the source’s

predicate mono0, then x = y.

(iii) Suppose E_{v} is continuously isomorphic to ℚ_{p}, with a = 1 or 16a^{2} < p. If y is tame, satisfies the

source’s squarefreeness condition, and satisfies mono0, then x satisfies mono0 and x, y have equal characteristic polynomials on every Weil element of degree zero.

The squarefreeness condition here has a specific meaning. For a tame-inertia generator, every repeated root z of its inertia polynomial must satisfy z^{qv−1} = 1. Neither this condition nor the commutator condition is replaced by a generic assertion of local–global compatibility. We retain the notation mono0 for the condi-tion N = 0, where N is the monodromy endomorphism. Indeed the source defines this condition on an isomorphism class by descent of N = 0 on a representative, and proves that equality of isomorphism classes preserves it. Its wdOf also uses Frobenius semisimplification, as specified by IsFrobSS, rather than replacing the monodromy operator by zero.

Source: AbelianVarietyTheory/Definitions/AutomorphicMembership/ MonodromyZeroOfWeilDeligneRepClassIff.lean:321,501--506; WeilDeligneParamMonodromyEqZeroIff.lean:336--355.

<!-- Source PDF page 338 -->

Definition 7.1 (The Galois row required by the source). For every choice of E, E, ℓ, ι above, every integer a ≥ 1, every cuspidal automorphic representation π of GL_{a}(𝔸_{E}), and every Hecke character χ of E^{+}, suppose that π is regular algebraic and that (π, χ) is a polarized pair in the source’s convention. The assertion Row_{0b} requires one triple

7.2 A finite-correspondence trace calculation

Proposition 7.2 (The holomorphic fixed-point formula). Let Z be a smooth projective complex scheme, purely of dimension d, and let c_{1}, c_{2} : Y → Z be finite etale morphisms. Suppose that their fixed-point scheme is finite and transverse. At a fixed point y, put z = c_{1}(y) = c_{2}(y), identify the tangent space at y with that at z by dc_{1}, and put A_{y} = dc_{2} (dc_{1})^{−1}. For every integer a ≥0,

```text
∑d ( ) ∑
```

[T^{a}] det(1 + TA_{y})

```text
(−1)^{b}Tr (c_{1})_{∗}c^{∗}_{2}| H^{b}(Z, Ω^{a}_{Z}) = . (173)
```

det(1 −A_{y})

```text
b=0 y:c_{1}(y)=c_{2}(y)
```

The trace map in the left side is the finite-etale trace on differentials, after identifying pullbacks of differentials by etaleness. In particular its direction is from Y to Z along c_{1}.

<!-- Source PDF page 339 -->

Proof. We use the coherent Lefschetz–Verdier formula, SGA 5, Expose III, Theorem 6.7, formula (6.7.2), and its residue description in 6.8–6.11. Here the base is Spec ℂ, the coherent complex is the vector bundle Ω_{Z}^{a}, one correspondence is (c_{2}, c_{1}), and the other is the diagonal. The reversal in this ordered pair makes direct image of the correspondence equal to trace along c_{1} after pullback along c_{2}. Properness follows from projectivity and finiteness. The complexes are perfect because Z is smooth, and all base Tor-independence conditions hold over a field. The diagonal is a regular immersion; the fixed-point transversality assumption makes its intersection with the correspondence Tor-independent and zero-dimensional. Thus the formula gives a sum of local residues, with no higher intersection terms. Proper coherent cohomology is finite-dimensional, so its alternating trace is defined.

We compute a residue without changing the global correspondence into a global self-map. Because c_{1} is etale, its completed local map at y identifies the local branch with the completed local ring at z. Choose regular parameters x_{1}, . . . , x_{d} there. On this branch c_{2} is expressed by power series F_{1}, . . . , F_{d}, and the fixed equations are x_{i} −F_{i}(x). Their linear coefficient matrix is 1 −A_{y}. Its determinant is nonzero by transversality, so these equations are again a regular system of parameters. The change-of-parameters rule for a zero-dimensional residue gives the factor det(1 −A_{y})^{−1}. This is the local calculation of SGA 5, III, 6.11–6.12, applied on the etale branch; it only uses the local power series, not the existence of a global map

```text
Z →Z.
```

The coefficient map on the fiber of Ω^{a}_{Z} is the a-th exterior power of the transpose of A_{y}. Its trace is [T^{a}] det(1 + TA_{y}): in a basis, both sides are the sum of the principal a-by-a minors. Multiplying by the residue factor gives the summand in (173). Summing the local terms proves the formula. For a > d both the exterior power and the coefficient vanish.

Proposition 7.3 (Descent across components). The formula above is unchanged if the proof is first made for integral components of Z and Y , and then assembled by finite clopen descent.

Proof. A smooth scheme over a field is regular. In a noetherian regular scheme the irreducible components are disjoint: two components through one point would give two minimal primes in its regular local ring, whereas a regular local ring is a domain. Consequently the finitely many irreducible components of Z are integral and clopen. The same applies to ∐ Y , which is smooth and proper because it is finite etale over Z.

Write Z = ∐_{j}Z_{j}, Y =_{r}Y_{r}. An integral Y_{r} maps under each c_{i} into a single Z_{j}. Cohomology of a finite clopen union is the direct sum of the component cohomology groups. If e_{j} and p_{j} are its inclusion and projection, the trace of an endomorphism u is ∑_{j} Tr(p_{j}ue_{j}), as is seen by taking the concatenated component bases. A component Y_{r} whose two images lie in distinct Z_{j}’s contributes only an off-diagonal block and hence contributes zero trace. It also has no fixed point. Each remaining Y_{r} contributes to exactly one diagonal block, to which the integral formula applies. Its fixed points are exactly its share of the fixed points of Y . Restricting a scheme to a clopen neighborhood preserves local rings and tangent maps, so it preserves each local determinant. Addition over the diagonal blocks proves the assertion, including the sign (−1)^{b} in each cohomological degree.

7.3 What the first geometric realization actually supplies

The geometric fixed-point formula is used in the Hodge-trace calculation of a tower of smooth projective varieties with Hecke correspondences. One takes an eigenspace of the tower’s Hecke action, cuts to a graded cohomological piece, and twists by a rank-one character. The twist shifts Hodge indices and scales Frobenius roots. This construction supplies the following placewise assertion; it does not yet supply the final row.

Proposition 7.5 (Untwisting a geometric eigenspace). Suppose the geometric construction has supplied a smooth projective Hecke tower ℋ, an eigensystem θ, an algebraic Hecke character κ, and integer shifts m_{τ}. Suppose the cohomological realization and comparison theorems used in Pack.rep hold. Then a single such geometric object supplies its corresponding witness in Proposition 7.4, with the twists and Hodge indices exactly as there stated.

Proof. Take the continuous semisimple graded eigenspace representation ρ_{0} associated to (ℋ, θ). The character construction gives a continuous one-dimensional ℓ-adic character ξ attached to κ, whose local Frobenius scalar is κ(v) and whose Hodge shift is −m_{τ} in the source convention. Set ρ = ρ_{0} ⊗ξ.

At a good place away from ℓ, the geometric Eichler–Shimura relation for ρ_{0} has roots sκ(v)^{−1}, with s running through the normalized Satake multiset of U. Twisting scales all roots by κ(v). The resulting multiset is exactly the original Satake multiset: the bijection on each entry is (sκ(v)^{−1})κ(v) = s. This also treats all multiplicities and recovers the annihilating polynomial with the source’s normalization, rather than its inverse twist.

<!-- Source PDF page 341 -->

At a good place above ℓ, smooth proper comparison makes ρ_{0} crystalline. The rank-one comparison and tensor compatibility keep ρ crystalline. The Hodge-trace assertion says the following: for every complex embedding τ over that place, there is a complex field automorphism σ_{τ} such that every required weight j occurs in the corresponding geometric Hodge group at degree j +m_{τ}, after changing coefficients by σ_{τ}. The Hodge comparison theorem is applied with ι replaced by σ_{τ} ∘ι. It therefore gives the required occurrence in the local jump multiset of ρ_{0}. Tensoring with ξ subtracts m_{τ}; its jump degree becomes j. The automorphism σ_{τ} can depend on τ, precisely as the Hodge-trace assertion allows. It is used to identify the comparison at that embedding; it does not require changing the chosen ρ.

At the distinguished lacunary place, these occurrences give a distinct required Hodge–Tate jumps in the jump multiset of ρ, yielding the rich-jump condition in VBase. Tensoring by a character preserves continuity and semisimplicity, and the geometric congruences outside one finite set give the remaining part of VBase. At any other place for which the same pack has a good Hodge assertion, the same argument gives its crystalline and jump clauses. At a place with a geometric Frobenius polynomial relation, tensor compatibility gives the corresponding Frobenius-annihilation clause; the same inverse scalar cancellation identifies its roots. The Satake multiset has cardinality a, as required in that clause.

Finally the plan-to-pack construction chooses the common standard base, a Kodaira–Spencer exponent and its tower, transfers the plan’s congruences to that tower, and applies its Hodge-trace theorem at the embedding just described. This preserves every place where the original plan supplied one of these properties. Applying the construction to the initial plan, then to the plan for each away-from-ℓ place, and then separately to the two plans at each above-ℓ place gives exactly the conjunction of existential assertions in Proposition 7.4. It does not combine those plans into one common plan.

Lemma 7.6 (A polynomial certificate for one joint eigencharacter). Let A be a finite-dimensional algebra over a field F, let T_{j} ∈A commute, and prescribe scalars α_{j} ∈F, with an arbitrary index set J. There is a finite linear combination s of words in J such that

```text

```

for suitable nonnegative integers N_{j}. The idempotent P is permitted to be zero.

Proof. Inside F × A, take the subalgebra D generated by (α_{j}, T_{j}). These generators commute, so D is commutative and finite-dimensional. Projection to F defines a character ϵ : D → F. For an integral element b ∈D, factor its minimal polynomial at c = ϵ(b) as

```text
m_{b}(X) = (X −c)^{k}r(X), r(c) ̸= 0.
```

Bezout for (X −c)^{k+1} and r gives a(X)(X −c)^{k+1}+q(X)r(X) = 1. The polynomial e(X) = q(X)r(X) has e(c) = 1, and both e^{2}−e and (X −c)^{k+1}e are divisible by m_{b}. Indeed subtracting the Bezout identity gives e^{2}−e = −a(X)(X −c)^{k+1}e, and (X −c)^{k+1}e = q(X)(X −c)m_{b}. Consequently e(b) is idempotent and (b −c)^{k+1}e(b) = 0.

Apply this construction to a finite F-basis b_{1}, . . . , b_{r} of D, and put z =∏_{i}e_{i}(b_{i}). The factors commute, so z^{2} = z and ϵ(z) = 1. Every (b_{i} −ϵ(b_{i}))z is nilpotent. The nilradical of the commutative ring D is an ideal: sums of nilpotents are nilpotent by the binomial expansion, and products with arbitrary ring elements are nilpotent. It is therefore an F-linear subspace. The linear map d →→(d−ϵ(d))z takes every basis element into it, so it takes all of D into it. Idempotence of z then gives, for each d, an exponent with (d−ϵ(d))^{N}z = 0.

An element of the generated algebra D is a finite linear combination of products of its generators. Write z = s((α, T)) in this form, using words to retain the source’s multiplication order. Its first projection is

<!-- Source PDF page 342 -->

s(α) = 1, and its second projection is the idempotent P = s(T). Apply the last annihilation identity to d = (α_{j}, T_{j}) and project to A. This gives all the stated powers simultaneously, without restricting the size of J.

Lemma 7.11 (The even integral cut has no fixed tangent direction). Let an abelian scheme over a complex base carry an 𝒪_{F} -action. Every nonzero a ∈𝒪_{F} acts by a finite etale surjective isogeny, and so does a product of such actions on a fiber power. In the local lattice calculation, if an integral endomorphism has complex eigenvalue e, and τ : F ↪→ℂ, then

```text
1 −τ(2a)e ̸= 0 (a ∈𝒪_{F} ).
```

Proof. For nonzero a, the finite quotient 𝒪_{F} /(a) is killed by its positive order M. Hence M = ab for an integer M > 0 and some b ∈𝒪_{F} . The corresponding endomorphisms commute and both composites are multiplication by M. Multiplication by M on a characteristic-zero abelian scheme is finite etale and surjective. Its differential is M times the identity. The differential of the a-action is therefore invertible. The two factorization identities also make the a-action surjective and put its kernel in the finite group scheme of M-torsion. Properness and these finite fibers make it finite; the differential criterion makes it etale. The product argument applies coordinate by coordinate, and conjugating by the tower’s specified isomorphisms preserves these properties.

For the second assertion, use the integral characteristic polynomial of the lattice endomorphism. Cayley– Hamilton annihilates it on the lattice and hence on its real span, which is the full complex vector space in the period model. Thus its complex matrix is annihilated by that monic integer polynomial, and each eigenvalue e is an algebraic integer. So are τ(a) and their product. If 1 −τ(2a)e = 0, then τ(a)e = 1/2 would be an algebraic integer. Substituting 1/2 in a monic integer polynomial of degree r, then multiplying by 2^{r}, would give an odd integer equal to zero. This is impossible. This proves the assertion even when a = 0.

Proposition 7.13 (Summing the fiber fixed points). On a local branch of a finite-etale correspondence, suppose a base fixed point has tangent matrix T from Proposition 7.12, and the fiber is a complex abelian variety A = V /Λ on which the branch is the affine map x →→Dx+b. Suppose DΛ ⊂Λ and det(1−D) ̸= 0. The sum of the local holomorphic Lefschetz terms over all fiber fixed points is

det(1 −yT) det(1 −yD) det(1 −D). det(1 −T)

For the even integral cut this is exactly its marked local weight used in Proposition 7.10.

Proof. Since 1 −D is invertible on V , it induces a surjective isogeny of the complex torus. The equation (1 −D)x = b has a solution, and its solutions are a torsor under Λ/(1 −D)Λ. The index of this lattice is the absolute value of the real determinant of 1 −D, namely | det_{ℂ}(1 −D)|^{2}. One can check the index by taking a Z-basis of the lattice and comparing fundamental parallelotope volumes; the real determinant of a complex matrix is its determinant times its complex conjugate. The number of fixed points is therefore exactly det(1 −D)det(1 −D).

The total tangent map is block triangular, with diagonal blocks T, D: differentiation of the map on the base gives the first block, while differentiation along the fiber gives the second. Consequently each fixed point has local term

det(1 −yT) det(1 −yD) det(1 −T) det(1 −D)^{.}

Multiplying by the number of fixed points cancels exactly the holomorphic fiber denominator and gives the displayed answer. It retains its antiholomorphic determinant factor; discarding that factor would change the root-weight identity.

For a fiber power and a diagonal integral endomorphism a, the eigenvalues of D are τ_{i}(a_{s})e_{i}, for all s, i. If every a_{s} is even, their factors at one in det(1 −D) are nonzero by Lemma 7.11. The base denominator is nonzero by the distinct-root assertion in the preceding proposition. Thus all the fixed points in this calculation are transverse. Group the eigenvalues by embedding type. At t the list is {µ}, at t^{̄} it is the conjugates of the other roots, and the remaining multiplicities are the prescribed ϵ_{τ}-lists. Expanding det(1 −yD)det(1 −D) now gives exactly the distinguished and remaining factors written in the proof of Proposition 7.10. Its base factor is B_{i}(y). This proves the final identification and its signs.

Lemma 7.14 (Even sign changes that are finite-adelic norms). Let M be a CM field, with conjugation c, and let S be a conjugation-stable set of complex embeddings with 4 | |S|. For every rational prime p, there are a ∈(M^{+})^{×} and u ∈(𝔸^{(}_{f}^{p)}⊗_{ℚ} M)^{×} such that τ(a) < 0 exactly at the embeddings in S, and

```text
uū = 1 ⊗a.
```

The positive signs hold at every embedding outside S, rather than only at a chosen set of representatives.

Proof. First take two distinct real places of K = M^{+}. Form a K-idele y equal to −1 there, to +1 at its other infinite places, and to one at all finite places. In the quadratic extension M/K, its Artin image is one: the two real components each give the nontrivial element, while all other factors are trivial. Finite global reciprocity, in the norm-quotient form used in Lemma 7.77, therefore writes y = h Nm(z) with h ∈K^{×} and

<!-- Source PDF page 349 -->

z an M-idele. At infinity a norm from ℂ^{×} is positive, so h is negative precisely at the prescribed two places. At every finite place 1 = h Nm(z_{v}), so h = Nm(z_{v}^{−1}). The finite components z_{v}^{−1} form one finite idele of norm h. This is the source’s two-place construction, including its finite norm equation.

Embeddings of a CM field come in pairs under conjugation. The set S therefore represents |S|/2 real places of M^{+}, an even number. Partition them into pairs. Apply the two-place construction to each pair and multiply the resulting elements and finite ideles. A place in the set acquires one negative factor, and every other factor is positive there; outside the set all factors are positive. Norms multiply, giving a finite idele of norm the desired nonzero a.

We spell out the tensor model in the statement. For any number field L, the canonical map

```text
𝔸_{f,ℚ} ⊗_{ℚ} L −→𝔸_{f,L}
```

is an algebra isomorphism. At each rational prime it is the usual product decomposition ℚ_{q} ⊗L =∏_{w|q}L_{w}. An integral basis of 𝒪_{L} identifies the integral lattice on both sides: completion of the finite free ring 𝒪_{L} is ∏_{w|q}𝒪_{Lw}, by the Chinese remainder theorem at powers of the primes above q. Thus coordinates in that basis are integral at almost all primes in both directions. This proves the restricted product, and not just the separate local, isomorphism. It respects field automorphisms and the diagonal copy of L. Transport the finite norm witness by this isomorphism and omit the factor at p. Multiplication and conjugation are preserved, giving exactly uū = 1 ⊗a.

Proposition 7.15 (The polynomial change to a definite pair). Fix the source’s unitary datum with one infinite place v of signature (1, n −1), all other signatures negative definite, and odd n. Fix an irreducible regular polynomial P_{0} of degree n, and a root µ at v. There is a polynomial A, depending only on P_{0}, µ, v, which converts every definite pair with polynomial P_{0} into a pair marked by µ, and conversely. It preserves the similitude element, its multiplier and the finite-adelic isometry class. The two operations are inverse on the source’s scalar-conjugacy classes.

Proof. We make the objects in this assertion explicit. Let C be the central simple algebra of the datum, with involution ∗. A pair has a unit β = β^{∗}, an invertible γ ∈C, and a rational multiplier c_{0} ̸= 0, satisfying

```text
γβγ^{∗}= c_{0}β.
```

Its regularity says that the minimal polynomial of γ has degree n and is separable. It also includes the specified finite-adelic trivialization of β. At a complex splitting ψ_{w} of C, use the Hermitian matrix H_{β,w} = G_{w}ψ_{w}(β^{−1}). A definite pair means that this matrix is positive definite at v and negative definite elsewhere. A marked pair means it has the original signature (1, n −1) at v, with a positive γ-eigenline of eigenvalue µ, and is negative definite elsewhere. These are the source’s sign conventions.

If neither kind of pair exists, the assertion is vacuous and take A = 1. Otherwise a pair fixes a positive multiplier c_{0}, and every conjugate root of P_{0} has squared absolute value c_{0}. For a definite pair, evaluate the similitude identity on an eigenvector of its definite Hermitian form and cancel its nonzero squared length. For a marked pair, its positive eigenline at v is nondegenerate and has a negative definite orthogonal complement. That complement is γ-stable: the similitude identity and the nonzero eigenvalue make orthogonality to the line invariant. On the line and on its complement the same definite calculation gives squared modulus c_{0}. At the other infinite places the whole form is negative definite. These assertions cover every complex embed-ding, using conjugation for the other representative at each infinite place. The eigenvalue list is exactly the

<!-- Source PDF page 350 -->

root list of P_{0}: its n independent powers remain independent after scalar extension, and the complex splitting of the central simple algebra is faithful. Hence the complex matrix has minimal-polynomial degree at least n, while its characteristic polynomial has degree n; Cayley–Hamilton and the mapped annihilating polynomial force both to equal the monic mapped P_{0}. The multiplier is then determined by |µ|^{2}, independently of the chosen pair.

Put M = F[X]/(P_{0}), with generator x. The common absolute-value identity equips M with conjugation extending that on F, and sends x to c_{0}/x. To verify this algebraically, compose the embedding of M at one root with complex conjugation. Its image is still in that embedded field, because the conjugate of x is c_{0}/x and the conjugates of the coefficients lie in F. Transporting back gives the required automorphism. It squares to one on F and x, and the absolute-value identity shows that every complex embedding intertwines it with complex conjugation. It is nontrivial on the CM field F. Its fixed field is therefore totally real and M is CM.

Choose the embedding η : M ↪→ℂ over v with η(x) = µ. Let S consist of the other embeddings over v, together with their conjugates. Separability gives exactly n embeddings over each embedding of F, and a CM embedding cannot equal its conjugate. Consequently |S| = 2(n −1), divisible by four since n is odd. Apply Lemma 7.14. It gives a = ̄a, positive at η and ̄η, negative at the other embeddings over v, positive at every other embedding, and a finite-adelic norm witness. Write a = A(x). This single polynomial is chosen before any particular pair with polynomial P_{0}.

For each such pair there is an embedding j : M ↪→ C with j(x) = γ. It is obtained by evaluating polynomials in γ; irreducibility of P_{0} makes this a field embedding. The similitude identity gives on all of

```text
M
β j(b)^{∗}= j(^{̄}b) β.
```

Check it first on F and x, where it is exactly the involution on coefficients and the similitude identity, and extend by addition, multiplication and inversion. Thus j(a)β is again symmetric and satisfies the same similitude identity.

Starting with a definite pair Q, set β_{P} = j(a)β_{Q}. In a γ-eigenbasis the Hermitian form H_{βQ,w} is diag-onal. Indeed distinct eigenvalues λ_{i} with |λ_{i}|^{2}= c_{0} satisfy λ_{i}λ_{j} ̸= c_{0} for i ̸= j, so the similitude identity forces all off-diagonal Gram entries to vanish. Every element j(b) is diagonal in the same basis, with entries the embeddings of b over w. Replacing β_{Q} by β_{P} therefore divides each real Gram entry by the correspond-ing embedding of a. At v it leaves the marked entry positive and makes the other n −1 entries negative. Elsewhere all entries remain negative. This is the required signature, with the same marked eigenline. Con-versely put β_{Q} = j(a^{−1})β_{P} . Multiplication of the marked form’s Gram entries by the embeddings of a makes them all positive at v, and keeps them negative elsewhere. Nonzero Hermitian diagonal entries with the same numbers of positive and negative signs give congruent forms: rescale each coordinate by the posi-tive square root of its absolute value and permute coordinates. This supplies the real trivializations required of the constructed pairs.

Map the finite norm witness u into the adelic algebra by j, and denote its image by U. It commutes with γ. The displayed involution identity gives

```text
Uβ_{Q}U^{∗}= j(uū)β_{Q} = j(a)β_{Q} = β_{P} .
```

Thus U transports the finite form, and its inverse transports it back. In particular an existing finite-adelic trivialization remains one after composing with this isometry. The two operations multiply by j(a) and j(a)^{−1}, so they are inverse on representatives with the same γ. They also respect conjugation and positive rational rescaling: polynomial evaluation commutes with conjugation, and the polynomial depends only on the common P_{0}. They therefore descend to inverse maps on the scalar-conjugacy classes.

Lemma 7.16 (Preservation of the orbital stabilizer weights). The two pairs in Proposition 7.15 have equal orbital terms for the same test functions, including the reciprocal stabilizer-cardinality factors and the aux-iliary local term at p.

Proof. For a regular irreducible γ, its centralizer in C is the field F[γ]. Indeed after a complex splitting, its distinct eigenvalues make its matrix centralizer the n-dimensional diagonal algebra. The n independent powers of γ already span a subalgebra of that dimension, proving equality by extension of scalars. The same centralizer identity holds after extension to the adelic coefficient ring: the centralizer is the kernel of the linear map x →→xγ −γx, and extension from a field preserves that kernel. It is consequently commutative there as well.

The rational centralizer group for a pair is

```text
Z_{β,γ} = {(y, s) : yγ = γy, yβy^{∗}= sβ}.
```

For β_{P} = A(γ)β_{Q}, every y commuting with γ commutes with the invertible factor A(γ). Cancelling that factor shows Z_{βP ,γ} = Z_{βQ,γ} as actual subgroups, with the same multiplier coordinate s.

Let (x, t) be a finite trivialization for Q. The compatible trivialization for P is (xU^{−1}, t), where Uβ_{Q}U^{∗}= β_{P} and Uγ = γU. For every element of the rational centralizer, commutativity of the extended centralizer gives

```text
xU^{−1}yUx^{−1}= xyx^{−1}.
```

Thus its embeddings in the finite adelic group, computed in these two trivializations, are equal. Their auxil-iary p-embeddings are also equal; they use the unchanged γ, c_{0}. The distinguished element of the centralizer is the same pair (γ, c_{0}).

The orbital term is the sum over the resulting double-coset orbits of the product of the two test-function values, multiplied by the inverse cardinality of its stabilizer. Equal embedded groups have equal orbit re-lations and stabilizers, and the preceding identities make the test arguments equal on every representative. Hence the terms are equal term by term. Changing a trivialization conjugates the embedded group; mul-tiplication by that conjugating element gives the inverse bijections of the orbit sets and their stabilizers. Conjugation-invariance under the level groups makes the summands independent of the chosen representa-tives. Therefore the calculation applies to the arbitrary trivializations selected in the definitions. Finally the condition for the auxiliary local term to exist depends only on γ, c_{0}. If it fails both terms are zero; if it holds, take the same witness in the two equal point sums.

Proposition 7.17 (Regrouping marks into the full root sum). Assume the finite-support assertion for the nonzero regular marked orbital terms of the chosen compact tests. Assume also that reducible polynomial classes have zero term, which is part of the source’s good-test condition. Then the marked-class sum equals the definite-class sum weighted by the sum over all roots:

```text
∑ ∑ (( ∑ )
```

c(P_{0}, µ_{P} ) term(P) = c(P_{0}, µ)) term(Q).

```text
[P] mmarked [Q] mdefinite,irr µ:P_{0}(µ)=0
```

On each side P_{0} denotes the polynomial of the class in that summand, with roots at the unique distinguished infinite place.

<!-- Source PDF page 352 -->

Proof. For each monic degree-n polynomial choose an ordering µ_{0}, . . . , µ_{n−1} of its complex roots. The relevant polynomials are separable, so this list has no repetitions. A regular pair has at most one positive eigenline mark. Its eigenspaces are one-dimensional. Distinct eigenspaces are orthogonal for its Hermitian form, by the similitude identity and their common squared modulus. Two different positive eigenlines would therefore span a positive definite plane, contrary to positive index one. Thus if a marked pair has mark µ_{i}, exactly one index in the ordered list gives its summand; all other mark conditions fail.

Split the marked sum into its n sums according to that index. A class with no mark contributes zero. A marked class with reducible polynomial has zero orbital term by hypothesis, so it contributes zero as well. For fixed i, the polynomial change in Proposition 7.15 is a bijection from the irreducible classes marked by µ_{i} to all irreducible definite classes. It preserves the polynomial, and Lemma 7.16 preserves every orbital term. Reindexing that sum therefore gives ∑_{[Q]}c(P_{0}, µ_{i}) term(Q).

The finite-support hypothesis justifies these reindexings and the interchange with the finite sum over i. It also implies finite support on the definite side: use any one root selector and the term-preserving bijection to transport the supporting set. Sum over i, then group the root weights inside each definite summand. This proves the formula, retaining each stabilizer factor exactly once and each root exactly once. No division by the number of roots or by the number of marks occurs.

Lemma 7.19 (Finitely many involution norm classes). Let E be a finite-dimensional reduced commutative ℚ-algebra with involution τ. Suppose some unit j satisfies τ(j) = −j. Fix a finite set of rational primes S. Among fixed units a = τ(a), consider those which, at every prime ℓ∈/S, are a rational local scalar times an involution norm, up to a local integral unit. There are only finitely many such classes modulo

```text
ℚ^{×}{eτ(e) : e ∈E^{×}}.
```

The same conclusion applies to the source’s two-sided integral-ratio formulation of this local condition.

<!-- Source PDF page 354 -->

Proof. A reduced finite-dimensional commutative algebra is a product of number fields: it is Artinian, has finitely many maximal ideals with zero intersection, and the Chinese remainder theorem identifies it with their field quotients. The involution either exchanges two factors, or fixes a factor with an involution on that field. On an exchanged pair its norm map onto the fixed subalgebra is surjective: (b, 1) has fixed norm (b, b), with the inter-factor isomorphism understood. On a stable field factor the involution is nontrivial, because a fixed involution would give j = −j in that factor, contrary to invertibility. Thus it gives a quadratic extension L_{i}/K_{i}. The fixed units of E modulo involution norms reduce to the products of K_{i}^{×}/N_{Li/Ki}L^{×}_{i}.

Enlarge S by the finitely many primes ramifying in these number fields and extensions. Away from it, each local quadratic factor is split or unramified. In an unramified quadratic factor, all units are norms and the valuation of a norm is even; this follows from local reciprocity, whose unit subgroup acts trivially on that unramified extension. Split factors have no norm restriction.

For a given fixed unit a, choose a nonzero integer D making both Da and Da^{−1} integral in every factor. Outside the primes dividing D, the element is a unit. At a prime dividing D but outside S, write the rational scalar in the local hypothesis as ℓ^{kℓ}u_{ℓ}, with u_{ℓ} an ℓ-adic unit. Set

```text
q = ∏ ℓ^{kℓ}∈ℚ^{×}.
ℓ|D, ℓ∈/S
```

At that prime, q differs from the specified scalar by a local unit, which is a norm in every unramified factor. At other primes q is a local unit. It follows that a/q is a norm at all places outside the fixed finite set above S. In the source’s formulation, the ratios and their inverses are integral after multiplication by an integer prime to ℓ; therefore they are local units. This proves the same implication from its exact two-sided equations.

Now record at the places above S and at infinity the local norm classes of a/q. There are finitely many possible tuples. Each local quadratic norm quotient has order at most two, by local reciprocity; at a real nonsplit place it is the sign quotient, and at a complex or split place it is trivial. Two elements with the same tuple differ by a local norm everywhere. The cyclic Hasse norm theorem in Proposition 10.46 then makes their quotient a global norm in every quadratic factor. They are the same involution-norm class. Choose one representative of each tuple that actually occurs, and assemble representatives in the product algebra. The resulting finite list represents all the required classes, with the factor q accounting for the rational scalar.

Lemma 7.20 (Finiteness from one denominator bound). Fix a number field F, a degree n, and a positive integer N. There are only finitely many monic polynomials P ∈ F[X] of degree n with the following properties: all conjugate roots have one common absolute value r_{P} > 0, and for every such root z, both Nz and Nz^{−1} are algebraic integers.

Proof. For a root z, every conjugate of the nonzero algebraic integer Nz^{−1} has modulus N/r_{P} . Its absolute norm to ℚ is a nonzero integer, so (N/r_{P} )^{d}≥1, where d is its degree. Thus r_{P} ≤N. In particular every conjugate of Nz has modulus at most N^{2}, and its degree is at most [F : ℚ]n.

There are finitely many algebraic integers of bounded degree with all conjugates in a fixed disk. Indeed their monic minimal polynomials have integer coefficients. Each coefficient is an elementary symmetric sum of conjugates, bounded by the corresponding binomial coefficient times a power of the radius. There are finitely many integer coefficient tuples in these bounds, and finitely many roots of each resulting nonzero polynomial. Apply this to Nz. Hence all the roots z, in one fixed complex embedding, belong to one finite set. A monic degree-n polynomial is determined by its root multiset; only finitely many multisets of size n can be chosen from that set. Injectivity of F ↪→ℂ then proves the assertion over F.

Lemma 7.21 (The cofinite local norm condition for pair ratios). Fix a regular pair (β_{0}, γ, c_{0}) and the com-pact support of an away-from-p test. There is one finite set of rational primes S such that every pair (β, γ, c_{0}) with a nonzero orbital test value satisfies the local scalar-norm hypothesis of Lemma 7.19 for

The ratio a commutes with γ, by comparing the two similitude equations and cancelling their nonzero common multiplier. Symmetry of β, β_{0} then gives τ(a) = a. The same equations make τ an involution of E. A nonzero purely imaginary element of the central CM field is an invertible element j ∈E with τ(j) = −j.

Choose an integral model of the algebra, its involution, β_{0}^{±1} and γ^{±1}. Invert one integer to clear their structure constants and the nonzero discriminant of the regular polynomial. Outside the resulting finite set, the order in E generated by γ is a maximal unramified etale order. The ambient central simple order is a matrix order over each local center. Here is the usual integral justification of that last assertion. The map from the algebra tensored with its opposite to its endomorphism ring is an isomorphism over its center; invert its determinant too. Its residue algebra is then central simple over a finite field, hence a matrix algebra by Wedderburn’s theorem. A primitive diagonal idempotent lifts over the complete discrete valuation ring: Newton iteration for e^{2}−e applies, since 2e −1 is invertible modulo the maximal ideal. Its corner has rank one, by reduction and Nakayama, and its column has rank n. The action on that column is an isomorphism onto its matrix endomorphism ring, since its reduction is one and its determinant is a unit. This proves the claimed matrix order. The finite-field input is the exact statement of Milne, Chapter IV, Theorem 4.1, p. 138.[23]

Enlarge the finite set by p and by the exceptional primes of the compact test support. At every remaining prime all test values lie in the integral unit group. A nonzero orbital summand provides a trivialization and a conjugating matrix k such that kγk^{−1} and its inverse are integral, and kβk^{∗}= λI for some rational local scalar λ ̸= 0.

The lattice k^{−1}𝒪^{n} is stable under the maximal etale order generated by γ. The representation has rank one over that order: regularity gives one occurrence of each root, and the sum of the local field degrees is n. A lattice of rank one over a product of unramified discrete valuation rings is a product of principal fractional ideals. Consequently k^{−1}𝒪^{n}= z𝒪^{n} for some z ∈E_{ℓ}^{×}, and m = kz is an integral invertible matrix.

```text
m(_{zτ}^{a}_{(z)}β_{0})m^{∗}= λI.
```

Both m and β_{0} are integral units. Hence a/(λzτ(z)) is an integral unit in the matrix order, and belongs to E_{ℓ}. The intersection of the centralizer with this order is its maximal etale order: in the rank-one etale module its centralizer is the order itself. The ratio is therefore a fixed unit of that etale order. Norms onto fixed units are surjective on its unramified quadratic factors by local reciprocity, and on its exchanged factors explicitly. It follows that a is a scalar times an involution norm at this prime. All excluded primes depended only on the fixed pair and the compact support, not on the varying pair.

Proposition 7.22 (Finiteness of the global marked sum). For the source’s degree-one compact regular tests, only finitely many marked scalar-conjugacy classes have nonzero orbital term. Thus the finite-support hy-pothesis in Proposition 7.17 holds for these tests.

The characteristic polynomial of left multiplication on the rational algebra is invariant under this conjugation. Its coefficients therefore have uniformly bounded denominators away from p. Precisely, one positive integer D, prime to p, makes each such coefficient belong to D^{−1}Z[1/p]. To see uniformity, write a rational basis of the algebra. The coefficient maps are polynomials in its coordinates. A compact adelic set has bounded coordinates at finitely many primes and integral coordinates elsewhere. The same argument applies to the compact inverse support.

At p, use the auxiliary test, where the degree is one and its twisting automorphism is the identity. Its nonzero summand puts the selected local matrices, their inverses, and the common multiplier c_{0} and its inverse in one compact set, up to conjugation. Choose k bounding their eigenvalue norms by p^{k}. Such a bound follows from bounded entries: for an eigenvector, a coordinate of maximum norm and the ultrametric inequality bound its eigenvalue by the maximum matrix entry. The other CM factors are adjoint inverses times c_{0}, by the similitude equation. Their roots are therefore bounded by p^{2k}. Together the selected and conjugate factors contain all roots of the rational left-multiplication characteristic polynomial, with their multiplicities.

Let d = dim_{ℚ} C. The ultrametric bound on each root and the elementary symmetric coefficient formula bound every coefficient by p^{2kd}. Taking N = Dp^{2kd} > 0 makes the coefficients of the characteristic polynomials of Nγ and Nγ^{−1} integral at p and at all other finite primes. Being rational, these coefficients are integers. Cayley–Hamilton proves that both elements are integral over Z. Every complex eigenvalue z therefore has both Nz and Nz^{−1} integral.

For a marked pair all conjugate roots have squared absolute value c_{0} > 0, by the definite orthogonal-complement argument in Proposition 7.15. Lemma 7.20 now leaves only finitely many possible polynomials.

For each one fix a contributing γ_{0}. All regular elements with this separable degree-n polynomial are conjugate in C^{×}. One can check descent of a conjugating matrix directly. The solution space of yγ = γ_{0}y is defined over F. Over an algebraic closure the two matrices with the same distinct eigenvalues have an invertible solution. The polynomial det(L_{y} : C →C) on that solution space is therefore nonzero. Since F is infinite, it is nonzero at some F-point, which is an invertible conjugator in C. Conjugate the varying pairs by it and transfer their finite trivializations too. Their multipliers have at most two values: determinants of the common similitude element fix c^{n}_{0}, which has at most two rational real roots as c_{0} varies.

Fix one of these multipliers and one reference β_{0}. Every ratio a = ββ_{0}^{−1} is a fixed unit in the regular commutative centralizer, for τ(b) = β_{0}b^{∗}β_{0}^{−1}. Lemma 7.21 gives its local norm conditions outside one finite set. Lemma 7.19 then gives a finite list of a_{0}’s with

```text
a = rea_{0}τ(e), r ∈ℚ^{×}, e ∈E^{×}.
```

Lemma 7.23 (Finiteness of regular orbital terms). For a fixed regular marked pair, the compact degree-one tests have finite support on its rational-centralizer double-coset space. Choose one coordinate in each pair and the multiplier freely; these are torus coordinates.

At each finite place, the orbit map modulo T has local continuous sections on the regular conjugacy orbit. This can be checked without an unproved properness assertion. Near the original solution its normalized ratio is near one. Its square root is defined by the convergent binomial series in the complete local algebra, after making that neighborhood sufficiently small. Multiplying the chosen conjugator by this centralizer square root corrects the form and gives a section in the similitude group.

These regular group orbits are closed. Within the closed regular polynomial fiber their classes are dis-tinguished by the local fixed-unit norm quotients, and there are finitely many of these, by local reciprocity. The local sections show that each class is open in that fiber, hence also closed. A compact subset of the orbit is consequently covered by finitely many compact section images, up to its local centralizer.

Away from finitely many primes the stronger integral assertion holds: the regular polynomial has unit discriminant, and the matrix and etale orders are those constructed in Lemma 7.21. Every stable lattice has rank one over that maximal etale order and is obtained by a centralizer element. The unramified unit-norm correction used there makes the remaining conjugator integral in the similitude group. Thus there is just the integral coset outside one finite set.

It follows that all adelic conjugators whose conjugates meet the fixed compact support belong to T(𝔸_{f})C for one compact set C. There are finitely many right level cosets in C. For the second, a positive fixed line splits the real Hermitian space into that line and its negative definite orthogonal complement. Its stabilizer at multiplier one is compact. Compact finite test support bounds the valuations of the rational multiplier at all primes, so there are finitely many possible positive multipliers. Rescaling by their positive square roots therefore bounds all real matrices fixing the line. The finite compo-nents have one denominator bound. Proposition 7.24 (The period-domain weighted marked count). The point’s contribution is the sum of these weights divided by the cardinality of its rational stabilizer. This is the source’s cxSumAtM definition. ## Complex uniformization and the marked period dictionary

<!-- Source PDF page 358 -->

7.4 Complex uniformization and the marked period dictionary

The analytic orbit count above uses actual complex points and tangent spaces, rather than just a set with the same cardinality. We make the required comparison explicit. The classical results used in this comparison are the following precise ones. A compact connected complex Lie group is its tangent space modulo the kernel of its exponential. Polarizable complex tori are equivalent to complex abelian varieties. The Appell– Humbert description gives the factors of automorphy of line bundles; a positive form gives an ample bundle. These statements are recorded in Milne’s Complex Multiplication, Proposition 2.1 and Proposition 6.1 with its Appell–Humbert and Lefschetz statements on pages 46–47 [34]. For a projective complex variety, algebraic and analytic sections and homomorphisms of coherent sheaves agree: Serre’s original GAGA, number 12, Theorems 1–3, pages 19–20 [24]. Here positivity, compactness and projectivity hold for the polarized abelian varieties under discussion; GAGA is used on these projective fibers, not on the nonproper PEL base.

<!-- Source PDF page 359 -->

Proposition 7.25 (The full polarized exponential dictionary). Let A/ℂ be an abelian variety of dimension g, and let L be a symmetric ample line bundle, rigidified at zero. Suppose its translation kernel is trivial, as required by the source’s KTriv. For every chosen nonzero vector in its rigidified fiber there are a surjective holomorphic homomorphism e : ℂ^{g} →A(ℂ), a full lattice Λ = ker e, a positive Hermitian form H, and a unitary semicharacter α : Λ →ℂ^{×} with the following simultaneous properties. The form E = Im H|_{Λ×Λ} is integral and perfect. The differential of e identifies ℂ^{g} with the algebraic tangent space at zero. Every algebraic group endomorphism of A lifts to a complex linear map of ℂ^{g}. For every integer n ≥0, algebraic sections of L^{⊗n} correspond bijectively to entire functions satisfying

```text
( )
```

f(z + λ) = J_{λ}(z)^{n}f(z), J_{λ}(z) = α(λ) exp πH(z, λ) +^{π}_{2}H(λ, λ) .

In the source’s order of the theta-group commutator, the Weil pairing of e(a/k) and e(b/k) is exp(−2πiE(a, b)/k) for every k > 0 and a, b ∈Λ.

Proof. Choose a complex basis of Lie(A). The exponential has derivative the identity, so is a local isomor-phism at zero. Its image is an open subgroup. Any open subgroup of a connected topological group is the whole group, since all its cosets are open and its complement is open. Thus the exponential is surjective, with discrete kernel. The quotient is compact because A is projective; a discrete subgroup of a finite dimen-sional real vector space has compact quotient precisely when it is a full lattice. This gives the exponential, its kernel, and real spanning, including the zero-dimensional case.

Apply Appell–Humbert to L^{an}. Its positivity is the positivity of the given ample line bundle. In the quotient description the action is (z, t) →→(z +λ, J_{λ}(z)t). The identity for a semicharacter says exactly that these maps compose as the lattice does. The vector represented by (z, 1) is a nowhere zero frame of e^{∗}L; if its coordinates in an algebraic local frame are u_{i}(z), then

```text
u_{i}(z) = J_{λ}(z)u_{i}(z + λ).
```

Multiplying this entire frame by one nonzero constant makes its value at zero the prescribed rigidification. This changes none of the factors J_{λ}. The u_{i} obey the source’s transition functions, are holomorphic and never zero where their algebraic frame is defined. This is the full IsAH/IsRig convention, including which side contains the factor of automorphy.

For clarity, perfectness uses principal polarization and is not a consequence of ampleness alone. Put

```text
Λ^{#}= {v ∈Λ ⊗ℝ : E(v, Λ) ⊂ℤ}.
```

Translating an Appell–Humbert bundle by v changes its factor by exp(πH(v, λ)). Changing frame by the exponential of πH(z, v) leaves the character exp(2πiE(v, λ)). The translated bundle is therefore isomorphic to L precisely when v ∈Λ^{#}. The translation kernel is Λ^{#}/Λ. The source’s KTriv sets this kernel to zero, so Λ^{#}= Λ. Nondegeneracy identifies Λ^{#} with Hom(Λ, ℤ); hence a →→E(a, −) is an isomorphism. This is the asserted integral perfect pairing.

The algebraic tangent vector at zero is a derivation of the local ring into ℂ. In smooth local coordinates it is the list of its values on the coordinates; the analytic directional derivative has exactly the same list. Consequently the derivative of e, which is the identity in our Lie basis, gives both uniqueness directions in the source’s dual-number tangent assertion. If f is a group endomorphism, its derivative F is complex linear. The two maps f ∘e and e ∘F agree near zero by uniqueness of the local group exponential. They agree everywhere: subdivide any z into m copies of z/m in that neighborhood and use the homomorphism law. In particular FΛ ⊂Λ.

A section pulled to the covering space is uniquely f(z) times the n-th power of the chosen frame. The displayed frame identity shows that descent is precisely the displayed theta functional equation. Thus all analytic sections, including those with n = 0, correspond to these entire functions. GAGA applies because

A is projective and L^{⊗n} is coherent, and identifies them with algebraic sections. Uniqueness follows either from descent or from the nonvanishing frame and surjectivity of e.

Finally consider lifts of translations by a/k and b/k on L^{⊗k}. In this frame their multipliers have the form C_{a} exp(−πH(z, a)) and C_{b} exp(−πH(z, b)). The constants cancel from the commutator. Its scalar is

```text
( )
```

exp(−πH(z, a)) exp(−πH(z + a/k, b)) = exp −π(H(a, b) −H(b, a))/k = exp(−2πiE(a, b)/k). exp(−πH(z, b)) exp(−πH(z + b/k, a))

Both points are killed by k, since a, b are periods. The source defines its Weil value by this same ordered theta-group commutator, so this proves the required sign as well as the scalar. Lemma 7.26 (Local period coordinates). Fix a polarized 𝒪-lattice (Λ, E), its specified action ρ : 𝒪 → M_{g}(ℂ), and a period embedding P_{0} : Λ → ℂ^{g}. Near P_{0}, period embeddings modulo complex linear change of coordinates have holomorphic coordinates in the vector space of symmetric, action-compatible infinitesimal period variations. If this vector space is W, its dimension is the local dimension of the period domain.

Proof. Extend P_{0} to the real isomorphism Λ ⊗ℝ ≃ℂ^{g}. Any nearby real linear period map is uniquely

```text
P = AP_{0} + BP_{0}, A, B ∈M_{g}(ℂ).
```

The coefficients are finite linear combinations of period values on a fixed integral basis. At P_{0} they are A = 1, B = 0, so A remains invertible nearby. Quotienting by left multiplication by A^{−1} normalizes the map to P_{0} + CP_{0}, where C = A^{−1}B. A change P →→HP changes (A, B) to (HA, HB), and hence leaves C unchanged. This proves uniqueness of the normalized coordinate.

Write the positive form of P_{0} as the Hermitian matrix M_{0}. The Riemann bilinear relation and the 𝒪-action become linear conditions on C^{t}M_{0}: symmetry and the intertwining conditions specified by ρ and its conjugate. This is the space W just stated. Lemma 7.27 (Periods in a holomorphic abelian family). Let A →X be an abelian scheme in characteristic zero, with its order action, relatively ample polarization bundle and torsion marking. Every holomorphic section through an exponential value has a local holomorphic logarithm with any specified initial lift.

Its inverse in the second variable, denoted h_{b}, is jointly holomorphic and

```text
h_{b}(v) =^{1}_{2}v + O(‖v‖^{2}).
```

This estimate can be made uniform in a smaller base neighborhood and a fixed vector ball: the holomorphic second-order remainder is bounded on a slightly larger polydisc, and the constant and linear terms are fixed. Write its bound as ‖h_{b}(v)−v/2‖≤C‖v‖^{2}. On a ball with radius at most 1/(8C), it follows that ‖h_{b}(v)‖≤ (5/8)‖v‖. The successive differences of 2^{r}h^{∘}_{b}^{r}(v) have norm at most

```text
2C‖v‖^{2}(25/32)^{r}.
```

Their geometric majorant is uniform in both variables. Consequently log_{b}(v) = lim_{r} 2^{r}h^{∘}_{b}^{r}(v) is jointly holo-morphic, vanishes at zero and has derivative the identity. Associativity and commutativity imply that inverse doubling commutes with the local group law. Applying this to its r-th iterate, the quadratic part of the mul-tiplication law is multiplied by 2^{r}(5/8)^{2r}, which tends to zero. Passing to the limit gives log_{b}(M_{b}(v, w)) = log_{b}(v) + log_{b}(w). The inverse function theorem, again with the base variable included, supplies the local exponential.

Extend this local exponential to all vectors by

```text
e_{b}(z) = [2]^{r}e^{loc}_{b} (z/2^{r})
```

for sufficiently large r. The local addition law shows that this expression is independent of r, agrees on overlaps and is a group homomorphism. Each point of the parameter-vector space has a neighborhood on which one r works, so the extension is jointly holomorphic. Its derivative is invertible; hence its image is an open subgroup of the connected complex fiber and is the whole fiber. The local inverse supplies a radius r_{0} > 0, independent of b after shrinking, such that e_{b}(z) = 0 and ‖z‖< r_{0} imply z = 0. Compose with one fixed linear isomorphism to make e_{b0} the specified initial exponential. This is possible because two exponentials differ by their invertible derivatives; equality near zero extends by subdivision as in Proposition 7.25.

For a section x(w) and base map b = β(w) with e_{β(w0)}(z_{0}) = x(w_{0}), multiply x(w) by e_{β(w)}(z_{0})^{−1}. The result is near the identity. Its local logarithm plus z_{0} is the requested holomorphic lift. This also explains why the lift can be prescribed at a nonzero vector.

Choose an integral basis of the kernel at b_{0}. Apply the preceding lifting property to the identity section with each of these initial kernel vectors. It gives holomorphic vectors P_{b}(λ_{j}) in the kernel. Extend them additively. They remain a real basis after shrinking. They generate the entire kernel, not just a sublattice: reduce any kernel vector modulo this varying lattice to its bounded fundamental parallelepiped. If extra reduced kernel vectors occurred arbitrarily near b_{0}, compactness would give a limiting vector in the initial kernel. Subtract its lattice representative; the result would be a nonzero kernel vector of norm less than r_{0}, a contradiction. Thus the kernel is exactly P_{b}(Λ), and it is a full discrete lattice.

Each order endomorphism has a holomorphic linear lift in these exponential coordinates. Indeed its local logarithm is a holomorphic additive germ, so equals its complex derivative; equality extends by subdivision. For any a ∈𝒪 and λ ∈Λ, the difference between its linear lift applied to P_{b}(λ) and P_{b}(aλ) is a continuous kernel vector which is zero at b_{0}. The uniform kernel radius forces it to be zero on a smaller connected neighborhood. It suffices to impose this on integral bases of the finite order and lattice, so one neighborhood works for all a, λ.

The alternating form is likewise constant. The torsion sections e_{b}(P_{b}(λ)/k) are holomorphic, and their Weil pairings are holomorphic with values in the finite group of k-th roots of unity. On a connected neigh-borhood each value is constant. By the negative exponential formula of the preceding proposition, its integer alternating form agrees with the initial form modulo every k > 0. Two integers congruent modulo every positive integer are equal. The equality therefore holds integrally. The marked N-torsion sections are con-stant in the same local torsion covering, and agree with e_{b}(P_{b}(t(a))/N) because they do so at b_{0}. A finite set of generators suffices for this assertion as well.

The linear action obtained so far need not equal the fixed matrix action ρ; it is conjugate to it. The source corrects this, rather than silently identifying the two. After complexification the finite order acts through a semisimple algebra, a product of matrix algebras. Proposition 7.28 (Marked complex points of the selected PEL model). Let D be the source’s PEL datum at p, and let M represent its moduli functor over a base with the specified complex action type. For N > 0 prime to p, its complex points are exactly the period embeddings P : Λ → ℂ^{D.g} with the following data, modulo marked integral isometry and complex linear intertwining. E = 2E_{1}, there is e_{0} prime to p with e_{0}Λ^{∗}⊂E_{1}(Λ).

Its prime-to-p genus is the genus of D, with the prescribed full marked similitudes at every torsion level. The point’s universal exponential has kernel PΛ, order action ρ, mark e(Pt(a)/N), and Weil value exp(−2πiE(a, b)/k).

Its order endomorphisms lift uniquely, preserve the lattice, and have adjoints given by the involution: compute their pullbacks on the polarization commutator, then use the Weil formula for every k to recover the integral equality E(ax, y) = E(x, ̄ay). The Lie trace condition identifies the central characters with the required type. A representation of the complexified order is determined by these multiplicities: each simple matrix factor is a sum of its standard module, with multiplicity equal to the corresponding central trace. Choosing matrix-unit bases gives the linear conjugacy to ρ. Transport the exponential and periods by that conjugacy.

A translation is in the kernel of the biextension exactly when E_{1}(v, Λ) ⊂ℤ. The moduli kernel condition says that this finite kernel is killed by an e_{0} prime to p. Here is also the full genus and marking check. For each positive n prime to p, a point killed by n is uniquely a class e(Pv/n), with v ∈ Λ/nΛ. E(f_{n}x, f_{n}y) ≡ν_{n} 2D.EF(x, y) (mod n).

Its lattice-preserving linear order action algebraizes by full faithfulness. Choose the ample line bundle with form E_{1}, and form its birigidified symmetric difference bundle on A × A. Proposition 7.29 (Holomorphic uniformization of the selected family). Suppose N ≥3, (N, p) = 1, and M is the smooth quasi-projective representing PEL model of the preceding proposition. Its complex points are a finite disjoint union of marked integral-lattice period domains modulo marked isometry. The period-to-point map is holomorphic; locally every holomorphic map to M(ℂ) lifts to a holomorphic period family. The universal abelian exponential is jointly holomorphic. These assertions persist on an open and closed complex component of a base change of M, with the pulled universal family.

Proof. The preceding proposition provides three exact properties: every point has a marked period descrip-tion, every permitted period occurs, and marked linearly equivalent periods give the same point. They are the source’s three FineAt clauses. Lemma 7.27 shows that the integral marked lattice class of a point is locally constant in every holomorphic chart. Thus it is locally constant on M(ℂ).

There are only finitely many values. Here one needs quasi-compactness of an algebraic scheme, not compactness of its complex points. Cover M by finitely many finite-type affine schemes, each with finitely many irreducible components. The complex points of an irreducible complex affine variety are connected. One direct reason for this last assertion is generic finite projection: on the complement of its discriminant, an irreducible variety is a connected finite unramified cover of a connected affine open. If the cover split, the elementary symmetric functions in the roots in one component would give a nontrivial factor of the defining irreducible function-field polynomial. These coefficients are holomorphic off the discriminant. The poly-nomial’s root bound gives polynomial growth after multiplication by a discriminant power, so they extend across it and are polynomials, by the Cauchy estimates on expanding polydiscs. This is the forbidden alge-braic factorization. The complement is dense in the original variety: the nonzero polynomial discriminant has empty interior on each smooth local branch, and smooth points are dense. Its connected closure is there-fore the whole variety. A locally constant function is constant on each such component, proving finite image. Choose one marked lattice (Λ_{i}, t_{i}, E_{i}) for each value.

For a permitted period P on Λ_{i}, choose its represented point u_{i}(P) and exponential. The classification proves surjectivity of these maps, disjointness for different i, and the exact fiber relation

```text
u_{i}(P) = u_{i}(P^{′}) ⇐⇒ P^{′}w = hP
```

for a marked integral isometry w and a complex linear isomorphism h. The choices themselves do not create a continuity assertion; we next prove it.

Let the algebraic base have local dimension d, and let the period coordinates of Lemma 7.26 have di-mension d^{′}. Lift a holomorphic base chart to periods by Lemma 7.27 and take their normalized coordinate Z(P). This is injective on a smaller chart: equal period coordinates give linearly equivalent periods and hence the same represented point. The holomorphic rank theorem implies d ≤d^{′}. For the reverse inequality take a countable collection of lifted base charts covering all complex points. Integral lattice isometries form a countable set, since their matrices in integral bases have integer entries. The group of linear coordinate changes commuting with the order action has a countable dense subset, as a subspace of a finite dimensional matrix space. Every small normalized period is represented in one base chart; transport its lattice by an integral isometry and approximate its linear change by that dense subset. The finite-nearness condition of the period chart remains valid after a sufficiently close approximation. Its normalized coordinate is invariant under all invertible linear changes. Thus an open subset of ℂ^{d′} is covered by countably many holomorphic images of open subsets of ℂ^{d}. If d < d^{′}, each image has real 2d^{′}-dimensional measure zero: on compact coordinate balls the map is Lipschitz, and subdivision into cubes gives a total covering volume bounded by a constant times ε^{2d′−2d}. A countable union of such images cannot contain an open ball. Hence d^{′}= d.

<!-- Source PDF page 365 -->

The resulting holomorphic map from a base chart to period coordinates is injective between equal di-mensional complex domains, and its derivative is invertible at every point. The source proves this last fact analytically. In dimension one, the first nonzero Taylor term of an injective germ has degree one, since degree greater than one gives multiple nearby inverse values. Induct on dimension: if the derivative is nonzero, a nonzero scalar component provides one coordinate and slicing by it reduces to the injective germ on a codimension-one slice. If the derivative were zero, the determinant of the derivative could not vanish identically nearby, since a holomorphic map of deficient rank on an open set cannot be injective. On its zero locus the nonzero-derivative case already proved forces the entire derivative to vanish. A nontrivial holomorphic zero locus has a regular hypersurface piece: take a derivative of minimal order nonzero along its zero set and apply the implicit function theorem. Restriction to this positive dimensional piece has zero derivative, hence is constant on small connected slices, contradicting injectivity. This proves the assertion in all dimensions.

The inverse function theorem now identifies a smaller base chart holomorphically with the normalized period chart. For any holomorphic period family, compose its normalized coordinate with that inverse. Its represented point must be the original chosen u_{i}(P), by the classification. This proves holomorphic depen-dence of u_{i}. The same argument gives a holomorphic family of linear changes between the given periods and the lifted chart periods: choose a finite set of period vectors giving an invertible complex matrix, and solve for the change of basis by matrix inversion. Thus the exponential attached to the given periods is the jointly holomorphic chart exponential composed with this holomorphic linear change. There is no remaining ambiguity: an automorphism of a polarized abelian variety preserving a full level N ≥3 is trivial. Its action on the lattice lies in a finite group, by positivity, and in the principal congruence subgroup of level N, which has no nontrivial torsion. This is seen without a finiteness assumption on a congruence group. Choose an odd prime q | N, or, if none exists, use 4 | N. A nontrivial finite-order matrix in this subgroup has a power of prime order r, still in the subgroup. Write it 1+q^{s}A, with an entry of A not divisible by q, where s ≥1 for odd q and s ≥2 for q = 2. If r ̸= q, the first binomial term in its r-th power has valuation s and every later term has larger valuation. If r = q, the first term has valuation s + 1 and every later term has valuation at least s+2. Either conclusion contradicts that the power is one. The finite order therefore was trivial. This is also the full-mark uniqueness used by the source. Finally the local lifting assertion is precisely Lemma 7.27, followed by a marked isometry to the chosen Λ_{i}.

For the last assertion, let j : X ↪→ M_{ℂ} be open and closed and pull back the universal object. The Cartesian square gives isomorphisms of the abelian fibers, and of the polarization and level data. It therefore transports each exponential, its kernel, pairing and mark in both directions. The complex points in the image are exactly the corresponding open and closed union of point classes. Smoothness is preserved by base change and open immersion; quasi-compactness and separatedness are preserved here because j is also closed. The above argument applies to the pulled family and gives exactly its period uniformization.
