7.7 Rank selection, tangent envelopes, and Hecke descent

Together with Subsection 7.5 (which establishes the positive-line and adelic lattice coordinates and the base Hecke point and tangent dictionary) and Subsection 7.6 (which constructs the admissible nonzero trace tests Spec/SpecTop, the integral congruence plans PlanEx, the selected projective Kuga–Sato tower KSAll, the Hodge-trace identity (174), and the cohomological realization and comparison package Steps), the geometric realization GeoOne is now established unconditionally (Corollary 7.44), modulo only the standard PEL moduli, definite-unitary vector realization, and étale, crystalline, and Hodge–Tate comparison theorems cited at their exact interfaces above (all verified axiom-free in the Lean source). We now pass from GeoOne to a single rank-a odd seed.

Proposition 7.45 (The source’s rank-selection transition). Assume the divisor theorem DivAll and the conju-gation, weight-gap and generic-multiplicity assertions used in seedFinOdd_of, in addition to GeoOne. Then the source obtains a single rank-a odd seed, rather than making an independent choice of rank-a represen-tation at each place.

Proof. For the fixed automorphic U, the weight-gap assertion first turns its prescribed sufficiently separated weight into the lacunary-weight hypothesis required by the geometric construction. To apply that construc-tion at a chosen place v, replace each of the two auxiliary places, when necessary, by its complex conjugate. The SameOr alternative makes the new place have the required restriction to ℚ(x); CplMem keeps it over ℓ. The conjugation assertions preserve respectively the elliptic local type and the Satake/lacunary-weight conditions. Their separation equivalences preserve the exclusions in the original sphericity hypothesis. This produces the placewise geometric witnesses of Proposition 7.4 for each desired v.

Apply DivAll once, using the geometric base witness. It produces one rank-a representation r and a comparison assertion universally quantified over every geometric witness satisfying VBase. This universal comparison, denoted hr in the proof, is the crucial order of quantifiers. For a place away from ℓ, choose its geometric Eichler–Shimura witness and apply the first part of hr. The generic-multiplicity assertion converts the seed’s generic Satake hypothesis into the multiplicity hypothesis used by that comparison. At a place above ℓ, choose the crystalline/jump witness and apply the second part of hr. Choose, separately, the Frobenius-annihilation witness and apply the last part of hr. These applications all concern the same r already selected by the divisor theorem. The FieldOK hypothesis also makes every place above ℓ split when that is required by the last comparison. Thus the use of separate geometric witnesses is logically valid; it is the universal comparison in the divisor theorem that puts their conclusions on one representation.

Here is the mathematical argument behind that universal comparison. For representations r of dimension a and ρ of dimension m, the source writes r ⊂ρ when an injective matrix intertwines their actions. It writes ρ ⊂r^{⊕q} when an injective intertwiner into some number of copies of r exists. Its names for these conditions are Inside and Covers. The latter condition is stronger than saying that r is one constituent of ρ.

Lemma 7.46 (Polynomial pinning). If an a-by-a matrix M has separable characteristic polynomial and a monic polynomial Q of degree a annihilates M, then Q = det(T −M).

Proof. Extend scalars to an algebraic closure. Every characteristic root α has a nonzero eigenvector v. Eval-uating Q(M)v gives Q(α)v = 0, hence Q(α) = 0. Separability gives a distinct characteristic roots. Their product ∏_{α}(T −α) therefore divides Q. Both polynomials are monic of degree a, so they are equal. Injec-tivity of extension of coefficients gives the equality over the original field.

Proposition 7.47 (Uniformity of the divisor construction). Suppose the divisor-extraction theorem gives, for each geometric ρ attached to U, a continuous semisimple rank-a representation r_{ρ} with r_{ρ} ⊂ρ ⊂r_{ρ}^{⊕q}, and with the prescribed Satake characteristic polynomials on an open dense set of good Frobenius elements. Suppose also the determinant and local subrepresentation/jump comparisons used in the source hold. Then one selected r works in the comparisons for every geometric ρ.

Proof. First fix the determinant character ψ attached to the central character of U. For a Satake multiset S_{v} of cardinality a, set ∏

```text
Q_{v}(T) = (T −ι^{−1}s).
s∈Sv
```

It is monic of degree a, and Q_{v}(0) = (−1)^{a} ∏_{s∈Sv}ι^{−1}s. The geometric Frobenius relation says that Q_{v} an-nihilates the relevant inverse Frobenius on ρ. The central-character comparison identifies (−1)^{a}Q_{v}(0) with ψ of that inverse Frobenius. Good split Frobenius elements outside a finite set are dense; inversion preserves density. Thus the divisor-extraction theorem applies to this dense family of annihilating polynomials with their fixed constant term.

The extracted r_{ρ} has an open dense locus where its characteristic polynomial is separable. Its intertwiner into ρ shows that Q_{v} also annihilates r_{ρ} at each relevant Frobenius. On that open dense locus, Lemma 7.46 identifies its characteristic polynomial with Q_{v}. Trivial inertia on ρ restricts to trivial inertia on r_{ρ}. This proves the defining good-place properties of the extracted divisor representation.

If r_{ρ} and r_{ρ}′ are two such divisor representations, exclude the union of their finite bad-place sets and intersect their two open dense separability loci. Good split Frobenius elements in this intersection are still dense. Both characteristic polynomials there equal Q_{v}, including the inverse-Frobenius convention just used. Continuity extends their traces to equal traces on all of G_{E}. The semisimple character criterion in characteristic zero then makes the two representations isomorphic. To recall its algebraic content, form the finite-dimensional algebra generated by their direct-sum image. Its semisimple quotient is a product of matrix algebras; the characters of its distinct simple modules are linearly independent, since evaluation on a matrix-unit diagonal in one factor reads the multiplicity of that simple module. Equality of characters therefore gives equal multiplicities and an intertwining isomorphism.

Choose a divisor r from one initial geometric witness. For any other witness ρ, apply extraction to obtain r_{ρ}, and use the isomorphism just proved to transport both embeddings to

```text
r ⊂ρ ⊂r^{⊕q}.
```

The determinant comparison gives det r = ψ. The source’s generic-multiplicity comparison now recovers the desired Frobenius eigenvalues of r from an Eichler–Shimura annihilating polynomial for ρ. Its local subrepresentation comparison passes crystallinity from ρ to r. The embedding into copies of r, together with the jump comparison, recovers all prescribed jumps, rather than only an inclusion of some jumps. Finally the determinant and Frobenius-annihilation comparison gives the crystalline Frobenius polynomial of r. These are precisely the three comparisons in DivAll, now universally quantified over the arbitrary ρ. This proves the asserted uniformity.

j̸=i^{ei −ej}

1.

Indeed equality with e_{k} −e_{l} would give e_{i} + e_{l} = e_{k} + e_{j}; cancelling common indices gives equal averages of two disjoint nonempty sets. Lemma 7.49 (Counting eigenvalues along idempotent cycles). Let K be algebraically closed of charac-teristic zero, and let p_{1}, . . . , p_{a} be nonzero orthogonal idempotents summing to 1. Suppose y is invertible and yp_{i} = p_{π(i)}y for a permutation π. Suppose also no eigenvalue of y occurs on nonzero eigenvectors supported in two different π-cycles. Then y has at least a distinct eigenvalues. If a nonzero polynomial of degree at most a annihilates y, its action on any fixed block p_{i}V , π(i) = i, is scalar.

Proof. For a cycle of length k, choose its initial index j. The nonzero space p_{j}V is stable under y^{k}. Choose an eigenvector v for that restriction, with y^{k}v = βv. Invertibility gives β ̸= 0. The polynomial T^{k}−β has k distinct roots in characteristic zero. For each such root λ, put

```text
∑k−1
w_{λ} = λ^{−m}y^{m}v.
m=0
```

Its p_{j}-component is v, since the intermediate cycle points are distinct. Thus w_{λ} ̸= 0. Shifting the sum, and using λ^{k} = β, gives yw_{λ} = λw_{λ}. It is supported on this cycle. Different cycles have disjoint sets of these eigenvalues by hypothesis. Adding their lengths therefore gives a distinct eigenvalues, with one chosen eigenvector indexed by every block.

Let q ̸= 0 be a degree-at-most-a annihilator. All those a eigenvalues are roots of q, so its roots are exactly these and are simple. On a fixed block, any eigenvector of the restriction must have the one eigenvalue λ_{i} assigned to that block: another assigned eigenvalue would contradict the cycle-disjointness hypothesis. Write q = (T −λ_{i})q^{′}, with q^{′}(λ_{i}) ̸= 0. The operator q^{′}(y) is injective on p_{i}V . Otherwise its kernel there is a nonzero y-stable space and has an eigenvector; its eigenvalue must be λ_{i}, which would make q^{′}(λ_{i}) = 0. Since q^{′}(y)(y −λ_{i}) = 0, injectivity on that block gives yp_{i} = λ_{i}p_{i}.

Lemma 7.50 (Scalar diagonal corners). Let X =∑_{i}e_{i}p_{i}, with the e_{i}’s distinct, over an algebraically closed characteristic-zero field. Choose also c so that y = X + sY + c is invertible; only finitely many c’s are forbidden by its characteristic polynomial. It preserves every p_{i}V . An eigenvector of y in that block is an eigenvector of Y , and its eigenvalue is e_{i} + sµ + c. Two different blocks cannot share such an eigenvalue: if µ = µ^{′}, this would give e_{i} = e_{j}; otherwise it would be one of the excluded values of s. Thus Lemma 7.49 applies with π = 1. Adding c to a matrix preserves the bound on the degree of an annihilator, by replacing its polynomial q(T) with q(T −c). The lemma therefore makes yp_{i} scalar. Lemma 7.51 (Passing the corner identities to the algebra). Let 𝔤 be a matrix Lie algebra, and let the p_{i}’s be as above. Suppose each off-diagonal block p_{i}Y p_{j}, i ̸= j, of an element of 𝔤 belongs to 𝔤, and an element of 𝔤 commuting with every p_{i} acts by a scalar on each p_{i}V . Then the algebra A generated by 𝔤 has scalar diagonal corners, and its off-diagonal blocks still belong to 𝔤.

Proof. Consider all matrices with these two properties. They are closed under addition and scalar multipli-cation, and contain scalar matrices. An element Y ∈ 𝔤 has these properties: subtract all its off-diagonal blocks. The result remains in 𝔤, is block diagonal, and so has scalar diagonal blocks by hypothesis.

For closure under products write (ab)_{ik} =∑_{j}a_{ij}b_{jk} in block notation. When i ̸= k, the terms j = i, k are scalar multiples of off-diagonal blocks. For the other terms, a_{ij}b_{jk} = [a_{ij}, b_{jk}], since the reverse product is zero by p_{k}p_{i} = 0. Thus every term lies in 𝔤. In a diagonal corner the term j = i is scalar. For j ̸= i, the bracket D = [a_{ij}, b_{ji}] belongs to 𝔤, is supported on the two diagonal corners i, j, and commutes with every p_{k}. Therefore Dp_{i} = a_{ij}b_{ji} is scalar on p_{i}V . Lemma 7.53 (The annihilator degree bound passes to tangents). Suppose every x ∈S is annihilated by a nonzero polynomial of degree at most a. The same holds for every x ∈Z(S), and, in characteristic zero, for every Y ∈𝔱(S).

After viewing these matrices as coordinate vectors, this is equivalent to vanishing of every (a + 1)-row determinant of the matrix whose columns are those vectors. Indeed dependence kills every such determinant, while independent columns have a + 1 independent rows and hence a nonzero minor. Each minor is a polynomial in the entries of x, defined over K, and the equivalence remains valid over every extension field. These equations already prove the assertion on Z(S).

For the tangent assertion put

```text
∑_{Y}k+1
```

U(t) = exp(tY ) = 1 + tZ(t), Z(t) = t^{k}.

```text
_{k≥0}(k + 1)!
```

The preceding lemma makes all these minor equations vanish on U(t). In the fraction field of K[[t]], they give a nonzero polynomial q of degree at most a with q(U(t)) = 0. The substitution T →→1+tT is invertible over this fraction field, so q(1 + tT) is nonzero, has the same degree, and annihilates Z(t). Their field-independent degree criterion now gives the required annihilator of Y .

Now U ⊂JV . Inductively, if U ⊂J^{k}V , decompose any v ∈V as u + w with u ∈U, w ∈W. For Z ∈ S, Zv = Zu ∈ J^{k+1}V . Taking spans gives U ⊂ J^{k+1}V for every k ≥ 1. Nilpotence of J forces U = 0. Each elementary factor 1 + E of u has E = p_{j}ap_{k}, j ̸= k, in the tangent Lie algebra, and E^{2}= 0. Finite-index tangent equality puts E in 𝔱(ρ(U)). Lemma 7.66 (From cosets to an open dense separability locus). Suppose Γ is a compact topological group, K a Hausdorff topological field of characteristic zero, and r continuous. If the conclusion of the preceding lemma holds, its separability locus is open and dense in Γ.

Proof. Openness follows by continuity of the resultant polynomial. To prove density, suppose a nonempty open set O lies in its zero set. Compactness gives finitely many left translates of O covering the group, or equivalently finitely many a’s such that each x has ax ∈O.

Equip Γ temporarily with the topology induced by the evaluation-kernel map into the prime spectrum of the polynomial ring in the entries of r. This topology is Noetherian, since that polynomial ring is Noetherian. Polynomial zero sets are closed in it. Left translations are homeomorphisms: pulling back a polynomial uses the linear substitution X →→r(a)X. Let X be an irreducible component containing 1. Its translates are irreducible components, of which there are finitely many. The stabilizer of X therefore has finite index; let U be its normal core, still of finite index.

Let Z be the polynomial zero set of the separability resultant. The finite translates a^{−1}Z cover Γ, because they already cover it with O in place of Z. Irreducibility gives X ⊂a^{−1}Z for one of them. For u ∈U, the equality uX = X and 1 ∈X imply u ∈X, hence au ∈Z. Thus an entire coset of a normal finite-index subgroup lies in Z, contrary to the preceding lemma. The original separability locus is consequently dense. Only the finite-cover step used the original compact topology.

Proposition 7.67 (The algebraic divisor extraction). Let Γ be a compact topological group, K an alge-braically closed Hausdorff topological field of characteristic zero, and ρ : Γ → GL_{N}(K) continuous and semisimple. Suppose S ⊂Γ is dense and each s ∈S has a monic degree-a polynomial P_{s} annihilating ρ(s). Suppose a lacunary a-eigenvalue tangent matrix exists, possibly over an extension of K. Finally suppose ψ : Γ →K^{×} is continuous and ψ(s) = (−1)^{a}P_{s}(0) for s ∈S. Then there is one continuous semisimple rank-a representation r, with

r ⊂ρ ⊂r^{⊕q}, det r = ψ,

whose separability locus is open dense. Its characteristic polynomial annihilates ρ(g) for every g. For s ∈S, charpol(r(s)) = P_{s} whenever either that characteristic polynomial is separable or the root multiset of P_{s} has the source’s multiplicative-genericity property.

The tangent, spectral and corner lemmas construct the envelope with scalar corners. The key proposition and the enlargement lemma give R containing ρ(Γ) with the same scalar corners, normalization and invariant-space preservation. Semisimplic-ity again supplies its nilpotent-obstruction property. Matrix-unit construction and finite matrix realization now give r ⊂ ρ ⊂ r^{⊕q}, semisimplicity and continuity. The two preceding lemmas give its open dense separability locus D.

For any polynomial q, intertwining gives q(ρ(g))A = Aq(r(g)). Since BA = 1, q(ρ(g)) = 0 implies q(r(g)) = 0. Conversely, if q(r(g)) = 0, then q(ρ(g))T = 0 for every intertwiner T, so the spanning property gives q(ρ(g)) = 0. In particular Cayley–Hamilton for r(g) proves the asserted annihilator, and each P_{s} annihilates r(s). Polynomial pinning gives charpol(r(s)) = P_{s} on S ∩D. This intersection is dense because S is dense and D is open dense. There det r(s) = (−1)^{a}P_{s}(0) = ψ(s). Continuity and Hausdorffness extend this equality to every g.

For the other pinning case, let M be the characteristic-root multiset of r(s). Every member is a root of P_{s}, because P_{s} annihilates its eigenvectors. Both multisets have cardinality a, and their products agree by the

<!-- Source PDF page 401 -->

determinant equality. The precise genericity condition is that no different cardinality-a multiset supported on the roots of P_{s} has that same product. It forces M = P_{s}.roots. Factoring both monic polynomials into their linear factors proves the last assertion.

Proposition 7.68 (The required Tate-twist invariant vanishing). Let K/ℚ_{ℓ} be finite and let C_{ℓ} be the comple-tion of an algebraic closure, with its usual Galois action and cyclotomic character χ_{cyc}. For every integer

```text

g(x) = χ_{cyc}(g)^{m}x (g ∈G_{K}) =⇒ x = 0.
```

Proof. Tate’s original Theorem 2 in Section 3, printed page 177, proves the vanishing of invariants of C(η) when the extension cut out by a continuous character η : G_{K} →K^{×} is, after a finite intermediate extension, totally ramified with group ℤ_{ℓ} [8]. Apply it to η = χ^{−}_{cyc}^{m}, so that the displayed eigenvector is an invariant of

```text
C(η).
```

We check that ramification hypothesis. Over ℚ_{ℓ}, the cyclotomic extensions are totally ramified, as fol-lows from the Eisenstein polynomial of a primitive ℓ^{r}-th root minus 1. The inertia subgroup of K has finite index in the inertia subgroup of ℚ_{ℓ}; therefore its cyclotomic image is open in ℤ^{×}_{ℓ}. After passing to a finite intermediate extension of the field cut out by η, its Galois image is a torsion-free principal-unit subgroup contained in the inertia image. It is ℤ_{ℓ}, and the remaining extension is totally ramified. A nonzero integer power has zero kernel on that torsion-free group, so this works for every m ̸= 0, including negative m and ℓ= 2 (where one uses 1 + 4ℤ_{2}).

For the source normalization, P.χ_{Q}(g) has norm one and hence comes from a unique unit of ℤ_{ℓ}, denoted chiZ(P)(g). Its residue modulo ℓ^{r} describes the action of g on every ℓ^{r}-th root of unity: the defining ap-proximation in P.χ_{Q} makes the exponents congruent modulo ℓ^{r}. A primitive root identifies this residue with that of the ordinary cyclotomic character. Equality at every r gives equality of the two ℤ_{ℓ} units, hence of their ℚ_{ℓ} images. The action on C_{ℓ} is the continuous extension of the action on its dense algebraic subfield. Thus both the character and action agree with Tate’s statement; arbitrary choices of the tied period data do not change this invariant calculation.

Proposition 7.72 (The period comparison supplies the lacunary tangent matrix). Let ρ : G_{E} → GL_{N}(ℚ_{ℓ}) be continuous. Suppose that for one place above ℓ, one permitted tied period model and bridge, and one induced embedding, its restriction is de Rham and its jump multiset contains a distinct lacunary integers. Proof. We first verify the established comparison being used. Fontaine’s Theorem 3.8(i), printed page 142, states that a de Rham representation is Hodge–Tate, that its canonical de Rham comparison is strictly com-patible with filtrations, and that its Hodge–Tate module is the associated graded de Rham module [41]. Its base field is complete discretely valued of characteristic zero with perfect residue field; the present base is finite over ℚ_{ℓ}. Dimension equality implies admissibility by Proposition 1.4.2(ii), since the de Rham period ring is Galois-regular by Proposition 3.6. We now check the source’s coefficients, model and embedding against this statement.

The source’s concrete period ring is the fraction field of the completion of W(𝒪_{C}^{♭}_{ℓ})[1/ℓ] at the kernel of θ, with its valuation filtration. This is the usual B_{dR} construction. The tied-model equivalence e_{D} respects the Galois action and every filtration step by its actD and fil fields. Its zD field fixes ℤ_{ℓ}, hence ℚ_{ℓ} after inversion. It also respects the algebraic coefficient embeddings: its om field gives a lift with the prescribed θ-residue, and that lift is unique for an algebraic element. Indeed its separable minimal polynomial has nonzero derivative at the residue; Hensel uniqueness in the complete discrete valuation ring identifies its lift. Thus 1 ⊗e_{D} identifies the two invariant spaces, coefficient actions and filtrations. The dimension condition called IsDR is consequently the ordinary one.

Explicitly, a model has coefficients in a finite extension L/ℚ_{ℓ}, and its dimension condition is

dim_{L} D = [K : ℚ_{ℓ}]N.

On forgetting L, this says dim_{K} D = [L : ℚ_{ℓ}]N, the dimension of the underlying ℚ_{ℓ}-representation. Hence the quoted admissibility criterion applies. Its continuity hypothesis also holds. The inverse of the bridge’s Galois identification is continuous: fixing a finite set of global algebraic elements pulls back to fixing their finite set of local algebraic images, an open subgroup. Compose with the given continuous ρ. Passing to its finite coefficient model preserves continuity, since L ↪→ℚ_{ℓ} has the induced topology.

Enlarge L if needed so that it contains all embeddings of K. s of the local algebraic closure, replace K by sK, and replace the local representation by h →→ρ(s^{−1}hs), retaining its coefficient matrices. Lemma 7.77 (Global reciprocity in the row’s convention). For a number field E, the global reciprocity map with geometric Frobenius convention has all the quotient, kernel and local compatibility properties assumed in Proposition 7.78. These apply to every number field and to every finite extension of ℚ_{ℓ}, respec-tively. They give compatible finite Artin maps, kill principal ideles, identify each finite abelian quotient with its norm quotient, and realize every open finite-index idele-class subgroup. The local convention there is arithmetic Frobenius. We invert the resulting maps to obtain the convention used here.[23]

Here are the inverse-limit and topology details. Write I = 𝔸^{×}_{E} and H = E^{×}I_{∞}^{0}. The product of the local Artin maps into a finite abelian extension has only finitely many nontrivial factors: outside the ramified places an idele component is a unit except at finitely many places. These products commute with restriction of finite extensions. They therefore define a continuous map into Gal(E^{ab}/E). Continuity follows by checking its finite coordinates. Each coordinate is onto, so the image is dense. Principal ideles are killed by reciprocity. The image of I_{∞}^{0} is trivial because a connected group has trivial image in a finite discrete group. Thus H is contained in the kernel.

```text

v|𝔪 v∤𝔪
```

satisfies HU_{𝔪} ⊂ HV ; one first chooses the finite compact-open part inside V , then absorbs the whole infinite identity component into H. The quotient I/(HU_{𝔪}) is the narrow ray class group for this modulus. Indeed weak approximation multiplies an idele by a principal element so that its components at v | 𝔪 lie in the specified congruence groups and all its real components are positive. The remaining valuations give a fractional ideal prime to 𝔪. Changing this principal adjustment changes that ideal by the ideal of a totally positive element congruent to one at the modulus, and these are exactly the changes killed in the ray class group. The converse uses the same adjustment to an idele representing such a principal ideal. This proves both the quotient identification and its finite index; it is the same narrow quotient as in Proposition 10.28.

The class-field existence theorem applied to this open finite-index subgroup of I/E^{×} gives a finite abelian extension whose Artin kernel in I is HU_{𝔪}. Since x does not belong to that kernel, it is not in the kernel of the inverse-limit map. This proves that the full kernel is precisely H.

The quotient I/H is compact. Choose finitely many fractional-ideal representatives for the ordinary ideal class group and fixed finite ideles with those valuation ideals. Multiplication by a principal idele puts every finite valuation ideal into one of these representatives. The remaining finite components lie in the compact group ∏_{v}𝒪_{v}^{×}. At infinity, division by I_{∞}^{0} leaves only the finitely many real signs. Thus a finite union of compact sets maps onto I/H. Its induced map into the profinite Galois group has compact, hence closed, image. The density already proved therefore gives surjectivity. The induced bijection from the compact Hausdorff quotient is a homeomorphism. Since the quotient homomorphism by a subgroup is open, the full Artin map is an open quotient map.

Theorem 7.87 (Unconditional closure of the uniform definite theta-lift theorem). Under the established global Eisenstein continuation (EisBL_k), anisotropic unitary Siegel–Weil formula (SiegelWeilStd_k), and unitary Siegel-set compactness (SiegelSetUnitary) (all of which are also proved unconditionally in the Lean repository), the uniform definite theta-lift theorem UpperTheory.TP.TLiftK holds. Explicitly, for every CM field E with F = E^{+}, base data B satisfying GoodK, integer n ≥ 1, and definite Hermitian space X of dimension n with X.J = I_{n}, there exists d_{0} = max{N, 2n} depending only on (E, B, n, X) such that for every d ≥d_{0}, every definite skew-Hermitian space W with W.J = δI_{d}, every admissible pair of splitting characters (χ_{X}, χ_{W} ) with archimedean exponents (m_{X}, m_{W} ), and every irreducible automorphic represen-tation U of U(X) whose infinite highest weights λ_{w} satisfy (190), there exists an irreducible automorphic representation U^{′} of U(W) satisfying IsLift: its infinite highest weights satisfy (191), and at every split finite place v of F its local components admit a nonzero equivariant theta pairing LocPair with those of U.

Proof. Fix (E, B, n, X) as in the statement. Proposition 7.85 supplies the doubled stabilizer and height (K, a, ϵ) and the integrability threshold t_{0} ∈ ℝ depending solely on (E, B, n, X); choose N ∈ ℕ with N > 2t_{0} and set d_{0} = max{N, 2n}. For any d ≥d_{0}, we have both d ≥2n and d/2 > t_{0}, and W.J = δI_{d} has δ ̸= 0 by definiteness. Good Darboux models and global Weil representations exist (pairEx_of_k), and the diagonal spaces X, W admit topological-group identifications e : U_{BC}(E, n) ≃ U(X)(𝔸_{F} ) and e^{′}: U_{BC}(E, d) ≃U(W)(𝔸_{F} ) matching rational, archimedean, finite, and split-place local factors (brEx).

The elliptic local-type perturbation has an explicit finite character calculation. Choose a small torsion-free compact open subgroup J ⊂ GL_{a}(E_{w0}) and a surjection ϑ : J →ℤ/ℓ^{m}ℤ, for which every nontrivial character eigenspace in an irreducible local representation forces that representation to be cuspidal. Choose J inside the stabilizer of a given algebraic automorphic form f. The finite-level construction gives a label b(g) ∈ ℤ/ℓ^{m}ℤ, constant on left rational cosets and at infinity, with b(gc) = b(g) + ϑ(c) on the chosen level subgroup. For each character ξ of this cyclic group, the function F_{ξ}(g) = ξ(b(g))f(g) is therefore an algebraic automorphic form of the same weight and has that local character type. Set

```text
G = −∑F_{ξ}.
ξ̸=1

The elementary character sum gives

```text
_{f(g) −G(g) =}{ℓ^{m}f(g), b(g) = 0,
0, b(g) ̸= 0.

Thus every constituent used for G has the required elliptic local type, while its error relative to f is bounded by |ℓ|^{m}_{ℓ} times the coefficient norm of f. Taking m above any prescribed lower bound makes the error arbitrarily small. The source’s torsion-free condition ensures the finite character label descends through the arithmetic stabilizers; the construction of such labels is an input to this perturbation, not an arbitrary global character assigned to J.

The weight-changing approximation first alters the weight only at the conjugate pair of embeddings over v^{′}, giving the large-gap weight there. The elliptic perturbation above is then made at w_{0}, keeping that weight. The source checks that the integral bounds for the Hecke operators survive this weight change: an operator component at an altered embedding is the identity, by the place-separation condition on its support. Thus the changed weight cannot alter the denominator contribution of that component.

To impose generic Satake parameters at finitely many places Z, the source uses one test operator at each z ∈Z whose eigenvalue is nonzero exactly when the chosen nonzero genericity polynomial is nonzero on the Satake parameter. Append these test eigenvalues, and the scaled Satake power sums at all controlled places above ℓ, to the original Hecke family. The scalars are chosen nonzero so the enlarged operators preserve the required integral bounds. Apply the weight and elliptic approximations to this entire family. In Lemma 7.88 take Q to be the product of the appended test-eigenvalue variables. It retains simultaneous nonvanishing at every z, while retaining approximation of every polynomial in all the other eigenvalues and power sums. Restricting back to those other coordinates is legitimate by renaming variables in the defining polynomial inequality. For the odd-seed version, replace Z by Z ∪W, where W is the finite set of controlled places above ℓ; this imposes their needed genericity too.

These are integer polynomial identities in group-indexed trace values. In (198) apply the corresponding identity polynomial. It vanishes for every Tr ρ_{i}, and its value at t is bounded by every positive error. Hence it vanishes at t. Extending t linearly to the group algebra gives a degree-a pseudocharacter. <!-- Source PDF page 439 -->

The algebraic realization theorem for pseudocharacters now gives a semisimple r : Γ → GL_{a}(ℚ_{ℓ}) with trace t. One precise reference is Chenevier, The p-adic analytic space of pseudocharacters of a profi-nite group and pseudorepresentations over arbitrary rings, arXiv:0809.0415v2, Proposition 1.27 and The-orem 2.12: over a characteristic-zero algebra, pseudocharacters correspond to determinants, and over an algebraically closed field such a determinant has a unique semisimple realization. We use only this algebraic statement, for the group algebra over ℚ_{ℓ}.

Continuity is checked separately. Let A be the algebra spanned by r(Γ). Since r is semisimple, A is a product of matrix algebras, acting on the representation with positive integer multiplicities. The trace pairing (u, v) →→ Tr(uv) on A is nondegenerate: on each matrix factor it is a nonzero integer multiple of the usual matrix trace pairing. Choose a basis r(g_{1}), . . . , r(g_{s}) from the spanning set. Its Gram matrix has entries t(g_{i}g_{j}) ∈L and is invertible. The coefficients of r(g) in this basis are obtained by applying its inverse to (t(gg_{j}))_{j}. They are continuous L-valued functions of g. Finitely many entries of the basis matrices lie in one finite extension L^{′}/L. Every entry of every r(g) lies in L^{′}, and is continuous. Inversion is continuous because r(g)^{−1}= r(g^{−1}). Thus r is continuous as a GL_{a}(L^{′})-valued representation. Algebraic uniqueness gives the stated uniqueness.

Proposition 7.98 (Finiteness at definite unitary level). For the definite unitary group G = U(X) over F = E^{+}, the adelic quotient G(F)\G(𝔸_{F} ) is compact and has finite invariant volume. For every compact open K ⊂G(𝔸_{F,f}), the class set G(F)\G(𝔸_{F} )/(G(F_{∞})K) is finite.

Proof. After extension to an algebraic closure, G is GL_{n}; it is thus connected and reductive. Its character group is generated by the determinant, and the nontrivial automorphism of E/F acts on this group by inver-sion. Hence it has no nontrivial F-rational characters. It also has no nontrivial rational unipotents: at a real place it is a compact unitary group, where a unipotent unitary matrix is diagonalizable with all eigenvalues one and therefore is the identity. The real embedding of the rational matrix entries is injective.

Borel, Some finiteness properties of adele groups over number fields, Theorem 5.6(i),(ii), now gives finite invariant volume and compactness; the rational-character and unipotent hypotheses have just been checked.

Theorem 5.1 gives the finite class set for the standard integral finite-adelic subgroup K_{0}. For general K, the intersection K ∩K_{0} has finite index in K_{0}, since it is open and K_{0} is compact. Refining each of finitely many K_{0}-classes by those finitely many cosets gives a finite class set at K ∩K_{0}, hence at K.

Proposition 7.99 (A common space for coefficient conjugates). The coefficient-conjugate automorphic forms used for one definite-unitary eigenform lie in a common finite-dimensional complex space.

Proof. Choose a common compact open finite level fixing the original form f. Its finite-dimensional infinite-type span expresses its infinite translates using finitely many polynomial matrix coefficients. These are polynomials in the coordinate functions g →→(g_{τ})_{ij}, allowing every complex embedding τ : E →ℂ. To recall why no inverse coordinates are missing, an irreducible compact-unitary highest weight can be shifted to a nonnegative weight by a determinant power. Its matrix coefficients then occur in tensor powers of the standard representation and the inverse determinant. On the compact unitary group the inverse determinant is the conjugate determinant, provided by the conjugate embedding coordinates already allowed. Thus a finite degree bound N suffices for the finitely many matrix coefficients of f.

Coefficient conjugation by σ ∈ Aut ℂ permutes the embeddings τ →→ στ and conjugates the scalar coefficients. It preserves this same degree bound N. The finite-level invariance is preserved on finite-adelic points by the equality with σf, and on all adelic points by rational invariance, density and continuity. There are only finitely many monomials of degree at most N in these finitely many coordinate functions; write P_{N} for their finite-dimensional span.

By Proposition 7.98, choose finitely many class representatives S. Let M consist of left-rational-invariant, right-level-invariant functions whose restriction to each sG(F_{∞}), s ∈ S, belongs to P_{N}.

M −→∏P_{N}.
s∈S

It is injective because every adelic point is a rational translate of a representative times an infinite point and a level element. The target is finite-dimensional, so M is finite-dimensional. The conjugate polynomial calculation puts every coefficient-conjugate form in M: on rational infinite points it is exactly the conjugated original polynomial, and equality extends to the infinite group by density and continuity. This is the common space required.

Proposition 7.100 (The common coefficient field). For a fixed algebraic automorphic representation, weight and level as in the source, the eigenvalues of the entire family of rational Hecke operators lie in one number field, hence under ι^{−1} in one finite extension of ℚ_{ℓ}.

Proof. Choose a nonzero level-fixed eigenform f. There is a finite-adelic point g_{0} where f(g_{0}) ̸= 0. Otherwise left invariance under rational points and density of rational times finite-adelic points, followed by continuity, would make f zero everywhere. For every field automorphism σ of ℂ, the coefficient-conjugation construction gives an automorphic form f_{σ}, agreeing with σ ∘f on finite-adelic points. In particular f_{σ}(g_{0}) = σ(f(g_{0})) ̸= 0. Rational Hecke coefficients commute with this construction, so f_{σ} is a joint eigenvector with eigencharacter σθ.

Joint eigenvectors with distinct eigencharacters are linearly independent. Indeed, in a shortest nontrivial linear relation, choose an operator separating one eigencharacter from another, apply that operator minus one of its eigenvalues, and obtain a shorter nontrivial relation. This is impossible. Since the forms f_{σ} lie in a common finite-dimensional space, only finitely many distinct tuples σθ can occur.

Each coordinate of θ is therefore algebraic over ℚ: a transcendental complex number has infinitely many images under complex field automorphisms, by extending a transcendence basis. The field generated by all coordinates has only finitely many embeddings into ℂ, since every such embedding extends to a complex field automorphism and is determined by that tuple. An algebraic extension of ℚ with a bounded finite number of embeddings is finite: otherwise its finite subextensions would have unbounded degrees and hence unbounded numbers of embeddings. Thus all coordinates lie in a single number field. The closure of its image under ι^{−1} is the completion at one place over ℓ, a finite extension of ℚ_{ℓ}.

Source: AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/SatakeParameters/ LinearIndependentSimulEigen.lean:23--84; TraceLimits/LimFinOddOf.lean:90--94,118--131.

The common finite-dimensional space in this proof is supplied by the conjugate-form construction at the prescribed finite level. It is important that the level is common: separate finite-dimensional spaces with unbounded dimensions would give no bound on the orbit of the whole eigencharacter.

Propositions 7.96 and 7.97 extend a polynomial-uniformly approximated Hecke eigensystem to one global continuous semisimple representation r : G_{E} → GL_{a}(ℚ_{ℓ}). (2) Embed ℚ into ℚ_{ℓ}; its image is dense. We next review the Breuil–Kisin prism and frame formalism used to propagate the de Rham and crys-talline properties across a pulled-back lattice-tower cover. For any finite extension K/ℚ_{ℓ} inside ℚ_{ℓ} with residue field k of cardinality ℓ^{aK} and uniformizer π ∈𝒪_{K}, the source constructs a Breuil–Kisin datum BK K consisting of 𝔖 = W(k)[[u]] (with Frobenius φ_{𝔖} extending Witt Frobenius by u →→u^{ℓ}), an Eisenstein mini-mal polynomial E(u) ∈W(k)[u] of π over W(k)[1/ℓ] whose constant term is ℓ times a unit, a compatible system of ℓ-power roots π^{♭} ∈𝒪_{ℂ}^{♭}_{ℓ} of π, and a Frobenius-equivariant evaluation map ev : 𝔖 → A_{inf} = W(𝒪_{ℂ}^{♭}_{ℓ}) sending u →→[π^{♭}] such that ev(E) generates ker(θ : A_{inf} →𝒪_{ℂℓ}) (nonempty_bk_of_finExt). Write ev_{W} : 𝔖 →W(ℂ^{♭}_{ℓ}) for the composition of ev with the natural inclusion incl_{W} : A_{inf} ↪→W(ℂ^{♭}_{ℓ}), and let 𝒪_{ℰ} ⊂ W(ℂ_{ℓ}^{♭}) be the ℓ-adic completion of ev_{W} (𝔖)[1/ev_{W} (u)]. Choosing a compatible system ε ∈𝒪_{ℂ}^{♭}_{ℓ} of ℓ-power roots of unity with ε^{(1)} ̸= 1, the element τ = ([ε^{1/ℓ}] −1)η ∈A_{inf} (for a unit η ∈A^{×}_{inf} solving φ(η) = ωη where ev(E) = ωξ_{ε}) satisfies φ(τ) = ev(E) τ and η([ε] −1) = ev(E) τ (exists_isPer).

For a continuous ℤ_{ℓ}-lattice representation ρ : G_{K} → GL_{d}(ℤ_{ℓ}) and a height bound N ≥ 0, a Breuil– Kisin preframe (Pre) of height N consists of T ∈ GL_{d}(W(ℂ^{♭}_{ℓ})) and A, A^{′} ∈ M_{d}(𝔖) such that AA^{′} = E^{2N}I_{d}, ev_{W} (E)^{N}φ_{W} (T) = T ev_{W} (A), and ρ(g) σ_{g}(T) = T for every g ∈G_{K} fixing π^{♭}. A Breuil–Kisin frame (Frame) is a preframe equipped with a Galois cocycle ε : G_{K} →M_{d}(A_{inf}) satisfying ρ(g) σ_{g}(T) = T incl_{W} (ε(g)) for all g ∈G_{K}. Such a frame is de Rham (Frame.IsDR) if for every m ≥0 there exist k ≥0 and β ∈M_{d}(𝔖) with β ≡ℓ^{k}I_{d} (mod E) and φ(ε(g)) σ_{g}(ev(β)) ≡ ev(β) (mod ev(E)^{m}) for all g ∈G_{K}; it is crystalline (Frame.IsCr) if ev(u) | (ε(g) −I_{d}) in M_{d}(A_{inf}) for all g ∈G_{K}. Proposition 7.102 (Breuil–Kisin frames on layers, tower limits, and transfer of de Rham and crystallinity). Let K, L_{0}/ℚ_{ℓ} be finite extensions in ℚ_{ℓ} such that every ℚ_{ℓ}-embedding K ↪→ℚ_{ℓ} lands in L_{0}, let (P, AI, T) be local period-ring data with compatible core C (Fits T C), let bk be a Breuil–Kisin datum for K with period τ, and let Cv be a lattice-tower cover of (L_{0}, r, Cl) for G_{K} in rank a ≥1. Assume that for every ρ_{1} ∈ Cl, every finite-extension model R of ρ_{1} over L ⊃ L_{0} is semistable (IsSst) with Hodge–Tate jump multisets mult_{V} (R, τ_{K}, n) = count_{n}(J(τ_{K})) for a fixed family of multisets J, and set N = max_{τ} ′_{, h∈J(τ} ′_{)} |h|.

1. Layer semistability, crystallinity, and filtration bounds. For every m ≥0, the rational layer represen-tation q_{Rep}(ρ^{′}_{m}) on ℚ^{d}_{ℓ}^{′m} is semistable, satisfies

$$
D_{\mathrm{dR}}(q_{\mathrm{Rep}}(\rho'_m))\le\mathrm{Fil}^{-N},\qquad D_{\mathrm{dR}}(q_{\mathrm{Rep}}(\rho'_m))\cap\mathrm{Fil}^{N+1}=0,
$$

and is crystalline whenever every ρ_{1} ∈ Cl is crystalline.

2. Uniform-height Breuil–Kisin frames on each layer. For every m ≥0, there exists a de Rham Breuil– Kisin frame F_{m} of uniform height N for ρ^{′}_{m}, which satisfies F_{m}.IsCr whenever q_{Rep}(ρ^{′}_{m}) is crystalline.

3. Limit-lattice Breuil–Kisin frame extraction. There exist a de Rham Breuil–Kisin frame F_{0} of height N for the limit lattice ρ and an integer r_{0} ≥ 0 such that for every n ≥ 0 there is m ≥ n with Link(bk, F_{0}.T, F_{m}.T, Π_{m}, n, r_{0}). Moreover, if F_{m}.IsCr holds for every m, then F_{0}.IsCr holds.

4. Recovery on the limit lattice and read model. The representation q_{Rep}(ρ) is de Rham, and is crystalline if F_{0}.IsCr holds. Consequently, every finite-extension model R of r over L ⊃L_{0} is de Rham, and is crystalline whenever every ρ_{1} ∈ Cl is crystalline.

Proposition 7.108 (Assembly of the local row). Suppose the construction has given, for every regular alge-braic polarized cuspidal π, one continuous semisimple weakly attached representation r, and the following upgrades for every such weakly attached r: spherical crystalline and Hodge comparison; the plain-toral local comparison; and the local comparison at first-congruence fixed vectors with the support-separation condition described below. Suppose also the local Langlands generic-support implications used below hold. Then these upgrades give the full row in Definition 7.1, retaining that same r.

Proof. First define the integer weight multiset. Regular algebraicity says that each infinitesimal-character entry has the form (a −1)/2 + n for an integer n. Consequently the entries (a −1)/2 −z are integers. Lift

<!-- Source PDF page 455 -->

them, with their multiplicities, to a multiset H_{τ} in ℤ. Polarization supplies one integer w such that complex conjugation reflects the infinitesimal-character multiset by the required affine map. Substitute the formula for H_{τ} into that affine equality. The resulting equality over ℂ is (H_{τc})_{ℂ} = ({w−h : h ∈H_{τ}})_{ℂ}. Injectivity of ℤ → ℂ gives the equality of integer multisets, including multiplicities. This chooses the same w, H before any local coefficient bridge is considered.

Let y = r_{c}(algNorm σ) at a fixed local component. Its dimension is a, by the dimension law for r_{c}. The associated Galois Weil–Deligne object also has dimension a, so the dimension clause is automatic.

For the commutator alternative assume N_{y} = 0. The local component of a cuspidal GL_{a} automorphic representation is generic. The generic local Langlands support implication in the source says that the com-mutator condition and N_{y} = 0 make its normalized support plain toral: all cuspidal support factors have rank one and are unlinked. The plain-toral upgrade applies to this weakly attached r. Away from ℓ it identifies its full local object with y. Above ℓ it supplies de Rham and potentially semistable comparison, N = 0, and equality of all Weil characteristic polynomials. Frobenius-semisimple Weil–Deligne objects with zero monodromy are semisimple Weil representations; equality of their characteristic polynomials on all Weil el-ements identifies them by the semisimple character criterion. Thus the above-ℓ objects are also equal. This proves the commutator clause in both places.

For the tame-squarefree alternative, genericity and the local support implication give a nonzero vector fixed by the first congruence subgroup K_{1}, and the following separation: distinct cuspidal support factors of rank at least two are not inertially equivalent. This is the source’s predicate Apart on the local representation; it is distinct from separation of two number-field places. The local upgrade at K_{1} therefore gives zero monodromy on the Galois side and equality of the two inertia characteristic polynomials. If a Weil element g has degree zero, write g = ϕ^{deg g}t with t in inertia. Then g = t, so the inertia equality is exactly the required equality for every degree-zero element. Equality of their characteristic polynomials at the identity also recovers their equal dimensions if needed, by taking the polynomial degree.

At a place above ℓ, split the local hypothesis into these same two alternatives. In the commutator case use the plain-toral upgrade. In the other case use the K_{1} upgrade and the support separation just proved. It gives de Rham and potentially semistable comparison together with the tame part of ⪯_{v}. If the commutator predicate is false, its implication in ⪯_{v} is vacuous; if true, the first alternative already gave equality. The de Rham comparison identifies its jump multiset with any integer multiset whose image is the required infinitesimal character. Apply it to the H_{τ} chosen at the start. The same argument works for every induced embedding and every bridge, since these are universal quantifiers in each upgrade.

Finally a spherical local component has a Satake multiset: existence of that multiset follows from its spherical vector and the spherical Hecke classification. Apply the spherical crystalline and de Rham upgrades to this multiset and the same weakly attached r. The de Rham comparison again gives the already chosen H_{τ}. This supplies the spherical clause at every bridge. Continuity, semisimplicity and all other clauses have now been checked for one triple r, w, H. Weakening the numerical place condition gives Row_{0b}.

Proposition 7.109 (Normalization of the twists and integer weights). The source’s algNorm σ is σ ⊗| det |^{(1−a)/2}. Its formula for the integer Hodge–Tate multiset has the same affine shift as the weight convention in BLGGT, Theorem 2.1.1.

Proof. The source defines ν^{s} by the s-power of the module character of additive Haar measure on the local field, and algNorm σ = σν^{(1−a)/2}. On a uniformizer ϖ, the module character is q^{−1}: the valuation ring is the disjoint union of q translates of ϖ𝒪, each of equal Haar measure. On a unit the module character is one, since it preserves the valuation ring. Multiplicativity therefore identifies this character with the normalized local absolute value. Twisting through the determinant gives the claimed normalization.

Use zero-based highest-weight coordinates λ_{0} ≥· · · ≥ λ_{a−1}. The infinitesimal-character entries are λ_{k} + (a −1)/2 −k. The source’s subtraction (a −1)/2 −z gives exactly k −λ_{k}. BLGGT defines the weight b using the dual algebraic coefficient representation, so in one-based coordinates b_{i} = −λ_{a−i}. Its Hodge–Tate entries are b_{i} + a −i, which after k = a −i become the same k −λ_{k}. This proves equality of the multisets, without imposing an ordering on the Hodge–Tate weights.

Source: AbelianVarietyTheory/PublishedTheorems/GaloisCohomology2/ GaloisRepOfPolarizedCuspidal.lean:24--26; Definitions/NonGaloisDescent/NonemptyEquivMultiProdOne.lean:203--206; Definitions/TwistedInnerProducts/IsSubquotientDetRepParInd.lean:47--61; BaseChangeDefiniteUnitary.lean:142--144.

There is a published theorem covering a substantial part of the desired conventional output. Barnet-Lamb, Gee, Geraghty and Taylor, Potential automorphy and change of weight, Theorem 2.1.1, constructs a continuous semisimple representation for a regular algebraic cuspidal polarized pair. It gives Frobenius-semisimplified local Langlands compatibility away from ℓ, de Rham restrictions and the stated Hodge–Tate weight formula above ℓ, and compatibility above ℓ at Iwahori level; spherical components are crystalline. This theorem is an appropriate candidate for replacing the full construction when only its stated conclu-sions are used. Its hypotheses are of the required CM, regular algebraic, cuspidal and polarized type. It is not yet a verified replacement for every clause in Definition 7.1: identification of every recognized local Langlands map with the conventional parameter, its arbitrary induced period-ring bridges, and the above- ℓ tame-squarefree/commutator alternatives must be matched explicitly. In particular, an Iwahori theorem cannot be applied to an arbitrary local component without a further argument.

For comparison, Caraiani’s Monodromy and local-global compatibility for ℓ= p, Theorem 1.1, proves the full Frobenius-semisimplified above-ℓ comparison for conjugate-self-dual cohomological cuspidal repre-sentations over CM fields, of rank at least two. Its theorem therefore removes the Iwahori restriction in that specific setting. Passing from a general polarized pair in this manuscript to that conjugate-self-dual setting requires a compatible Hecke twist or base-change-and-descent argument; it is not a change of notation. Rank one is a separate class-field comparison.

Proposition 7.115 (Recognized local Langlands adapters and generic support implications). Let w be a finite place of a number field E with prolongation A ⊂Ω and h : IsPlaceOver A w.

(a) (RecTExists) The recognition predicate IsRecT h rc holds when there exist a local Artin map a : W_{Ew} →E_{w}^{×} satisfying IsLocalArtin h a (unique by artEx) and the twelve compatibility axioms LawsTa ha rc (dimension, rank-one matching with a, Langlands segment additivity, cuspidal-to-irreducible mapping, unramified twist ν^{s}, central-character norm, and on Good representations: twisting, cen-tral character, duality, injectivity, K_{1}-fixed-to-tame preservation, and the depth-zero Green/Deligne– Lusztig inertial formula TypeLaw). For every (E, Ω, A, w, h), there exists r_{c} satisfying IsRecT h rc.

(b) (plainTor_of_tor) For any r_{c} satisfying IsRecT h rc and any generic irreducible x of GL_{a}(E_{w}), if y = r_{c}(x) satisfies Tor y (every commutator [s, t] in W_{Ew} has characteristic polynomial (X −1)^{dim y} on y) and mono0, then x is plain toral (PlainTor x).

(c) (mixed_of_tame and guard_tame) Suppose a ≥ 1, σ is a local component of a cuspidal π at w with E_{w} ≃ℚ_{p} continuously (IsQp w), and r_{c} satisfies IsRecT h rc. If y = r_{c}(algNorm(σ)) is tame (TmWy), squarefree in the source’s sense (Sqf y), and satisfies mono0, then σ has a nonzero K_{1}-fixed vector and algNorm(σ) satisfies Apart.

Proof. For (a), artEx gives the unique local Artin map a, cuspEx constructs the cuspidal correspondence r matching rank-one characters via a and depth-zero ℚ_{g}-cuspidals via regular characters and TypeLaw, and exists_isLExt extends r uniquely via Langlands segment sums to all irreducible representations, satisfying all axioms of LawsT (recTExists).

Before proving (b) and (c), we record two linear-algebraic facts (AbConv.dim_one and tor_of_fix). First, if ρ : W_{Ew} → GL_{d}(ℂ) is an irreducible semisimple Weil representation such that every commutator [σ, t] (σ ∈ W_{Ew}, t ∈ I_{Ew}) has characteristic polynomial dividing (X −1)^{m}, then semisimplicity of ρ([σ, t]) forces its squarefree minimal polynomial to divide X −1, so ρ([σ, t]) = I_{d}. Thus every ρ(t) (t ∈ I_{Ew}) commutes with ρ(W_{Ew}), hence acts as a scalar by Schur’s lemma. Choosing a nonzero eigenvector v of ρ(frob_{h}), the line ℂv is stabilized by both frob_{h} and I_{Ew}, hence by all of W_{Ew}; irreducibility forces d = 1 (dim_one_of_dvd). Second, if a tame Weil representation y has the property that every eigenvalue z of a tame inertia generator γ satisfies z^{qw−1} = 1, then semisimplicity gives ρ(γ)^{qw−1} = I. By tameness, Frobenius conjugation acts by ρ(frob_{h} γ frob^{−}_{h}^{1}) = ρ(γ)^{qw} = ρ(γ), so ρ(frob_{h}) commutes with ρ(γ) and hence with all of ρ(I_{Ew}); therefore ρ(W_{Ew}) is abelian and Tor y holds (tor_of_fix).

For (b), because x is generic and mono0(r_{c}(x)) holds, its unlinked Langlands datum has all segments of length 1 (split), giving an unlinked supercuspidal support list l with r_{c}(x) = ∑_{u∈l}r_{c}(u). For each u ∈l, r_{c}(u) is irreducible by LawsT.cusp, and its commutator characteristic polynomial χ_{rc(u)([s,t])} divides χ_{rc(x)([s,t])} = (X −1)^{dim rc(x)}. By dim_one_of_dvd, u.1 = dim r_{c}(u) = 1 for every u ∈l. Thus x is plain toral.

For (c), set x = algNorm(σ), which is generic by isGeneric_of_isLocComp and twist invariance (generic_algNorm). By split, x has an unlinked supercuspidal support list l with r_{c}(x) = ∑_{u∈l}r_{c}(u). Since r_{c}(x) is tame, every summand r_{c}(u) is tame (isTame_of_mem_weilDeligneListSum). We claim that every u ∈l has depth zero (DZ u, i.e., a nonzero K_{1}-fixed vector, proved in dz_of_cusp): let d = u.1, fix a Weil element φ of degree −1 (so a(φ) is a uniformizer of E_{w}), and set c = det(r_{c}(u)(φ)) ̸= 0. The family argument needs a uniform estimate for Galois cohomology and a way of imposing finitely many eventual conditions on one family. Lemma 8.7 (A scalar restriction kernel). Let R be a discrete valuation ring and M an R-module all of whose cyclic submodules have finite length. Suppose G acts continuously on the discrete module M by scalars, U ⊴G, G/U is abelian, and a finite set T ⊂G generates a dense subgroup modulo U. Then

Proof. Write gm = c(g)m, and let a generate the ideal generated by all c(g) −1. Let Z be the module of continuous cocycles vanishing on U. Subtracting a coboundary shows that Z surjects onto the kernel in the statement. Evaluation Z →M^{T} is injective: the zero set of a cocycle vanishing on U ∪T is a closed subgroup containing a dense subgroup of G. Thus all cyclic submodules of Z have finite length. Comparing z(gh) and z(hg) gives

```text

```

since the commutator belongs to U, where z vanishes. Hence (c(g)−1)z is a coboundary, and the restriction kernel is a quotient of Z/aZ.

For such a module Z, length(Z/aZ) ≤ length Z[a]. Indeed a finite-length submodule F has length(F/aF) = length F[a], so its image in Z/aZ has length at most length Z[a]. If this bound is finite, say b, but the quotient had length greater than b, successively adjoining representatives outside the preceding image would give a finitely generated, finite-length submodule whose image has length at least b + 1, a contradiction. The inequality is automatic for an infinite bound. Finally evaluation embeds Z[a] into M[a]^{T}, and M[a] = M^{G} by the definition of a.

Lemma 8.10 (Finite abelian obstruction). Let Q be a finite abelian group acting by scalars on an O-module M with finite-length cyclic submodules. Then

length_{O} H^{2}(Q, M) ≤|Q|^{2} length_{O} M^{Q}.

If U ⊴G is open in a profinite group and G/U is abelian, the cokernel of

```text
H^{1}(G, M) −→H^{1}(U, M)^{G/U}
```

has length at most [G : U]^{2} length_{O} M^{G}.

Proof. Write c(g) for the scalar action and let a generate the ideal of all c(g) −1. For a 2-cocycle F, define β_{g}(x) = F(g, x) −F(x, g). The three cocycle identities at (g, x, y), (x, g, y), (x, y, g), and commutativity of Q, give

```text
dβ_{g}(x, y) = (c(g) −1)F(x, y).
```

Thus aZ^{2}⊆B^{2}, and H^{2}(Q, M) is a quotient of Z^{2}/aZ^{2}. Every cyclic submodule of Z^{2} has finite length, because evaluation embeds it into a finite product of cyclic submodules of M. The cokernel-versus-kernel argument in Lemma 8.7 applies to multiplication by a on Z^{2}. Moreover evaluation embeds Z^{2}[a] into (M[a])^{Q×Q}= (M^{Q})^{Q×Q}. This proves the first assertion.

For completeness the transgression used in the second assertion is the obstruction to extending an invari-ant cocycle on U. Choose a section s : G/U →G, which is continuous because the quotient is finite and discrete. Invariance of the class allows the conjugated cocycle at each s(q) to be corrected by a cobound-ary. Extend these choices to a 1-cochain on G using g = us(q). Its failure to satisfy the cocycle identity depends only on the two quotient coordinates and takes values in M^{U}; the identity d^{2} = 0 makes it a 2-cocycle. Changing the corrections changes it by a 2-coboundary. If the resulting class is zero, subtracting a lifted 1-cochain on the quotient removes the failure, so the original class is the restriction of a cocycle on G. This gives an injection of the restriction cokernel into H^{2}(G/U, M^{U}). Apply the first assertion to M^{U}; its quotient invariants are M^{G}, and its cyclic submodules retain finite length.

Lemma 8.22 (The convex-body argument). Let Λ be a full lattice in a real vector space of dimension d, of covolume v. A convex, symmetric measurable set of volume greater than 2^{d}v contains a nonzero lattice vector. For d ≥1, if a real symmetric matrix G satisfies z^{t}Gz ≥1 for every nonzero z ∈ℤ^{d}, then

G > 0, det G ≥d^{−d}.

Proof. If a measurable set B has volume greater than v, its translates by Λ cannot be disjoint: intersect them with a measurable fundamental parallelepiped P, and translate back. If disjoint, countable additivity would give ∑

vol(B) = vol((B + λ) ∩P) ≤ vol(P) = v.

```text
λ∈Λ
```

Apply this to B =^{1}_{2}A. Two points of B whose difference is a nonzero lattice vector give a point of A, since b_{1} −b_{2} =^{1}_{2}(2b_{1}) +^{ 1}_{2}(−2b_{2}). This proves the convex-body assertion.

The quadratic form of G is nonnegative on rational vectors: multiply by a denominator to reduce to an integer vector. By continuity it is nonnegative on all real vectors. For δ > 0, G_{δ} = G + δI is positive definite and still has integral minimum at least one. The open ellipsoid x^{t}G_{δ}x < 1 contains no nonzero integer vector. Its volume is vol_{√}(B_{d})/^{√}det G_{δ}, so the first assertion bounds it by 2^{d}. The unit Euclidean ball contains the cube with side 2/ d; therefore det G_{δ} ≥d^{−d}. Let δ decrease to zero. Continuity of determinant gives the same positive lower bound for det G. A nonnegative symmetric matrix of positive determinant is positive definite, by diagonalising it.

Proposition 8.26 (The normal-cone complex and its orbit bound). Let X_{p} consist of (p+1)-tuples of vertices of ℛ whose normal cones have a common point in the open cone of linear forms strictly positive on nonzero positive semidefinite forms. Face maps delete entries. Its augmented integer chain complex is exact. The GL_{N}(O_{L})-stabilisers have order at most s = 3^{dN}, and

```text
( )dN(p+1)
```

|X_{p}/ GL_{N}(O_{L})| ≤A_{p} := I_{0}^{1+dN} (2R + 1)^{d}+ 1 .

Proof. We spell out the geometric properties of the complex. Near a positive form, only finitely many of the inequalities q_{h}(y) ≥ 1 can be active: compare with a fixed positive form and use discreteness of the embedded integral lattice. Thus ℛ is locally polyhedral. It lies in the positive cone by Lemma 8.23. A linear form strictly positive on the semidefinite cone has bounded sublevel sets there: on the compact unit section of that cone it has a positive minimum. Its minimum on the nonempty closed set ℛ is attained and its minimising face is compact. That face has a vertex, since a nonempty compact polyhedron has one. Consequently the normal cones of the vertices cover the open dual cone. They are locally finite there; a compact dual subregion bounds the associated minimising primal forms, where local polyhedrality gives only finitely many vertices. Every finite intersection with the open dual cone is convex.

The augmented complex of tuples in this cover is acyclic. One direct verification is the usual convex-cover double complex: take singular chains in the finite intersections in one direction and alternating deletion in the other. In one direction, convex contraction gives homology only in degree zero, namely the tuple complex. In the other, subdivide a singular simplex until its pieces lie in members of the cover; its augmented finite cover complex is a simplex and is exact. The resulting homology is that of the convex open dual cone, which is ℤ in degree zero. For closed polyhedral members, carry out this argument with small open thickenings on the compact support of any given finite chain. Local finiteness makes the relevant collection finite; empty intersections remain empty for sufficiently small thickening on that compact set. Thus the tuple nerve and its finite-chain filling are unchanged. This proves the claimed augmented exactness.

For any allowed tuple, all its vertices have common minimal vectors spanning L^{N}. To see this, average its vertices and examine the vectors minimal at the average. They are minimal at each vertex: each cor-responding value is at least one and their average is one. If their L-span were proper, at each embedding

<!-- Source PDF page 489 -->

Decreasing the averaged form slightly in that direction preserves the active inequalities and, by local polyhedrality and positivity, the inac-tive inequalities. It decreases the common strictly positive linear functional, contradicting the normal-cone minimum condition. Choose N independent common minimal vectors as columns of A. Lemma 8.23 gives | Norm det A| ≤I_{0}. Move A to one of the at most I_{0}^{1+dN} representatives of Lemma 8.24. Every vertex of the moved tuple lies among the nearby vertices counted in Lemma 8.25. Choosing such an encoding for each orbit is injective: equal encoded matrices and vertex tuples give the same orbit. This proves the formula for

```text
A_{p}.
```

A vertex stabiliser permutes its finite set of minimal vectors, which spans the full vector space; hence it is finite. Reduction modulo 3 is injective on any finite subgroup of GL_{N}(O_{L}). Indeed, in the integer representation on O_{L}^{N}, a nonidentity finite-order matrix congruent to one modulo 3 would give one of prime order p. Write it 1 + 3^{a}B, a ≥1, with B not identically divisible by 3. The binomial expansion of its p-th power has leading term p3^{a}B of strictly smaller 3-adic valuation than all other terms, for p ̸= 3 and also for p = 3; it cannot equal one. Since O_{L}/3O_{L} has 3^{n} elements, its matrix ring has 3^{nN2}= 3^{dN} elements. This bounds every tuple stabiliser, which is a subgroup of a vertex stabiliser.

Lemma 8.27 (Torsion from an exact permutation complex). Suppose an augmented complex · · · → ℤ[X_{1}] →ℤ[X_{0}] →M →0 of G-modules is exact through degree m −1. Suppose X_{p} has at most A orbits and stabilisers of order at most s ≥1, for p ≤m, and each boundary of a generator of X_{m+1} has ℓ^{1}-norm at most b ≥1. Then

| tors H_{m}(G, M)| ≤b^{A}s^{mAsm}.

Proof. For m = 0, coinvariants have at most A generators, and their relations have Euclidean norm at most their ℓ^{1}-norm, hence at most b. Choose linearly independent relation columns spanning their rational span. Hadamard’s inequality bounds their nonzero-volume determinant by b^{r}, r ≤A; the index of the full relation lattice in its saturation is no greater, since adding relations decreases that index. This proves the torsion bound b^{A}.

For the induction, put K = ker(ℤ[X_{0}] → M). The shifted augmented complex resolves K. The homology exact sequence of 0 → K → ℤ[X_{0}] → M → 0 compares the desired torsion with that of H_{m−1}(G, K) and H_{m}(G, ℤ[X_{0}]). The latter is the sum, over the at most A orbits, of the stabiliser homology, by the explicit induced-module bar resolution. For a finite group of order at most s, positive-degree homology is killed by its order (sum the translates in the bar resolution) and has at most s^{m} generators (the rank of the degree-m bar group). Its order is therefore at most s^{sm}. Thus |H_{m}(G, ℤ[X_{0}])| ≤ s^{Asm}. The shifted induction gives b^{A}s^{(m−1)Asm−1}. Their product is at most b^{A}s^{mAsm}. In this exact-sequence comparison the intervening positive stabiliser homology is finite, so taking its quotient cannot create torsion from an uncontrolled free quotient.

Take the inverse limits on the integral side and direct limits on the torsion-dual side of these compatible finite duality sequences. The finite H^{1} groups satisfy the Mittag–Leffler condition: for each fixed finite target the descending images eventually stabilise. Hence their derived inverse limit is zero. The continuous cochain descriptions then identify the inverse limit degree-two groups with H^{2}(T); the direct limit groups on the other side are the groups with coefficients A. Pontryagin duality interchanges these limits and reverses exact sequences. The finite perfect pairing between localisation kernels therefore identifies the integral kernel with 𝒮_{ℓ}(L, E)^{∨}; exactness at the last two terms gives the displayed sequence. The same limit argument applied to the finite local duality pairing identifies its local degree-two term as H^{0}(A)^{∨}. nonzero finite quotient, where the finite perfect pairing detects it. This checks both injectivity and that no extra limit cokernel has been inserted. Lemma 8.32 (Detecting a global power at degree-one primes). Let F/L be a finite Galois extension of number fields, µ_{q} ⊂F, q ≥1, and β ∈F^{×}. If β is a q-th power in the residue field at every prime P of F, outside a fixed finite set, for which O_{L} →O_{F} /P is surjective, then β ∈(F^{×})^{q}.

Proof. If it is not a q-th power, the Kummer extension F(β^{1/q})/F is nontrivial and Galois. Choose an automorphism nontrivial on a q-th root, and extend it to a Galois closure M/L. It fixes F. Chebotarev’s theorem gives a prime of L with that conjugacy class of Frobenius, outside the finite excluded set, all ramified primes, the primes above q, and the numerator and denominator primes of β. Choose the prime of M so that its Frobenius is the chosen automorphism itself. Its restriction to F is one, so the intervening residue degree over L is one, which is the required surjectivity. At this prime a q-th power residue of β would make Frobenius fix a root of X^{q}−β. It fixes µ_{q}, so fixing one root would fix all; the chosen action fixes none. This contradicts the residue-power hypothesis. Here Chebotarev is used only for a finite Galois extension of number fields and a conjugacy class, with finitely many primes removed. A precise reference is Milne, Class Field Theory, v4.03 (2020), V, Theorem 3.23, printed p. 164.^{12}

Combining Propositions 8.33 and 8.31 cancels the factor q^{r2(L)}. It gives the class-character bound, inde-pendent of ν, assumed in Proposition 8.21. The cancellation explains why a finite-level count can bound the intrinsic cohomology group: every finite set of unramified equivariant characters on ker χ_{ℓ} descends to one sufficiently high cyclotomic layer and is killed by ℓ^{ν} at a still higher common level. Artin reciprocity iden-tifies its lifts with the class characters just counted. Restriction from the Selmer group to ker χ_{ℓ} is injective: the quotient cyclotomic image is procyclic, and a scalar cocycle there is a coboundary, since multiplication by χ_{ℓ}(γ)^{−E}−1 ̸= 0 is surjective on ℚ_{ℓ}/ℤ_{ℓ}. Thus each finite subset of the Selmer group has cardinality at most the same bound, forcing the group to be finite. The necessary common-level descent also preserves local triviality at ℓ; an arbitrary continuous extension of characters would not suffice for this step.

The actual cycles and functionals in this argument are constructed in Proposition 8.50 and Lemma 8.47.

Lemma 8.53 supplies the common-level passage. The filtered rank statement follows below from the checked stable-cohomology theorem; the torsion and integral-duality bounds have been proved in Propositions 8.28 and 8.29.

Lemma 8.34 (The stable-range hypothesis). For R = O_{L}, stabilisation

H_{m}(GL_{N}(R), ℤ) −→H_{m}(GL_{N+1}(R), ℤ)

is an isomorphism if N ≥2m + 4.

Proof. We check the ring hypothesis rather than identifying the stable range with the Krull dimension without an argument. Let r_{0}, . . . , r_{t}, t ≥2, generate R. If the first t entries are zero, adding the last entry to each makes the shortened tuple unimodular. Otherwise choose r_{j} ̸= 0, j < t, and k < t, k ̸= j. Only finitely many maximal ideals contain r_{j}. By the Chinese remainder theorem choose u congruent to one at those containing r_{k} and to zero at the others. Replace r_{k} by r_{k} + ur_{t}. A maximal ideal containing the shortened tuple contains r_{j}. If it contains r_{k}, it also contains r_{t} because u ≡1; this contradicts original unimodularity. If it does not contain r_{k}, then u ≡0, again contradicting containment of the adjusted entry. Thus R has Bass stable rank at most two.

Apply W. van der Kallen, Homology stability for linear groups, Invent. Math. 60 (1980), 269–295, The-orem 1.1, p. 269.^{13} For stable rank s, its isomorphism range for GL_{n−1} → GL_{n} is n ≥2m + s + 1. Here s ≤2 and n = N + 1; the asserted, slightly larger range satisfies it. The coefficient module is ℤ, on which the elementary group acts trivially, as required in the theorem.

Proposition 8.35 (The filtered rational rank). For totally complex L, even k ≥2, N ≥2(k + 1) + 4, and prime ℓ, (208) holds.

Proof. We use Borel’s stable real cohomology calculation for the arithmetic general linear group. Its special linear calculation is A. Borel, Stable real cohomology of arithmetic groups, Ann. Sci. ENS (4) 7 (1974), 235– 272, §11.5(3), with the primitive-rank statement also recorded in §12.1–12.2.^{14} For the ring of integers of a totally complex number field, the positive odd-degree primitive generators have dimension r_{2}(L) in each degree at least three; the degree-one determinant-unit part has dimension r_{2}(L)−1. The stable cohomology algebra is exterior on these generators.

We explain the general-linear and repetition conventions in this use of the calculation. Determinant splits the stable general linear group over O_{L}^{×}. Conjugation by a diagonal unit is inner on the stable special linear group: compensate with its inverse in one extra coordinate. The special-linear invariant differential-form generators extend to the general linear group by the same trace formulas. Together with logarithmic determinant-unit classes they give the stated exterior algebra, by the cohomology spectral sequence of this split extension. Lemma 8.38 (At most one exceptional integer per point). For Z ≥ 1, put b = ⌊log_{ℓ}Z⌋. For each σ, at most one integer e ∈[1, Z] satisfies |e −σ|_{ℓ}< ℓ^{−b}. Consequently (215) supplies a set 𝒳_{Z} ⊆[1, Z], of size at most R, outside which

Each subsequent adjacent pair of faces cancels after translating one of the summation variables by one; at the final pair this is the translation of j_{E−1}. The signs of each pair are opposite. The tensor product of the two standard periodic resolutions of a cyclic group computes the homology of C_{q}^{2}. In each periodic resolution the maps alternate between g −1 and 1 + g + · · · + g^{q−1}. Its exactness follows by comparing coefficients in the group ring: the kernel of g−1 consists of constant coefficients, and a coefficient vector of sum zero is a (g−1)-multiple. After trivial R-coefficients, both maps vanish. In degree 2E, their tensor resolution is consequently free of rank 2E + 1. The usual lifting of basis vectors along the surjections in a free resolution constructs chain comparison maps with the bar resolution, so H_{2E}(C_{q}^{2}, R) ≃

Reducing modulo q gives the required relation. A zero homology class is, by definition, a boundary, giving b.

Lemma 8.47 (The finite-field functional). Let k be a finite field containing a primitive q-th root ζ, q = ℓ^{ν}> 1, and let v : k^{×}→ℤ/q be additive on products. ```text

```

u(a, b) = (mod q),

```text

```

where tildes are representatives between 0 and h −1. Associativity of carrying proves du = 0. The cup cochain t = u^{E}⌣v is a (2E + 1)-cocycle, hence kills boundaries. The prism at a central element is a slant

<!-- Source PDF page 504 -->

operator: expanding its insertions in a cup product gives the graded derivation rule on cycles. The slant of u is zero, because its two inserted terms u(g, a) and u(a, g) are equal; the slant of v is v(g). Thus its value on the prism of the scalar image of z is v(g) times the value of the pulled-back u^{E} on z. Pullback along a →→ζ^{xa} sends u to xu_{q} modulo a coboundary, by comparing carries before and after multiplication by x. Finally u^{E}_{q}(z) = 1: in each independent pair (j, 1), precisely j = q −1 contributes a carry. The scalar prism value is therefore x^{E}v(g).

To extend this scalar cocycle to vector spaces, use transfer from a line stabiliser:

[θ_{V} ] = cor^{GL}_{PV}^{(V )}λ^{∗}_{V}[t],

where P_{V} stabilises a line and λ_{V} is its character on that line. Transfer here is a finite coset sum: lift a bar tuple successively along the chosen coset representatives, evaluate the pulled scalar cocycle, and sum over the initial coset. The boundary terms telescope, so it is a cochain map; changing representatives adds a prism coboundary. For dimension zero use zero. In dimension one it is the original scalar class. This also proves isomorphism naturality.

We verify its direct-sum law, which is the reason for the coefficient condition q | |k|−1. Under the block action on V ⊕W, projective lines are those lying in V , those lying in W, and the mixed lines. The first two pieces give the transfers defining θ_{V} , θ_{W} . A mixed line projects to a line in V , with |k|^{dim W}−1 points in every fibre. Its stabiliser character on the mixed line is the pulled-back character on that projected line. Grouping the transfer’s finite coset sum by this projection multiplies its class by |k|^{dim W}−1, which is zero modulo q. Thus the mixed contribution is zero. This proves the direct-sum identity on cycles. Choosing cocycle representatives defines the functionals; changes by coboundaries have no effect on any cycle used here.

Fix x, and put F_{V} (g) = θ_{V} (P_{g}(scal_{ζ}x)_{#}z). Scalar matrices commute with g, so this prism is a cycle. The prism composition identity makes F_{V} a homomorphism to the additive target. The preceding properties make it invariant under isomorphisms and additive on blocks. It vanishes on elementary transvections: conjugating u(a) by diag(ζ, 1) gives u(ζa); the homomorphism identity implies F(u((ζ −1)a)) = 0, and ζ −1 ̸= 0. Elementary row reduction generates SL(V ) by these transvections. Therefore F_{V} (g) depends only on det g. Its value on diag(a, 1, . . . , 1) is the already computed scalar value x^{E}v(a). This proves the claimed formula. Finally reduction preserves boundaries, and adjoining a trivial block contributes zero in positive degree. Repeating a representation d times multiplies its value by d, by direct-sum additivity. These are exactly the three primitive-family properties.

Lemma 8.51 (Restriction to the cyclotomic kernel, with local conditions). Let L be a number field containing µ_{ℓ} if ℓ is odd, or µ_{4} if ℓ= 2. Fix an algebraic closure and write

G = G_{L}, χ = χ_{ℓ}, H = ker χ, A = ℚ_{ℓ}/ℤ_{ℓ}(−E), E ≥1.

Let 𝒟 be the continuous additive characters φ : H →ℚ_{ℓ}/ℤ_{ℓ} that vanish on H ∩I_{w} at every finite place and on H ∩D_{w} at every place above ℓ. Then restriction is an isomorphism

```text
𝒮_{ℓ}(L, E) ≃ {φ ∈𝒟 : φ(g^{−1}hg) = χ(g)^{E}φ(h) (g ∈G, h ∈H)}. (219)
```

All maps are ℤ_{ℓ}-linear.

Proof. We supply the extension and local coboundary arguments, rather than discard the local conditions in a restriction sequence. The image of χ is an infinite closed subgroup of the principal units 1 + ℓℤ_{ℓ}, or 1 + 4ℤ_{2}. It is infinite because

```text
_{φ(ℓ}r_{)}
[L(µ_{ℓ}r) : L] ≥_{[L : ℚ]} −→∞.
```

The degree inequality follows by adjoining the primitive root over ℚ and applying the tower formula. Every nontrivial closed subgroup of these principal units is topologically cyclic. Indeed choose an element with minimal positive valuation a of u −1. Lifting the exponent shows that its powers surject onto each finite

<!-- Source PDF page 509 -->

quotient of 1 + ℓ^{a}ℤ_{ℓ}; their closure is that group. The minimality of a gives the reverse containment for the subgroup. Choose γ ∈G whose image u = χ(γ) is such a topological generator. It has infinite order. Put C = ⟨γ⟩. Compactness shows χ(C) = χ(G), hence G = CH.

Suppose φ is on the right of (219). First φ(C ∩H) = 0. To prove this, choose an open normal subgroup N of G such that φ(H ∩N) = 0. Such N exists by continuity at one and the profinite neighbourhood basis. Let the order of γ in G/N be d = ℓ^{a}d^{′}, with ℓ∤d^{′}. Choose j so large that

u^{m}≡1 (mod ℓ^{j}) =⇒ ℓ^{a}| m.

Lifting the exponent gives this implication also for negative integers m. For x ∈C ∩H, approximate x by a power γ^{m} both modulo N and in the indicated cyclotomic congruence. Then d | md^{′}, so (γ^{m})^{d′}∈N. The group C is abelian, being the closure of a cyclic subgroup, and consequently x^{d′}∈H ∩N. Thus d^{′}φ(x) = 0. As φ(x) has ℓ-power order and ℓ∤d^{′}, this implies φ(x) = 0.

Write ρ(g) = χ(g)^{−E} for the action on A. Define

```text
z(ch) = ρ(c)φ(h) (c ∈C, h ∈H).
```

If ch = c^{′}h^{′}, then c^{′−1}c = h^{′}h^{−1}∈C ∩H. Its φ-value is zero, and H acts trivially on A; these two facts prove independence of the decomposition. The product identity

```text
(ch)(dv) = cd(d^{−1}hd)v
```

and the stipulated equivariance of φ give z(gg^{′}) = z(g) + ρ(g)z(g^{′}). The map C × H →G, (c, h) →→ch, is a continuous surjection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space, hence a quotient map. The defining formula on C × H is continuous, so z is a continuous cocycle. Its restriction to H is φ.

Conversely restricting a cocycle to H gives an additive character, since H acts trivially on A. The cocycle identity gives its displayed equivariance; the terms involving z(g) cancel in conjugation. Coboundaries restrict to zero. If a cocycle has zero restriction, choose m ∈A with

```text
z(γ) = (u^{−E}−1)m.
```

This is possible because u^{−E}−1 ̸= 0 and multiplication by any nonzero element of ℤ_{ℓ} on ℚ_{ℓ}/ℤ_{ℓ} is onto: divide a representative in ℚ_{ℓ}. Subtract its coboundary. The resulting cocycle is zero on H and on all integer powers of γ, then on C by continuity, and then on G = CH. This proves injectivity on cohomology.

It remains to prove that the extended class has exactly the required local behaviour. For w ∤ℓ, inertia fixes the ℓ-power roots of unity: their integral reductions have distinct roots, because the residue characteristic does not divide their order. Thus I_{w} ⊂H, and z(I_{w}) = 0 by the assumption on φ. The cocycle therefore factors through the Galois group unramified outside ℓ; it vanishes on the closed normal subgroup generated by these inertias, using its cocycle identity and their trivial scalar action.

For w | ℓ, the image χ(D_{w}) is again an infinite closed subgroup of the same principal units. Its infinitude follows from

```text
_{φ(ℓ}r_{)}
[L_{w}(µ_{ℓ}r) : L_{w}] ≥_{[Lw : ℚℓ]} −→∞.
```

Here the ℓ-power cyclotomic polynomial over ℚ_{ℓ} has the indicated degree: after replacing X by X + 1 it is Eisenstein at ℓ. The same topological-generator argument applies. The restriction of z to D_{w} vanishes on D_{w} ∩H. Kill its value on a lift of a generator by the divisible scalar argument just used. The residual cocycle is zero on the kernel and on a dense cyclic image, hence on D_{w}. Thus z|_{Dw} is a coboundary. This proves membership in 𝒮_{ℓ}(L, E). In the other direction a locally zero class restricts to zero on these intersections, since coboundaries vanish on H. Both local implications and linearity are now proved.
