Proposition 8.52 (One common operator for every cyclotomic layer). Retain the preceding hypotheses and put χ(G_{L}) = 1 + ℓ^{c0}ℤ_{ℓ}, with c_{0} ≥ 2 when ℓ = 2. Let L_{m} = L(µ_{ℓ}c_{0+}m). There are a single compact ℤ_{ℓ}-module X and, for every E ≥1, a continuous automorphism T_{E}, independent of m, such that

s_{ℓ}(L_{m}, E) = length_{ℤℓ} coker(T_{E}^{ℓm}−1). (220)

Lengths may initially be infinite; the equality includes finiteness in either direction. The generator γ, X, and the untwisted action are fixed before E and m vary.

Proof. All L_{m} have the same infinite cyclotomic extension L_{∞}, and the same cyclotomic kernel H = G_{L∞}. Their group inside G_{L} is

```text
G_{m} = χ^{−1}(1 + ℓ^{c0+m}ℤ_{ℓ}).
```

The lifting-the-exponent calculation shows [G_{L} : G_{m}] = ℓ^{m} and that γ^{ℓm} generates its cyclotomic image. It also shows uniqueness: a finite cyclotomic field of degree ℓ^{m} is this field, since its fixing group is the corresponding principal congruence preimage. In particular this identification is valid for any abstractly given layer after embedding it into the fixed closure.

The module 𝒟 in Lemma 8.51 is common to all these fields. Indeed the inertia group in G_{m} is I_{w} ∩G_{m}, and its intersection with H is I_{w} ∩H; the same statement holds for decomposition groups above ℓ. Every place of each layer is obtained this way. Thus no local vanishing condition is weakened. On 𝒟 define

```text
(τ_{E}φ)(h) = χ(γ)^{−E}φ(γ^{−1}hγ).
```

Conjugation preserves the collection of local subgroups, so this is an automorphism of 𝒟. Its invariants under the group G_{m} are precisely ker(τ_{E}^{ℓm}−1). Lemma 8.53 (A common finite level for finitely many characters). Let L have largest ℓ-power root level c, with the root hypotheses of Lemma 8.51. Suppose every cyclic cyclotomic layer

```text
F = L(µ_{ℓ}ν), ν ≥c, γ(ζ) = ζ^{1+ℓc},
```

has at most B characters ϑ : Cl(F) →ℤ/ℓ^{ν} satisfying

```text
ϑ(γ^{−1}a) = (1 + ℓ^{c})^{E}ϑ(a).
```

Then 𝒮_{ℓ}(L, E) is finite and

```text
ℓ^{sℓ(L,E)}= |𝒮_{ℓ}(L, E)| ≤B.
```

Proof. Take a finite subset of 𝒮_{ℓ}(L, E). Represent each of its restrictions to H by the continuous cocycle z : G_{L} →A constructed in Lemma 8.51. Each has finite image, since G_{L} is compact and A is discrete. At each of the finitely many places w | ℓ choose m_{w} with z(g) = (χ(g)^{−E}−1)m_{w} on D_{w}. Choose a common K annihilating the images of all these cocycles and all their m_{w}’s by ℓ^{K}. The same K handles all conjugate decomposition groups. In fact the cocycle formula shows that a conjugate local coboundary has parameter ρ(g)m_{w} −z(g); scalar units preserve the annihilator, and both terms are killed by ℓ^{K}.

Choose ν ≥ c, K and put U_{ν} = χ^{−1}(1 + ℓ^{ν}ℤ_{ℓ}). Every ρ(u) −1, u ∈ U_{ν}, is divisible by ℓ^{ν}. Thus z|_{Uν} is an additive character: its cocycle multiplication formula has trivial action on every value of z. It is unramified at every finite place. Away from ℓ the original cocycle vanishes on inertia; above ℓ its local coboundary formula is zero on D_{w} ∩U_{ν}. It also remains equivariant for the whole G_{L}, because

```text
z(gug^{−1}) = ρ(g)z(u) + (1 −ρ(u))z(g) = ρ(g)z(u).
```

All its values lie in A[ℓ^{ν}].

We use the unramified reciprocity theorem in precisely its Hilbert-class-field form: for a totally complex number field F, Artin induces an isomorphism from Cl(F) to the Galois group of its maximal abelian ex-tension unramified at all finite places.^{15} Here F is totally complex because it contains the stipulated nonreal root of unity. The character z|_{Uν} therefore factors uniquely through Cl(F). No splitting condition at ℓ is needed for this factorization; its stronger vanishing has already been checked. Identify A[ℓ^{ν}] with ℤ/ℓ^{ν} by a →→a/ℓ^{ν} mod ℤ_{ℓ}. Conjugation naturality of Artin gives, for its class character ϑ,

```text
ϑ(γ^{−1}a) = (1 + ℓ^{c})^{E}ϑ(a).
```

To check the normalization, conjugation by a lift of γ carries a prime Frobenius to that of γP, and the preceding equivariance uses the scalar χ(γ)^{−E}; inverting γ gives the stated scalar. Such a lift exists with cyclotomic value exactly 1 + ℓ^{c}, since the full image is the principal group at level c.

Different original classes give different finite class characters: equality at this common finite level im-plies equality of their restrictions to H, and restriction is injective by (219). Thus the arbitrary finite subset has at most B members. An infinite set would have a subset of size B + 1, so the entire module is finite. A finite ℤ_{ℓ}-module is a direct sum of cyclic ℓ-groups; successively dividing by a subgroup of order ℓ shows its order is ℓ to its module length. Applying the same finite-subset bound to the full module proves the assertion.

s_{ℓ}(L_{m}, e) ≤s_{ℓ}(L_{j0}, e) + R(m −j_{0})_{+}.

Lemma 8.59 (Characters across an index-two subgroup). Let U be an open subgroup of index two in a profinite group V , and let S ⊂ U be stable under conjugation by V . Write 𝒞(V, S) for the continuous homomorphisms V → F_{2} vanishing on S. If |𝒞(V, S)| ≤n, then

```text
|𝒞(U, S)| ≤n^{2}.
```

The same upper bound holds when the index divides two. Finiteness of the left side is part of the conclusion.

Proof. Choose σ ∈ V \ U. Conjugation by σ induces an involution c on 𝒞(U, S), since σ^{2} ∈ U and characters kill inner conjugation. For P = ker(1 + c), define t(φ) = φ(σ^{2}). If t is nonzero choose φ_{0} ∈P with t(φ_{0}) = 1; otherwise put φ_{0} = 0. For φ ∈P, the character

```text
φ̃ = φ + t(φ)φ_{0}
```

is invariant under c and kills σ^{2}. It extends to a character ψ_{φ} of V by assigning value zero to σ: write an element in the two open cosets as uσ^{a}, a = 0, 1, and assign ̃φ(u). In multiplying two such forms, conjugating u does not change its value, and the sole carry σ^{2} has value zero. This proves multiplicativity; openness of U proves continuity. The extension still kills S. Let ϵ be the quotient character V /U → F_{2}, which also kills S. The map

```text
P −→𝒞(V, S), φ −−→ψ_{φ} + t(φ)ϵ
```

is injective: its value at σ records t, and its restriction to U then recovers ̃φ and φ. Hence |P| ≤n.

On 𝒞(U, S), N = 1 + c satisfies N^{2}= 0 in characteristic two. Its kernel is P, and its image lies in P. Every nonempty fibre of N is a coset of its kernel. Therefore the whole space is finite of size at most n^{2}. For index one the spaces are equal and the bound is immediate because n ≥1.

Lemma 8.60 (The cost of allowing one tame prime). Let V be a closed subgroup of an absolute Galois group. Suppose full inertia at a prime p ̸= ℓ lies in V , and the places above p have at most k orbits under V . If the space of F_{ℓ}-valued characters with a specified set of allowed ramified primes has size at most ℓ^{a}, then allowing p in addition raises this bound to at most ℓ^{a+k}.

<!-- Source PDF page 517 -->

Proof. Choose one place in each orbit. Wild inertia there is pro-p, hence has no nonzero continuous additive character to F_{ℓ}. The ℓ-primary tame inertia quotient is procyclic, so choose an element that generates it. Restriction of a character is determined by its value at that element. Record these at the at most k chosen places. If two newly allowed characters have the same record, their difference vanishes on full inertia at each chosen place, and then at every place above p, by conjugation invariance of additive characters. It belongs to the old space. Each record fibre consequently injects into that old space by subtracting a chosen member. There are at most ℓ^{k} records. This proves both finiteness and the asserted cardinality bound.

Proposition 8.61 (A uniform rank for the varying two-prime bases). Fix the abelian field K belonging to M, of degree n_{M}, and put K_{∞} = K(µ_{2}∞). There is an integer g, depending only on M, such that every admissible pair q, d has

```text
( √^{√} )
```

X K(i, −q, −d) generated by at most R = 4(g + 6n_{M}) elements over ℤ_{2}.

Here X is the locally split cyclotomic module of Proposition 8.52. In particular R is chosen before q, d.

Proof. We first state exactly the established Iwasawa input used for this fixed abelian base. For the cyclo-tomic ℤ_{p}-extension of a finite abelian number field, the unramified Iwasawa module is finitely generated over ℤ_{p}. This follows from its finite torsion ℤ_{p}[[T]]-module structure and Ferrero–Washington’s µ = 0 theorem. A precise account is R. Sharifi, Iwasawa Theory, Proposition 3.2.11, Theorem 6.2.1 and the mod-ule structure Theorem 2.1.22; the locally split module is identified in Proposition 3.2.20.^{16} The hypotheses include p = 2; no odd-prime eigenspace assertion is being used here. To spell out the algebraic conse-quence, the structure theorem gives a pseudo-isomorphism to a sum of modules ℤ_{p}[[T]]/(f(T)^{a}), with f distinguished, and no summand ℤ_{p}[[T]]/(p^{b}), since µ = 0. The displayed summands are finite free over ℤ_{p} by division by the monic distinguished polynomial. The kernel and cokernel of the pseudo-isomorphism are finite. Noetherianity of ℤ_{p} therefore proves finite generation over ℤ_{p} itself.

Apply this at p = 2 to the fixed field K(i). Its unramified Iwasawa module has finite F_{2}-dimension g modulo two. By unramified Artin reciprocity, the continuous characters of G_{K∞} unramified at every finite place thus have at most 2^{g} elements.

There are at most 2n_{M} places of K_{∞} above q, and at most 4n_{M} above d. Indeed in ℚ(µ_{2}∞)/ℚ, a decomposition group at an odd prime p has image the closure of the powers of p in ℤ^{×}_{2}. Corollary 8.62 (The fixed and two-prime tower inputs). The tower estimates needed in Proposition 8.41 hold for every fixed admissible abelian base and for the two-prime bases of Lemma 8.42. In the latter case their rank R is uniform before the auxiliary primes vary.

Take a cyclotomic field containing all the character values. Each of its Galois automorphisms permutes the characters of Gal(E/ℚ) and preserves their parity. It also preserves primitive conductors: the kernel and every factorization through a smaller modulus are preserved by an injective coefficient automorphism. The primitive Bernoulli finite sum therefore commutes with that automorphism. Thus the parity product is fixed by the whole Galois group, and is rational. It is integral by the first part, hence is an integer. Every factor is nonzero by Lemma 8.63. The product is consequently nonzero. There are at most n factors, each bounded as above, and the bound is at least one. Taking absolute values and logarithms gives the claimed estimate, also when the parity set is empty and the product is one.

Proposition 8.68 (The reciprocity law used in a Kolyvagin step). Let ℓ be odd, O a finite coefficient discrete valuation ring over ℤ_{ℓ}, D_{O} = Frac(O)/O, and α : G_{ℚ} → O^{×} a continuous character. Put β = χ_{ℓ}α^{−1}. Let 0 ̸= a ∈O, and choose w_{0} ∈D_{O} with annihilator aO. Suppose c, n : G_{ℚ} →D_{O}[a] are continuous cocycles for α, β, respectively. Let N ̸= 0 be divisible by ℓ, and let q ̸= ℓ be prime. Assume the following local conditions, at every conjugate place:

1. Away from the primes dividing Nq, α ≡1 (mod a), and c = n = 0 on inertia.

2. At primes dividing N other than q, c(g) = (α(g) −1)m_{v} on the decomposition group, with am_{v} = 0.

3. At q, both α, β are one modulo a on the decomposition group, and c is zero on inertia.

Then for g ∈D_{q}, τ ∈I_{q}, and y ∈O with n(τ) = yw_{0},

```text
y c(g) = 0.
```

Proof. Use B = O/aO and the identification ι : B →D_{O}[a], ̄z →→zw_{0}. It is injective by the annihilator condition and surjective because D_{O}[a] is a cyclic module of length v_{O}(a). Choose r ≥1 with a | ℓ^{r}; then B is a finite ℤ/ℓ^{r}-algebra. Write c = ιc^{′}, n = ιn^{′}, and reduce α, β to B^{×}. They satisfy αβ = χ_{ℓ} mod B. The cocycle and local conditions pass to these reductions by injectivity of ι. We prove n^{′}(τ)c^{′}(g) = 0 in B.

Let λ : B →ℤ/ℓ^{r} be any ℤ/ℓ^{r}-linear map and form

```text
w(g, h) = λ(n^{′}(g)α(g)c^{′}(h)).
```

The two cocycle identities and αβ = χ_{ℓ} give

```text
χ_{ℓ}(g)w(h, k) −w(gh, k) + w(g, hk) −w(g, h) = 0.
```

For example expand the two middle terms; the n^{′}(g)α(g)α(h)c^{′}(k) terms cancel, and the remaining terms agree because α(g)β(g) = χ_{ℓ}(g). Thus w is a continuous two-cocycle with coefficients ℤ/ℓ^{r}(1). It factors through the Galois group unramified outside Nq. Indeed the common kernel of the scalar characters and both cocycles contains all the excluded inertias and is closed and normal; the identity

```text
c^{′}(gug^{−1}) = c^{′}(g) + α(g)c^{′}(u) + α(gu)c^{′}(g^{−1})
```

shows its normality, and the same calculation applies to n^{′}.

At v | N, v ̸= q, write the local coboundary parameter as m^{′}_{v}∈B. Then the local restriction of w is the coboundary of

```text
b_{v}(g) = −λ(n^{′}(g)α(g)m^{′}_{v}).
```

Expanding db_{v}(g, h) gives exactly w(g, h); the cross terms cancel by the product character identity. At all excluded primes the local class is unramified of degree two and is zero. The sum of the local invariants of the global degree-two class is zero. This is the degree-two localization exactness in Milne, Arithmetic

<!-- Source PDF page 526 -->

Duality Theorems, I, Theorem 4.10(b), already used in Proposition 8.29. At the real place the odd-primary cohomology vanishes by averaging over its group of order two. All invariants except possibly that at q have therefore vanished; the invariant at q is zero too. The local invariant is injective for these coefficients by finite local Tate duality. Consequently w|_{Dq} is a coboundary.

We spell out the local consequence, since the unramified condition on c^{′} matters. Fix a Frobenius σ at q. Any continuous additive homomorphism from D_{q} that vanishes on I_{q} and at σ is zero: it factors through D_{q}/I_{q} ≃ ℤ̂, where the powers of Frobenius are dense. For every unramified character x : D_{q} → ℤ/ℓ^{r}, apply this observation to the B-valued homomorphism

```text
h −−→x(h)c^{′}(σ) −x(σ)c^{′}(h).
```

It gives x(h)c^{′}(σ) = x(σ)c^{′}(h). The function f(g) = λ(n^{′}(g)c^{′}(σ)) is a ℤ/ℓ^{r}(1)-cocycle on D_{q}: the two reduced actions are trivial there, and λ is scalar-linear. Moreover

```text
f(g)x(h) = x(σ)λ(n^{′}(g)c^{′}(h)) = x(σ)w(g, h).
```

Thus its cup product with every unramified x is zero. The unramified subgroups are exact annihilators under local Tate duality: Milne, I, Theorem 2.6, printed pp. 30–31. Its hypotheses hold here because the module ℤ/ℓ^{r} is finite and unramified, and q ̸= ℓ. Hence f is unramified. The cyclotomic character is trivial on inertia at q, so every coboundary vanishes there, and f(τ) = 0. We have proved λ(n^{′}(τ)c^{′}(σ)) = 0. Apply the Frobenius-density observation again to g →→λ(n^{′}(τ)c^{′}(g)). It is zero for every g ∈D_{q}.

Finally these linear maps λ separate the points of B. To see this, decompose its finite ℤ_{ℓ}-module into cyclic modules ℤ/ℓ^{si}, s_{i} ≤ r. A nonzero coordinate is detected by projection followed by multiplication by ℓ^{r−si} into ℤ/ℓ^{r}. It follows that n^{′}(τ)c^{′}(g) = 0. Since n^{′}(τ) = ̄y, applying ι gives y c(g) = 0, as required.

For a general I, choose a prime P of rational prime norm outside M in the inverse ideal class of I. The Hilbert class field and Chebotarev provide such a prime. t∈(ℤ/F)^{×}

Lemma 8.74 (Choosing a prime with two prescribed values). Use the hypotheses on α, F, M of Proposi-tion 8.73. Let r ∤F be prime, T ̸= 0, and let c, ν : H →D_{O}[M] be continuous homomorphisms equivariant under α and β = χ_{ℓ}α^{−1}, respectively. If c ̸= 0, there is an admissible prime q ∤T, a place A | q, and a Frobenius φ ∈H at A such that

```text
c(φ) ̸= 0, ν(H) ⊆Oν(φ).
```

Proof. Choose ρ^{M} = r, and put J = H ∩ Stab(ρ). This is an open subgroup. We use the following elementary radical calculation. If an equivariant homomorphism f : H →W[M], of character γ, vanishes on J, then

```text
(γ(g) −χ_{ℓ}(g))f(u) = 0 (g ∈G_{ℚ}, u ∈H). (229)
```

Indeed uρ = ξρ with ξ ∈µ_{M}. If k represents χ_{ℓ}(g) mod M, then gug^{−1}ρ = ξ^{k}ρ = u^{k}ρ. Thus gug^{−1}= u^{k}v with v ∈J. Applying f gives γ(g)f(u) = kf(u) = χ_{ℓ}(g)f(u); the last equality uses Mf(u) = 0.

Let B = ker c, an open subgroup of H. It does not contain J: otherwise (229), with γ = α, and the unit α(δ) −χ_{ℓ}(δ), would force c = 0. The compact group H has finite image under ν. The cyclic submodules of D_{O} are totally ordered by inclusion: a nonzero element represented by π^{−j}v, v ∈O^{×}, generates exactly D_{O}[π^{j}]. Choose u_{∗} ∈ H with maximal cyclic module Oν(u_{∗}). It contains the entire image of ν. If that image is zero put K = B. Otherwise put

```text
P = 𝔪_{O}ν(u_{∗}), K = {u ∈H : ν(u) ∈P}.
```

This too is an open subgroup, and J is not contained in it. For if it were, apply (229) to ν mod P. For a lift g of −1 mod F, α(g) + 1 ∈MO ⊂𝔪_{O}. Consequently 1 −α(g) is a unit: otherwise their sum 2 would be in 𝔪_{O}, contrary to ℓ̸= 2. But β(g) −χ_{ℓ}(g) = β(g)(1 −α(g)) is then a unit, forcing ν(u_{∗}) ∈P. This means ν(u_{∗}) = vν(u_{∗}) for some v ∈𝔪_{O}. As 1 −v is a unit, it forces ν(u_{∗}) = 0, a contradiction. For φ /∈K, its coefficient in ν(φ) = vν(u_{∗}) is a unit; thus ν(φ) generates the O-span of ν(H).

The third subgroup to avoid is C = G_{ℚ(µF ℓ)}. We claim J ⊂⊂C. Choose u, g ∈G_{ℚ} acting on µ_{Fℓ} as 1 + F and −1. The first is a unit modulo Fℓ, since ℓ| F. Then u ∈H, and

```text
gug^{−1}u ∈J.
```

For verification, write uρ = ξρ and g^{−1}ρ = ηρ, with ξ, η ∈µ_{M} ⊂µ_{F} . The element u fixes η, g inverts ξ, and gug^{−1} fixes ξ, giving gug^{−1}uρ = ρ. Its action on µ_{Fℓ}, however, is (1 + F)^{2}. If it lay in C, then Fℓ| F(F + 2), whence ℓ| 2, which is impossible.

We need one element of J outside K ∪B ∪C. Here is the group argument with its oddness hypothesis explicit. A group cannot be the union of two proper subgroups: elements outside each give, if necessary,

<!-- Source PDF page 536 -->

their product outside both. Suppose a group J is a union of three proper subgroups A, B, C, and each x ∈J has x^{k} ∈B for one fixed odd integer k. Choose x /∈B ∪C and y /∈A ∪C. The covering forces x ∈A, y ∈B, and xy ∈C. Now x^{2}y lies in neither A nor C: membership in A would put y in A, and membership in C, together with xy ∈ C, would put x in C. Thus x^{2}y ∈ B, so x^{2} ∈ B. Since k = 2j + 1, also x = x^{k}(x^{2})^{−j} ∈B, a contradiction. Apply this argument to the three intersections with J. Here x^{M} ∈B, since c(x^{M}) = Mc(x) = 0, and M is odd. We obtain a nonempty open set

```text
V = J \ (K ∪B ∪C).
```

All the subgroups removed are open and closed; thus V is open in G_{ℚ}.

By Lemma 8.43, there are q ∤TFℓr, a place A | q, and a Frobenius φ ∈V . For precision, Chebotarev gives a finite quotient conjugacy class contained in the image of V ; choosing the prime above q chooses the required member, so no conjugacy-invariance of V is being assumed. Since φ ∈H, its action on µ_{F} gives q ≡1 (mod F); write q = 1 + Fk. Since φ /∈C, ℓ∤k. It fixes ρ, whereas Frobenius acts on its residue by the q-th power. As q ̸= r, ρ is a local unit, and

ρ = φρ ≡ρ^{q}= ρ r^{N0k} (mod A).

It follows that r^{N0k}≡1 (mod q). Thus ord_{q}(r) | N_{0}k, which is prime to ℓ. This proves admissibility. The exclusions from B and K give the two required values.

Proposition 8.75 (Discharging the descent inputs). In the notation of Proposition 8.17, take z = z_{b} from

Proposition 8.73. If a_{0}z | M, then all three construction, prime-choice, and reciprocity assertions preceding that proposition hold. Consequently

length_{O} 𝒞(1) ≤v_{O}(z).

Proof. The construction is Proposition 8.73, with w = 1/M mod O, whose annihilator is (M). We check that the normalized cocycles and these homomorphisms meet exactly the prime-choice and reciprocity hy-potheses.

Since a_{0} | M, α|_{H} acts trivially on D_{O}[a_{0}]. For a cocycle c ∈𝒞(n) its restriction to H is additive, killed by M, and has conjugation character α: expand the cocycle identity for gug^{−1}, and cancel c(g) + α(g)c(g^{−1}) = 0. It is nonzero if c ̸= 0. Indeed if it vanishes on H, the commutator gδ_{0}g^{−1}δ_{0}^{−1} lies in H, where δ_{0} is the normalizing element with α(δ_{0}) −1 a unit. Comparing c(gδ_{0}) and c(δ_{0}g), using c(δ_{0}) = 0, gives (α(δ_{0}) −1)c(g) = 0. Thus c = 0. Lemma 8.74 applies to c|_{H}, ν_{L}, with T =∏L.

For reciprocity a homomorphism on H must first be extended to a global cocycle. There is d ∈G_{ℚ} with β(d) −1 a unit, since β(d) −1 = −α(d)^{−1}(α(d) −χ_{ℓ}(d)). For an equivariant ν : H →D_{O}, define

```text
n(g) = −(β(d) −1)^{−1}ν(gdg^{−1}d^{−1}).
```

Every commutator lies in H, and the map is locally constant. The identity

```text
[gh, d] = g[h, d]g^{−1}[g, d]
```

and equivariance show that n(gh) = n(g) + β(g)n(h). For u ∈ H, ν([u, d]) = (1 −β(d))ν(u), so n(u) = ν(u). Every value of n is a scalar multiple of a value of ν; in particular any annihilator of ν(H) also kills n.

Let (a^{′}) = ann(ν(H)) and (a) = ann(ν(τ)) at the new prime. Then a | a^{′}| M, and both are nonzero. Write a^{′} = ae, and choose w_{0} of annihilator (a^{′}). Since a^{′}ν(τ) = 0, some y ∈ O has ν(τ) = yw_{0}.

<!-- Source PDF page 537 -->

Proposition 8.68 then gives y c(φ) = 0. Its local hypotheses are met as follows. At primes outside Fnq both cocycles are unramified; inertia lies in H, where the extension agrees with ν. At primes over F, the defining local coboundaries for c have primitives killed by a_{0}, hence by a^{′}. At the additional primes over n, c is zero on decomposition groups. At q, the decomposition group lies in H: its inertia fixes µ_{F} and its Frobenius acts by q ≡1 (mod F). Both α and β are therefore one modulo a^{′} there. Finally c is unramified at q. These are precisely the local conditions used in that reciprocity proposition.

To pass from y to e, use the total divisibility order in the discrete valuation ring. If y | a^{′}, write a^{′}= yt. Then tν(τ) = a^{′}w_{0} = 0, so a | t; write t = as. Cancelling a ̸= 0 from ae = yas gives e = ys, and hence e c(φ) = 0. If a^{′}| y, then ν(τ) = 0, so a is a unit. Since a_{0} | a in the descent step, a_{0} is a unit and c = 0, giving the same conclusion.

The remaining kernel identification in the descent is also exact. If c(φ) = 0, then its restriction at q is zero, because it is unramified there and a Frobenius topologically generates the unramified quotient. Conjugation equivariance transports this vanishing to every place over q. Thus the kernel of evaluation imposes exactly the extra splitting condition in 𝒞(nq). All three inputs of Proposition 8.17 are now proved; applying it gives the claimed bound.

Lemma 8.77 (The exceptional residual cyclotomic character). Let ℓ be odd, O as above, and α : G_{ℚ} →O^{×} a character congruent to χ_{ℓ} modulo the maximal ideal (π) of O. Suppose α is unramified outside ℓ. Then its everywhere-unramified, ℓ-locally trivial group of classes in H^{1}(ℚ, D_{O}(α)) is zero.

Proof. Choose t in inertia at ℓ acting on µ_{ℓ} by inversion. Such a t exists by the inertia surjectivity used in Lemma 8.72. Since ℓ is odd, α(t) −1 ≡−2 (mod π) is a unit. Every cohomology class has a unique cocycle representative c with c(t) = 0: subtract the coboundary of (α(t)−1)^{−1}c(t). If its restriction to G_{ℚℓ} is a coboundary, the primitive must be zero, by evaluating at t. Thus this normalized c vanishes on G_{ℚℓ}. At every other prime inertia acts trivially on the coefficient module; being a coboundary on inertia means that c itself vanishes there.

First suppose πc = 0. The values lie in the residue vector space D_{O}[π], which is killed by ℓ, and the action of G_{ℚ} on it is the scalar mod-ℓ cyclotomic character. Compose with any additive F_{ℓ}-linear functional D_{O}[π] → F_{ℓ}. The resulting cocycle z has the mod-ℓ cyclotomic action and vanishes on inertia at every finite prime. Identify F_{ℓ}(1) with µ_{ℓ} using a primitive root. The elementary Kummer description gives

```text
a ∈ℚ^{×}, θ^{ℓ}= a, gθ = ζ_{ℓ}^{z(g)}θ.
```

For completeness this description follows from multiplicative Hilbert 90 for the root-valued cocycle. In a

```text
−z(g)
```

finite Galois extension through which it factors, choose x for which the sum ∑_{g}ζ_{ℓ} g(x) is nonzero; such an x exists by linear independence of distinct field automorphisms. Call the sum θ. Changing the index gives the displayed transformation law, so θ^{ℓ} is fixed and lies in ℚ^{×}.

Because z vanishes on inertia, θ is inertia-fixed at each prime. In an unramified local extension its valuation is integral. Thus ℓ | v_{p}(a) for every rational prime p. Unique factorization in ℚ^{×} then gives a = y^{ℓ}, y ∈ℚ^{×}: divide each prime exponent by ℓ and absorb the sign, since ℓ is odd. Therefore θ/y ∈µ_{ℓ}, and z is a coboundary, say z(g) = (χ_{ℓ}(g) −1)j. Its normalization z(t) = 0, with χ_{ℓ}(t) −1 = −2 ̸= 0, gives j = 0, so z = 0. Linear functionals separate the points of a vector space, hence c = 0.

A locally constant cocycle on the compact group G_{ℚ} has finite image, and every element of D_{O} is killed by a power of π. Thus some π^{k} kills c. Induct on k. The cocycle π^{k−1}c satisfies the same normalization and local conditions, and is killed by π; it is zero by the case just proved. Apply the induction hypothesis to c with the smaller exponent. This proves that every normalized representative, and hence every class, is zero.

Theorem 8.78 (The good-prime Bernoulli character bound). Inequality (206) holds. In particular the minus estimate of Proposition 8.16 has no remaining Euler-system input.

Proof. First let ψ be primitive of conductor f, order prime to ℓ, and parity ψ(−1) = (−1)^{e+1}, and put α = (χ_{ℓ}^{e}ψ)^{−1}. We prove the bound for its classes over ℚ with coefficients D_{O}(α). At p ̸= ℓ, the cyclotomic character is trivial on inertia, so the action there is ψ^{−1}. A nontrivial root of unity of order prime to ℓ differs from one by a unit of O. Indeed, if x^{h}= 1, x ̸= 1, and ℓ∤h, then ∑^{h}_{i=0}^{−1}x^{i} = 0; reducing x ≡1 modulo the maximal ideal would imply h = 0 in its residue field, a contradiction. Primitivity also ensures that at every prime dividing f some inertia element acts nontrivially under ψ. Otherwise ψ would be trivial on the kernel removing that prime-power component of (ℤ/f)^{×}, and would factor through a proper divisor of its conductor. Inertia maps onto this component by the cyclotomic inertia surjectivity. Outside f, it acts trivially.

If α(g)−χ_{ℓ}(g) is a nonunit for every g, then α ≡χ_{ℓ} (mod π). On inertia away from ℓ this implies ψ^{−1}≡ 1 (mod π). The preceding prime-to-ℓ root-of-unity observation forces ψ = 1 there, so α is unramified outside ℓ. Lemma 8.77 gives zero for the class group in question, which proves the desired inequality.

Otherwise Lemma 8.76 applies. Choose a lift δ_{0} of complex conjugation. The character α(δ_{0}) = −1 exactly, so α(δ_{0})−1 = −2 is a unit. Normalize every cocycle by c(δ_{0}) = 0. Every class under consideration has such a representative in 𝒞(1) for some nonzero a_{0}, with the ramification set the primes dividing fℓ. Here are the local and finiteness details. Its finite image is killed by one nonzero scalar. At ℓ, choose a local coboundary primitive and include its annihilator in that scalar. At a prime p | f, p ̸= ℓ, the class is an inertia coboundary, say c|_{Ip} = (α −1)m_{p}. Choose g_{p} ∈ I_{p} with α(g_{p}) −1 a unit. Any scalar killing c kills m_{p} by evaluating at g_{p}. Moreover the same primitive works on the entire decomposition group: subtract its coboundary; the resulting cocycle vanishes on inertia, and comparison at g_{p} and d^{−1}g_{p}d gives (α(g_{p}) −1)c(d) = 0 for every decomposition element d. Thus c(d) = 0. Conjugating places sends the primitive to α(σ)m_{p} −c(σ); the same scalar kills it. Outside fℓ the coefficient character is unramified, so the local inertia coboundary condition means literal vanishing on inertia. These verifications give exactly the defining conditions of 𝒞(1).

length_{O} 𝒞(1) ≤v_{O}(z_{b}) ≤v_{O}(A_{ψ}).

Thus the full class group has length at most v_{O}(A_{ψ}).

Lemma 8.81 (The split-place choice used by the local cover). Let E/E^{+} be CM, with complex conjugation c. If a finite prime v of E differs from cv, then the prime v_{0} below it splits in E. There is an E^{+}-embedding E →E_{v}^{+}_{0} inducing either of the two primes, and one may choose a uniformizer of E_{v}^{+}_{0} for the corresponding split Hecke operator. The abstract conjugation of the host is this c whenever its complex embeddings satisfy the host conjugation rule.

Proof. Choose x ∈v with cx /∈v. Such an x exists, since inclusion of one of the distinct maximal ideals in the other would imply equality. The elements

```text
a = x + cx, b = x cx
```

are in O_{E}+, with a /∈ v_{0} and b ∈ v_{0}. The polynomial T^{2}−aT + b consequently has the simple root 0 modulo v_{0}; its derivative there is the unit −a. Hensel lifting gives a root in O_{Ev}+_{0}. As x /∈ E^{+}, the same

polynomial is its degree-two minimal polynomial, and E = E^{+}(x). Sending x to the lifted root defines the desired embedding. Composing with c gives the other choice. There are no other primes over v_{0}: if a third maximal ideal w existed, choose z ∈w outside both v and cv. This is possible by taking one element for each exclusion and, if necessary, their sum. Then z cz ∈w ∩O_{E}+ = v_{0}, so z cz ∈v, contradicting the two exclusions and primality of v. Thus the two embeddings give exactly the two primes, and the orientation required for the conjugate-prime Hecke operator can be chosen. The local field has a uniformizer by its discrete valuation; it is the uniformizer used in the statement.

Finally fix a complex embedding ι : E ↪→ℂ. The host rule says ι(c_{host}z) = ι(z). Complex conjugation on a CM field has the same property. Injectivity of ι therefore gives c_{host}z = cz for every z.

Proof. We give the simultaneous decomposition argument. A split endomorphism of a finite-dimensional space is the direct sum of its generalized eigenspaces: the factors (T −λ)^{d} for its distinct eigenvalues are pairwise coprime, and their Bezout identities give complementary polynomial projections. Every operator commuting with it preserves these spaces. Thus a finite commuting set can be decomposed successively in this way. For an arbitrary set S, choose a finite subset whose decomposition has the maximal possible num-ber of nonzero summands; that number is at most dim V . Each additional s ∈S preserves these summands. If it had two eigenvalues on one, decomposing that summand would increase their number, a contradiction. Hence every s has one eigenvalue on each summand. Successive refinement, or the same polynomial pro-jections, shows that these are exactly the joint generalized eigenspaces. On each summand simultaneous triangularization of the commuting nilpotent remainders makes every diagonal entry a character of A. It takes values in O, since the eigenvalues of the generators do. Distinct characters give disjoint summands: some generator distinguishes them, and its two generalized eigenspaces are disjoint. We have proved

```text
V =⊕V_{ψ} =⊕P_{𝔪}, P_{𝔪} ∩Q_{𝔪} = 0.
ψ 𝔪
```

Only finitely many characters and groups occur. No semisimplicity of the Hecke action has been assumed.

Summing over the distinct, exhaustive labels proves (233). Lemma 8.96 (A compact reproducer for the selected lowest vector). Let σ be an irreducible admissible continuous unitary representation of the real unitary group G, and let w be a K-finite vector for its maximal compact subgroup K. Then there is a continuous compactly supported scalar function α on G such that

```text
∫_{G}α(g)σ(g)w dg = w.
```

The integral is absolutely convergent, and α is bounded.

Proof. There is nothing to prove if w = 0; take α = 0. Otherwise let

```text
𝒱 = {σ(ϕ)w : ϕ ∈C_{c}(G)}, σ(ϕ)w =∫_{G}ϕ(g)σ(g)w dg.
```

This is a linear subspace. It is invariant under G, since left translation of ϕ is still continuous with compact support. It is nonzero: choose a nonnegative compactly supported function of integral one in a neighborhood of 1 on which Re⟨w, σ(g)w⟩> ‖w‖^{2}/2. Its integral applied to w has nonzero inner product with w. Thus its closed invariant span is all of H, by irreducibility; equivalently 𝒱 is dense.

Choose the finite list of irreducible K-types occurring in the K-span of w. Compact-group character projection gives a continuous function e on K whose averaging operator

```text
T(v) =∫_{K}e(k)σ(k)v dk
```

fixes w and has range in the sum of those isotypic spaces. Explicitly, for normalized∑ K-Haar measure take e(k) =_{τ}(dim τ)χ_{τ}(k). Character orthogonality makes this the identity on the indicated types and zero on the others. This orthogonality follows by averaging an operator between two irreducible finite dimensional unitary representations: the average intertwines them, so is zero for distinct types and is scalar, with scalar fixed by its trace, for equal types. Admissibility makes the resulting range finite dimensional.

The subspace T(𝒱) is consequently finite dimensional and closed in H. Continuity of T and density of 𝒱 show that T(w) = w lies in its closure, hence in T(𝒱). Choose ϕ ∈C_{c}(G) with T(σ(ϕ)w) = w. Fubini on the compact support gives

```text
T(σ(ϕ)w) = σ(α)w, α(g) =∫_{K}e(k)ϕ(k^{−1}g) dk.
```

The function α is continuous, by uniform continuity on compact neighborhoods of its support, and its support lies in the compact set K supp ϕ. It is bounded there and zero elsewhere. Finally ‖α(g)σ(g)w‖= |α(g)|‖w‖, so compact support and local finiteness of Haar measure give absolute integrability.

In the selected data w belongs to the algebraic sum of lowest K-type subspaces. A vector in such a sum is a finite sum; the sum of its finitely many finite dimensional stable subspaces is again finite dimensional and stable. Thus it is K-finite, as required here.

Proof. We give the finite dimensional argument underlying the source’s Bochner inequality. Here ρ_{C}(a), respectively ρ_{N}(a), is half the number of indices above a of the same, respectively different, sign minus half the number below a of that sign. Thus ρ = ρ_{C} + ρ_{N}, with ρ(a) = (n −1)/2 −a. The compact Casimir eigenvalue on a highest vector of weight η is

```text
c_{K}(η) = ‖η + ρ_{C}‖^{2}−‖ρ_{C}‖^{2}.
```

To check this normalization, pair the terms E_{ab}E_{ba}, E_{ba}E_{ab} for equal-sign a < b. The raising operator kills the highest vector, and the commutator contributes η_{a} −η_{b}. The diagonal terms contribute ∑_{a}η_{a}^{2}. Their sum is ‖η‖^{2}+ 2⟨η, ρ_{C}⟩, as asserted.

Write L_{0} = V and ∑

```text
L_{j+1} = L_{j} + E_{ab}L_{j}.
```

different signs a,b

Each L_{j} is finite dimensional and compact-stable. For compact E_{ab}, commuting it across a noncompact E_{cd} produces δ_{bc}E_{ad} −δ_{da}E_{cb}, whose nonzero terms are again noncompact. This proves stability inductively. It also shows that ∪_{j}L_{j} is the full generated module. The Casimir is central, by cancellation of the same commutator formula in its double sum. Consequently Ω= c_{λ} on every L_{j}.

First exclude a highest vector z ̸= 0 of weight Λ −α_{ab}, a < b of different signs, where α_{ab} = e_{a} −e_{b}. Pair the Casimir terms using the order which is the usual raising order on compact roots and the opposite order on noncompact roots. The adjoint signs give the exact identity

```text
c_{λ}‖z‖^{2}=(‖η + ρ∑_{C} −ρ_{N}‖^{2}−‖ρ_{C} −ρ_{N}‖^{2})‖z‖^{2}
−2 ‖E_{ba}z‖^{2}, η = Λ −α_{ab}.
a<b
```

different signs

Indeed the compact raising terms vanish; each reversed noncompact pair contributes its diagonal commutator and the negative of twice the squared norm of its remaining operator. The diagonal commutator sum is 2⟨η, ρ_{C} −ρ_{N}⟩. Dropping the final nonpositive sum, substituting η + ρ_{C} −ρ_{N} = λ −α_{ab}, and using ‖α_{ab}‖^{2}= 2, would imply

```text
0 ≤2 −2(λ_{a} −λ_{b}) + 4⟨ρ_{C}, ρ_{N}⟩.
```

But 2⟨ρ_{C}, ρ_{N}⟩≤npq. For completeness, if o_{a} is the number of indices opposite to a, then |2ρ_{C}(a)| ≤n, |2ρ_{N}(a)| ≤o_{a}, and ∑_{a}o_{a} = 2pq. Summing 2ρ_{C}(a)ρ_{N}(a) ≤no_{a}/2 proves the bound. Since λ_{a} −λ_{b} ≥ h > npq + 1, we have the required contradiction.

We next quantify the cost of entering a new layer. Let 𝔭_{ℂ} be the span of the different-sign matrix units, with its orthonormal matrix-unit basis. On B_{j} = 𝔭^{⊗}_{ℂ}^{j}⊗V use the tensor compact action, and define the contraction

```text
Φ_{j}(X_{1} ⊗· · · ⊗X_{j} ⊗v) = E(X_{1}) · · · E(X_{j})v.
```

Its image together with L_{j−1} is L_{j}. This follows by induction, commuting a compact factor to the right and then using compact stability of V . The contraction is compact-equivariant, directly from the displayed commutator relation.

On B_{1} the compact Casimir expands as

```text
Ω^{B}_{K}^{1}= nI + c_{K}(Λ)I + 2C,
```

where C = ∑ ad(e_{ab}) ⊗E_{ba}. The adjoint identities show that C is symmetric. Every highest

same-sign a,b weight occurring in B_{1} has form Λ+α_{rs} for different-sign r, s. Here is the elementary weight argument used in the source. Write a highest tensor as a matrix-indexed family F_{rs} ∈V , and choose a nonzero coordinate

<!-- Source PDF page 583 -->

maximizing r −s. The raising equation in that coordinate has extra coordinates with strictly larger r −s, which therefore vanish. This coordinate is a highest vector of V ; its weight is Λ. The diagonal equations then give the asserted tensor weight. For j tensor factors, the same argument maximizes ∑_{i}(r_{i} −s_{i}) and gives a sum of j noncompact roots.

On such a highest vector the eigenvalue θ of C is

```text
θ = λ_{r} + ρ_{N}(r) −λ_{s} −ρ_{N}(s) + 1 −n/2.
```

If r < s, the opposite-index counts give ρ_{N}(r) −ρ_{N}(s) ≥ 2 −n/2, and hence θ ≥ h −n + 1 > 0. Indeed each endpoint contributes its other endpoint to its above or below opposite-sign count, while their total opposite-sign counts sum to n. If s < r, the reversed inequality gives θ ≤−h −1 < 0. These are all eigenvalues: each eigenspace of C is compact-stable, and a nonzero finite dimensional compact-stable space contains a highest vector. Thus B_{1} = W_{−}⊥W_{+}, where C is negative on W_{−} and at least h −n + 1 on W_{+}.

The image Φ_{1}(W_{−}) is zero. Otherwise its nonzero compact-stable image has a highest vector, which can be lifted to a highest vector in the orthogonal complement of the kernel of Φ_{1}. The preceding calculation gives its weight Λ −α_{ab}, a < b of different signs. This is impossible by the first part of the proof. In B_{j}, a tensor whose slices at one position lie in W_{−} therefore contracts into L_{j−1}. Move that position to the last one; the last-position contraction is zero. The change from permuting two positions is a commutator of two noncompact operators. It is compact and can be moved through the remaining operators to V ; every resulting word has at most j −1 noncompact factors. This proves the assertion for any position.

Now let z ∈L_{j}∩L^{⊥}_{j−1}, j ≥1, be a nonzero highest vector of weight η. Restrict the map (I−proj_{Lj−1})Φ_{j} to the orthogonal complement of its kernel in B_{j}. It is an injective compact intertwiner onto its image, and z is in this image. Its inverse gives a nonzero highest lift P of z. The slice observation shows that P is orthogonal to every tensor with a W_{−} slice, so each of its one-position slices lies in W_{+}. For clarity, project any fixed slice onto W_{−}, insert that projection into the fixed other coordinates, and pair with P. The resulting inner product is the squared norm of that projection, so it must vanish. This proves the slice claim without an assumption that P is a pure tensor.

Expanding the compact Casimir on B_{j} gives

```text

i=1
```

The first term is nonnegative: it is a sum of a compact generator times its adjoint. Summing the preceding one-slice lower bounds gives

```text

```

The norm ‖P‖^{2}> 0 cancels from this inequality. The compact Casimir eigenvalue formula proves that it is indeed c_{K}(η) on P.

Finally decompose a highest vector in L_{m} by the successive orthogonal differences

```text
⊕m
L_{m} = V ⊥ (L_{j} ∩L^{⊥}_{j−1}).
j=1
```

All projections preserve its highest equations, since each summand and its orthogonal complement are compact-stable. For weight η = Λ, every nonzero positive-layer component would satisfy c_{K}(Λ) ≥ c_{K}(Λ) + 2j(h −n + 1), which is impossible. Thus only the component in V remains.

Lemma 8.110 (Taylor closure of the generated module). Let σ be a strongly continuous unitary representa-tion of U(p, q). Suppose the operators of Lemma 8.109 are its derived action on a common invariant domain D. For any finite dimensional compact-stable V ⊂D on which the Casimir is a real scalar c, the Hilbert closure of its algebraically generated module is σ(G)-stable.

Proof. We retain the layers L_{k} from the preceding proof; the gap assumption and irreducibility of V are not needed here. The commuting symmetric diagonal operators have a simultaneous orthonormal eigenbasis on V . Their finite set of real weights ν has a bound ‖ν + ρ_{C}‖≤ R, R ≥ 0. Commuting a diagonal operator through E_{ab} adds the weight α_{ab}. Induction on k therefore spans L_{k} by weight vectors of weights ν + α_{1} + · · · + α_{j}, j ≤k, where all α_{i} are noncompact roots. An eigenvector of a different weight cannot lie in their span: a product of diagonal operators minus the unwanted eigenvalues kills any given finite list_{√} while acting nontrivially on that eigenvector. Since every root has Euclidean norm_{√} 2, every highest weight η in L_{k} satisfies ‖η + ρ_{C}‖≤R + 2k. Finite dimensional compact complete reducibility and the compact Casimir formula now give

```text
ℜ⟨Ω_{K}x, x⟩≤((R +^{√}2k)^{2}−‖ρ_{C}‖^{2})‖x‖^{2} (x ∈L_{k}).
```

The noncompact adjoint sign in the full Casimir gives the exact energy identity

```text
c‖x‖^{2}= ℜ⟨Ω_{K}x, x⟩− ∑ ‖E_{ab}x‖^{2}.
```

different signs a,b

Indeed a term E√_{ab}E_{ba} pairs with x as minus ‖E_{ba}x‖^{2}; swapping a, b reindexes the sum. Put d = ‖ρ_{C}‖^{2}+ c and A = R+ max(0, −d). For a Hermitian noncompact X, let S = ‖X‖_{F}. Cauchy–Schwarz in its matrix entries and the energy identity imply

```text
‖E(X)x‖≤S(A +^{√}2k)‖x‖, x ∈L_{k}.
√ √ √ √
```

Here (R + 2k)^{2}−d ≤ R + 2k + max(0, −d); squaring the nonnegative right side verifies this. Moreover E(X)L_{k} ⊂L_{k+1}. Iteration yields

```text
m∏−1_{√}
‖E(X)^{m}x‖≤S^{m} (A + 2(k + ℓ)) ‖x‖.
ℓ=0
√
```

For r_{√} 2S < 1, this majorant multiplied by r^{m}/m! is summable by the ratio test: its successive ratio tends to r 2S.

The orbit t →→σ(e^{tX})x has m-th derivative σ(e^{tX})E(X)^{m}x. This follows inductively from the derived-action hypothesis and the one-parameter group law. Taylor’s integral remainder, unitarity and the preceding majorant therefore give

```text
∑_{(t −t0)}m_{√}
σ(e^{tX})x = σ(e^{t0X})E(X)^{m}x if |t −t_{0}| 2S < 1.
m≥0^{m!}
```

Explicitly its remainder is at most_{√} |t −t_{0}|^{m}‖E(X)^{m}x‖/m!, which tends to zero by the same ratio estimate. Choose an integer N > 2S. Induction over j = 0, . . . , N in this Taylor formula, at t_{0} = j/N and t = (j + 1)/N, shows that σ(e^{jX/N})x belongs to the closed generated space for every algebraic x. Every term involves E(X)^{m}x, which is still in the algebraic generated space. At j = N we obtain invariance under e^{X}; continuity extends it to the closure.

The compact group preserves the algebraic generated space. On V this is assumed; on words it follows from σ(k)E(X)σ(k)^{−1}= E(kXk^{−1}), obtained by differentiating the group identity. Compact conjugation preserves the noncompact subspace. Finally every g ∈U(p, q) has polar decomposition g = ke^{X} with such k, X, as used above. It follows that the closed generated space is invariant under every σ(g).

Proposition 8.111 (Rigidity of lowest-type coefficients and the resulting isometry). Let (σ_{i}, H_{i}, D_{i}, E_{i}, V_{i}), i = 1, 2, have the hypotheses of Lemma 8.109, with the same sign pattern and parameter λ. Suppose each σ_{i} is strongly continuous and unitary, each E_{i} is its derived action on D_{i}, and each V_{i} is stable under the compact group. If φ : V_{1} →V_{2} is a compact-equivariant linear isometry, then

```text
⟨φv^{′}, σ_{2}(g)φv⟩= ⟨v^{′}, σ_{1}(g)v⟩ (g ∈G, v, v^{′}∈V_{1}).
```

It extends uniquely to a unitary intertwiner between the closed cyclic spaces generated by V_{1} and φV_{1}. For irreducible σ_{i}, these spaces are H_{i}.

Proof. We first prove the orthogonality assertion used by the source. Work in one such representation, and let j : V → H be a compact intertwiner satisfying ⟨jv^{′}, v⟩ = 0 for all v, v^{′} ∈ V . We claim that jV is orthogonal to the whole algebraic module generated by V .

Extend j to a continuous linear operator J : H →H by orthogonal projection onto V , followed by j. For a compact Lie algebra element Z, differentiate the constant function

```text
t −−→⟨Jσ(e^{tZ})v, σ(e^{tZ})y⟩= ⟨jv, y⟩, v ∈V, y ∈D.
```

The equality uses compact equivariance of j and unitarity of σ; the compact orbit of v stays in V , so J acts as j on it. Using the two compact elements e_{ab} −e_{ba} and i(e_{ab} + e_{ba}) for equal-sign a, b, and adding their differentiated identities, gives

```text
⟨JE_{ab}v, y⟩= ⟨jv, E_{ba}y⟩.

It extends by completeness to an isometry of the closed cyclic spaces. Its image contains every orbit vector on the second side and is closed, so it is onto that closed cyclic space. On orbit sums it intertwines the group actions; continuity proves this on the closures. For an irreducible unitary representation any nonzero closed invariant cyclic space is the whole space. The irreducible compact types here are nonzero, so the last assertion follows.

Lemma 8.113 (The L^{2} model embedding and its smooth-vector regularity). Let G = U(p, q) with signature ε, maximal compact subgroup K = {k ∈U(n) : kJ = Jk} ^{∼}= U(p) × U(q), and Haar measure µ. Let λ ∈ℝ^{n} be strictly decreasing with opposite-sign gap at least h > npq + 1, and let (τ, V_{τ}) be an irreducible finite dimensional unitary representation of K of highest weight Λ = λ + ρ_{N} −ρ_{C}, with unit highest vector w_{τ}. Suppose Ψ : G → End(V_{τ}) satisfies the five model-coefficient axioms (IsPsiFor):

(i) Ψ(k_{1}gk_{2}) = τ(k_{1})Ψ(g)τ(k_{2}) for all k_{1}, k_{2} ∈K and g ∈G;

(ii) Ψ(1) = I_{Vτ} ;

(iii) Ψ ∈C^{∞}(G, End(V_{τ})) (locally extending smoothly on Mat_{n}(ℂ));

operator and c_{λ} = ‖λ‖^{2}−‖ρ_{C} + ρ_{N}‖^{2};

(v) Ψ ∈L^{2}(G, µ; End(V_{τ})).

Fix a nonzero vector v_{0} ∈V_{τ}. Define the scalar functions j_{v0}(v)(g) = ⟨v_{0}, Ψ(g)v⟩ and the linear map J_{v0} : V_{τ} → L^{2}(G, µ) sending v to the class of j_{v0}(v), where L^{2}(G, µ) carries the right-regular representation

```text
(R(g)f)(x) = f(xg).
```

(a) The action R is strongly continuous and unitary on L^{2}(G, µ). The map J_{v0} is injective and K-equivariant (R(k)J_{v0} = J_{v0}τ(k)), the scalar c = ‖J_{v0}w_{τ}‖_{L}2 is strictly positive, and

```text

It is nondegenerate because Y = JXJ = −X^{∗}∈𝔲(p, q) gives tr(XY ) = −‖X‖^{2}_{F}. Conjugation Ad(g) preserves this nondegenerate real bilinear form, so | det Ad(g)| = 1. Thus µ is both left- and right-invariant, and R is a strongly continuous unitary representation on L^{2}(G, µ).

For (a), square-integrability (v) implies that each continuous linear contraction g →→⟨v_{0}, Ψ(g)v⟩ lies in L^{2}(G, µ), and v →→ J_{v0}v is ℂ-linear because the inner product is linear in its second argument. Right K-equivariance (i) gives

Lemma 8.120 (Uniqueness of σ-finite left-invariant measures and Haar upgrade). Let U ⊆ Mat_{n}(ℂ) be a closed subgroup of GL_{n}(ℂ), and let µ_{0} be a strong Haar measure on U.

(a) Let ν be any σ-finite Borel measure on Mat_{n}(ℂ) such that ν(U^{c}) = 0 and (L_{a})_{∗}ν = ν for all a ∈U. Then there exists a constant c ∈[0, ∞) such that ν = c µ_{0}.

(b) In particular, if ν is locally finite on compact subsets of Mat_{n}(ℂ) (as in HaarUnique), then ν = c µ_{0} for some c ∈[0, ∞); if µ is a weak Haar measure on U (as in HaarUniqueSF), then µ = c µ_{0} for some c ∈(0, ∞), and consequently µ is also a strong Haar measure on U.

Proof. Because U is closed in the second-countable locally compact σ-compact Hausdorff space Mat_{n}(ℂ) and inversion a →→ (det a)^{−1} adj(a) is continuous on U ⊆ GL_{n}(ℂ), U is a second-countable σ-compact locally compact topological group, the inclusion ι : U ↪→ Mat_{n}(ℂ) is a closed measurable embedding, and ℬ(U ×U) = ℬ(U)⊗ℬ(U). Define the restricted Borel measures ̃µ_{0}(E) := µ_{0}(ι(E)) and ̃ν(E) := ν(ι(E)) on U. Since µ_{0}(U^{c}) = ν(U^{c}) = 0, we have ι_{∗}µ̃_{0} = µ_{0} and ι_{∗}ν̃ = ν. Moreover, ̃µ_{0} is nonzero, bi-invariant on U, and finite on compacts – hence σ-finite by σ-compactness of U – while ̃ν is σ-finite and left-invariant on U.

Part (a) is the standard noncommutative determinant calculus in U(𝔤𝔩_{n}): column/row antisymmetry in R, C follows by commuting adjacent entries via [C_{ab}(x), C_{cd}(x −1)], and induction on p comparing the sum of column expansions with the sum of row expansions proves (p + 1) cminor = (p + 1) rminor, hence cminor = rminor. For (c), the r = 0 case is immediate because every entry in the product involves only E_{ij} (0 ≤i, j < k) and l intertwines each factor with D_{ij}. When r > 0, apply three peeling phases to l∘cminor(E, ι_{cast}, ι_{succ}, x). First, for m = r, r −1, . . . , 1, every row index i ∈{0, . . . , k +r +m−1} has strictly smaller block number than the last column index k + r + m; expanding along the last column shifts x →→x −1 at each step and retains only the unique simple pair (k + r + m −1, k + r + m) (with sign (−1)^{(k+r+m−1)+(k+r+m−1)}= 1), peeling off the factor ∏^{r}_{j=0}^{−1}ψ_{k+r+j,k+r+j+1} and reducing to the (k+r)×(k+r) minor on rows [0, k+r−1], columns [1, k+r] at parameter x−r. Proposition 8.134 (Interlacing walk from λ_{T} (t) to λ_{48}). Let k ≥1, r ≥0, t ∈ℕ, h ∈ℝ, and u ∈ℝ^{k}, v ∈ ℝ^{k−1}, b ∈ ℝ^{2r+2} satisfy IsHCPar(λ_{48}), interlacing, half-integral differences, and b_{j+1} −b_{j} ≥ h for all 0 ≤j ≤2r. Let 𝒫 be any predicate on ℝ^{2r+k+1} closed under single ±1 steps preserving IsHCPar, opposite-sign gap ≥ h for ε_{48}, and the avoidance condition u_{l} ̸= λ_{s} ±_{2}^{1} (StepClosed). Then 𝒫(λ_{T} (k, r, u, b, t)) implies 𝒫(λ_{48}(k, r, v, b)).

Proof. Observe first that for any strictly decreasing λ ∈ℝ^{n}, |λ_{a} −λ_{c}| ≥h for all opposite-sign (a, c) holds as soon as λ_{a} −λ_{a+1} ≥h at every adjacent sign change ε_{48}(a) ̸= ε_{48}(a + 1) (adjGap): any opposite-sign pair a < c contains an adjacent sign change a ≤m < c, so λ_{a} −λ_{c} ≥λ_{m} −λ_{m+1} ≥h. Moreover, by definition of ε_{48}, every adjacent sign change satisfies m ≥k −1.

Stage 1 (raising the tail). For 1 ≤j ≤2r + 2, define raisePar(j) ∈ℝ^{2r+k+1} by raisePar(j)_{a} = u_{a} −^{1}_{2} (a < k), −b_{a−(k−1)} (k ≤ a < j + k −1), and −b_{a−(k−1)} −(a −(k −1))t (a ≥ j + k −1). Then raisePar(1) = λ_{T} (k, r, u, b, t). For each 1 ≤ j ≤ 2r + 1, moving from raisePar(j) to raisePar(j + 1) increments coordinate s = j + k −1 by +1 exactly jt times. Using −b_{0} ≤u_{k−1} −_{2}^{1} (from −b_{0} < u_{k−1} and u_{k−1} −(−b_{0}) ∈ℤ +^{1}_{2}) and b_{q+1} −b_{q} ≥h, every intermediate point µ along this segment is strictly decreasing, satisfies µ_{a} −µ_{a+1} ≥h for all a ≥k −1 (hence has opposite-sign gap ≥h), retains IsHCPar, and satisfies µ_{j+k−1} +^{1}_{2} < µ_{l} +^{ 1}_{2} = u_{l} for every 0 ≤l < k (since l < k ≤j +k −1), so u_{l} ̸= µ_{j+k−1} +^{ 1}_{2}. Applying the +1 closure hypothesis jt times for j = 1, . . . , 2r + 1 transports 𝒫 to raisePar(2r + 2).

Stage 2 (lowering the head). For 0 ≤i ≤k, define walkPar(i) ∈ℝ^{2r+k+1} by walkPar(i)_{a} = u_{a}−^{1}_{2} (a < i) and λ_{48}(a) (a ≥i); then walkPar(k) = raisePar(2r+2) and walkPar(0) = λ_{48}. For i = k−1, k−2, . . . , 0, interlacing gives λ_{48}(i) < u_{i}, and half-integral differences give u_{i} −λ_{48}(i) = N +^{1}_{2} for a nonnegative integer N ∈ℕ, so moving from walkPar(i+1) to walkPar(i) decrements coordinate i by −1 exactly N times through points y = λ_{48}(i) + m (m = N, . . . , 1). At each such point, monotonicity gives strict decrease; for any adjacent sign change a ≥k −1, either a > i (where the gap is unchanged from λ_{48}) or a = i = k −1 (where y ≥λ_{48}(k −1) = −b_{0}, so y −(−b_{1}) ≥b_{1} −b_{0} ≥h). Finally, for any l < k, u_{l} ̸= y −^{1}_{2}: if l < i then u_{l} > u_{i} > y −^{1}_{2}; if l = i then y −^{1}_{2} ≤ u_{i} −1 < u_{i}; and if l > i then i < k −1 and interlacing gives u_{l} < v_{i} = λ_{48}(i) < y −^{1}_{2} (as y ≥ λ_{48}(i) + 1). Applying the −1 closure hypothesis N times for i = k −1, . . . , 0 yields 𝒫(λ_{48}).

Proof. Since p(ε_{48}) = k + r ≥1 and q(ε_{48}) = r + 1 ≥1, the first and third branches of h > h_{need}(ε_{48}) in (282) immediately yield StepGap(ε_{48}, r, h) (gapLap_stepGap). By Proposition 8.133, the predicate λ →→ BesselNZ(ε_{48}, λ, u) is StepClosed for gap h, so Proposition 8.134 gives BesselNZ(ε_{48}, λ_{48}, u). Applying Proposition 8.127 upgrades this to BesselAll(ε_{48}, λ_{48}, u).

Since h > 2(n+2qt)^{3}+t+3 ≥160q^{2}n^{2}+t+3, we obtain h (ε ) < h. Finally, for any x < y with ε (x) ̸= ε (y), we must have y ≥k (since ε ≡ true on need 48 48 48 48 {0, . . . , k−1}), so strict decrease of λ_{48} gives λ_{48}(x)−λ_{48}(y) ≥λ_{48}(y−1)−λ_{48}(y) = b_{y−k+1}−b_{y−k} ≥h, proving GapLap(ε_{48}, λ_{48}, h).

## Same-realization kernel, mass, and loop estimates for the spectral link

8.18 Same-realization kernel, mass, and loop estimates for the spectral link

Proposition 8.85 derives the uniform spectral link LinkS from the four kernel bounds (236) and the total row-count estimate (237) on the same selected realization with thresholds independent of the index i. The abstract row-pair decomposition and its numerical closure are already proved in Lemmas 8.86–8.87 and Proposi-tion 8.88, while the local discrete-series compression, weighted reproducing kernel, Bessel integrability, and rank-one Bessel nonvanishing inputs are established in Propositions 8.90–8.116 and Theorems 8.125–8.138. In this subsection we reconstruct the full chain of same-realization Poincaré, mass–volume, multi-level re-cursion, carrier, loop, non-generic, and degenerate kernel estimates around theoremS_closedP that supply all four kernel bounds (236) uniformly along any selected family realization.

## The covolume estimate and its uniformity

## 9 The covolume estimate and its uniformity

This section reconstructs the numerical and lattice argument used in F-12. Its geometric inputs are kept explicit. In particular, proving a numerical implication from eight estimates does not prove that the required geometric data satisfy those estimates.

## Lattices, heights and an integral orthogonal cut

<!-- Source PDF page 680 -->

9.1 Lattices, heights and an integral orthogonal cut

Let K be a totally complex number field, let n_{K} be the number of its infinite places, and let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space. Choose one embedding σ : K → ℂ at each infinite place and a positive definite Hermitian norm at that place. A lattice means a finitely generated 𝒪_{K}-submodule of V . Its rank is the dimension of its K-span. Realizing the lattice in the direct sum of the complex spaces at these places gives a discrete integer lattice of real rank 2n_{K}r, where r is its K-rank. All covolumes are taken in its own real span.

The source’s height and normalized slope are

log h(L) h(L) = 2^{nKr}| disc K|^{−r/2} covol(L), rµ(L) = − . (335)

```text
n_{K}
```

At rank zero the lattice is zero, its height is one, and the second equation reads 0 = 0. These conventions are needed in the cut argument when the bad part vanishes.

<!-- Source PDF page 681 -->

Lemma 9.1. Let ϕ : V →W be K-linear, let L be a lattice, and set L_{0} = L∩ker ϕ, I = ϕ(L) and r = rk I. Suppose the operator norm at place v is at most c_{v} ≥0. For the quotient norm on L/L_{0},

```text
h(I) ≤∏c^{2}_{v}^{r}h(L/L_{0}), h(L/L_{0}) = h(L)/h(L_{0}). (336)
v
```

Source: Formalism/HarderNarasimhan/HarderNarasimhanProofs/HtImage.lean:289--476; GramBlock.lean:10--228; StatementPl.lean:108--119.

Proof. Write ρ for the real realization. The sublattice ρ(L_{0}) is saturated in ρ(L): if a nonzero integer multiple of x ∈ L lies in L_{0}, then that same multiple of ϕ(x) is zero, and the characteristic-zero vector space has no such torsion. Equivalently, the quotient is the torsion-free integer group I. A basis of L_{0} as an integer group can therefore be extended to an integer basis of L. Project the additional basis vectors orthogonally off ⟨ρ(L_{0})⟩_{ℝ}. They form a basis of the quotient lattice Q. In orthonormal coordinates adapted to this subspace, the basis matrix is block triangular. Taking its determinant gives

covol(L) = covol(L_{0}) covol(Q).

The factors in (335) multiply in the same way because the ranks add. This proves the equality in (336).

The realized map kills the real span of L_{0}, so it induces a linear map from the span of Q to the span of I and an integer-group isomorphism Q →I. Both spans split orthogonally by infinite places, with real dimension 2r in each part. To see the dimension assertion, the K-span of L/L_{0} has dimension r; at each chosen complex embedding it becomes a complex r-space, hence a real 2r-space. The realized map preserves these parts and has norm at most c_{v} on part v.

Choose an orthonormal basis within each part. If c_{v} = 0 on a nonzero part, the image determinant is zero and the inequality follows directly. Otherwise divide that part’s map by c_{v}. Each resulting part is a contraction. Its Gram matrix is positive semidefinite and its quadratic form is at most the identity quadratic form; the real Hermitian spectral theorem therefore puts all its eigenvalues in [0, 1]. Its determinant is at most one. Undoing the scaling and taking the square root of the Gram determinant bounds the volume multiplier by ∏_{v}c_{v}^{2r}. 9.6 Finite generation and fullness of the integral lattice

Lemma 9.17 (Integral functionals force finite generation). Let K be a number field, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, and let L ⊆ V be an 𝒪_{K}-submodule. Suppose that for every x ̸= 0 in V there are a number field K_{x} extending K and a K-linear map ϕ_{x} : V →K_{x} such that

```text
ϕ_{x}(x) ̸= 0, ϕ_{x}(L) ⊆𝒪_{Kx}. (C.20)
```

Then L is finitely generated over 𝒪_{K}. The detecting field and functional may depend on x.

Source: Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/DivisorProofs/FgIntOfForallIsIntegral.lean:7--51.

Proof. We prove by induction on dim_{K} W that L ∩W is a finitely generated abelian group for every K-subspace W ⊆V . The assertion is immediate for W = 0. Otherwise choose 0 ̸= x ∈W and a functional from (C.20). The kernel of its restriction to W is proper, because it does not contain x, so its dimension is smaller. The image of L ∩W is an additive subgroup of 𝒪_{Kx}. This ring is a finitely generated free abelian group, hence is noetherian as a ℤ-module; its subgroup is finitely generated. Its kernel is L ∩(W ∩ ker ϕ_{x}), which is finitely generated by induction. Lift a finite set of image generators and add a finite set of kernel generators. Every element of L ∩W subtracts an integer combination of the former to leave an element of the kernel, so this combined finite set generates it over ℤ. Taking W = V gives finite abelian generators of L. Their 𝒪_{K}-span is contained in L, and contains their ℤ-span L, so they also generate L over 𝒪_{K}. This is exactly the source’s dimension induction; no common field for all the functionals is assumed.

Proof. We first explain the extension step used in both assertions. Let F be an intermediate field of ℂ/k and σ : F → ℂ a k-embedding. Choose finitely many generators s_{1}, . . . , s_{a} of R/k. The algebra A = F[s_{1}, . . . , s_{a}, r^{−1}] ⊂ℂ is nonzero and of finite type over F. A maximal ideal of A has residue field finite over F, by the following elementary form of Zariski’s lemma: a field generated as an algebra by finitely many elements over a field is a finite algebraic extension. Indeed, after choosing a maximal algebraically independent subset of the generators, the remaining generators are integral over a localization of the resulting polynomial ring at one nonzero polynomial; a polynomial ring in at least one variable cannot become a field after inverting just that polynomial (choose an irreducible polynomial not dividing it, or use T −a over an infinite field). Integrality would force that localized ring to be a field, a contradiction. Here every F contains ℚ and is infinite. Thus the independent subset is empty. Embed this finite residue extension into the algebraically closed field ℂ, extending σ. Its restriction to R agrees with σ on R ∩F, and does not kill r, since r is a unit in A.

If c were transcendental, then for every z ∈ ℂ transcendental over k the isomorphism k(c) ≃ k(z) sending c to z, followed by this extension step with r = 1, would give ρ(c) = z. The elements algebraic over a number field form a countable set: there are countably many polynomials and finitely many roots of each nonzero polynomial. Thus the transcendental elements of ℂ are uncountable. This contradicts the assumed countability of the values of c.

For the second assertion use F = k^{̄}∩ℂ and its identity embedding. The same maximal-ideal construction has its image in F, because F is algebraically closed. The images of the finitely many generators of R are algebraic over k, and hence belong to one finite extension K^{′}/k. Restrict the target to that field. Agreement on R ∩F and the nonvanishing of r were built into the construction. The argument proves the simultaneous fixing clause, not just the fixing of one chosen coordinate.

A symmetric bundle has semicharacter with square 1: inversion changes the semicharacter to its inverse, whereas symmetry preserves it. The prod-uct θ_{i}(Fz)θ_{j}(Fz) consequently has the transformation law for the source bundle to the power 2nN; the two target semicharacter factors cancel. By the specified theta-section correspondence it is an algebraic section t_{ij}. In local trivializations the same nonzero frame factor occurs for every j, so on t_{ii} ̸= 0,

They satisfy all its relations: evaluate on every complex point, use the displayed identity, and use that the source is reduced. They therefore define morphisms on those open sets. The open sets cover, because at every Fz some s_{i} is nonzero; complex closed points detect an omitted closed subset on this variety. This gives an algebraic morphism inducing z →→Fz on the universal covers. The same reasoning on A×A, which is smooth and reduced, proves preservation of addition; F0 = 0 proves preservation of the identity. Thus this is precisely the source’s construction through products of theta sections and their ratios.

Lemma 9.59 (Descent and integral extension of the full CM family). Lemma 9.68 (The section bases in the key construction). For a principally polarized abelian scheme f : A → Spec R over a local Noetherian ring and every m ≥1, the module H^{0}(A, L^{m}) is free of rank m^{g}, has no higher cohomology, and commutes with arbitrary base change. The precise formulas are [20, Theorems9.11,9.14 and Proposition9.18(iv), pp.131–135]. They hold in every characteristic, so apply to every geometric fibre here. The scheme morphism f is proper, smooth and of finite presentation; the in-vertible sheaf L^{m} is finitely presented and flat over R. By [14, Tag0B91, Lemma36.30.4], Rf_{∗}L^{m} is perfect and commutes with arbitrary derived base change. Represent it over the local ring by a bounded complex of finite free modules. Cancel every unit differential entry as a two-term identity summand. The resulting complex has all differentials in the maximal ideal. Its tensor product with the residue field therefore has zero differentials, but its cohomology is concentrated in degree zero with dimension m^{g}, by the geometric-fibre calculation and faithful descent from an algebraic closure. The minimal complex consequently has only one nonzero term, R^{mg}, in degree zero. This proves both the vanishing and freeness over R. The arbitrary derived base-change assertion now becomes ordinary base change of this one free module. In the source’s local-function model, restriction to the trivializing charts identifies this module with its section coordinates, as in the section dictionary in Proposition 10.27.

## 10 Geometric inputs and the integral Hodge–Tate comparison

The geometric assertions entering the covolume estimate have different mathematical contents. We first resolve the integral annihilator assertion. Its conclusion concerns integral kernels, although the Hodge–Tate exact sequence used to prove it is an exact sequence over a field. The passage between them requires torsion freeness and clearing denominators.

Lemma 10.1 (The valuation-ring hypotheses give the usual complete field). Let C be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, let v : C →ℝ_{≥0} be a multiplicative nonarchimedean valuation, and let O be its ring of integers. Suppose 0 < v(p) < 1 and O is separated and complete for the powers of p. Then C = O[1/p] is complete for v, and the given ℤ_{p}-algebra structure on O is the usual one. After rescaling the valuation by a positive real power, C is a complete nonarchimedean extension of ℚ_{p}.

Proof. Regard O as a subring of C. This is legitimate for the source’s abstract ring O: saying that its algebra map identifies it with the integers of v includes injectivity and the condition that its image consists of the elements of valuation at most one. For any z ∈ C, choose m so that v(p)^{m}v(z) ≤ 1. Then p^{m}z ∈ O, proving C = O[1/p]. Moreover

```text
p^{m}O = {z ∈C : v(z) ≤v(p)^{m}}.
```

Both inclusions follow by dividing by p^{m}. These sets form a neighborhood basis of zero in O, so its valuation topology and its p-adic topology agree.

A Cauchy sequence in C is bounded. Indeed, its sufficiently late terms differ from one fixed term by elements of valuation at most one, and the finitely many earlier terms have a finite maximum valuation. Multiplication by one power of p therefore places the entire sequence in O. It is Cauchy for the powers of p by the preceding equality. Completeness of O gives a limit there; dividing by the fixed power gives a limit in C. This proves completeness.

For a ∈ ℤ_{p} and every m, write a = a_{m} + p^{m}b_{m} with a_{m} an integer and b_{m} ∈ ℤ_{p}. Any unital ring map ℤ_{p} →O sends b_{m} into O, so the image of a differs from a_{m} by an element of p^{m}O. Separation makes

<!-- Source PDF page 757 -->

this image uniquely determined. Thus the given algebra structure is the continuous extension of the integer map. It extends to the usual embedding of ℚ_{p} into C. Normalize v by its positive real power for which v(p) = p^{−1}. If an integer is prime to p, a Bezout relation with p shows that its valuation is one: if both terms of that relation had valuation less than one, their sum could not be one. The normalized restriction to ℚ is therefore the usual p-adic absolute value, and completeness gives the assertion about ℚ_{p}.

Lemma 10.2 (The integral factorization used in the source). Let O be a domain, f : M →W an O-linear map and ϕ : M →O a linear functional. Suppose ker f ⊆ ker ϕ and κW ⊆ im f. Then there is an O-linear ℓ: W →O such that

```text
ℓ(f(y)) = κϕ(y) (y ∈M).
```

Proof. On im f define g(f(y)) = ϕ(y). If f(y) = f(y^{′}), then y −y^{′}∈ ker f, so ϕ(y) = ϕ(y^{′}). This proves that g is well defined; the same formula proves additivity and O-linearity. By the hypothesis on κ, the map w →→κw takes W into im f. Compose it with g. For w = f(y) the result is g(κf(y)) = g(f(κy)) = κϕ(y), which proves the formula.

This is the quotient-by-the-kernel construction of FarguesExactOfPrismatic.lean, lines 18–34. It does not require extending a functional arbitrarily from a submodule.

Lemma 10.3 (Clearing the denominators of a surjective map). Let F be the fraction field of a domain O, let W be finite free over O, and suppose f : M →W becomes surjective over F. Then some 0 ̸= κ ∈O satisfies κW ⊆ im f. If F = O[1/p], one may take κ = p^{a} for an integer a ≥0.

Proof. Choose a finite basis w_{1}, . . . , w_{d} of W. For each i, choose a preimage of w_{i} under f_{F} . An element of F ⊗_{O} M is a finite sum of fractions times elements of M, so multiplying by a common nonzero denominator gives m_{i} ∈M and s_{i} ̸= 0 with f(m_{i}) = s_{i}w_{i}. This equality follows first after localization and then in W, because a free module over a domain injects into its localization. Take∏ κ = ∏_{i}s_{i}. Multiplying m_{i} by _{j̸=i}s_{j} gives a preimage of κw_{i}. Linear combinations give the assertion for all W. When the localization is O[1/p], all the chosen fractions have denominators powers of p; taking the largest required power, and increasing it to account for each chosen preimage, gives the final assertion.

Background fact 10.4 (The precisely used Hodge–Tate theorem). Let C/ℚ_{p} be an algebraically closed complete nonarchimedean field and let G be a p-divisible group over O_{C}. Its Tate module is finite free over ℤ_{p}, and its completed invariant cotangent module ω_{G} is finite locally free over O_{C}. Write Lie G = ω_{G}^{∨}. The freeness of this completed module is verified again for the project’s finite-level model below. The Hodge– Tate sequence is

```text
α^{∗}_{∨α}
```

0 −→ Lie G ⊗_{OC} C(1)−−−→^{G} T_{p}G ⊗_{ℤp} C−−→^{G} ω_{G}∨⊗_{OC} C −→0.

The two arrows are dual under the Cartier Tate pairing. The exact sequence and its arrows are [52, Theo-rem 12.1.1 and the description immediately after Remark 12.1.2, pp. 98–99]. The cotangent and Lie modules here are those of the p-adic formal group, not those obtained by taking the tangent sheaf of the generic-fiber torsion sheaf.

Proposition 10.5 (Integral annihilator equality). Let G and C satisfy Fact 10.4. Choose a generator ζ of ℤ_{p}(1) and use it to write the Cartier pairing as a perfect pairing

```text

```

Let f = α_{G} : M → ω_{G}∨ and g = α_{G}∨ : N → ω_{G} be the integral Hodge–Tate maps. Then, for every

```text
x ∈M,
```

f(x) = 0 ⇐⇒ B(x, y) = 0 for every y ∈ ker g. (G.1)

Equivalently, f(x) = 0 if and only if there are 0 ̸= c ∈O_{C} and ℓ: ω_{G} →O_{C} such that cB(x, y) = ℓ(g(y)) for every y ∈N.

Proof. We first work over C. A finite-dimensional linear map g_{C} : N_{C} →(ω_{G})_{C} has

im(g_{C}^{∗}) = (ker g_{C})^{⊥}

in N_{C}^{∗} = M_{C}, using B_{C} for the identification. One inclusion follows by evaluation on a kernel vector. For the other, a functional vanishing on ker g_{C} factors through its image: send g_{C}(y) to its value on y. This is well defined by the vanishing. Extend a basis of the image to a basis of the target and extend that functional linearly, giving a preimage under g_{C}^{∗}. By Fact 10.4, its image is ker f_{C}. Hence

ker f_{C} = (ker g_{C})^{⊥}. (G.2)

Every element of ker g_{C} is a fraction of an integral kernel element. To check this explicitly, write it as p^{−a}y with y ∈N. Its image under g vanishes after inverting p. Therefore some power p^{b} kills g(y), and p^{b}y ∈ ker g. Thus the original element equals p^{−a−b}(p^{b}y). In particular the integral kernel spans the rational kernel. This argument is also the usual flat-localization identity C ⊗ ker g = ker g_{C}.

If B(x, ker g) = 0, the preceding spanning assertion gives B_{C}(x, ker g_{C}) = 0. Equation (G.2) then gives f(x) = 0 after localization. The target ω_{G}∨ is free over the local domain O_{C}, so it injects into its localization; hence f(x) = 0 integrally. Conversely, if f(x) = 0, (G.2) implies that B(x, y) is zero in C for each integral y ∈ ker g. The inclusion O_{C} ↪→C makes it zero in O_{C}. This proves (G.1).

For the factorization formulation, g_{C} is surjective by the Hodge–Tate sequence for G^{∨}. Lemma 10.3 supplies 0 ̸= κ ∈O_{C} with κω_{G} ⊆ im g. If the right side of (G.1) holds, apply Lemma 10.2 with ϕ(y) = B(x, y). It gives ℓ with κB(x, y) = ℓ(g(y)). In the reverse direction such a factorization gives cB(x, y) = 0 on ker g; cancellation of c ̸= 0 in the domain proves the right side of (G.1).

The project proves the last equivalence using an integral prismatic sandwich and the stronger bound p^{2}ω_{G} ⊆ im g. The numerical exponent two is absent from the statement FarguesExact: it only asks for (G.1). The proof just given establishes that entire statement with a common nonzero denominator, rather than asserting that rational surjectivity is integral surjectivity.

Lemma 10.6 (The root system and normalization of the pairing). Suppose ζ_{0} = 1, ζ_{n}^{p}_{+1} = ζ_{n} in O_{C}, and ζ_{1} ̸= 1. Then (ζ_{n}) generates the Tate module of µ_{p}∞. Any O_{C}-bilinear form having the prescribed scalar Cartier values on pure Tate tensors is the form B in Proposition 10.5.

Proof. Repeated powering gives ζ_{n}^{pn} = 1 and ζ_{n}^{pn−1} = ζ_{1} ̸= 1 for n > 0. Since p is prime, its order is exactly p^{n}. Every p^{n}-th root of unity lies in O_{C}: its valuation has p^{n}-th power one and so is one. In the algebraically closed characteristic-zero field C, these roots form a cyclic group of order p^{n}, generated by ζ_{n}. Write any compatible root system uniquely as (ζ_{n}^{an}), a_{n}∈ℤ/p^{n}ℤ. Compatibility says exactly that a_{n+1} reduces to a_{n}. Such a system is an element of ℤ_{p}, and conversely every element gives such a system. Thus multiplication by (ζ_{n}) identifies ℤ_{p} with this Tate module.

For t ∈T_{p}G and u ∈T_{p}G^{∨}, the Cartier pairing is consequently aζ for one uniquely determined a ∈ℤ_{p}. Its scalar value in O_{C} is the image of a. The hypothesis on a form specifies exactly this value at (1⊗t, 1⊗u). Multiplication by the two O_{C} coefficients specifies its value at every pair of pure tensors. Tensor products are spanned by pure tensors, so additivity in each argument gives equality of the forms everywhere.

10.1 Matching the project model

The following identifications specify the conversion required to apply Proposition 10.5 to the project, rather than merely replacing one theorem name by another.

<!-- Source PDF page 759 -->

Its PDivGroup presents G[p^{n}] as the spectrum of a finite projective commutative Hopf O-algebra A_{n} of rank p^{nh}. The surjective transition homomorphisms are the closed inclusions of the p^{n}-torsion subgroup; the equality of their kernels with the torsion ideals is precisely that assertion on coordinate algebras. Thus these are exactly the finite-group and kernel conditions in Tate’s definition [8, §2.1, p. 161]. Their associated group is the resulting p-divisible group, with its p-adic formal cotangent module. The rank-zero level is the trivial group: its rank-one augmented algebra is O, as the unit and counit split it and their finite projective complement has rank zero at every prime.

Lemma 10.7 (Freeness of the completed cotangent model). For this system over O = O_{C}, put W_{n} = ω_{G[p}n_{]} = I_{n}/I_{n}^{2}, n ≥1. Then

W_{n+1}/p^{n}W_{n+1} ≃W_{n}, lim W_{n} ≃O^{d}

```text
←−_{n}
```

for a fixed finite integer d. Consequently the source’s completed ω_{G} is finite free and torsion free.

Proof. The differential of multiplication by an integer a on the cotangent space of a commutative group is multiplication by a. Indeed, the differential of the group law at the identity is addition: restricting it to either coordinate gives the identity, which determines that linear map on the direct sum. Iteration gives the assertion for positive a. Since [p^{n}] is zero on G[p^{n}], it follows that p^{n}W_{n} = 0.

Formation of invariant cotangent modules commutes with base change: the augmentation ideal modulo its square is equivalently the module representing derivations at the identity, and the universal derivation commutes with tensoring the base ring. Thus W_{n} equals the cotangent module of G[p^{n}] over O/p^{n}. This is a truncated Barsotti–Tate group of level n. The finite-level cotangent theorem says that its invariant cotangent module is finite locally free over O/p^{n}; the precise cited statement is Illusie [9, Corollary 2.2.5, p. 164], applied to the implication from a truncated Barsotti–Tate group to its two locally free cotangent modules. Its hypothesis p^{n}= 0 holds on this base. Since O/p^{n} is local, W_{n} is finite free over that ring.

The transition identifies G[p^{n}] with the kernel of [p^{n}] on G[p^{n+1}]. For a kernel of group schemes, the cotangent sequence at the identity is right exact. Here it is

```text
W_{n+1}−→^{pn} W_{n+1} −→W_{n} −→0.
```

To see the right exactness directly, present the kernel by its fiber product with the identity section. Its coordi-nate algebra is the corresponding tensor product, and the universal rule for differentials of a tensor product gives the cokernel of the two cotangent maps. The identity section has zero relative cotangent module; the remaining map is the differential of [p^{n}] computed above. This proves the first displayed isomorphism.

Reduction modulo p shows that the ranks of all W_{n} are one fixed d. Choose a basis at level one. Lift it successively along the surjective transition maps. Any such lifts at level n + 1 form a basis: relative to an existing basis of the free module W_{n+1}, their determinant is a unit modulo p, so is a unit in the local ring O/p^{n+1}. The adjugate identity then inverts the matrix. We obtain compatible basis isomorphisms W_{n} ≃ (O/p^{n})^{d}. Taking inverse limits and using the assumed p-adic completeness and separation of O gives lim_{←−}W_{n} ≃O^{d}. An element of O^{d} killed by a nonzero element of the domain O has every coordinate zero. This proves the last assertion.

The source’s Tate module uses O-valued points, whereas the published theorem writes C-valued points. These are equal at every finite level. Indeed, a homomorphism A_{n} →C sends each element to one integral over O, because A_{n} is finite over O. A root z of a monic polynomial with coefficients in O has valuation at most one: if v(z) > 1, its leading term has strictly larger valuation than every lower term and cannot cancel their sum. Thus its image lies in O. The factorization is unique since O ↪→ C is injective. These factorizations commute with the transition maps, so the two inverse-limit Tate modules agree.

<!-- Source PDF page 760 -->

For an augmented coordinate algebra, the invariant cotangent module is I/I^{2}, where I is the augmen-tation ideal. The source takes the compatible inverse limit of these modules at finite level. This is the completed invariant cotangent module of the associated p-adic formal group. Its Lie is the O-linear dual of this completed cotangent module. In particular one must not take the tangent space after passing first to the characteristic-zero torsion sheaf, where each finite level is etale and would give the wrong answer.

Finally the source’s dlogLinear sends c ⊗u to c times the pullback of dt/t under the Cartier character G →µ_{p}∞ represented by u. This is α_{G}∨ in the publication. Its hodgeTateLinear first uses biduality to regard a Tate vector as a character of G^{∨}, and then takes this same pullback. This is α_{G}. The description of α_{G} on page 99 of the cited theorem is exactly this construction. Biduality makes the pairing the Cartier pairing used for the transpose arrow, and Lemma 10.6 fixes its scalar normalization for every primitive root system allowed in the source.

The source locations are ToSpanSingletonConstGenInjective.lean, lines 12–29, 369–375, 523– 533, 962–970, 1062–1073 and 1088–1095.
