10.2 The prismatic normalization and its Hodge quotient

The separate prismatic input in the Hodge-bundle package requires a functor, not merely the existence of individual modules. We record the part whose precise normalization is already checked against the published construction.

Lemma 10.8 (The perfectoid base hypotheses). The ring O in Lemma 10.1 is an integral perfectoid ring. It is therefore among the quasisyntomic bases of prismatic Dieudonne theory.

Proof. It is p-complete by assumption and has no p-torsion, being a subring of a characteristic-zero field. Choose ϖ ∈C with ϖ^{p} = p. Its valuation is v(p)^{1/p} < 1, so ϖ ∈O and ϖ^{p} = p. Frobenius on O/p is surjective: given a lift x ∈O, choose y ∈C with y^{p} = x. Then v(y)^{p} = v(x) ≤1, so y ∈O. Its kernel on O/p consists of the classes of z with v(z)^{p} ≤v(p), equivalently v(z) ≤v(ϖ), equivalently z ∈ϖO. Thus Frobenius gives the required isomorphism O/ϖ ≃ O/p. These are the integral perfectoid criterion for a p-torsion-free complete ring, with ϖ^{p}= p. Equivalently, C is complete and uniform, with surjective Frobenius on O/p and nondiscrete valuation: the elements p^{1/pa} have valuations tending to one from below. The implication from integral perfectoid to quasisyntomic is the precise established base-ring fact in [10,

Example 3.17(2)].

Put A = W(O^{♭}) and let φ be its Witt Frobenius. Fix a compatible primitive cyclotomic system ϵ = (1, ζ_{p}, ζ_{p}2, . . .) and put

```text
µ = [ϵ] −1, ξ =_{[ϵ}^{[}_{1/}^{ϵ]}_{p}^{ −}_{] −}^{1}_{1}, ξ̃ = φ(ξ).
```

The quotient notation denotes the finite geometric sum, so it is an element of A. The untilt map is θ : A →O with kernel (ξ). The initial prism used by the cited prismatic Dieudonne functor is


In particular its prismatic ideal is generated by φ(ξ), whereas the Hodge quotient used below is by ξ. These two generators must not be identified. The choice of this prism and the distinction of the two quotient maps are [10, Example 1.10(1) and the beginning of §4.3, pp. 43–44].

10.6 Seminegativity on a complete curve

Background fact 10.23 (The characteristic-zero Lie positivity theorem). Let C be a smooth projective con-nected curve over a characteristic-zero field, let K = k(C), and let G/C be a smooth group scheme of finite type. If a subbundle F ⊂ Lie G is ample and its generic fiber is a Lie subalgebra, then that fiber is the Lie algebra of a connected unipotent algebraic subgroup of G_{K}. This is [18, Theorem 2.6,§2.4], read in the original author’s preprint, pp. 14–16. Its footnote 4 on p. 14 explains that the quasi-projectivity in its formulation is automatic for a smooth finite-type group scheme over a smooth curve.

Proposition 10.24 (The exact semiabelian seminegativity input). Let C/k be a smooth projective geometri-cally connected curve in characteristic zero, and let G/C be a semiabelian scheme in the source’s sense. If a vector bundle W admits a monomorphism W → Lie G, then

deg det W ≤0.

Thus SemiAbelianLieSeminegative holds, including monomorphisms whose cokernel has torsion.

Proof. The source group is smooth, separated and quasi-compact over the noetherian curve, hence is of finite type. Its Lie sheaf is the usual finite-rank vector bundle. Its commutative group law makes the Lie bracket zero, so every generic subspace is a Lie subalgebra. Every geometric fiber, in particular the geometric generic fiber, is an extension of an abelian variety by a torus.

<!-- Source PDF page 772 -->

Such a group has no nontrivial connected unipotent subgroup in characteristic zero. Indeed, after alge-braic closure a unipotent group has a filtration by additive groups. A homomorphism from G_{a} to an abelian variety extends to P^{1} by properness and is constant; abelian varieties have no rational curves. A homomor-phism from G_{a} to a torus is also zero, since invertible regular functions on A^{1} are constant. Induction through that filtration shows that any connected unipotent subgroup of the semiabelian group is trivial.

Suppose that the maximal Harder–Narasimhan slope of E = Lie G were positive. Its first Harder– Narasimhan term F is a nonzero semistable subbundle of positive slope. In characteristic zero such a bundle on a complete curve is ample; equivalently the positive-slope part has positive minimal slope. This is the curve-bundle ampleness criterion used in the proof of Bost’s theorem, loc. cit., pp. 16–17. Fact 10.23 would give a nonzero connected unipotent subgroup with Lie algebra F_{K}. The preceding paragraph excludes it. Hence µ_{max}(E) ≤0.

Saturate the image of W in E, obtaining a subbundle W^{sat}. Over the discrete valuation local rings of the smooth curve, a torsion-free coherent module is free; thus this saturation and its locally free quotient have the usual bundle meaning. Moreover W^{sat}/W is torsion, so

deg W = deg W^{sat}− length(W^{sat}/W) ≤ deg W^{sat}.

Every subbundle has slope at most µ_{max}(E), so deg W^{sat}≤0. This proves the inequality. For rank zero it is the empty determinant of degree zero. The source interNum of a line on this curve is its ordinary degree, by the one-difference calculation in Proposition 10.18. Thus the inequality is exactly its stated one. All argu-ments and the cited theorem apply over the original characteristic-zero field; alternatively a field extension multiplies curve degrees by positive factors and gives the same conclusion.

10.7 Deformation across the stated divided-power thickening

Background fact 10.25 (Grothendieck’s general abelian deformation theorem). Let S_{0} ↪→S be a thickening with locally nilpotent divided powers. Abelian schemes over S are equivalent to pairs consisting of an abelian scheme A_{0}/S_{0} and a locally direct summand of its crystalline H^{1}(A_{0}/S) extending the Hodge submodule ω_{A0}. Morphisms are exactly the morphisms on S_{0} whose crystalline pullback preserves these submodules. This is the named deformation theorem in [19, Chapter V,§4,p. 116]. The original French text on pp. 114– 115 explicitly uses the general nilpotent crystalline site: there is no privileged prime and no assumption that some prime be nilpotent in the base. It also identifies its crystal at a lift with H_{dR}^{1} and gives the natural Hodge exact sequence.

We describe its cohomology convention. The source category consists of affine test schemes mapping to A_{0} and their nilpotent divided-power affine thickenings, with coefficient functor sending one to its thickening ring. Its category cochain complex is the usual product complex on composable chains of morphisms, with alternating faces. Its cohomology is crystalline cohomology of the structure sheaf. Indeed affine objects form a basis of this crystalline site. The structure sheaf is acyclic on them, since restriction to the opens of an affine thickening is its quasi-coherent structure sheaf. Proposition 10.29 (Holomorphic sections and the source atlas). The source field SerreHolomorphicSections holds for every supplied AnRead atlas.

Proof. Let Y /ℂ be smooth and projective and let B be the supplied invertible sheaf. Serre’s comparison theorem, [24, §12, Theorem 1, p. 19, with q = 0], states that restriction gives a bijection H^{0}(Y, B) −→ H^{0}(Y^{an}, B^{an}). The invertible sheaf is coherent since Y is noetherian. Smoothness makes Y reduced, so Serre’s variety formulation applies. If Y has several components, they are finitely many disjoint smooth projective varieties; apply the theorem to each and take their product.

It remains to identify its target with the target actually specified. An AlgChart is an open partial home-omorphism whose coordinate functions are evaluations of regular functions giving an etale map to affine space. In the usual analytification this map is locally biholomorphic: its Jacobian is invertible, and the complex inverse function theorem applies. Since the supplied homeomorphism agrees with these coordi-nate evaluations, its local inverse is precisely that holomorphic inverse. Its restriction to every sufficiently small open is therefore an ordinary holomorphic coordinate chart. Conversely, the charts cover all complex points. Differentiability on the open target domains in HoloOn is thus equivalent to ordinary holomorphicity, independently of the chosen atlas.

The compatibility in fibSec is s_{i} = g_{ij}s_{j} on the overlap of the trivializations of B. Accordingly a tuple in holSec glues to a unique analytic section of B^{an}. There is an additional detail in this model: each s_{i} is a function on all complex points, and fibSec requires it to be zero outside its trivializing open. An analytic section therefore recovers exactly one such tuple by extending its local coefficient functions by zero. No holomorphicity across the boundary of that open is required by HoloOn. These operations are inverse. The analogous algebraic gluing identifies B.Sec with H^{0}(Y, B), and the source’s secVal is exactly restriction/evaluation, with that same zero extension. Conjugating Serre’s bijection by these two identified gluing maps gives the claimed bijection, including equality of all the tuple entries outside their domains.

Remark 10.38 (Reconciliation with Berthelot–Breen–Messing, dual Lean paths, and callers). Theorem 10.37 matches the degree-two case of Berthelot–Breen–Messing [65, §2.5, Proposition 2.5.2, Lemma 2.5.3, and

10.10 Semistable reduction, arithmetic inputs, and toroidal compactifications

Proposition 10.45 (Semistable reduction in the fixed p-adic closure). The source’s SemistableReductionSt holds with its specified intermediate fields and integral-closure rings.

Proof. Let K ⊂ℂ_{p} be finite over ℚ_{p}, and let A/K be the abelian variety of the supplied polarized object. Its valuation ring 𝒪_{K} is the integral closure of ℤ_{p} in K: an element of negative valuation cannot be integral, by comparing valuations in a monic equation; the integral closure is the finite valuation ring of the finite ex-tension of the complete discretely valued field ℚ_{p}. In particular it is a complete noetherian discrete valuation ring.

The semistable reduction theorem supplies a finite separable extension E/K such that the identity com-ponent of the special fiber of the Neron model of A_{E} is an extension of an abelian variety by a torus. We use the original arithmetic proof, Deligne’s appendix in [27, Expose I, §6, Theorem 6.1, pp. 21–24]. That theorem and the following paragraph permit a finite separable fraction-field extension. Its finite-residue-field case suffices here. If dim A = 0, A = Spec K and the constant trivial group over 𝒪_{K} supplies the conclusion directly.

Embed E into the fixed algebraically closed field ℂ_{p} extending the given embedding of K: a primitive element has a root of its minimal polynomial there, and its irreducibility makes this map injective. Let K^{′}

<!-- Source PDF page 795 -->

be its image. Then K ⊂K^{′}, K^{′} is finite over K and hence over ℚ_{p}. Its valuation ring is exactly the source’s integralClosure(ℤ_{p}, K^{′}). Transport the semistable model through the isomorphism E ≃K^{′}.

Let 𝒜/𝒪_{K}′ be the Neron model, and let G = 𝒜^{0} be its open subgroup with connected geometric fibers. This is the identity component of the Neron model, rather than its possibly disconnected whole special fiber. It is a smooth separated group scheme of finite type, hence quasi-compact. Its generic fiber is A_{K}′, an abelian variety; its geometric special fiber is the semiabelian variety supplied by the theorem. These are all the geometric fibers of this trait, so G satisfies precisely the source IsSemiAbelian predicate.

The generic-fiber isomorphism G_{K}′ ≃A_{K}′ followed by the projection A_{K}′ →A gives the specified φ. The defining square is cartesian and respects the group laws, since the first map is a group isomorphism and the second is base change along K ⊂K^{′}. It is therefore exactly an IsGrpPullback witness. No extension of the polarization to the semiabelian group is demanded by this source contract, and none is needed in constructing these witnesses.

Proposition 10.47 (Landherr’s invariant test in the source convention). The field LandherrSt holds with the source’s linear-first-variable hermitian forms and matrix action.

Proof. Let E be its CM field, let ̄ denote its complex conjugation, and let F = E^{̄} be its maximal totally real subfield. Thus E/F is quadratic and ̄ is its nontrivial automorphism. For the supplied matrices define

```text

a,b a,b
```

```text
G^{′}.
```

Landherr’s original classification proves that the dimension, the signatures at the real places nonsplit in E, and the local norm-residue invariants of the determinant are a complete set of invariants. See [28, pp. 246–247, the invariant definition and induction proving equivalence]. This is equivalence of forms, not equivalence after multiplication by an arbitrary scalar, which is considered separately on p. 248.

The two forms have the same dimension r. The columns of the source’s invertible Q form a complex basis; its gram condition says that in that basis the form is the stated diagonal matrix. Hence its number of positive squares is min(r, p_{0}) and its number of negative squares is r−min(r, p_{0}). The same p_{0} is supplied for G and G^{′} at each embedding, so their signatures agree at every real place of F. The determinant hypothesis says det G^{′}/ det G = zz̄ = N_{E/F} z; its left side is nonzero, so z ̸= 0. After any completion this remains a norm. Thus all the local determinant norm-residue invariants agree as well.

Landherr’s test gives an E-linear isometry with invertible matrix γ and G^{′}= γ^{T}Gγ̄ in this convention. Indeed, expansion of the two finite sums gives


An invertible matrix is precisely an element of the source group GL_{r}(E), so this equality supplies its re-quested witness with no transpose or conjugation change in the vector action. If r = 0, both underly-ing spaces are zero, the unique empty matrix is the identity of GL_{0}(E), and the same assertion follows directly.

Lemma 10.48 (A cuspidal Whittaker line, including q = 2). Let σ be a cuspidal irreducible representation of GL_{d}(𝔽_{q}) in the Green parametrization. For any nontrivial additive character ψ of 𝔽_{q}, its subspace on which the upper unitriangular group acts by

has dimension one.

Proof. Write H_{j} = GL_{j−1}(𝔽_{q}) ⋉𝔽^{j}_{q}^{−1} for the mirabolic subgroup of GL_{j}, whose last row is (0, . . . , 0, 1), and write V_{j} for its last-column vector subgroup. Embed H_{j} in the first j coordinates of GL_{d}. Let N_{j} be the unitriangular subgroup consisting of matrices

```text
(^{I}_{0}^{jB}_{u}), u ∈U_{d−j}.
```

On N_{j}, restrict the character in the statement. Let E_{j} be its isotypic subspace in σ. In particular E_{d} = σ, and E_{1} is the desired Whittaker space. The last-row condition defining H_{j} shows that H_{j} preserves this character, and hence E_{j}.

For j ≥2 we claim E_{j}^{Vj} = 0. A vector in that fixed space is fixed by all entries in rows 1, . . . , j −1 and columns j, . . . , d: the column j entries are V_{j}, and the others belong to N_{j}, where the selected character is trivial on these rows. These entries form the unipotent radical of the proper (j −1, d −j + 1) parabolic. Cuspidality says that its fixed space in σ is zero, proving the claim.

Over ℂ, the finite abelian group V_{j} acts diagonally on E_{j}. All of its occurring characters are therefore nontrivial. Conjugation by GL_{j−1}(𝔽_{q}) ⊂H_{j} acts transitively on the q^{j−1}−1 nontrivial characters: write them as v →→ψ(ℓ(v)) for nonzero linear functionals ℓ. Thus their isotypic spaces all have the same dimension. The space for ℓ(v) = v_{j−1} is exactly E_{j−1}, since adjoining this character to the one on N_{j} gives the one on N_{j−1}. Consequently

dim E_{j} = (q^{j−1}−1) dim E_{j−1}.

For d = 1 the unitriangular group is trivial and that same degree is one. This proof also works when q = 2: it uses neither a nontrivial multiplicative character of 𝔽_{q} nor a restriction q > 2.

Lemma 10.49 (Distinct cuspidal blocks). Let σ_{i} be pairwise nonisomorphic cuspidal representations of GL_{di}(𝔽_{q}) and n = ∑_{i}d_{i}. Inflating their exterior tensor product to the block upper triangular parabolic P and inducing to GL_{n}(𝔽_{q}) gives an irreducible representation. Its Whittaker space for a nondegenerate upper-unitriangular character is one-dimensional. Two such inductions are isomorphic exactly when the multisets of their cuspidal blocks agree.

Proof. We spell out the intertwining calculation. For two ordered block decompositions, their parabolic dou-ble cosets are classified by the dimensions of the intersections of successive steps of the two flags: a matrix (m_{ij}) of nonnegative integers whose row sums and column sums are the respective block sizes. Choose bases successively in these flag intersections; they give permutation-matrix representatives and the block descriptions of the intersections of the parabolics.

The finite-group Mackey calculation is obtained by writing an induced function separately on each double coset, then evaluating at its representative. An intertwiner there must factor, on each block, through invari-ants under the upper rectangular groups determined by its nonzero m_{ij}. If a row contains two nonzero entries, the first such group is a proper parabolic unipotent radical of σ_{i}, so its invariant space is zero by cuspidal-ity. Applying the same argument to the other inducing representation excludes a column with two nonzero entries. Thus a surviving incidence matrix is a matching of blocks of equal dimensions. Its intertwining space is ⊗_{i} Hom(σ_{i}, σ_{π}^{′}_{(i)}). Schur’s lemma makes this one-dimensional for a matching of identical cuspi-dal representations and zero otherwise. In the self-intertwining calculation pairwise distinctness leaves only the identity matching. The induced representation has endomorphism algebra of dimension one. Maschke’s theorem decomposes it into irreducibles, with endomorphism dimension equal to the sum of the squared multiplicities. It is therefore irreducible. The same matching calculation proves the last assertion.

For the Whittaker calculation, the orbits of U_{n} on GL_{n}/P are the usual flag cells indexed by shuffles of the ordered blocks. This follows by row elimination; diagonal matrices may be moved across each per-mutation representative into P, so passing from the upper triangular group to U_{n} adds no cells. For a cell representative w, evaluation of induced functions gives its contribution as

Hom_{Un∩wPw}−1(ψ_{n}, σ^{w}).

If its block labels are not in decreasing order, some two adjacent coordinates have increasing block labels. Their elementary root subgroup lies in U_{n}∩w rad(P)w^{−1}. The inflated representation is trivial there, whereas ψ_{n} is nontrivial there, so that contribution is zero.

There is exactly one remaining shuffle: it reverses the order of the blocks and preserves the internal order in each block. On this cell the relevant intersection is the product of the block unitriangular groups. The restricted character is nondegenerate on each block, and the contributing space is the tensor product of their Whittaker spaces. Each factor is one-dimensional by Lemma 10.48; the cell therefore contributes exactly one dimension. This proves the claimed Whittaker dimension.

Background fact 10.51 (The closed bottom alcove). Let K be algebraically closed of characteristic p > 0, let G be a split connected reductive group, and choose positive roots R^{+}. If a dominant weight µ satisfies

```text
⟨µ + ρ, α^{∨}⟩≤p (α ∈R^{+}),
```

then its induced module ∇(µ) is simple. The inequality is weak.

Proof. Use the integral canonical map c_{µ} : ∆_{ℤ}(µ) →∇_{ℤ}(µ) and its Jantzen filtration. Andersen–Kulkarni’s sum formula [29, Corollary 5.1, author preprint p. 12] has the form

```text
∑ch ∆^{i}(µ) = ∑ ∑ v_{p}(m) χ(µ −mα).
i>0 α∈R^{+} 0<m<⟨µ+ρ,α^{∨}⟩
```

Their hypotheses are an algebraically closed field of arbitrary prime characteristic and a reductive group; there is no lower bound on p. Every integer m in this sum is strictly less than p, so every coefficient v_{p}(m) is zero. On the left each weight multiplicity is a sum of nonnegative integers. Consequently ∆^{1}(µ) = 0.

Lemma 10.55 (Number-field models and integral weight lattices). Every dominant integral weight in the polynomial model used above has a characteristic-zero rational model. Its extension to a characteristic-zero discrete valuation ring has a full finite free lattice stable under its integral general linear group. The same assertions hold for finite tensor products over the embeddings of a number field, after a finite splitting extension.

Proof. Fix ν and use the finite monomial basis of polynomials with column degrees ν_{j}. The finitely many generic column-addition equations defining V_{ν} are integer linear equations: expand each substitution in the auxiliary variable t and compare its finitely many coefficients. Consequently there is one map of finite free integer modules B : ℤ^{a}→ℤ^{b} for which

Λ = ker B, V_{ν,ℚ} = ker(B ⊗ℚ). (AG.25)

The subgroup Λ is finite free, being a subgroup of ℤ^{a}. It is a full lattice in the rational kernel: multiplying the finitely many rational coordinates of any vector by a common denominator gives a vector in Λ. Flatness gives V_{ν,ℂ} = V_{ν,ℚ}⊗ℂ. Thus this is an actual rational model of the polynomial space, rather than a rationality assertion inferred from its character.

Let 𝒪 be a characteristic-zero discrete valuation ring, with fraction field E. As a torsion-free ℤ-module it is flat, so Λ⊗𝒪 is exactly the kernel of B⊗𝒪. It is finite free and becomes V_{ν,E} after inverting the uniformizer. If g ∈ GL_{N}(𝒪), substitution X →→g^{T}X preserves integer-coefficient polynomials and commutes with all right column operations. It therefore preserves this kernel. Its determinant is a unit, so multiplication by det(g)^{c} is integral for every integer c, including negative c. Apply the same argument to g^{−1} to obtain equality of the lattice with its image. This is precisely stability for the action (AG.11). No lowest-alcove assumption is needed in this characteristic-zero construction.

For a finite collection of embeddings, choose a finite normal number-field extension containing their im-ages and splitting the relevant unitary groups. Their defining Hermitian matrix equations identify each split factor with a general linear group, and its specified algebraic weight is the corresponding determinant twist of V_{ν}. Tensor the models (AG.25) for these finitely many factors. Matrix substitution and tensor products are defined over that number field and give the required complex representation after the selected embed-ding. At a place where the specified matrices are integral, the tensor product of the lattices just constructed is stable.

More generally a prescribed compact subgroup admits a stable full lattice without an integrality choice for the splitting matrix. Start with any lattice Λ_{0} in the local model. Continuity of its finitely many representation matrix entries on a compact group K gives a common denominator: gΛ_{0} ⊆ π^{−m}Λ_{0} for all g ∈ K. The 𝒪-span of all gΛ_{0} then lies between Λ_{0} and π^{−m}Λ_{0}, so is finite free, full, and K-stable. Stability follows because left multiplication permutes the elements of K. This last argument also handles the finitely many places where a chosen splitting matrix has denominators.

Proposition 10.57 (Good Chern forms in the source model). Both clauses of GoodChernWeil hold.

The coordinates are genuine analytic coordinates: composing with local algebraic étale co-ordinates gives an injective holomorphic map between open subsets of ℂ^{dim X}, hence a biholomorphic map. The metric entries and its inverse determinant have at most powers of the sum of absolute logarithms of the boundary coordinates.

Put θ = ∂H H^{−1} in row-frame notation. The source conn is its transpose. Its form bound gives Poincaré growth for each entry of θ: the reciprocal coordinate weight is 1/(|z_{a}| | log |z_{a}||) in a punctured direction and one in the other directions. Lemma 10.58 (The unitary moduli problem and its level). Let E, H, D, l, c be the CM field, host, lattice da-tum, level and coefficient field in ToroidalCompactification. The moduli scheme in that assertion is the fine PEL moduli scheme for the self-dual symplectic 𝒪_{E}-lattice (D.La, D.EF), with the indicated determinant condition and a neat compact open level. w + ̄w = 1. (AG.31)

The form D.EF is alternating and unimodular over Z. Its adjoint identity is precisely ⟨ax, y⟩ = ⟨x, ̄ay⟩. The real endomorphism J in the datum has square −1, preserves this form, commutes with E, and makes ⟨Jx, x⟩ positive definite. Thus it gives the polarizable PEL Hodge structure. The trace identities in Datum.dom specify multiplicities p, q on the two sets of embeddings distinguished by the chosen square root of −H.d. The reflex field is contained in that imaginary quadratic field: the characteristic-polynomial coefficients are invariant under every automorphism preserving those two sets. Consequently they are defined over the field K_{A} used for the source moduli problem. The maximal-order condition in Lan’s Condition 1.4.3.10 holds because the order here already is 𝒪_{E}.

For a principally polarized abelian scheme (A, λ) with this action, write 𝒫_{λ} = (1, λ)^{∗}𝒫_{A} for its symmet-ric Poincaré biextension on A × A. Set

L = (1, w)^{∗}𝒫_{λ}. (AG.32)

The biextension laws, Rosati identity and (AG.31) identify

We check the level carefully. Put 𝔪 = l.Mb and M = l.M. The identities 𝔪𝔪̄ = (M) and 𝔪+ ̄𝔪 = 𝒪_{E} split the M-torsion lattice into its two complementary summands. The map η, killed by 𝔪, records the ̄𝔪-summand of a symplectic full M-level structure; this is exactly the last identity in Obj.geom. The map η_{A} records the full A-level structure. Its specified primitive root fixes the Weil-pairing multiplier. Thus these are finite étale level structures with the symplectic liftability condition, rather than arbitrary torsion sections. There is a useful exact version of this comparison over c.F, which contains the selected M^{′} = lcm(M, A)-th root of unity. Fix the compatible M-th root. The two 𝔪-primary and ̄𝔪-primary summands are isotropic and are in perfect Weil duality. The map η identifies the latter summand. Perfect duality with the fixed root therefore determines the other summand uniquely. This recovers a full symplectic M-level map. Its restriction to the common gcd(M, A)-torsion agrees with η_{A}: on one summand this follows from Obj.geom, and on the other from that same perfect duality. The two maps consequently combine to a full M^{′}-level map. Conversely restricting such a map recovers η, η_{A}. The liftability condition is preserved: locally a change of primitive root rescales the complementary summand, with the same multiplier, and gives an integral symplectic similitude. Thus after this coefficient extension the level is exactly the specified component of principal level M^{′}. This argument uses the Weil pairing; fixing a half-level map alone in a similitude group would not give this conclusion.

The stabilizer of the first level map is contained in the full principal congruence subgroup of level M. Indeed an isometry fixing this map has (g −1)D.La ⊂𝔪D.La. Taking its symplectic adjoint gives (g^{−1}− 1)D.La ⊂𝔪̄D.La; multiplication by g gives the same containment for g −1. Intersecting the two coprime ideals gives (g −1)D.La ⊂MD.La. The extra A-level only decreases the stabilizer.

Here is also a direct neatness check. Choose an odd prime ℓ | M, which exists since M ≥ 3 is odd. Every eigenvalue of a matrix congruent to 1 modulo ℓ has the form 1 + ℓu, with u integral over Z_{ℓ}; apply its characteristic polynomial to g −1. Every product of integral powers of these eigenvalues still lies in 1 + ℓZ_{ℓ}. This group contains no nontrivial root of unity. For an order prime to ℓ, distinct roots of unity remain distinct modulo the maximal ideal. For order ℓ^{a}> 1, the valuation of ζ −1, normalized by v(ℓ) = 1, is 1/(ℓ^{a−1}(ℓ−1)) < 1, as follows by evaluating the ℓ^{a}-cyclotomic polynomial at 1. Splitting the order into these two parts proves the claim. It applies equally to the intersection of any adelic conjugate of this level with the rational group, by using the conjugate Z_{ℓ}-lattice. Hence the level is neat.

Finally the source uses geometric multiplicities and represents its functor initially on reduced schemes. Over a reduced characteristic-zero base, the geometric multiplicity condition is equivalent to the characteristic-polynomial determinant condition: the coefficient differences vanish at all geometric points, hence vanish in the reduced coordinate rings. Both the usual fine PEL scheme and the specified source scheme are smooth and therefore reduced. Applying their two representing properties to their universal objects gives maps in both directions; uniqueness makes both composites identities. This identifies the schemes and their universal objects. The PEL tangent space is a product, over the [E : Q]/2 conjugate pairs, of p-by-q matrix spaces. Its dimension is exactly D.dim = [E : Q]pq/2, including the zero-dimensional case pq = 0.

Proposition 10.60 (Characteristic-zero toroidal input). The full assertion ToroidalCompactification, and hence field p1 of the Hodge-bundle package, holds with the source moduli problem and HasLogKS convention.

Proof. We use the corrected author version of Lan’s Arithmetic Compactifications of PEL-Type Shimura Varieties, revised 14 March 2021, whose theorem numbering agrees with the book [33]. Proposition 7.3.1.4, p. 567, supplies compatible projective smooth admissible cone decompositions. Theorem 6.4.1.1(1)–(5),

<!-- Source PDF page 810 -->

pp. 519–522, supplies the smooth proper compactification, its universal semi-abelian family, boundary and logarithmic Kodaira–Spencer isomorphism. Theorem 7.3.3.4, pp. 571–575, makes this compactification a projective scheme.

We may impose the no-self-intersection refinement explicitly. Barycentrically subdivide the smooth fans, compatibly at every cusp and face. A new ray is the sum of the primitive rays of an old cone. In a smooth cone the old rays are part of a lattice basis, so the cones indexed by chains of faces are still smooth: their new generators have triangular coordinate matrix with diagonal entries one. Color a new ray by the dimension of that old cone. A chain contains at most one ray of each color, and every cusp equivalence preserves the colors. It therefore cannot identify two different rays of a new cone. The construction respects faces and lattice quotients. It is projective: a star subdivision is the normalized blowup of its torus-invariant monomial ideal; a small rational strict perturbation of the old support function gives its support function. There are finitely many cusp and cone orbits, so the perturbations can be chosen simultaneously, and a common denominator makes them integral.

All PEL hypotheses were checked in Lemma 10.58. We work over the coefficient number field, so all primes forbidden in the integral construction are invertible. The order is maximal, and the prescribed level is neat. These facts respectively give the required maximal-order condition, smooth integral-model base change, and absence of stabilizers. The dimension is the one computed in that lemma. Smooth projective base change to c.F preserves each of these properties.

The universal group is abelian precisely on the open moduli scheme. At a boundary point its torus has positive rank, since a nonzero boundary cone has a nonzero toric character direction. Thus the open immersion has exactly the abelian locus required in Model.ab_gen; its image is dense. The reduced boundary is a relative normal-crossings divisor. The preceding refinement prevents identifications of its branches, while neatness removes their stabilizers. Its components are consequently smooth without self-intersections. In a regular local ring their distinct local equations form part of a regular system of parameters. Lift these equations and the remaining parameters to a sufficiently small affine neighborhood; equality with the reduced boundary ideal can also be arranged there, since all ideals are coherent. This is exactly the Zariski-local condition FinalTheorems.Snc, not merely an assertion after an unspecified étale cover.

We also need the source’s line bundle on the whole semi-abelian family. On each normal connected com-ponent Lan’s Theorem 3.4.3.2, pp. 203–204, extends the dual family and the Poincaré biextension. Extend the action and polarization by the uniqueness in Proposition 10.31, and define L by (AG.32) on this extended biextension. The biextension calculation (AG.33) works on the entire family; its rigidification, symmetry, cubical identity, Rosati identity and primitive normalization therefore extend as well. On the interior it agrees with the specified universal line by the inverse construction in Lemma 10.58. This supplies all fields of the source SAB and its pullback comparison, with no arbitrary extension of an interior line bundle.

Take this scheme and family for Y . Normality and flatness follow from smoothness over the field; projectivity, the open dense immersion and the line comparison have just been verified. Finally Lemma 10.59 converts the cited logarithmic cotangent isomorphism into the full quantified HasLogKS assertion. This proves all three conjuncts of the requested input, also when the boundary or the moduli scheme is empty.

Lemma 10.61 (The prescribed fan and its boundary ideal). For a finite projective 𝒪_{E}-module X, the con-ditions IsPolFanOn turn the cones IsCone into a smooth admissible projective decomposition of the cone of nonnegative balanced forms with rational radical. They are compatible under quotient maps. At principal level n, the primitive monodromy generators are nδ_{i}, where the δ_{i} are its primitive generators at level one. The corresponding boundary ideal has order ϕ(nδ_{i}) on the i-th ray.

Proof. Write L_{X} for the lattice of integral symmetric balanced forms. A source cone is the nonnegative span of its generators δ_{1}, . . . , δ_{m}. The part-of-a-basis condition makes it a rational smooth cone. The covering clause covers precisely the rational closure of the positive cone: the definition of psdCone is a pullback of

<!-- Source PDF page 811 -->

a positive definite form on a projective quotient. The radical of a nonnegative form is saturated, and its quotient lattice is torsion-free, hence projective over the Dedekind ring 𝒪_{E}. Thus the two descriptions of this rational closure agree.

The strict supporting functional in IsStrict exposes each cone. More explicitly it gives an integer N > 0 and a rational linear form ℓ/N ≥ ϕ on the positive cone, with equality on its generators. If an integral nonnegative β has equality, the last clause says that some positive multiple of β is a nonnegative integral combination of those generators. Thus β belongs to that cone. On any other source cone the difference ℓ/N −ϕ is linear and nonnegative. Its zero set there is the face generated by exactly the rays on which it vanishes. Those rays are integral and hence belong to the first cone. This proves that intersections are common faces. The source face condition includes all such faces.

The same argument characterizes the domains of linearity. If ϕ is linear on a rational polyhedral cone, choose a rational point in its relative interior and a covering source cone. The supporting difference is non-negative and linear on the first cone and vanishes at an interior point. It therefore vanishes identically there, so every integral generator belongs to the second cone. This is exactly the strict linearity condition for a po-larization function. The integral and positive clauses give its positive integral values. Positive homogeneity and superadditivity have the required orientation: the function is concave in the usual convention, and the associated ideal is 𝒪(−B_{ϕ}). On the smooth cones its linear expressions agree on common faces, so this is the continuous piecewise linear function in the fan topology.

There are finitely many cone orbits. Indeed the last clause of IsPolFanOn moves every set of rays into one fixed finite set; there are only finitely many subsets of that set. The source InvFun.inv makes the function unchanged on pullback under every surjection. A cone supported on a quotient corresponds to the same cone in the face with that radical: the lattice of forms vanishing on the kernel is a saturated direct summand, and the strict supporting inequalities restrict to it. This verifies compatibility at the lower-rank cusps as well as invariance under automorphisms. These are precisely the decomposition and polarization-function conditions in Lan’s Definitions 6.1.1.7–6.1.1.12, 6.3.3.4 and 7.3.1.1–7.3.1.3.

A symmetric balanced unipotent is integral at level one; it acts trivially on the full n-torsion precisely when all its bilinear entries are divisible by n. Thus its lattice is nL_{X}. Division by n identifies a basis of this lattice with one of L_{X}, and the generators become nδ_{i}. This is the source’s exact definition of levelForms.

Lemma 10.63 (Hodge power minus the fan divisor). Let f : X^{tor} → X^{min} be the toroidal-to-minimal morphism for a neat PEL level, and let B_{ϕ} be the Cartier divisor of Lemma 10.61. Write ω = det e^{∗}Ω^{1}_{G}. A positive power of ω is generated by global sections, and

ω^{a}⊗𝒪(−B_{ϕ}) is ample for all a ≫0 (AG.41)

over the affine noetherian base of the integral model. Both assertions persist after extension to a coefficient field.

Proof. Lan’s Theorem 7.2.4.1(2)–(3), pp. 552–553, identifies a positive power of ω with the pullback of an ample line M on the projective minimal compactification. Choose a power M^{N} generated by global sections over the affine base. Its pullback is generated too; this proves the first assertion.

For the second assertion use exactly the ideal 𝔧 = 𝒪(−B_{ϕ}) of Definition 7.3.3.1, whose identification with (AG.37) has been checked. Theorem 7.3.3.4 says that, for some d_{0} > 0, X^{tor} is the normalization of the blowup of the ideal f_{∗}𝔧^{d0}, and the coherent ideal pullback is 𝔧^{d0}. On a blowup Proj ⊕_{a≥0}I^{a}, this is its relatively ample tautological line 𝒪(1). Normalization is finite here because the base is excellent. Its pullback is relatively ample: the finite map onto the blowup is surjective, so the finite-surjective ampleness criterion applies on every affine open of the base. Thus 𝔧^{d0}, and hence 𝔧, is f-ample.

For completeness the last step only uses ordinary relative ampleness. If L is f-ample and M is ample on the target over an affine base, then L ⊗f^{∗}M^{a} is ample for all sufficiently large a; see [14], Tags 0892 and 0C4K. The finite-surjective criterion just used is Tag 0B5V, and the positive-power criterion is Tag 02NN. The schemes are projective of finite type over the affine noetherian base, so the quasi-compactness hypotheses in these criteria hold. ## Resolution and principalization in the geometric input

## 11 Resolution and principalization in the geometric input

The covolume argument uses two separate characteristic-zero statements. Their precise scheme-theoretic forms matter: principalization must respect an existing boundary, and resolution must make the entire inverse image of the nonsmooth locus a simple normal crossings divisor. We verify both forms here against the published resolution theorem.

Definition 11.1 (The boundary and blowup conventions). A reduced divisor E on a smooth k-scheme has simple normal crossings if, at every point x, its ideal on some affine neighbourhood is generated by a product of distinct members of a regular system of parameters of 𝒪_{X,x}. Outside E the product is empty and is 1. A smooth centre Z has normal crossings with E if, in such a neighbourhood, the ideal of Z is generated by a subset of the same parameters. After blowing up Z, the new boundary is the reduced inverse image of

```text
E ∪Z.
```

Source: ReciprocityTheory/AnalyticForms/RegularLocalRings/FinalTheorems.lean:6--21,93--97; Development/AutomorphicSpectrum/PublishedTheorems/Geometry2/NotSubsetOfDenseCompl.lean:14--30.

Here a regular system of parameters means exactly a set of generators of the maximal ideal whose car-dinality is the Krull dimension. This is the source’s Rsp. Its Snc includes regularity of the ambient stalk at

<!-- Source PDF page 819 -->

every point. Thus the convention is a Zariski local simple normal crossings condition, with squarefree local equation; a merely normal crossings condition after an unspecified field extension would not suffice. All blowups below are ordinary scheme blowups. Their inverse-image ideal is locally generated by a nonze-rodivisor, and they are terminal among morphisms with that property, by the Stacks Project, Tags 02OS and 0806 [50]. These are exactly the two clauses of the source’s FinalTheorems.Blowup; in particular the universal property ranges over every scheme over X.

Background fact 11.2 (The published characteristic-zero theorems). For a reduced separated finite-type scheme over a characteristic-zero field, there is a finite sequence of blowups with smooth centres ending in a smooth scheme, isomorphic over the original smooth locus. For a marked ideal (M, N, E, ℐ, d), where M, N are smooth, E is an ordered simple normal crossings boundary transverse to N, ℐ is coherent and d > 0, there is a finite sequence of admissible smooth-centre blowups making its cosupport empty. Admissibility means that the centre lies where the order of the current ideal is at least d and has normal crossings with the current boundary; the controlled transform divides the pulled-back ideal by the dth power of the exceptional ideal.

These are Bierstone–Milman, Theorem 1.1, p. 611, and Theorem 1.3, p. 614, with Definitions 2.1–2.2, pp. 618–619 [49]. We use their scheme formulation over arbitrary characteristic-zero fields. The boundary in Definition 2.1 is explicitly simple normal crossings, with smooth components. We do not require any further functoriality assertion.

Proposition 11.3 (Principalization with the source’s initial boundary). Let k be a characteristic-zero field, and let X be a separated quasi-compact smooth k-scheme of pure relative dimension d. Let ℐ be a quasi-coherent ideal and let E be a reduced closed subset satisfying the simple normal crossings condition at its points. Assume that no irreducible component of X is contained in V (ℐ). Then there exist a smooth k-scheme X^{′} and a finite sequence s : X^{′}→X of smooth-centre blowups, all with normal crossings with their current boundaries, such that

ℐ𝒪_{X}′ is an effective Cartier ideal, V (ℐ𝒪_{X}′)_{red} has simple normal crossings.

The sequence is an isomorphism over X \ V (ℐ). With the successive boundaries defined by Definition 11.1, it is precisely a SncBlowup.IsSncBlowupSeq.

Source: Development/AutomorphicSpectrum/PublishedTheorems/Geometry2/NotSubsetOfDenseCompl.lean:57--66 (\lean {PrincipalisationCharZero}).

Proof. Smoothness is locally of finite presentation. Quasi-compactness therefore makes X finite type over k; hence it is noetherian. Its quasi-coherent ideal is coherent. Since k has characteristic zero, it is perfect, so regular finite-type k-schemes are smooth over k. The source’s local boundary equations imply that every component of E is smooth and that any collection meeting at a point is given there by distinct parameters. There are finitely many components. Order them arbitrarily, thereby obtaining the boundary required in Fact 11.2. At points outside E, its ideal is the unit ideal; after shrinking to an affine open disjoint from E, the empty product verifies the same convention there.

Apply the marked-ideal theorem to (M, N, E, ℐ, d) = (X, X, E, ℐ, 1). Transversality to N = X is automatic. The hypothesis excluding whole components makes the ideal nonzero at each generic point. Each centre lies in the cosupport of the current controlled transform and has the stated parameter description. The ambient schemes and centres are smooth over k. Induction on the blowups therefore gives exactly the source’s inductively defined sequence: its boundary step is reduced inverse image of the old boundary and centre, which is the union of the strict old components and the new exceptional component. Repetitions of a component in this union have no effect on its reduced closed subset.

<!-- Source PDF page 820 -->

For completeness, the conclusion about the total ideal follows from the controlled-transform conclusion. Write ℐ_{j} for the controlled transform on X_{j}, and write H_{j} for the exceptional Cartier ideal at the jth blowup π_{j}. By its transformation rule,

```text
ℐ_{j−1}𝒪_{Xj} = H_{j}ℐ_{j}.
```

Repeated substitution expresses the total pulled-back original ideal as ℐ_{t} times a product of pulled-back exceptional Cartier ideals. The empty final cosupport for marking 1 means ℐ_{t} = 𝒪_{Xt}: at each local stalk an ideal of order zero contains a unit. The remaining factors are invertible effective Cartier ideals. Their divisors are supported on the final simple normal crossings boundary. In regular parameters their product is therefore a unit times z_{1}^{a1}· · · z_{r}^{ar}, with a_{i} ≥0. Its generator is a nonzerodivisor, because the regular local ring is a domain. Shrinking the affine neighbourhood preserves both that property and the equality of the ideal with this principal ideal. This verifies EffCartier in the source’s affine form. The radical ideal is generated by the squarefree product of those z_{i} for which a_{i} > 0; hence it verifies Snc.

For a reduced separated finite-type k-scheme X over any characteristic-zero field, there is a finite sequence of blowups s : X^{′}→X such that X^{′} is smooth, s is an isomorphism over the smooth locus U of X/k, and the reduced inverse image of X \U has simple normal crossings. Proof. Apply the first part of Fact 11.2 to obtain a smooth Y and a blowup sequence r : Y →X that is an isomorphism over U. Over a perfect field the smooth and regular loci agree for a finite-type reduced scheme. In particular U contains each generic point of X. Each centre in the stated resolution lies over the original singular locus; equivalently its sequence is the identity over U. The resulting Y has no component supported over X \U: blowing up a generically nonzero ideal is birational on each component, as is seen by restricting its Rees algebra to that generic point. Thus r^{−1}U is dense in every component of Y .

Let 𝒥 be the ideal of the reduced closed subset X \ U, and set ℐ = 𝒥 𝒪_{Y} . It is coherent and is the unit ideal on r^{−1}U, so it vanishes on no entire component of Y . Principalize it by Proposition 11.3, with empty initial boundary, obtaining t : Y^{′}→Y . If the smooth components have different dimensions, apply the proposition to each pure-dimensional open and closed part. There are finitely many such parts; the resulting blowups on their disjoint union give one finite sequence (insert identity steps on the other parts). This removes the pure-dimension restriction in that application.

The composite s = r ∘t is a finite blowup sequence: concatenate the two lists of centres. The source’s Resolution.IsBlowupSeq imposes no smooth-centre restriction, so in particular accepts this sequence. It is an isomorphism over U, since both r and t are isomorphisms there. Its reduced inverse image of X \ U is exactly the reduced support of ℐ𝒪_{Y} ′, which has simple normal crossings by principalization. The ambient Y^{′} is smooth, so all of its stalks are regular. This proves every conjunct of the source statement, including the condition on the whole inverse image, rather than only on the exceptional divisors listed by a chosen resolution algorithm.

Both results are used in the fifteen-input geometric package before the point-separation and Arakelov es-timates produce the covolume bounds. They supply slots 1 and 2 of that package. They do not by themselves prove the remaining Hodge, toroidal, metric or quantitative inputs.

The source’s separate state-ment GlobalTheory.Published.Principalisation holds: if Y is integral, smooth of relative dimension d and projective over a characteristic-zero field, and 0 ̸= ℐ is an ideal, its principalization may be chosen integral, smooth of that same dimension and projective over the field. Source: Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/PublishedTheorems/Divisors2/GeometricallyConnectedOfIsIsoRestrict.lean:13--19,118--125.

Proof. Projectivity gives quasi-compactness and separatedness. The nonzero ideal on the integral scheme vanishes on no entire component, so Proposition 11.3 applies, with empty initial boundary. Its centres are smooth and contained over V (ℐ): on the inverse image of its complement the total ideal is a unit, and the controlled-transform relation in that proof makes the controlled ideal a unit as well. No admissible centre can meet that open set. Thus its sequence satisfies exactly the source’s IsSmoothBlowupSeq f (I.support).

Each blowup of an integral scheme in a generically nonzero coherent ideal is integral. On an integral affine chart its nonempty blowup charts are rings A[ℐ/f] inside Frac A, hence domains; their common dense open is the unchanged complement of the ideal, so their union is reduced and irreducible. That open is nonempty because the original ideal is nonzero. These observations also apply at each subsequent step. Each blowup is projective, being the relative Proj of its finitely generated Rees algebra. Its composite with the original projective morphism is therefore projective.

The resulting scheme is smooth by the proposition and birational to Y . Its function field has transcen-dence degree d over k. On an integral smooth scheme the relative dimension is locally constant, and its constant value equals this transcendence degree; therefore the new scheme is smooth of relative dimension d. The isomorphism on the complement, effective-Cartier property and simple normal crossings conclusion were already proved in Proposition 11.3. All extra conjuncts in this Hodge-package formulation are now verified.

These are polynomial equations defining an affine algebraic group. Over an algebraic closure K of F, K ⊗_{F} E = K × K, with conjugation interchanging the factors. Write J = (J_{1}, J_{1}^{t}). The unitary equation for a pair (A, B) is B^{t}J_{1}A = J_{1}, so

B = J_{1}^{−t}A^{−t}J_{1}^{t}, det B = (det A)^{−1}.

Consequently projection to A is an algebraic isomorphism G_{K} ≃ SL_{m,K}; its inverse is regular because inverse matrices on determinant-one matrices are adjugates. For completeness, the elementary structural

facts about this last group can be seen as follows. Elementary root subgroups 1+aE_{ij} generate SL_{m} over an algebraically closed field by row reduction, and their products are connected; hence the group is connected. A nonzero ideal in its characteristic zero Lie algebra, decomposed under the diagonal torus, contains either a matrix unit or a nonzero diagonal matrix. Bracketing the latter with a suitable matrix unit gives the former; brackets [E_{ij}, E_{jk}] = E_{ik} and [E_{ij}, E_{ji}] = E_{ii} −E_{jj} then give all of 𝔰𝔩_{m}. This proves absolute almost simplicity. Finally embed K in ℂ. The analytic group SL_{m}(ℂ) retracts onto SU(m) by polar decomposition. On a small ball about x_{0}, the holomorphic quotient R_{j}/T_{j} has constant absolute value ρ. Restriction to complex lines and the maximum modulus theorem show that it is a constant C, with |C| = ρ. At each point of the ball the simultaneous proportionality therefore gives R_{i} = CT_{i} for every i, including those for which T_{i} vanishes. Restrict each difference R_{i} −CT_{i} to the complex line segment joining the nearby point to an arbitrary point in a smaller ball. The one-variable identity theorem makes it zero there. This proves relative closedness and the assertion, without imposing a finite index set.

For the last clause, indefinite Hermitian Gram–Schmidt writes any allowed frame as a unit frame times an invertible triangular matrix, preserving the order of its positive and negative columns. Its triangular weight character is a product of integer powers of nonzero diagonal entries, so is nonzero. Apply proportionality at the unit frame and cancel that common character. We obtain the pointwise hypothesis on all of U, and the preceding argument applies. The allowed frame domain is connected: its quotient by the connected triangular group is the connected space of ordered positive and negative Hermitian flags, and its fibers are connected.

We need the elementary bound that a rank-ρ free abelian group has at most m^{ρ} subgroups of index m. For m = p, each such subgroup is the kernel of a nonzero linear form on 𝔽^{ρ}_{p}, with two forms giving the same kernel exactly when proportional. Their number is (p^{ρ}−1)/(p −1) ≤p^{ρ}. Every subgroup of index p^{k} is contained in one of index p^{k−1}: choose a subgroup of order p in its nonzero finite abelian quotient. Above each rank-ρ subgroup there are at most p^{ρ} choices for the next index-p subgroup. Induction bounds the number of index-p^{k} subgroups by p^{kρ}, even though different chains can end at the same subgroup. A subgroup of index m contains mℤ^{ρ}. The Chinese remainder decomposition of (ℤ/m)^{ρ} separates its quotient into primary components, with respective orders p^{vp(m)}. Self-duality of L, L^{′} consequently gives equal indices [L : M] = [L^{′} : M] = m, and [M^{∗} : L^{′}] = [L^{′} : M] = m. The preceding subgroup count in the rank-ρ group M^{∗} allows at most m^{ρ} possibilities for L^{′}. There are at most m^{2ρ} pairs, proving the claimed count. For an alternating form the integral dual has the same transposed-matrix description, so its sign changes no index.

Lemma 15.25 (A good prime without a density theorem). For every CM field E and positive integer m, there are a rational prime q and a prime ideal P ⊂𝒪_{E} such that

q ∤m, |𝒪_{E}/P| = q, P + P = 𝒪_{E}, q ∤2 disc E. (SS.23)

Source: Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/SiegelThetaTransformation/ExistsGoodSplitPrimeCmField.lean:17--324.

Proof. Choose an integral primitive element θ for E/ℚ. This uses only separability and an infinite base field: for two separable generators, all but finitely many rational numbers c make their distinct embeddings take distinct values on α + cβ, so that this element has the full extension degree. Repeat for finitely many generators and multiply by a nonzero integer to make it integral. There is an integer d ̸= 0 with d𝒪_{E} ⊆ℤ[θ]. For the source’s choice, use the determinant of the trace matrix of 1, θ, . . . , θ^{e−1}. Its entries are integers and its determinant is nonzero: the trace matrix is the transpose times itself of the Vandermonde matrix of the

<!-- Source PDF page 864 -->

distinct conjugates. For integral x, each trace Tr(xθ^{j}) is an integer. Cramer’s rule consequently makes d times every coordinate of x in this power basis integral, proving the assertion.

Conjugation cannot fix θ, since then it would fix the field it generates, whereas CM conjugation is non-identity. Put δ = θ −θ ̸= 0 and choose the nonzero integer

B = 2m d disc E Norm_{E/ℚ}(δ).

We recall the elementary polynomial prime-divisor argument used in the source. If f ∈ℤ[T] is nonconstant with c = f(0) ̸= 0, write f = c + Tg. Then f(cBt) = c(1 + Bt g(cBt)). The polynomial 1 + BTg(cBT) is nonconstant and hence takes an integer value of absolute value greater than 1. A prime divisor q of that value divides f(cBt) and does not divide B, since the value is 1 modulo every prime dividing B. Apply this to the characteristic polynomial of multiplication by θ on 𝒪_{E}. It is monic of positive degree and its constant coefficient is, up to sign, Norm(θ) ̸= 0. Because θ is primitive, this is also its minimal polynomial. We obtain q ∤B and an integer a with f(a) = 0 modulo q.

The map ℤ[θ] →𝔽_{q} sending θ to a extends to 𝒪_{E}: after inverting d the two orders are equal, and d is a unit modulo q. Its image contains the prime field, so it is onto. Its kernel P is maximal and has norm q. If P = P, conjugation induces an automorphism of 𝔽_{q} and is therefore the identity. It would kill δ, so q would divide Norm(δ). For clarity, this last implication follows directly by reducing the integral multiplication matrix of δ modulo q: if its determinant were nonzero, δ would be a unit in 𝒪_{E}/q𝒪_{E} and hence in its quotient by P, contradicting its zero image. This contradicts q ∤B. Distinct maximal ideals are comaximal, giving P + P = 𝒪_{E}. The remaining assertions in (SS.23) follow from the other factors of B. (1) Unitarity (un): Every γ ∈D.grp lies in U(X) by Lemma 15.49(c).

(2) Lattices (lat): Every L ∈ D.lats is self-dual (hence finitely generated over 𝒪_{E}) and satisfies span_{E} L = E^{r} by Lemma 15.49(d).

(3) Stability (stab): For γ ∈D.grp and L ∈D.lats, γL ∈D.lats by Lemma 15.49(d).

(4) Schwartz–Bruhat regularity (sb): Φ(L, Λ) ∈𝒮_{ℚ}(n, g) for all L ∈D.lats and Λ ∈ Vset(E, n, M) by

Proposition 15.51(a).

(5) Norm and tail bound (norm): Since D.𝔪 ̸= 0, the quotient ring 𝒪_{E}/D.𝔪 is finite, hence D.J ≤ GL_{r}(𝒪_{E}/D.𝔪) is finite and nonempty (1 ∈ D.J), giving a := |D.J| > 0. Put b(L, L^{′}) := [L : L ∩L^{′}]^{−n/2} and θ := 0.65 < 1. By Proposition 15.52(a), ⟨Φ(L, Λ), Φ(L, Λ)⟩ = a and |⟨Φ(L, Λ), Φ(L^{′}, Λ)⟩| ≤a b(L, L^{′}) for all L, L^{′}∈D.lats and Λ ∈ Vset(E, n, M). On the rational vec-tor space E^{r} of dimension ρ := [E : ℚ]r, the alternating form E_{X} is nondegenerate (if E_{X}(u, v) = 0 for all v, testing the symplectic basis vectors bas(e_{j}) kills every symplectic coordinate of u, forcing u = 0), and each L ∈ D.lats is a finitely generated ℤ-lattice equal to its integral E_{X}-dual. Since n ≥ 4ρ + 4, Lemma 15.21 (eq. (SS.14)) implies that ∑_{L}′_{∈D.lats, L}′_{̸=L}b(L, L^{′}) converges and is at most 0.65.

(6) Multiplier norm and covariance (mu): Fix γ ∈ D.grp and L ∈ D.lats. By Lemma 15.49(c),(d), γ ∈ U(X), there exists k ∈ D.J with D.Red((γβ_{i})_{i}, k), and γL ∈ D.lats. Put c := µ(γ, L)λ(k), so ω(γ)v_{0}(L) = c v_{0}(γL) by (376). Because ω(γ) preserves the inner product on 𝒮_{ℚ}(n, g) and both v_{0}(L) and v_{0}(γL) have squared norm 1,


for every Λ ∈ Vset(E, n, M).

15.3.4 Normalized local class and harmonic valuation estimates

We now prove the uniform harmonic valuation lower bound chBound_host across all finite places of the host field, the ℓ-primary isotropic class-sum estimate ell_part and its translated-product companion bound_of_trivAt assembled in class_bound, and the resulting unconditional verification of inequality (SS.5) and exists_smul_short_nonneg.

Lemma 15.73 (Host-field Galois, discriminant, conjugation, and vdH bounds). Let D : D7 and let H : Host D.host.E be a host datum for the CM field E := D.host.E, with conductor N_{host} := D.host.condN and normalized discriminant ramification function

v_{p}(| disc E|) vdH(p) := (p ∈ℕ).

```text
[E : ℚ]
```

(a) (hostField_galois_degree_discr_conj_moves_primes) E/ℚ is Galois of degree [E : ℚ] = 4 D.R.ord;

every rational prime p | disc E divides N_{host}; and for every prime p | N_{host} and every prime ideal 𝔭 ⊂𝒪_{E} with p ∈𝔭, there exists x ∈𝔭 such that H.bar(x) /∈𝔭.

(b) (vdH_le_natAbs) For every p ∈ℕ, 0 ≤ vdH(p) ≤| disc E|.

Source: Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/RingsOfIntegers/HostFieldGaloisDegreeDiscrConjMovesPrimes.lean:18--56; Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/RingsOfIntegers/HostFieldGaloisDegreeDiscrConjMovesPrimesStatement.lean:12--13; Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/PrimeDiscriminants/SlopeTestRemainingChoices.lean:28--33; Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/CyclotomicBounds/RamifiedDiscriminants/VdHLeNatAbs.lean:4--11.

Proof. For (a), the Galois property, [E : ℚ] = 4 D.R.ord, and the divisibility of N_{host} by every prime divisor of disc E are directly supplied by the host-field construction (D.host.galois, D.host.der.finrank_{E}, and D.host.der.discr_{p}rimes.1). Evaluating at any complex embedding φ : E ↪→ℂ identifies H.bar(x) = D.host.conj · x for every x ∈𝒪_{E} (host_bar_eq_smul), and H.bar is an involution. Let p | N_{host} be prime and let 𝔭 ⊂𝒪_{E} be a prime ideal containing p. Since (p) ⊂ℤ is maximal and (p) ⊆𝔭 ∩ℤ ⊊ℤ, 𝔭 lies over (p). ## 16 Maximal slopes, scalar extension and measure normalization

The slope below is the normalized slope of the squared Hermitian norm convention in (335). In particular a uniform multiplication of norms by e^{H} costs 2H in slope. The lattices are finite over the rings of integers of totally complex number fields. Norms are Hermitian, positive definite and compatible with complex conjugation.

Lemma 16.1 (The largest sublattice of maximal slope). A nonzero Hermitian lattice L has a largest sublattice of maximal slope. It is saturated in L. Any additive automorphism of L which carries 𝒪_{K}-submodules to 𝒪_{K}-submodules and preserves its global real norm preserves this sublattice; in particular this holds for a semilinear isometry.

Source: Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/DivisorProofs/ MaxSlopeExtendedLatticeGaloisLe.lean:20--73; MaxSlopeSqFieldExtensionLeComparableNorms.lean:26--49.

Proof. Saturating a sublattice within its vector-space span keeps its rank and divides its covolume by a positive integer. It therefore increases its degree. Among saturated sublattices of a fixed rank and slope at least a given t, only finitely many occur. To see this in the real realization, choose an integral basis of L. The wedge of an oriented integral basis of a rank-k saturated integer sublattice is a primitive vector of the discrete lattice ∧^{k}L. Its Euclidean norm is the sublattice covolume. A lower bound for the slope is an upper bound for that norm, with a fixed field/rank normalization. A bounded ball contains only finitely many vectors of a discrete finite-rank lattice. The primitive wedge determines the real span and hence its saturated intersection with L. There are only finitely many ranks. Taking t = µ(L) proves attainment of the maximal slope θ.

The degree is supermodular:

deg A + deg B ≤ deg(A ∩B) + deg(A + B), rk A + rk B = rk(A ∩B) + rk(A + B).

For the degree inequality, project a basis of B orthogonally off the real span of A and use the quotient covolume formula. Projection can only decrease the relevant Gram volume, by the contraction argument of

Lemma 9.1. The finite index between the sum lattice and its saturation only strengthens the inequality. The rank identity is the vector-space dimension formula. If A, B have degree θ times rank, the intersection has degree at most θ times its rank. These two formulas force A + B to have degree at least θ times rank, hence equality.

The sum of all maximal-slope sublattices is a finite sum, since L is Noetherian. The preceding argument makes this sum a maximal-slope sublattice containing every other one. Its saturation again has slope at least θ and so equals it by maximality. An isometry preserves ranks and covolumes; its image of this largest sublattice has the same universal property and is therefore equal to it. This proves the canonical invariance used in the source.

## Assembly of the ordinary RH argument

## 17 Assembly of the ordinary RH argument

We now give the actual final composition, distinguishing its mathematical implications from the task of constructing their inputs. In particular, an input bundle is not an additional established theorem merely because it is expressed as a Lean structure.

## From a connected arithmetic family to zero-freeness

<!-- Source PDF page 967 -->

17.1 From a connected arithmetic family to zero-freeness

The family and analytic sections give the following mechanism. A primitive character ψ determines a cyclic level and a class 𝒢_{ψ} of admissible arithmetic families. The host existence assertion at a fixed λ > 1 supplies the allowed starting data. The family-selection conclusion gives positive window exponents e_{D}, e_{L} and ε_{1} > 0 such that for every 0 < ε < ε_{1} an admissible family exists on the corresponding window, with those same e_{D}, e_{L}. Its core comparison bounds the logarithmic prime sum, while its pole-data formula and Landau argument exclude an L-zero to the right of 1/2.

Proposition 17.1. Suppose the following three assertions have been established with the definitions and uniform quantifiers of the preceding sections:

<!-- Source PDF page 968 -->

(i) Green’s finite-field character parametrization in the project’s polynomial-label form;

(ii) the window bound VWin for every primitive character;

(iii) a nonempty compatible family-selection bundle HypsAlt with its closed two/three local bound and

definite-side condition.

Then ZF, hence EC and ordinary RH, hold.

Source: Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/ThetaCorrespondence/ThetaPairLifts/ThirdPlaceSeries/TopPlug.lean:12--18; Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/CharacterBoxes/ZeroFreeAllOfTopG.lean:26--34.

Proof. Choose an element of the nonempty bundle in (iii). This use of nonemptiness eliminates into the proposition to be proved; it does not require choosing one element uniformly over all future primitive char-acters. Green’s result in (i) supplies the source’s shape assertion for this bundle. Applying its family-selection implication gives TopG, whose quantifiers are: for every λ > 1 and every family request G, host existence for G and the prescribed eventual V -bound on every family in its class imply connected family selection in that class.

Take λ = 3/2, which satisfies 1 < λ. For each primitive ψ, apply (ii) to ψ and then the source’s host construction supplyChi to obtain host existence for G = 𝒢_{ψ} at this λ. Membership of a family in this class includes the pointwise V -bound; after the threshold Fm.x_{1} + 1 it supplies the eventual hypothesis needed by TopG. Thus TopG gives the window exponents and the families just described for this ψ.

The other class-membership component is the explicit-formula condition EFamC for the cyclic level. Its source constant is 4, with threshold Fm.x_{1}+1; the family’s size identities identify its local scale and exponent with the requested ones. The connected-family witness also supplies the chain tie on that same family. We therefore have every premise of the tied-window zero-freeness criterion, including the core estimate and the pole-data formula, with the original shared window exponents. That criterion gives L(s, χ_{ψ}) ̸= 0 for Re s > 1/2. Since ψ was arbitrary, this is ZF. Propositions 2.4 and 2.3 complete the implication.
